Mishna: a stoned ox is judged by twenty-three judges, since Exodus 21:29 equates the ox's death to the owner's death.
Abaye asks Rava: from where do we know that the phrase and also its owner comes to teach that the ox's death is like the owner's death?

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Should we say the verse teaches that the ox's owner is liable to be executed?
Rava: if so, the verse should have written only the owner, and stayed silent; the added phrase shows the ox's death is parallel to the owner's.
Abaye: had the verse been written this way, I would have said the owner is executed by stoning.
Rejected: an owner whose ox killed should not get the harsher stoning when a man who kills himself gets the sword.
Perhaps the phrase shall be put to death is meant to lighten the sentence to strangulation, depending on which method is considered more severe?
Rejected: Exodus 21:30 allows a ransom for an owner, and Numbers 35:31 forbids ransom for a murderer, so the owner cannot be liable to death.
On the contrary, the added phrase is needed exactly for this point: a man who kills pays with his life, while the owner of an ox may redeem himself with money.
Hizkiyya's school taught a baraita from Numbers 35:21: the striker is executed for his own murder, but not for his ox's killing.
Do we apply a halakha from a specific one-time event, the ox at Sinai, to the general rule about stoned animals?
Rami bar Yeḥezkel's baraita: the verse Whether animal or man equates the animal's judgment to a person's, so twenty-three judges.
Mishna: the dispute concerns the judgment of a lion or a wolf, and whether it requires twenty-three judges.
Reish Lakish: the dispute applies only if the animal has killed, which implies such animals can be tamed and have owners.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: the dispute applies even without a killing, implying such animals are not tameable and have no owners.
Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer says whoever kills such a dangerous animal first acquires it.
What does the killer acquire under each Sage's view, and what does it mean for Reish Lakish's case, since the Sages treated the animal as condemned?
The acquisition is in the sense of merit before Heaven, a religious credit for having removed the danger.
A baraita following Reish Lakish: the disagreement concerns only animals that killed, and Rabbi Eliezer's merit is before Heaven alone.
Mishna: Rabbi Akiva says these animals are judged by twenty-three judges.
Rabbi Akiva's view seems identical to the first tanna's, so what is new in his statement?
The difference concerns a snake, which Rabbi Akiva excludes from the twenty-three-judge requirement.
Mishna: the court judges cases involving an entire tribe that sinned, in the Great Sanhedrin.
In what way did this tribe sin, since a tribe that broke Shabbat would not fit the rule?
The mishna must be about a tribe that was led astray into idol worship, since the Torah distinguishes individuals from multitudes only for idolatry.
Would this mean an idolatrous tribe is treated like an idolatrous city, and whose opinion would that be?
A baraita on idolatrous cities: Rabbi Yoshiya sets the threshold at ten to one hundred people; Rabbi Yonatan sets it at a majority of the tribe.
Even Rabbi Yonatan speaks only of a majority of the tribe, and Rav Mattana applies the Mishna to the case here.

16a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Frames the case as a tribal Nasi who has sinned.
Rav Adda bar Ahava cites Exodus 18:22 'every great matter' to mean matters concerning a great person.
Ulla gives Rabbi Elazar's alternative: the case parallels the seventy-one judges of the initial land division.
If so, lots, Urim VeTummim and all of Israel should be needed, which is not halakha; so why?
Resolution: the mishna follows Rav Mattana and concerns the Nasi of a tribe who sinned.
Ravina: the mishna concerns a tribe that was subverted into idolatry.
Replies to the difficulty: such a tribe is tried by the multitude, though executed as individuals.
Rav Hama bar Yosei citing Deuteronomy 17:5: one takes out a man or woman to the gates, not the whole city or tribe.
Asks the source for the rule that a false prophet is tried only by the Great Sanhedrin.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina: a verbal analogy of 'presumptuousness' from the rebellious elder, tried by seventy-one.
Objection: the rebellious elder's presumptuousness carries capital punishment, which twenty-three judges can decide.
Reish Lakish derives it from the word 'word' in both verses, since the elder defies the seventy-one court.
Why not instead derive the elder's trial from the false prophet's presumptuousness?
This tanna derives halakhot only from the word 'word', not from the presumptuousness analogy.
Asks the source that the High Priest is tried only by the Great Sanhedrin.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: Exodus 18:22 'every great matter' covers the High Priest.
Baraita objects: 'great matter' means a difficult matter, as shown by Exodus 18:26.
Rav Adda's view stands: another baraita reads 'great' as matters concerning a great person.
Why are two verses needed to teach one halakha?
One verse is for the general command and one confirms that the matter was carried out correctly.
The other tanna argues that the two verses must teach two distinct rules, so both words are needed.
Rabbi Elazar asks: if a High Priest's ox kills, is it judged by seventy-one or twenty-three judges?
Abaye: since the question is raised only for the ox, it is clear his other property is judged ordinarily.
Asks why this is not obvious and why it would need to be stated.
Abaye taught it lest 'every great matter' be read as all of the High Priest's cases going to the Great Sanhedrin.
Mishna: the king may not take the nation out to an optional war without the Great Sanhedrin.
Asks from where this rule is derived.
Rabbi Abbahu reads Numbers 27:21 as the king, the anointed war priest, and the Sanhedrin as 'congregation'.
Challenge: the Sanhedrin may only consult the Urim VeTummim, so the king might still decide war alone.
Rav Aha bar Bizna's story of David's lyre and dawn study shows David consulting the Sages each morning.
The Sages petition David about the nation's sustenance; David tells them to support one another.
The Sages reply with the lion and cistern parable: the nation cannot sustain itself from its own resources.
David orders war, and they consult Ahithophel, the Sanhedrin and the Urim VeTummim.
Rav Yosef asks which verse is the source of this aggada.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Verses in Chronicles and Samuel name Ahithophel as counselor, Benaiah as the Sanhedrin and Ebiathar as the Urim VeTummim.
Another verse on Benaiah over the Kereti and Peleti explains these as the Sanhedrin's decisiveness and wondrous conduct, setting the consultation order.
R. Yitzhak asks for the verse showing that David's lyre woke him at midnight.
Psalm 57:9 'awake my glory' is cited: the self-playing lyre has awakened, so David must study Torah until dawn.
Mishna: Jerusalem or the Temple courtyards may be extended only by a court of seventy-one judges.
Asks from where this halakha is derived.
Rav Shimi bar Hiyya cites Exodus 25:9 'and so shall you do' as applying the Tabernacle pattern to future generations.
Rava objects with a baraita: vessels need anointment only in the Tabernacle, so 'and so shall you do' should require it later too.
The baraita stands: the verse says 'them' in the Tabernacle context, so anointment applies only to those vessels.
Suggests the vessels could be sanctified by anointment or by service in future generations.
Rav Pappa: the verse ties sanctification to service, so service itself consecrates the vessels.
Asks why the word 'them' is needed if the verse only teaches service sanctification.
Without 'them' one would think both anointment and service apply later, so the word limits anointment to those vessels.
Mishna: a lesser Sanhedrin for the tribes may be appointed only by a court of seventy-one judges.
Asks from where this halakha is derived.
Moses appointed lesser courts while standing in the place of the seventy-one, so the Great Sanhedrin appoints them.
Baraita derives from Deuteronomy 16:18 the obligation to appoint judges and officers for the nation, tribes and cities.
Rabbi Yehuda says one court must oversee all appointments; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says each tribe judges its own. Mishna: idolatrous cities need the Great Sanhedrin.
Asks the reason, in the mishna's rule that an idolatrous city is decided only by the Great Sanhedrin.
Rabbi Oshaya's exegesis of Deuteronomy 17:5 shows that a man or woman goes to the gates, not the whole city.
Mishna: an idolatrous city may not be designated by a book, that is, by written testimony.
The reason: Deuteronomy 13:14 says 'from your midst', excluding a ruling based on a document.
Mishna: three adjoining cities may not be designated as idolatrous, but one or two may.
Baraita derives the rule of one or two cities from the plural 'your cities' in Deuteronomy 13:13, and from 'one' excluding three.
Rav's two positions: in one court only two adjoining cities may be designated; he later holds that this is never permitted.
Asks the reason for Rav's view.
Due to desolation, so that no large swaths of Eretz Yisrael remain uninhabited; Reish Lakish permits designation in separate regions.
Rabbi Yohanan holds that they may not designate cities at all, due to desolation.
Baraita in accordance with Rabbi Yohanan: in Eretz Yisrael two cities may be designated, one in Judea and one in the Galilee, but not near the frontier.
Asks the reason for the frontier restriction.
Gentiles may hear of a desolate border city and invade and destroy Eretz Yisrael.
Asks why this is not derived from 'from your midst' itself, which excludes the frontier.
This baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, who derives the halakha by interpreting the reason stated in the verse.
Mishna: the Great Sanhedrin was seventy-one judges; Rabbi Yehuda holds seventy, since Moses is not counted.
Asks the reasoning of the Rabbis, who count Moses among the seventy-one.
Numbers 11:16 'gather Me seventy men' and 'they shall stand there with you' shows Moses stands at the head and is counted.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda reads 'with you' as referring to the Divine Presence resting on Moses, so Moses is not counted among the seventy.
The Rabbis cite Numbers 11:17 and Exodus 18:22 to show 'with you' means similar to you, so the Great Sanhedrin is derived from the lesser one.
Baraita narrative: Moses selects seventy elders by lot from seventy-two candidates, avoiding envy among the tribes.
Analogy with the redemption of the firstborn in Numbers 3:45-47, offered as a parallel to Moses's lottery difficulty.
Narrative of the Levite redemption lots, with twenty-two thousand slips and two hundred seventy-three five-shekel slips.
Rabbi Shimon: Eldad and Medad stayed in the camp by choice, and God rewarded their humility with lasting prophecy.
Asks what prophecy Eldad and Medad actually uttered.
Two opinions: they foretold Moses's death and Joshua's leadership, or they foretold the quail that came afterward.
Rav Nahman: they prophesied about Gog and Magog, citing Ezekiel 38:17 and reading 'shanim' as 'shenayim', two prophets.
Asks who the two prophets are who spoke one prophecy in the same passage.
They are Eldad and Medad, who prophesied together in the same passage with one prophecy.
The Master's baraita: all prophets prophesied and then stopped, but Eldad and Medad prophesied and did not stop.
Asks from where we know that the other prophets stopped.
Objection: if 'they did not add' shows prophecy stopped, then the great voice at Sinai not adding would show it stopped too.
Reply: the wording here reads 'they prophesied' and there 'they are prophesying still', so the prophecy continued.
If Moses had died, 'my master Moses' in Numbers 11:28 is read as referring to him after his death.
Asks why Joshua called them to imprison, if they prophesied without any link to Moses.
Public prophecy near Moses would resemble a student teaching a halakha before his teacher, which is improper conduct.
Asks whether Moses would be content with all the people prophesying, and what Joshua's command to imprison them means.
Joshua asked that public responsibilities be placed on them, so they would cease prophesying on their own.
Asks from where the mishna derives the need to add three more judges to a lesser Sanhedrin.
The derivation: a conviction by a majority of two cannot be reached in a court of twenty-three judges, except by adding judges.
Objection: with twenty-three judges, a majority of two never occurs in a split vote, so the derivation fails.
Abbahu: the case arises only when judges are added and one abstains, giving an even court, which works per Rabbi Yehuda's seventy.
Abbahu: when judges are added, the court is ab initio an even number, so the court is set up as even from the start.
Asks why this would not be obvious, and what the novelty of Abbahu's statement is.
Lest one think a judge who says I do not know still counts and may later speak, Abbahu teaches he no longer counts.
Rav Kahana: in a capital case where all judges voted to convict, the defendant is acquitted.
The reason is that a trial must be deferred overnight to allow a possibility of acquittal, and no one remains to argue for it.
Rabbi Yohanan: members of the Great Sanhedrin must be dignified, wise, of good appearance and age, skilled in sorcery and fluent in seventy languages.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: a Sanhedrin member must be able to render a creeping animal ritually pure by Torah law, through reasoning.
Rav's own statement: he will demonstrate the argument and render the creeping animal pure.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A fortiori argument: a snake that kills and spreads impurity is pure, so a creeping animal that does neither should surely be pure.
Rejection: the argument fails, since a creeping animal is like an ordinary thorn, which can kill yet remains pure.
Rav: a city lacking two men fluent in all seventy languages and one listener cannot host a lesser Sanhedrin. Beitar and Yavne had such experts.
Objection from a baraita: three language experts make a wise Sanhedrin and a fourth leaves no higher court, so two is not enough.
Glossary of attributions: standard phrases and names used to introduce statements by Sages across Babylonia and Eretz Yisrael.
Objection: Rav Huna himself says in the school of Rav, so that phrase cannot refer to Rav Huna.
Reply: the phrase refers to Rav Hamnuna, and Western phrases identify Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina.
Objection: a report says Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina's view was sent from there, so the phrase cannot be his.
Reply: reverse the attribution, so the phrase refers to Rabbi Elazar and the Western dispute concerns Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina.
Mishna: a city is eligible for a lesser Sanhedrin with 120 men, according to the first tanna.
Asks what the number 120 is meant to accomplish.
Twenty-three judges, three rows of students, and idlers of the synagogue, plus scribes, bailiffs, litigants and witnesses, total 114 men.
Baraita lists ten communal requirements for a Torah scholar to reside, raising the count to 120; Rabbi Akiva adds fruit; Rabbi Nehemya requires 230.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The population needed for a lesser Sanhedrin is 277: Rabbi Nehemya's 230 plus 47 extra for possible added judge pairs.
Asks why a baraita attributed to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gives 278 rather than 277.
Reply: the two baraitas differ because one follows Rabbi Yehuda with seventy judges and the other follows the Rabbis with seventy-one.
Baraita derives from Exodus 18:21 the number of ministers at each level, totaling 78,600 judges of the Jewish people.
Chapter closing formula: this ends the chapter on monetary cases.
Mishna on the High Priest: he judges and testifies, performs halitza and levirate marriage, and he is restricted from mourning rites and comforting.
Mishna on the king: he does not judge, testify, or perform halitza; Rabbi Yehuda says this is his prerogative; a king may marry a king's widow.
Rabbi Yehuda's view is supported by David marrying Saul's widows, drawn from II Samuel 12:8.
Asks why the mishna's rule that the High Priest judges others is needed, since it seems obvious.
Objection: if others do not judge him, he cannot judge others; yet Zephaniah 2:1 seems to suggest otherwise.
Reply: the High Priest's judging role is taught as the counterpart to the king's rule, or the mishna teaches the baraita's separate halakha.
Baraita: a High Priest who kills intentionally is executed; if unintentionally, he is exiled and treated as an ordinary person in all other halakhot.
Asks why the baraita needs to state the intentional case if it is obvious.
Objection: the unintentional case is also obvious and needs no mention.
Reply: without the clause one might think the High Priest, who has no return from exile, is exempt from exile; he is in fact exiled.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A High Priest who kills, or who was killed, never leaves the city of refuge; the baraita therefore asserts he is exiled.
Asks why not say the High Priest is not exiled at all, since he could never return home.
Deuteronomy 19:3 'every manslayer may flee there' includes even a High Priest in the term every.
Baraita: a High Priest who transgresses a positive mitzva and a prohibition is treated as an ordinary person in all his halakhot.
Clarifies that the baraita does not require the High Priest to transgress, but addresses the case where he does.
Asks whether this is obvious, or whether it could be thought that the High Priest is judged by seventy-one for all matters.
Mishna: an entire sinning tribe, a false prophet, or a High Priest is judged only by the Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one.
Rav Adda bar Ahava's verse, Exodus 18:22, is read as referring to capital matters, so the baraita's leniency is needed.
Rejects the suggestion that all cases of the High Priest go to seventy-one judges, since the verse says great matter, a capital one.
Mishna: the High Priest testifies before the court, and others testify concerning him.
Asks how the High Priest may testify, given a baraita on Deuteronomy 22:1 that permits ignoring lost items in some cases.
Baraita: ignoring lost property is allowed for a priest near graves, an elder of dignity, or heavier work, so the High Priest may ignore duties.
Rav Yosef: the High Priest testifies only about a king, since this does not compromise his dignity.
Objection: the mishna says the king neither testifies nor is testified about, so testimony about a king is excluded.
Rabbi Zeira: the High Priest testifies about a king's son, though the Gemara objects that a king's son is an ordinary person.
Rav Yosef's meaning is instead that the High Priest testifies before the king himself.
Objection: a king is not seated on the Sanhedrin, so testimony before a seated king seems impossible. Reply: a special arrangement honors the High Priest.
A king may not be seated on the Sanhedrin, nor may a king or High Priest be seated on a court for intercalating the year.
Exodus 23:2 'do not answer in a riv' is read as 'rav', so one whose stature frightens judges may not be seated.
A king's soldiers and a High Priest's cold concern disqualify them from intercalation rulings, since they have a stake in the outcome.
Rav Pappa: the High Priest's ruling teaches that the year's weather follows the months of the non-intercalated calendar.
Objection: the Sages heard three cattle herders giving weather signs, which contradicts Rav Pappa's inference.
The three herders' weather signs for Adar, which had not yet come to pass when the Sages intercalated that year.
Objection: can the Sages have relied on cattle herders to determine halakha?
Reply: the Sages relied on their own calculations, and the herders' signs were supported by that conclusion.
Mishna and Gemara: the High Priest performs halitza but does not consummate levirate marriage, whether the widow was betrothed or married.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the positive mitzva of levirate marriage does not override the prohibition for a betrothal widow.
The first intercourse is forbidden by decree lest a second occur; a baraita states the same rule for one whose yevama is forbidden.
Baraita on Leviticus 21:12: the High Priest does not leave with the bier but after it; Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda differ on how far he goes.
Explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning about sanctity and impurity, and why Rabbi Yehuda requires a stricter separation due to grief.
Mishna and baraita: when the High Priest consoles others, he stands in a line; the anointed High Priest does not come near him.
The reason is that a distraught High Priest would think others are glad at his grief, so the former High Priest keeps his distance.
Rav Pappa draws three lessons from the baraita about the deputy High Priest, the consoling line and where mourners stand.
Baraita: formerly mourners stood while all passed, but two quarrelsome families led the Sages to reverse the custom.
A parenthetical mnemonic: returned, walk and converse, marking the next set of customs.
Rami bar Abba's reports of Rabbi Yosei's local customs, and Rav Menashya's report that consolation requires at least ten people.
Mishna: when the High Priest is consoled, the people say we are your atonement, and he responds with a blessing.
Asks what the High Priest should say when he consoles others.
A baraita states that he says may you be consoled when he consoles others, since saying it on being consoled would be a curse.
Mishna: a king neither judges nor is judged; Rav Yosef says this applies only to the kings of Israel, not the house of David.
Jeremiah 21:12 'O house of David, execute justice' shows kings of the Davidic line judge.
Objection: if others do not judge the king, how can he judge, given Zephaniah 2:1 'adorn yourself first'?
Reply: the rule applies to kings of Israel, not the house of David.
Asks the reason that others do not judge the kings of Israel.
Illustrated by Yannai's slave who killed a person, and Shimon ben Shatah's request that Yannai appear with him to be judged.
Shimon ben Shatah tells Yannai to stand, since he stands before the Creator; Yannai agrees to stand only at the words of the whole court.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shimon ben Shatah's judges are struck down by Gabriel; from this the Sages rule that a king neither judges nor testifies, and the mishna's rule on halitza.
Objection: Rav Ashi holds that a king's honor is not waived, so Rabbi Yehuda's permission for a king to perform halitza seems impossible.
Reply: a mitzva is different, since a king is not disgraced by waiving honor to perform one; the mishna then rules no one marries a king's widow.
Baraita: the Sages told Rabbi Yehuda that the verse means David married women of the royal house, namely Merab and Michal.
Rabbi Yosei's students ask how David could marry two sisters while both were alive.
Rabbi Yosei: Michal was married after Merab died. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha: the betrothal to Merab was in error, as David's words to Ish-bosheth show.
Asks the biblical source by which Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha derives the error.
Rav Pappa: David's words Michal is my wife but Merab is not indicate that the earlier betrothal was void.
Asks what made David's betrothal to Merab an error.
Saul promised riches and a daughter for killing Goliath; a loan forgiven as betrothal does not betroth, so the betrothal to Merab failed.
Narrative: Saul gave Merab to Adriel and set the price of a hundred foreskins; Saul and David dispute whether a loan plus a peruta betroths.
Alternative reading: all agree the peruta governs, and Saul and David dispute the worth of foreskins, one saying none, the other enough for dogs.
Asks what Rabbi Yosei derives from the verse Deliver me my wife Michal.
Rabbi Yosei habitually derives meaning from mixed or apparently contradictory verses.
II Samuel 21:8 says Michal's five sons were borne to Adriel, and the Tosefta reads this as Michal's betrothal being effected by transgression.
Objection: Saul gave Michal to Palti, so how can the verse say she was given to Adriel?
Reply: the verse equates Merab's betrothal to Adriel with Michal's to Palti, both effected in transgression.
Asks how the verse can say the five sons of Michal were borne to Adriel, if Merab bore them.
Merab bore them and died, and Michal raised them, so the children bear her name, showing raising an orphan is credited as birth.
Mnemonic for the following Amoraic derivations, listing the names of the Sages cited.
Rabbi Hanina: Ruth 4:17 'a son born to Naomi' shows the raiser of a child is credited as its parent.
Rabbi Yohanan: Jered, Heber and Jekuthiel's mother Bithiah raised Moses, so the sons are credited to her, as with Moses's name.
Rabbi Elazar: Psalms 77:16 'children of Jacob and Joseph' shows Joseph sustained the nation, so they bear his name.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani: Moses taught Aaron's children, and Numbers 3:1-2 credits Aaron with having sired them.
Rav Yehuda: Isaiah 29:22 'who redeemed Abraham' means Jacob spared Abraham the burden of raising the twelve tribes.
Rabbi Yohanan: Palti was named Paltiel because God saved him from sin, and he placed a sword between himself and Michal.
Objection: II Samuel 3:16 calls Palti Michal's husband, and weeping suggests he knew she was David's wife.
Rabbi Yohanan: Joseph's strength is Boaz's humility, and Boaz's is Palti's, with Rav explaining vayyilafet as Boaz's restraint.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Boaz's strength is surpassed by Palti ben Laish's humility, as stated earlier.
Rabbi Yohanan asserts a teaching that he will ground in a verse.
A Proverbs verse is read as naming Joseph and Boaz, with Palti ben Laish surpassing them.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman, citing Rabbi Yonatan, offers a second verse-based teaching.
Proverbs 31:30 is read as praising Palti ben Laish above Joseph and Boaz.
Alternative reading: the three phrases describe the generations of Moses, Joshua and Hezekiah.
Another reading ties the phrases to Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Ilai's hard-pressed generation.
Mishnah: a relative of the king does not leave the palace gate to accompany a bier.
Rabbi Yehuda permits the king's relative to follow the bier if he wishes.
Rabbi Yehuda's proof: David followed Abner's bier, as II Samuel 3:31 states.
The Sages reply that David's act was only to appease the people, so the Mishnah's rule stands.
Baraita: where women customarily follow the bier, they do so; otherwise they walk in front.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that women always walk in front of the bier.
Rabbi Yehuda's proof: David followed Abner's bier, so he presumably did not walk among women.
The Sages reply that the king's following was only to appease the people, and they were appeased.
David moved between the men and the women during the procession, which supports the Sages' reply.
II Samuel 3:37 shows the people understood the king did not order Abner's killing.
Rava offers a homiletic reading of a verse about the people coming to David.
II Samuel 3:35 says all the people came to comfort David.
The written word means to destroy and the read word means to comfort, so the people first intended harm.
Why was Abner punished with death? Rav Yehuda asks this in Rav's name.
Rav answers that Abner should have protested against Saul and did not.
Rabbi Yitzchak says Abner did protest but was not answered; both views read one verse.
II Samuel 3:33 has the king lament Abner's death, saying his hands and feet were not bound.
The one who says Abner did not protest reads the verse as a rebuke for his silence.
Why did Abner not protest, given the verse about falling before the children of iniquity?
For the view that Abner protested, David was astonished at the verse's wording.
If Abner did protest, why does the verse say he fell before the children of iniquity?
According to the view that he protested, what was the reason he was punished?
Rav Nachman son of Rabbi Yitzchak answers that Abner delayed David's kingdom two and a half years.
The Gemara quotes the Mishnah: the mourner reclines on the dargash during the meal of comfort.
What is a dargash?
Ulla answers that a dargash is a bed of fortune kept for decoration and not used for sitting.
The Sages challenge Ulla: why seat the mourner on something never permitted before?
Rava defends Ulla: the dargash is like food and drink, permitted now only in mourning.
If the dargash is a bed of fortune, a baraita says it need only be stood up, not overturned.
If it were a bed of fortune, why would the mourner not be required to overturn it?
Baraita: one who overturns a bed in mourning overturns all the beds in his house.
Rebuttal: the dargash may resemble a bed set aside for vessels, which need not be overturned.
This resolution is itself difficult, and the difficulty is raised against it.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: the mourner loosens the dargash's straps and it falls on its own.
If the dargash were a bed of fortune, would it have straps at all?
Ravin reports a sage's account of Rav Tachlifa asking leatherworkers in the market about the term.
Rav Tachlifa asks what a dargash is.
The leatherworker answers that a dargash is a leather bed.
Rabbi Yirmeya, citing Rabbi Yochanan, begins to distinguish a dargash from an ordinary bed.

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that a bed's weaving sits inside its posts while a dargash's straps are tied around them.
Objection raised from a Mishnah in Kelim about when wooden vessels become susceptible to impurity.
The Mishnah's rule: a bed or crib becomes complete once rubbed with fish skin.
If a bed is woven on its back side, the fish-skin rubbing would seem unnecessary.
Why is rubbing with fish skin needed at all, if the weaving covers the smooth wood?
Proposes that both bed and dargash are woven inside, differing only in whether straps pass through holes or loops.
Rabbi Yaakov, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, rules like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on the dargash.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Ami says a mourner stands up a long-posted bed, which suffices.
Mishnah: the king may conscript for an optional war only on the authority of a seventy-one judge court.
The king may breach fences to make his own road, and no one may protest his road's width.
All the people plunder for the king, who takes the first share of the spoils.
The Gemara recalls that the court-of-seventy-one rule was already taught earlier in the tractate.
The rule is repeated because the Mishnah lists all the king's matters and so includes it.
Shmuel holds that the king may perform all the actions described in the biblical passage on kingship.
Rav holds that the passage was stated only to instill fear of the king.
Rav supports this with Deuteronomy 17:15 about setting a king whose dread should fall upon the people.
A parallel tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Yosei permits all the king's actions described in the passage.
Rabbi Yehuda holds the passage was stated only to frighten the people into accepting a king.
Rabbi Yehuda's support is Deuteronomy 17:15 about the king's dread falling upon the people.
Rabbi Yehuda teaches that three commandments applied on entering the land, beginning with appointing a king.
The other two commandments are cutting off Amalek's seed and building the Chosen House.
Rabbi Nehorai holds the king passage was a response to the people's complaint, not a commandment.
Deuteronomy 17:14 is cited: the people say they will set a king like the surrounding nations.
Rabbi Eliezer says the elders of Samuel's generation asked properly for a king.
I Samuel 8:6 is cited: the elders asked for a king to judge them.
The common people, however, spoiled the request.
I Samuel 8:19-20 shows the people demanding a king to judge them and lead their battles.
Rabbi Yosei teaches the same three commandments of entering the land.
He lists the three commandments: appoint a king, cut off Amalek, and build the Chosen House.
Rabbi Yosei admits he does not know which of the three commandments comes first.
Exodus 17:16 is read as showing that appointing a king comes before the war against Amalek.
The Gemara concludes that appointing a king is the first commandment to fulfill.
A throne is a term for a king, as I Chronicles 29:23 shows Solomon sitting on the Lord's throne.
The Gemara admits it still does not know whether the Temple or the war against Amalek comes first.
Deuteronomy 12:10-11 is cited as indicating that Amalek's seed should be cut off first.
The conclusion from that verse is that cutting off Amalek's seed comes first.
II Samuel 7:1 shows David had rest from his enemies before he planned the Temple.
II Samuel 7:2 shows David then said he dwelt in a cedar house while the Ark dwelt in curtains.
Reish Lakish says Solomon initially ruled over the supernal worlds.
I Chronicles 29:23 is cited for Solomon sitting on the Lord's throne at first.
Ultimately, Solomon ruled over only the lower worlds.
I Kings 5:4 is cited: Solomon ruled from the River to Gaza.
Rav and Shmuel explain the place names Tiphsah and Gaza differently.
Just as he ruled over Tiphsah and Gaza, he ruled over the whole world.
Ultimately, Solomon ruled only over Israel.
Ecclesiastes 1:12 is cited: I, Koheleth, was king over Israel.
Ultimately, Solomon ruled only over Jerusalem.
Ecclesiastes 1:1 is cited: Koheleth, son of David, king in Jerusalem.
Ultimately, Solomon ruled only over his bed.
Song of Songs 3:7 is cited: the bed of Solomon with mighty men around it.
Ultimately, Solomon ruled only over his staff.
Ecclesiastes 2:10 is cited: this was my portion from all my labor.
Rav and Shmuel disagree whether the word this refers to the staff or to the cloak.
Did Solomon return to reign over the whole world, or not?
Rav and Shmuel disagree: one says he returned to kingship, the other says he did not.
Explains each view: he was king and then an ordinary person, and either did or did not return to kingship.
Mishnah repeated: the king breaches fences to create a road for himself.
Baraita: treasures of kings go to the king, and the rest of the spoils are split half to the king and half to the people.
Abaye asks Rav Dimi, or Rav Acha, why the rest of the spoils are split between the king and the people.
Abaye asks from where this halakha is derived.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: I Chronicles 29:22 is cited: Solomon was anointed as leader alongside Tzadok the priest.
The leader is compared to Tzadok: half the shewbread for him, half for his brothers.
From where do we know that the High Priest himself takes half of the shewbread?
A baraita cites Leviticus 24:9, inferring the shewbread is split half to Aaron and half to his sons.
Mishnah: the king may not add many wives, beyond the permitted eighteen.
Rabbi Yehuda says he may marry many wives, provided they do not turn his heart away.
Rabbi Shimon says even one wife who turns his heart away is forbidden.
If so, why does the verse say many wives? It must forbid even wives like Abigail.
Does Rabbi Yehuda interpret the verse's rationale while Rabbi Shimon does not? Didn't we hear the reverse elsewhere?
A baraita rules that one may not take collateral from a widow, whether she is poor or wealthy.
Deuteronomy 24:17 is cited: you may not take a widow's garment as a pledge.
Rabbi Shimon allows collateral from a wealthy widow, but not a poor one, against Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Shimon's reason: returning the pledge gives the widow a bad name among her neighbors.
Explains that Rabbi Shimon means: taking and returning the pledge makes neighbors suspect her.
Concludes that Rabbi Yehuda does not interpret the verse's rationale while Rabbi Shimon does.
Generally Rabbi Yehuda does not interpret rationales, but here the verse itself states the rationale.
Deuteronomy 17:17 is cited: the reason is that his heart should not turn away.
Rabbi Shimon would object: if the verse gives the rationale, it should simply end after the prohibition.
Rabbi Shimon infers that the phrase about the heart teaches a separate rule for a single wife.
The verse's prohibition therefore applies even to wives like Abigail, not only to the many.
From where do we derive the number eighteen permitted for the king?
II Samuel 3:2-5 lists six sons born to David in Hebron, from six different wives.
II Samuel 12:8 has Nathan say he would add like these and like those, giving eighteen wives.
Ravina objects: the verse yields twelve from the first pair, and twenty-four in total.
A baraita states the king may not marry more than twenty-four women, following Ravina.
On the reading of the letter vav as adding, the total becomes forty-eight women.
A baraita states the king may not marry more than forty-eight women.
What is the reasoning of our Mishnah's tanna for limiting the number to eighteen?
Rav Kahana: the repeated word kahenna equates the two phrases, so each means six.
But David also had Michal, so he had at least seven wives.
Rav: Eglah is Michal, called a calf because she was dear to him, as Judges 14:18 shows.
Did Michal have children, given that the verse says she had none?
II Samuel 6:23 is cited: Michal had no child until the day of her death.
Rav Chisda: she had no child until her death, but at the moment of death she had one.
Where does the verse count these children, since they were born in Hebron while Michal's incident was in Jerusalem?
II Samuel 6:16 shows the Michal incident occurred in Jerusalem, after David's arrival there.
Rav Yehuda, or Rav Yosef, says Michal was punished immediately and could have no children afterward.
Revised: she had a child until the incident, and none from that point on.
II Samuel 5:13 says David took more wives and concubines in Jerusalem, beyond eighteen.
What is the difference between wives and concubines in that verse?
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: wives have a marriage contract and betrothal, concubines have neither.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: David had four hundred sons of captive women, who sat in gold carriages.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: David's daughter Tamar was born of a captive woman before her mother converted.
II Samuel 13:13 is cited: Tamar asks Amnon to speak to the king, who would not refuse her.
If she were a daughter of marriage, would David have permitted her to Amnon?
Rather, learn that Tamar was born of a captive woman who converted later, so she was not David's daughter.
II Samuel 13:3 introduces Amnon's friend Jonadab, described as a very wise man.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: a wise man for wickedness, meaning Jonadab was wise in evil.
II Samuel 13:4 is cited: Amnon was becoming thin day by day.
II Samuel 13:4-9 recounts Jonadab's plan, and Tamar prepares food before Amnon.
Rav: Tamar prepared various kinds of fried food for Amnon.
II Samuel 13:15 says Amnon hated Tamar with exceeding great hatred.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers: during the rape, a hair of hers tied around his member and severed it.
Suggests Tamar was tied to Amnon and made him a eunuch, through the hair.
But if the hair was tied to him, what did she do to deserve this?
Rather, she tied the hair on purpose to take revenge, and that is why he hated her.
Rava's homiletic reading of Ezekiel 16:14 shows Jewish women had no pubic hair, so Tamar could not do this, unless she was a gentile's daughter.
II Samuel 13:19 is cited: Tamar tore her garment of many colors and put ashes on her head.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha taught that Tamar built a great fence through her public outcry.
If such a thing could happen to royal daughters, all the more so to ordinary women, and to licentious women.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, says that at that moment the Sages issued a decree.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Seclusion with a forbidden woman is a Torah prohibition, according to Rabbi Yohanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak.
From where in the Torah is the prohibition of seclusion derived?
Deuteronomy 13:7 is cited: if your brother, the son of your mother, entices you.
Does not the son of a father also entice? Why specify the son of the mother?
The verse teaches that a son may be secluded only with his mother, while others are forbidden seclusion with all forbidden relatives.
Rather, the Sages decreed against seclusion of a man with a single woman.
I Kings 1:5 is cited: Adonijah son of Haggith exalted himself, saying he would be king.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: the phrase exalted himself shows he sought a throne that did not fit him.
The verse continues: Adonijah prepared chariots, riders, and fifty men to run before him.
What was the novelty of these preparations, since other wealthy people do the same?
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: the runners had their spleens removed and soles hollowed, to increase their speed.
Mishnah: the king may not accumulate many horses or much silver and gold, beyond what he needs, and writes a Torah scroll for himself.
When the king goes to war or judgment, the Torah scroll goes with him, and he reads from it all his days.
Baraita: the verse forbids the king to accumulate many horses.
The baraita infers the king may keep horses for his chariot and riders, but not for personal pleasure.
How do I realize the meaning of horses in the verse?
The horses meant are idle horses, which serve only to glorify the king.
From where is it derived that even one idle horse is prohibited?
Deuteronomy 17:16 is cited: the word for horses appears in the singular, so one idle horse is included.
Since even one idle horse is prohibited, why does the verse use the plural horses?
Its purpose is to teach that the king transgresses once for each and every idle horse.
Otherwise I would say even enough horses for his chariot and riders are prohibited, which is unreasonable.
No, the verse is needed to permit horses beyond necessity for the army.
Mishnah: the king may not accumulate much silver and gold, only enough for his soldiers' provisions.
Baraita: one might think even enough silver for soldiers' provisions is prohibited.
The double word to him is cited as a limiting indication.
The king may accumulate enough silver and gold to provide soldiers' sustenance.
Otherwise I would say even enough silver for soldiers' provisions is prohibited, which is unreasonable.
No, the phrase is needed to permit a comfortable military financial cushion.
What does the phrase for himself exclude, when applied to the wives verse?
Rav Yehuda raises a contradiction between I Kings 5:6 (forty thousand stalls) and II Chronicles 9:25 (four thousand).
Reconciles: either forty thousand stables each with four thousand stalls, or four thousand stables with forty thousand stalls each.
Rabbi Yitzchak raises a contradiction about the value of silver in Solomon's days.
II Chronicles 9:20 says silver was worthless, while I Kings 10:27 says the king made silver like stones.
Reconciled: before Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter silver was worthless, and after, it was valuable.
Rabbi Yitzchak: after the marriage, Gabriel planted a pole in the sea, and Rome was built on the sandbar.
Why were the rationales of Torah commandments not revealed?
Two verses' rationales were revealed, and Solomon, the greatest man, failed in both.
Deuteronomy 17:17 is cited: the king shall not add many wives to himself.
Solomon said: I will add many wives but I will not turn away, so it is permitted.
I Kings 11:4 says his wives turned away his heart when he was old.
Deuteronomy 17:16 is cited on the prohibition against many horses.
Solomon said: I will accumulate many horses and I will not return.
I Kings 10:29 says a chariot came up from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver.
The king writes a Torah scroll for his own sake.
A baraita: the king fulfills the mitzva only if he does not beautify himself with his ancestors' scroll.
Rava: each person must write his own Torah scroll, even if he inherited one from his ancestors.
Deuteronomy 31:19 is cited: now write for yourselves this song.
Abaye objects from the baraita that a king, unlike an ordinary person, may not rely on an inherited scroll.
No, the baraita teaches that the king writes two scrolls, one as every Jew does and an extra one.
Deuteronomy 17:18 is cited: he shall write for himself a second Torah.
Deuteronomy 17:18 continues: he shall write a copy of this Torah.
Baraita: the king writes two scrolls, one that travels with him and one kept in his treasury.
The traveling scroll is made very small, like an amulet, and hung on his arm.
Psalm 16:8 is cited: I have set the Lord always before me, at my right hand.
He may not enter the bathhouse or the bathroom with the scroll.
Deuteronomy 17:19 is cited: it shall be with him and he shall read in it.
The verse says the scroll should stay in a place appropriate for reading from it.
Mar Zutra: the Torah was first given in Ivrit script and in the sacred tongue, Hebrew.
It was given again in Ezra's days in Ashurit script, with Israel keeping Ashurit and Hebrew, and commoners Ivrit and Aramaic.
Who were these commoners?
Rav Chisda says they were the Samaritans, the Kutim.
What is Ivrit script?
Rav Chisda says it is the Libona script.
Rabbi Yosei: Ezra was worthy to receive the Torah, had Moses not come first.
Exodus 19:3 and Ezra 7:6 both use the going up language for Moses and Ezra.
Just as the going up for Moses concerns Torah, so does Ezra's going up concern Torah.
Deuteronomy 4:14 is cited: the Lord commanded me to teach you statutes and ordinances.
Ezra 7:10 is cited: Ezra set his heart to seek and teach the Torah, statutes and ordinances.
Though the Torah was not given by Ezra, the script was changed through him.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ezra 4:7 is cited: the letter was written in Aramaic script and set forth in the Aramaic tongue.
Daniel 5:8 is cited: the wise men could not read the writing or explain it to the king.
Deuteronomy 17:18 is cited: he shall write for himself a second Torah.
The word second teaches that the script is one apt to be changed.
The script is called Ashurit because it came up with the Jews from Ashur.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the Torah was first given in Ashurit, changed to Libona'a after sin, and restored after repentance.
Zechariah 9:12 is cited: return to the stronghold, I will render double unto you.
It is called beautiful script, shemaushert, because it is beautiful and straight.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, citing Rabbi Eliezer ben Perata and Rabbi Elazar HaModai, holds the script never changed.
The script never changed at all, according to this view.
Exodus 27:10 is cited: just as the poles were not changed, so the hooks were not changed.
Esther 8:9 is cited: the Jews' script and language were not changed, just as the language stayed Hebrew.
If the script never changed, the second Torah means two scrolls the king writes, one carried with him and one in his treasury.
The carried scroll is made very small, like an amulet, and hung on the arm.
Psalm 16:8 is cited: I have set the Lord always before me.
What does the other Sage, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, derive from the word I have set?
Rav Chana bar Bizna, citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida: one praying should see the Divine Presence as opposite him, from I have set.
According to Rabbi Shimon, who says the script never changed, what does they could not read mean?
Rav says it was written in a gimatriya code, using letter substitution.
What did Daniel explain to them?
Daniel explains the words mene, tekel, and parsin as God numbering, weighing, and dividing the kingdom.
Shmuel, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Ashi each offer a different reading of the written letters.
Mishnah: one may not ride the king's horse, sit on his throne, or use his scepter.
One may not see the king while he is having his hair cut, naked, or in the bathhouse.
Deuteronomy 17:15 is cited: set a king over you whose fear will be upon you.
Rav Yaakov, citing Rabbi Yochanan: Abishag was permitted to Solomon as a king, but forbidden to Adonijah as a commoner.
What was the story of Abishag?
I Kings 1:1-4 is cited: King David was old, and Abishag was found to minister to him.
Abishag asks David to marry her, he refuses because of his eighteen wives, and he sends for Bathsheba.
I Kings 1:15 is cited: Bathsheba went in to the king in the chamber.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: Bathsheba wiped herself with thirteen cloths, matching the number of words in the verse.
Rav Shemen bar Abba: divorce is so severe that David was permitted to seclude with Abishag but not to divorce for her.
Rabbi Eliezer: anyone who divorces his first wife, even the altar sheds tears over him.
Malachi 2:13 is cited: the altar is covered with tears, because the Lord no longer accepts the offerings.
Malachi 2:14 is cited: the Lord has been witness between you and the wife of your youth.
Rabbi Yochanan, or some say Rabbi Elazar, holds a man's wife dies only if creditors demand a debt he cannot pay.
A man's wife dies only if creditors demand money he owes, and he has none.
Proverbs 22:27 is cited: why should he take away your bed from under you?
Rabbi Yochanan: when a man's first wife dies, it is as if the Temple were destroyed in his days.
Ezekiel 24:16 is cited: I take away the desire of your eyes with a stroke, yet you shall not weep.
Ezekiel 24:18 and 24:21 are cited, linking the death of a wife to the Temple's profanation.
Rabbi Alexandri: for any man whose wife dies in his lifetime, the world is dark for him.
Job 18:6 is cited: the light shall be dark in his tent, a metonym for the wife.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: his steps get shorter.
Job 18:7 is cited: the steps of his strength shall be constrained.
Rabbi Abbahu: his counsel falls.
Job 18:7 is cited: his own counsel shall cast him down.
Rabba bar bar Chana, citing Rabbi Yochanan: matching a couple is as difficult as splitting the Red Sea.
Psalm 68:7 is cited: God makes the solitary dwell in a house, bringing out prisoners.
The verse is read as like bringing out prisoners, and bakkosharot as crying and singing, recalling the Red Sea.
Is matching really so difficult, when Rav Yehuda says a Divine Voice announces matches forty days before formation?
No difficulty: the predestined match is the first marriage, the difficult match is the second.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman: everything lost has a substitute, except one's wife of youth.
Isaiah 54:6 is cited: a wife of youth, can she be rejected?
Rav Yehuda taught Rav Yitzchak his son that a man finds calm only with his first wife.
Rav Yehuda's teaching: a man finds peace of spirit only in his first wife.
Proverbs 5:18 is cited: let your fountain be blessed and rejoice in the wife of your youth.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yehuda tells his son Rav Yitzchak that the woman described is such as his mother.
Didn't Rav Yehuda once read Ecclesiastes 7:26 to his son, saying a woman is more bitter than death?
Ecclesiastes 7:26 is cited: I find the woman more bitter than death, whose heart is snares and nets.
Resolves the contradiction: the mother is difficult at first but afterward conciliatory, so both statements hold at different times.
Rav Shmuel bar Unya, citing Rav: a woman is raw material, bound only to the one who first made her a vessel.
Isaiah 54:5 is cited: for your Maker is your husband.
A baraita: a man dies primarily to his wife, and a woman's death concerns her husband.
Ruth 1:3 is cited: Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died.
A woman dies only to her husband.
Genesis 48:7 is cited: Rachel died on me, as Jacob told Joseph.
Restates the Mishnah: one may not see the king while he is having his hair cut.
Baraita: the king cuts his hair daily, the High Priest between Shabbatot, and an ordinary priest every thirty days.
Explains the king's daily cut via Isaiah 33:17, and the High Priest's weekly cut as tied to the weekly new priestly watch.
An ordinary priest cuts his hair once every thirty days.
Ezekiel 44:20 is cited: the priests shall not shave their heads or let long hair grow.
A verbal analogy links long hair for priests to long hair for the nazirite.
Numbers 6:5 is cited: the nazirite lets the hair of his head grow long.
Just as the nazirite's term is thirty days, so the priest's hair cut interval is thirty days.
A mishna is cited: a nazirite term of unspecified length is thirty days.
From where do we derive that thirty days is the minimum nazirite term?
Rav Mattana: the word yihye in Numbers 6:5 has the numerical value of thirty.
Rav Pappa suggests that priests should not let their hair grow at all, but shave instead.
Abaye replies that the wording and long hair permits somewhat long hair, not very long.
If so, should priests still cut their hair every thirty days after the Temple's destruction?
The restriction on long hair parallels the wine prohibition, which applies only at the time of Temple entry.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says priests are always forbidden wine, but the destruction ruined and confused the rules.
Abaye infers: nowadays priests drink wine in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, so the Rabbis prohibit it.
The wine prohibition exists because a priest fit for Temple service is needed once the Temple is rebuilt.
The same reasoning should apply to hair, so a priest fit for service is needed.
Here it is possible for the priest to cut his hair and enter the Temple immediately.
There too one can sleep a little and enter, as Rav Acha says walking a mil or sleeping dispels the effect of wine.
Rav Naḥman and Rabba bar Avuh: the wine's effect is dispelled only for a quarter-log, not more.
Rav Ashi: priests drunk on wine desecrate the service so were forbidden, but long-haired priests were not decreed against.
A baraita lists those sentenced to death by Heaven: priests with long hair or drunk on wine.
Leviticus 10:9 is cited: drink no wine or strong drink when you enter the Tent of Meeting, that you not die.
From where do we derive that long-haired priests are also punished with death?
The verses juxtapose drunk priests and long-haired priests, so they share the same penalty.
Ezekiel 44:20-21 is cited: no priest drinks wine when entering the inner court.
Just as drunk priests are liable to death by Heaven, so long-haired priests are likewise liable.
Parallel reasoning would make long-haired priests desecrate the service as drunk priests do, which poses a difficulty for Rav Ashi.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi: until Ezekiel came, who taught this halakha? How can a Torah law derive from Ezekiel's verse juxtaposition?
Rav Ashi replies: Rav Chisda says we did not learn the rule from Moses until Ezekiel taught it.
Ezekiel 44:9 is cited: no stranger uncircumcised in heart and flesh shall enter My Sanctuary.
If Ezekiel taught that rule, who said it before Ezekiel came?
Rather, the halakha is learned as a tradition, and Ezekiel gave it support by writing a verse.
The tradition covers the death penalty for violating the restriction, not the desecration of service.
What is the meaning of they shall trim only their heads, from Ezekiel 44:20?
A baraita: it means a lulyanit haircut.
What is a lulyanit haircut?
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: it is a unique haircut.
What is the unique haircut like?
Rav Ashi: the hair is cut so that the head of one row is at the side of the bottom of the next row.
The Sages asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi what the High Priest's haircut was.
He told them to look at the haircut of ben Elasa, his son-in-law, who wore the High Priest's style.
A baraita: ben Elasa spent his money on haircuts only to display the High Priest's haircut.
Chapter-end marker: this closes the chapter beginning with High Priest.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: each litigant picks a judge and the two picked judges choose a third, per Rabbi Meir.
The Rabbis say the two chosen judges choose one more judge for themselves.
Rabbi Meir: each litigant may disqualify the judge chosen by the other.
The Rabbis: disqualification requires evidence of relation or other flaw, not if the judges are fit or ordained experts.
Rabbi Meir: each litigant may disqualify the witnesses of the other litigant.
The Rabbis: witnesses may be disqualified only with evidence of relation or other flaw, not if they are fit.
Why must each litigant choose a judge, when three judges would suffice to decide the case?
Each litigant asks for a specific judge; the two must agree on a third, and even a debtor may object.
Does not Rabbi Elazar say only a creditor may refuse the court, while a debtor is compelled to appear before the local court?
Rabbi Yochanan: the Sages taught that rule about the laymen's courts in Syria.
Here too the mishna speaks of the Syrian laymen's courts, not of courts of experts.
Rav Pappa: even expert courts apply, as in the courts of Rav Huna and Rav Chisda, where the parties are not burdened.
If the mishna meant each side chose a full court of three, the courts would then need to choose more judges, which is difficult.
What is the point of each litigant choosing one judge, if the two then choose a third?
The mishna means each litigant picks one judge, and the two judges pick a third.
Why do they do this procedure?
Rabbi Zeira in the West: this selection produces a true judgment, since each party trusts the judge he chose.
Restates the Rabbis' view that the two chosen judges choose a third.
Suggests that Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree about Rav Yehuda's statement about witnesses signing.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: witnesses do not sign a document unless they know who signs with them.
Rabbi Meir does not accept Rav Yehuda's statement, while the Rabbis do, on this suggested reading.
Rejects that reading: everyone accepts Rav Yehuda's statement.
Everyone agrees the judges' consent is needed; the dispute concerns the litigants' consent.
Rabbi Meir requires the litigants' consent, while the Rabbis do not.
Returns to the matter: Rav Yehuda's statement about witnesses signing.
A baraita: the scrupulous Jerusalemites signed, judged, and dined only with known co-participants.
Restates the mishna: a litigant may disqualify the judge chosen by the other.
Rabbi Yochanan: the Sages taught this about the Syrian laymen's courts, not about experts.
The latter clause of the mishna implies Rabbi Meir also speaks of experts, since the Rabbis limit disqualification to fit judges.
The mishna means: judges who are fit become like court-ordained experts, and cannot be disqualified.
A baraita: the Rabbis told Rabbi Meir a litigant cannot disqualify a judge accepted by the public as an expert.
A baraita: one may keep disqualifying judges until he accepts a court accepted as expert, per Rabbi Meir.
Witnesses are like experts, so why does Rabbi Meir let each litigant disqualify the other's witnesses?
Reish Lakish: a holy mouth would not say this, so the text should read his witness, singular, referring to one witness.
For what purpose does a single witness testify, if monetary testimony requires two witnesses by Torah law?
The ruling teaches that a litigant may retract his agreement to accept a single witness as two.
Mishna: if one litigant says my father, or three herders, are trusted to judge for me, the offering party may retract.
Rabbi Meir: one may retract; the Rabbis say one cannot retract and must accept the verdict.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Dimi son of Rav Nachman: this refers to a litigant who accepted one of these people as a judge alongside two fit judges.
Both mishnayot are needed: one case concerns a father as judge, the other a single witness accepted as two.
Conversely, the dispute must also be stated for the father case, since Rabbi Meir might concede to the Rabbis there.
Since the mishna says his judge in the first clause but his witnesses in the second, does it mean only two witnesses?
Rabbi Elazar: the case is that the litigant and another person come to disqualify the witnesses.
Can a litigant testify to disqualify the other side's witnesses, when his own testimony is tainted by conflict of interest?
Rav Acha bar Ika: the case is a challenge to the witness's fitness, which cannot be disregarded because of conflict of interest.
If the challenge concerns theft or another transgression, is the litigant's testimony not still tainted by conflict?
It is a family flaw, so Rabbi Meir accepts the testimony, while the Rabbis reject it as tainted by conflict.
Rav Dimi, citing Rabbi Yochanan: the dispute concerns a case with two sets of witnesses for one litigant.
Rabbi Meir requires the litigant to substantiate the witnesses, so with one set everyone agrees there is no disqualification.
Rav Ami and Rav Asi asked Rabbi Yochanan what the law is when only one set of witnesses is there.
If only one set is there, everyone agrees a litigant cannot disqualify them, so the question must be understood otherwise.
If the second set is later found to be related or disqualified, can the first set's litigant claim the disqualifying party was unable to disqualify?
Rabbi Yochanan: the first pair already testified validly, so their testimony cannot be disqualified afterward; some attribute this to Rav Ashi.
Do Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree on the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?
A baraita: for a land claim with a deed and presumptive ownership, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi judges by the deed, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel judges by presumption.
Rather, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel means a claim may be judged on either the deed or presumptive ownership.
The dispute concerns whether a litigant must substantiate all his evidence, and everyone agrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
When Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree, it follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's position.
The Rabbis could reply that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi spoke only of presumptive ownership claims, not of a deed.
A deed-based claim cannot rely on presumption, but two sets of witnesses are independent, so even Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi concedes no substantiation is needed.
When Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported Rabbi Yochanan's different reading of the dispute.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the mishna's two cases, disqualified witnesses with fit judges and the reverse, reasoning that disqualifying one group disqualifies the other.
Rava objects that disqualifying the judges in the latter case would nullify the whole claim, since no witnesses would remain to testify.
Replies in support of the mishna: the dispute applies only when a second, untouched set of witnesses exists, so disqualifying this set does not predetermine the outcome.
Asks what the law is if no second set of witnesses exists, and whether the litigant may then disqualify them, linking this to Rav Dimi's reading.
Explains the practical difference: Ravin holds Rabbi Meir applies the miggo principle, while Rav Dimi holds it does not, so each claim must be proven.
Reish Lakish objects that Rabbi Meir could not have held that a litigant may silence a witness, since such a view is too strange for a sage of his stature.
Proposes emending the mishna to read the singular, so the rule concerns only a witness who testifies alone.
Asks whether Reish Lakish really spoke of Rabbi Meir with such reverence, given Ulla's account of Reish Lakish's own sharpness in study.
Ravina answers that anyone who studies Rabbi Meir's Torah seems to uproot mountains, so Reish Lakish's reverence was fitting; the remark shows mutual esteem.
Introduces an example of mutual esteem: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules that insulating cold food on Shabbat is forbidden.
Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, contradicts him, saying his father permitted insulating cold food on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi retracts and defers to the elder Rabbi Yosei, who already issued a ruling on the matter.
Rav Pappa states that the episode shows how deeply the Sages loved one another.
Argues that had Rabbi Yosei lived, Rabbi Yishmael would have sat as Rabbi Yehuda's student, yet Rabbi Yehuda still deferred to Rabbi Yosei's ruling.
Rabbi Oshaya asks the meaning of the verse about two staves, named Graciousness and Binders.
Explains the staves: Graciousness refers to Torah scholars of Eretz Yisrael who treat each other kindly, and Binders to those of Babylonia who harshly disagree.
Brings a second verse about two anointed ones and two olive trees, offered as support for the same contrast between the two communities.
Rabbi Yitzhak interprets the verses: scholars of Eretz Yisrael are pleasant like olive oil, while those of Babylonia are bitter like an olive.
Quotes Zechariah's vision of a measure carried between heaven and earth to the land of Shinar, as scriptural basis for the next interpretation.
Rabbi Yoḥanan, in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai, interprets the measure as flattery and arrogance that descended to Babylonia.
Asks whether arrogance really descended to Babylonia at all.
Objects that the Master taught ten kav of arrogance descended to the world, with Elam taking nine and the rest of the world taking one.
Answers that arrogance did descend to Babylonia but passed on to Elam; the verse's wording shows a house was intended for Babylonia but never built there.
Objects that the Master taught poverty is a sign of arrogance, and poverty descended to Babylonia, not to Elam.
Asks what kind of poverty is meant.
Cites the verse about a little sister without breasts as scriptural basis for speaking of poverty in Torah.
Rabbi Yoḥanan identifies that poverty with Elam, which merited learning Torah but did not merit teaching it.
Asks the homiletic meaning of the name Babylonia.
Rabbi Yoḥanan reads the name as mixed with Bible, Mishna and Talmud, praising Babylonian learning.
Cites Lamentations' verse about dwelling in dark places as the scriptural basis for the next opinion.
Rabbi Yirmeya reads the same verse as criticizing the Babylonian Talmud, which is less clear than the Talmud of Eretz Yisrael.
Mishna's case: a litigant designates a relative, or three unqualified herders, as judges, all of whom are disqualified from judging.
Rabbi Meir holds that the party who made the offer may retract it.
The Sages hold that the offer cannot be retracted, and the litigant must accept the verdict.
Mishna's second case: one obligated to swear is offered instead a vow by the life of one's head.
Rabbi Meir holds that the offerer may retract and require the oath.
The Sages hold that once a vow is accepted in place of an oath, the agreement cannot be retracted.
Rav Dimi explains the relative-as-judge case: the relative served on a three-judge panel alongside two fit judges, not as the sole judge.
Shmuel holds the dispute concerns a claimant's offer to forgive, while if the defendant offered payment all agree it can be retracted.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the reverse: the dispute concerns a defendant's offer to pay, not a claimant's offer to forgive.
Asks whether Rabbi Yoḥanan's dispute applies only to the defendant's offer, or to both kinds of offer.
Brings Rava's ruling as support: the dispute applies only to the defendant's offer, with all agreeing on the forgiveness case.
Objects: if so, Rava follows Rabbi Yoḥanan; but if the dispute covers both offers, Rava's ruling matches neither Shmuel nor Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Replies that Rava is offering his own explanation of the dispute, not stating the view of either Sage.
Rav Aḥa bar Taḥlifa objects to Rava from the mishna's latter clause, where Rabbi Meir allows retraction of the vow and the Sages forbid it.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that the mishna may refer to a defendant who takes an oath and pays nothing, making the claimant's suggestion equivalent to forgiving the debt.
Rejects the objection: the mishna refers to a claimant who takes an oath and collects, so the suggestion equals agreeing to pay what he claims.
Objects that on Rava's reading the first clause already taught the case where the defendant says I will give you, with unfit judges.
The former clause concerns making the outcome depend on others' decision, the latter on the claimant's own decision.
Explains why both cases must be taught: otherwise one might think Rabbi Meir allows retraction only in the decision-of-others case, and the Rabbis only in the other.
The converse is also needed: without both cases one might think the Rabbis concede to Rabbi Meir in the first case, so the mishna must state both.
Reish Lakish holds the dispute concerns retraction before the verdict; after the verdict everyone agrees the acceptance cannot be retracted.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the reverse: the dispute concerns retraction after the verdict is issued.
Asks whether Rabbi Yoḥanan's dispute is limited to retraction after the verdict, or applies to both the before and after cases.
Brings Rava's statement as a resolution of the dilemma: a relative or disqualified judge accepted may be retracted before the verdict, not after.
Objects: if Rava follows Rabbi Yoḥanan the dispute is only after the verdict, but if it covers both cases Rava matches neither Reish Lakish nor Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Concludes that Rava's statement shows the dispute concerns retraction after the verdict, confirming the reading.
Rav Naḥman bar Rav Ḥisda writes to Rav Naḥman bar Ya'akov asking which case the dispute concerns and whose view the halakha follows.
Rav Naḥman bar Ya'akov replies that the dispute concerns retraction after the verdict, and the halakha follows the Rabbis.
Rav Ashi gives a different version of the letter, asking whether the dispute concerns the defendant's offer to pay or the claimant's offer to forgive.
Rav Naḥman bar Ya'akov's reply in Rav Ashi's version: the dispute concerns the defendant's offer to pay, and the halakha follows the Rabbis.
Reports that the study halls of Sura and Pumbedita each teach a different version of the question and answer.
Rav Ḥanina bar Shelemya reports a question sent to Shmuel: may a party retract his acceptance of judges after a formal act of acquisition was made?
Shmuel replies that nothing can be retracted once an act of acquisition has been performed.
Mishna's list of those disqualified as witnesses for unseemly conduct: dice players, usurers, pigeon-flyers and traders in Sabbatical produce.
Rabbi Shimon explains the name for traders in Sabbatical produce: the term changed once tax collectors became numerous.
Rabbi Yehuda limits the disqualification to those who have no other occupation; those with another trade remain fit to testify.
Asks what a dice player does that disqualifies him from testifying.
Rami bar Ḥama explains that gambling is an asmakhta, a conditional consent that does not effect acquisition, so the winner is a robber.
Rav Sheshet rejects that reasoning: gamblers consent knowingly, so the disqualification is because they are not engaged in the settling of the world.
Asks what practical difference lies between Rami bar Ḥama's and Rav Sheshet's explanations.
Raises a difficulty against Rami bar Ḥama from the mishna's Rabbi Yehuda clause, which supports Rav Sheshet's reason about occupations.
Presses the difficulty: if the Rabbis dispute Rabbi Yehuda, the problem remains, since Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says Rabbi Yehuda's statements in the Mishna are authoritative.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the phrasing when does this halakha apply signals only that the speaker is clarifying the Sages' earlier statement, not disputing it.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that the 'when' phrasing means explanation for all, while 'in what case' signals disagreement, yet Rabbi Yehuda's phrasing here is explanatory.
Replies that one should not set one man's statement against another's: Rami bar Ḥama holds the Sages disagree even with this phrasing, while Rabbi Yoḥanan holds they do not.
Asks whether they really do not disagree, citing a baraita that disqualifies a dice player whether or not he has another occupation, which fits Rami bar Ḥama.
The baraita reflects Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Tarfon, who treats a dice bet as an asmakhta, making the winner a thief; the mishna's Rabbis differ.
The mishna disqualifies a lender at interest, and Rava extends the disqualification to the borrower as well.
Asks why Rava extends the rule to the borrower, since the mishna teaches only the lender.
The mishna's wording refers to a loan that comes with interest, and so it disqualifies all parties who participate in the loan.
Recounts a case: two witnesses testified that bar Binittos lent at interest, and Rava disqualified him from witnessing and judging.
Asks how Rava could disqualify bar Binittos, since by Rava's own rule the witness who borrowed from him is wicked and not a valid witness.
Explains Rava's consistency: a person is his own relative and cannot make himself wicked, so only the testimony about bar Binittos is accepted.
Recounts a slaughterer who sold tereifa meat, was disqualified by Rav Naḥman, and later grew his nails and hair out of remorse, hoping to be restored.
Rava objects that the slaughterer may be feigning repentance in order to regain his position.
Rav Idi bar Avin's remedy: the suspect must return a valuable lost item or remove tereifa meat from his possession in a place where he is unknown.
The mishna lists those who fly pigeons among those disqualified from bearing witness.
Asks what the term those who fly pigeons means, and what its Aramaic equivalent is.
Babylonian Sages explain it as betting on pigeon races: if your pigeon arrives first, you receive a sum from me.
Rabbi Ḥama bar Oshaya explains the term as referring to an ara, one who trains pigeons to bring him the pigeons of others.
Asks why the one who reads the term as pigeon races does not also read it as referring to an ara.
Replies that an ara is not a robber, since the pigeons he takes dwell on others' property, and taking them is prohibited only as a matter of peace.
Asks the converse: why the one who reads it as an ara does not also read it as pigeon wagers.
Replies that a pigeon bettor is the same as a dice player, since both gamble on games of chance, and this type is already listed in the mishna.
Asks how the other Sage, who reads the term as pigeon wagering, would respond to this claim.
The mishna teaches both types of gambler, since a dice bettor depends on his own decision and a pigeon bettor depends on his bird's decision.

Both teachings are needed: if the mishna had mentioned only dice bets dependent on one's own decision, one might think the gambler is a thief only there, since he does not resolve to transfer the money.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A gambler who stakes on his pigeon may know he cannot guarantee the result and so resolves to pay; a dice gambler relies on pure chance, so both types must be taught.
Objects from a baraita: the dice player is not limited to pispasim stone dice, but includes those who play with nutshells or pomegranate shells.
The baraita states that repentance is accepted only once the gamblers break their dice and abandon the occupation entirely, even playing for nothing.
The baraita states that both lender and borrower at interest are disqualified, with repentance requiring tearing up the notes and lending to no one, even gentiles.
The baraita extends the pigeon-flying disqualification to training any domesticated animal, wild animal or bird, not only pigeons.
Repentance for those who train animals is accepted once they break their fixtures and stop even in the wilderness, where no one can be robbed.
Merchants of Sabbatical produce regain fitness once another Sabbatical year arrives and they cease dealing in its produce.
Rabbi Neḥemya adds that verbal repentance is not enough: the merchant must also declare the profit given to the poor.
Explains the objection: if the pigeon-flyer category covers animals in general, the parallel is a domesticated animal raced against another, and the ara case is unclear.
Answers that the baraita speaks of the wild ox, which can be lured, and it follows the view that the wild ox is a species of domesticated animal, as in Kilayim.
A baraita states that the Sages added robbers and forcers of transactions to the list of those disqualified from bearing witness.
Asks why the Sages needed to add robbers, since a robber is already disqualified by Torah law.
Replies that the addition covers one who steals an item found by a deaf-mute, imbecile or minor, who acquire by rabbinic law only.
Explains that the Sages initially thought such finds rare, or that taking them was only a matter of peace; once they saw it was actual robbery, they disqualified the thieves.
Similarly, forcers of transactions were excused at first because they paid and acted only occasionally, but once they snatched regularly the Sages decreed disqualification.
A baraita adds shepherds of others' fields, tax collectors who overcharge, and customs officials who collect illegally to the disqualified list.
Shepherds were initially excused as incidental trespass, but when they deliberately grazed others' fields, the Sages decreed their disqualification.
Tax collectors and customs officials were excused while they took the set amount, but once they took more the Sages disqualified them.
Rava holds that the disqualified shepherd includes both the herder of small livestock and the herder of large livestock.
Asks whether Rava really says this, given that Rava elsewhere distinguishes the two kinds of herders.
Rava's statement appears to disqualify small-livestock shepherds in Eretz Yisrael but not large-livestock herders, even there, which conflicts with the broader claim.
Resolves the conflict: that ruling concerns herders who graze on their own land, not those who herd on public land.
Offers a proof for Rava: the mishna's phrase three cattle herders trusted suggests cattle herders are generally disqualified, presumably from testifying.
Rejects the proof: the disqualification concerns sitting as a judge, and the mishna's wording about three herders fits that reading.
Asks why the mishna specifies three cattle herders if the rule concerns judging, since any three unlearned people would also be disqualified.
The mishna means that litigants may accept even herders who live in the fields and are not proficient in business ways.
Rav Yehuda holds that an ordinary shepherd is disqualified unless he is known not to graze in others' fields, while an ordinary tax collector is fit unless known to overcharge.
Recounts that Rabbi Zeira's father, a tax collector for thirteen years, warned the sages with Isaiah's hint to hide while the head collector passed.
The father warned the ordinary townspeople that the head collector would take from father and son in turn, so the taxes could be assessed in advance.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Recounts that Rabbi Zeira's father, a tax collector, reduced the town's levy and on his deathbed returned money he had taken, showing some collectors were God-fearing.
Rabbi Shimon says the collectors were initially called gatherers of Sabbatical produce and later called merchants of it.
