Asks what Rabbi Shimon is actually teaching in this statement.
Rav Yehuda explains: initially gatherers were fit and merchants disqualified, since gathering was a fitting act and selling was not.
Explains that once those paying the poor to gather grew numerous, gathering became a business, so both categories were disqualified.
The children of Raḥava object that the mishna should say merchants grew abundant, not tax collectors, if this explanation were right.
Offers a different explanation: the collectors' arnona tax forced Sabbatical sowing, so gatherers became fit while merchants stayed disqualified.
Recounts that Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Zarnokei and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak went to intercalate the year in Asya, joined by Reish Lakish, who wanted to watch.
Reish Lakish sees a priest plowing in the Sabbatical year; the Sages suggest a defense that he works for a gentile landowner as a hired hand.
Reish Lakish sees a priest pruning vines; the defense is that he needs the branches for an olive-press basket, and Reish Lakish plays on the word for basket.
Asks which incident came first, since a priest pruning vines should have offered the hired-hand defense, implying the order of the two incidents.
Asks what distinguishes a priest, and why Reish Lakish assumed this man was one.
Replies that priests are suspected of desecrating the Sabbatical year.
A baraita rules that a se'a of teruma fallen into a hundred se'a of Sabbatical produce is nullified, but a smaller mixture must be left to rot.
Asks why the mixture must rot, since the owner could sell it to a priest at teruma value, paying only for the teruma se'a.
Rav Ḥiyya cites Ulla: the prohibition on selling to priests shows priests are suspected of consuming Sabbatical produce after its removal time.
Recounts that the two Sages, annoyed by Reish Lakish, took the ladder away so he could not join them on the roof.
Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yoḥanan whether people suspected of desecrating the Sabbatical year may intercalate the year.
Reish Lakish answers his own question: as in the cattle herders' case, the Sages relied on their own calculations, so this may be similar.
Reish Lakish reverses: the cattle herders case differs, since the Sages afterwards counted the year themselves, whereas here a wicked conspiracy is not counted.
Rabbi Yoḥanan remarks that the problem Reish Lakish raises is a difficult one.
Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Shimon complain to Rabbi Yoḥanan that Reish Lakish called them cattle herders and he did not rebuke him.
Rabbi Yoḥanan dismisses the complaint: even if called shepherds, they are disqualified witnesses, and Reish Lakish is correct.
Asks the source of the halakha that a conspiracy of wicked people is not counted as part of a group.
Shebna, Hezekiah's minister, taught 130,000 students, more than Hezekiah's 110,000, offering the source of the principle about the wicked.
Recounts Shebna's note shot over the wall to Sennacherib announcing his surrender, supported by the psalm verse about the wicked bending the bow.
Hezekiah fears God may follow the majority, so that since most submitted, the faithful will be handed over as well.
Isaiah replies that this is a conspiracy of wicked people, which is not counted, so they are not considered the majority.
Recounts Shebna carving a tomb among the house of David's graves, and Isaiah's rebuke that God will wind and cast him away.
Rav holds that the wandering of a man is more severe than that of a woman, based on the verse's wording.
Cites the Isaiah verse about winding round and round as the textual basis for the next interpretation.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina says Shebna contracted leprosy, drawing on the shared root in the leprosy laws of Leviticus.
Cites the continuing Isaiah verses about being rolled like a ball into a wide land as the basis for the next baraita.
A baraita holds that Shebna sought shame for his master's house, so his glory turned to shame, and Gabriel blocked his camp at the gate.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Recounts the Assyrians' mockery of Shebna after his camp abandons him, and their brutal punishment of him dragged on thorns.
Rabbi Elazar says Shebna was a hedonist, one who enjoyed luxury.
Supports Rabbi Elazar by comparing the word for steward in Isaiah with the word for companion used of Abishag in Kings.
Brings the next verse from Psalms, asking what the Righteous One has done when the foundations are destroyed, as a basis for interpretation.
Rav Yehuda, Rav Eina and Ulla each read the verse differently: Hezekiah's camp, the Temple, or the wicked man's intentions.
Asks how the reading about Sennacherib's intentions fits, since the word for foundations also means intentions.
Shows the Temple reading also fits, citing the mishna about the foundation stone called the Shetiyya stone.
Asks where righteous people are ever called foundations, on the reading that the verse refers to Hezekiah.
Answers with I Samuel 2:8, where the world is set on the Lord's pillars, and Isaiah's word tushiyya, identifying the righteous as the foundations.
Rabbi Ḥanan explains the name tushiyya for the Torah: it weakens a person's strength, was given in secret against the Satan, and rests on ungrounded matters.
Ulla holds that concern is effective even against Torah study, citing Job's verse that frustrates the crafty so their hands accomplish nothing.
Rabba holds that concern is ineffective for those who study Torah for its own sake, reading Proverbs to mean the Lord's counsel stands forever.
The mishna's view that these people are disqualified only without another occupation is followed, as Rabbi Abbahu reports Rabbi Elazar's ruling.
Rabbi Elazar holds that all these disqualifications require a proclamation in court before they take effect.
Rav Aḥa and Ravina dispute whether a shepherd requires a proclamation of disqualification.
Asks how Rav Yehuda's statement that an ordinary shepherd is disqualified works on the view that a proclamation is required.
Explains that the court proclaims the disqualification of a known regular shepherd, without proving he grazed on others' land.
Recounts that Rav Pappa bar Shmuel wanted to validate a gift deed signed by two robbers, since no proclamation had been made about them.
Rava objects: a proclamation is needed only for a rabbinically defined robber, while a Torah-defined robber is disqualified automatically.
Gives a mnemonic for the categories of disqualification discussed: something, forbidden relations, and thieves.
Rav Naḥman rules that those who eat the forbidden other thing are disqualified as witnesses, meaning those who take charity from gentiles.
Clarifies that taking gentile charity disqualifies only when done publicly and only if one could sustain himself privately, not when it is his livelihood.
Rav Naḥman holds that one suspected of forbidden relations due to rumor is fit to testify.
Rav Sheshet challenges him: a rumored offender receives forty lashes, so how can he be fit to testify?
Rava reconciles: Rav Naḥman concedes that one suspected of adultery is disqualified from testimony about a married woman's status.
Ravina, or Rav Pappa, limits the disqualification to testimony that removes a woman's married status, not testimony that establishes it.
Asks why a suspect should be assumed to lie to make a woman married, and answers that forbidden relations are not preferable to him.
Rav Naḥman rules that a thief during the harvest months is not called a thief and so is not disqualified.
Explains Rav Naḥman's ruling as limited to a tenant farmer taking a small amount of finished produce, where he may assume it is compensation.
Recounts that Rav Zeviḍ disqualified two tenant farmers who stole a kav of barley and a cluster of dates, since those amounts are not small.
Recounts gravediggers who buried a person on the festival; Rav Pappa disqualified them after excommunication, while Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua deemed them fit.
Rav Pappa objects to Rav Huna: they are wicked people, since they violated a Torah prohibition.
Rav Huna replies that they believed they were performing a mitzva by burying the dead.
Rav Pappa presses that he had already excommunicated them for this, yet they kept burying on the festival.
Rav Huna replies that they reasoned excommunication was not for wrongdoing, since the mitzva of burying the dead atones for desecrating the festival.
Opens the discussion of the conspiring witness, whose testimony about place and time is refuted by two other witnesses.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye holds that a conspiring witness is disqualified retroactively, nullifying any testimony he gave from the time he first testified.
Rava holds that the disqualification applies only from the point he is established as a conspiring witness, not retroactively.
Explains Abaye's reason: from his testimony he is a wicked man, and the verse forbids putting a wicked man in the position of witness.
Explains Rava's reason: conspiring-witness disqualification is a novelty against logic, so it applies only from its novelty onward.
Offers another explanation of Rava: retroactive disqualification would nullify transactions validated by the witnesses, harming purchasers.
Asks what practical difference lies between the two explanations of Rava's view.
Reports that Rav Pappi ruled in accordance with Rava, while Mar bar Rav Ashi says the halakha follows Abaye.
States that the halakha follows Rava except in six cases, given by a mnemonic, where it follows Abaye.
Everyone agrees that one who eats non-kosher meat out of appetite is disqualified, as he is suspected of also testifying falsely for gain.
For one who eats non-kosher meat to show insolence, Abaye disqualifies him while Rava holds he is fit.
Explains the positions: Abaye relies on the general prohibition against a wicked witness, while Rava requires a monetary transgression, as the word for unjust suggests.
Objects to Rava from a baraita listing robbers and oath-breakers as disqualified, which seems to include non-monetary oath violators.
Replies that both kinds of oath in the baraita concern monetary matters, and the plural refers to oaths in general.
Objects to Abaye from a baraita that mentions only monetary transgressors, such as robbers and usurers, and so refutes his view.
Suggests the dispute parallels a tannaitic one: Rabbi Meir disqualifies a conspiring witness for all of Torah, while Rabbi Yosei distinguishes capital and monetary cases.
Proposes that Abaye follows Rabbi Meir and Rava follows Rabbi Yosei, explaining each Sage's rule on lenient and stringent inferences.
Rejects the proposal: all agree on Rabbi Yosei's view, so Abaye and Rava must disagree about what Rabbi Meir holds.
Abaye derives from Rabbi Meir that insolent meat-eaters are disqualified, while Rava limits Rabbi Meir's rule to a monetary conspiring witness, who is bad to people as well.
Concludes that the halakha follows Abaye.
Asks how the halakha can follow Abaye when his opinion seems to have been refuted.
Replies that the refuting baraita reflects Rabbi Yosei's view, which Abaye does not accept.
Asks why Abaye's view is not simply the view of Rabbi Yosei, since the halakha follows him in disputes with Rabbi Meir.
Replies that a mishna without attribution teaches Rabbi Meir's view, and an unattributed mishna sets the halakha.
Asks where the tanna taught such an unattributed mishna.
Answers with a case: the Exilarch ordered an investigation of a killing, and witnesses who came to refute the first pair were themselves tested, showing the principle in action.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Opening fragment glossing an object in the preceding story: the handle of a spear.
Rav Abba bar Ya'akov challenges bar Ḥama: what does he hold, since Rabbi Yosei would make the witness fit for capital cases?
Rav Pappi replies that the principle applies only where no unattributed mishna follows Rabbi Meir, and here one does.
Asks which mishna shows an unattributed teaching following Rabbi Meir, noting the cited Nidda mishna is inconclusive and may reflect Rabbi Yosei.
Suggests the mishna may concern judges disqualified by lineage, such as converts and mamzerim, rather than by sin.
Argues that the latter clause of the mishna must refer to lineage disqualification, since a conspiring witness is disqualified in every case, so the first clause does too.
Brings a mishna from Rosh HaShana listing disqualified witnesses, including Sabbatical traders, and the principle that women's testimony is generally not accepted.
Asks whose view that mishna records, since Rabbi Yosei would admit a woman's testimony in capital cases from the monetary-wicked, which seems to conflict.
Concludes the mishna follows Rabbi Meir, who disqualifies monetary transgressors even in capital matters, so the halakha follows him.
Recounts that after this ruling one of the witnesses against bar Ḥama was disqualified and bar Ḥama acquitted, and he honored Rabbi Pappi.
Mishna listing the relatives disqualified from testifying for or against one another, including in-laws and stepsons.
Rabbi Yosei says that version reflects Rabbi Akiva, and the original mishna disqualifies only paternal relatives fit to inherit, judged at the time of trial.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that a former relative who became unrelated remains disqualified if his former wife's children still link them, and a litigant's son-in-law counts.
One who loves or hates a litigant is disqualified: a groomsman as a lover, and one who refused to speak to the litigant for three days as a hater.
The Rabbis reply that Israel is not suspected of false testimony out of love or hatred.
Asks from where the rule that relatives are disqualified is derived.
Derives the rule from a baraita on Deuteronomy 24:16, reading each part of the verse as limiting testimony between fathers and children.
Explains the verse's clauses: fathers are not put to death by their children's testimony, and children not by their fathers' testimony.
Asks how this fits Exodus 34:7, which says God visits the iniquity of fathers upon children.
Replies that the Exodus verse refers to children who adopt their ancestors' deeds as their own.
Cites a baraita on Leviticus 26:39 to show that punishment for fathers' sins applies only when the children adopt those deeds.
Asks whether Leviticus 26:37, that they shall stumble one upon another, shows that all Jews are guarantors for one another.
Replies that verse refers to cases where others could have protested the sin and did not, so they are punished for not protesting.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Derives disqualification of fathers and sons, and of brothers' relatives, from the plural wording of the verse.
Asks where this derivation comes from.
If the verse would otherwise need no plural, the plural shows relatives of brothers are also disqualified.
Asks the source for disqualifying the children of brothers from testifying together about others.
Rami bar Hama: this is logical reasoning, since conspiring witnesses are only punished together.
Rava objects that brothers' testimony in a three-year possession case would conflict with that reasoning.
Reply: the conspiracy here comes from other witnesses, not from the relative, so the reasoning still stands.
Derives the disqualification from superfluous plural wording in the verse about children and fathers.
Asks where the disqualification of maternal relatives is derived from.
The repeated word fathers is superfluous for paternal relatives, so it teaches the maternal case.
Asks the source for disqualifying a witness who testifies in favor of a relative.
The repeated phrase shall not be put to death teaches testimony for relatives is also excluded.
Asks the source for applying relative disqualification to monetary cases, not only capital ones.
The verse one manner of law makes monetary and capital law follow the same rules.
Rav's position: relatives of my paternal uncle and of my in-laws are mutually disqualified as witnesses.
Asks why a third-generation witness about a first-generation relative is not covered by the mishna.
The mishna's son-in-law refers to the son-in-law of one's son, which covers a third-generation witness.
Asks why the mishna does not simply say son of his son.
Mentioning the son-in-law teaches in passing that a husband is like his wife in this context.
Notes a baraita counting relatives that contradicts reading the mishna as referring to the grandson.
The mishna means the actual son-in-law, who is treated as a more distant relative.
If so, a witness about his father's son-in-law is like a third-generation witness about a second-generation relative, which Rav permits.
Rav rules instead according to Rabbi Elazar's baraita, which disqualifies the uncle's grandson as well.
Asks how Rav squares Rabbi Elazar's view with his own permitting third-generation testimony about second-generation relatives.
Rav follows Rabbi Elazar on one point and disagrees with him on another.
Rav's reason is that the verse's phrase for the children includes the grandchildren of one's brother.
Rabbi Elazar derives his view from the verse's wording for the children, extending the disqualification to them.
Rav Naḥman: the brother, son and sister's son of my mother-in-law cannot testify for me, as the tanna also taught.
Rav Ashi reports a question he heard in Ulla's study hall about relatives of one's father-in-law.
Ulla points out that the mishna's list answers that question from the younger generation's perspective.
Narrative aside: Rav arrived at a certain place to buy something.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether a man may testify about the wife of his stepson.
In Sura the version of Rav's answer: a husband is like his wife, so the son's wife is like a daughter-in-law.
In Pumbedita the other version: a wife is like her husband, so the stepson's wife is disqualified.
Rav Huna citing Rav Naḥman derives from the verse about the uncle's wife that a wife is like her husband.
The mishna lists the mother's husband's son, which seems identical to his brother, already disqualified.
Rabbi Yirmeya: the mention is needed only for a half brother of a half brother, who is not biologically related.
Rav Ḥisda deems the testimony of a half brother of a half brother fit.
The Sages object that Rabbi Yirmeya's ruling disqualifies this half brother, asking if Rav Ḥisda heard it.
Rav Ḥisda replies that he did not hear it, meaning he does not hold that opinion.
If so, the earlier difficulty returns: the mother's husband's son is the same as his brother.
The mishna covers both a paternal half brother and a maternal half brother.
Rav Ḥisda: the fathers of a groom and a bride may testify about each other, since they are like a lid on a barrel.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana: a man may testify about his betrothed wife, since they are related only after marriage.
Ravina limits this to testimony that removes money from her, not testimony that awards her money.
Rejects Ravina's limit: testimony for or against her money is equally unreliable, so no distinction applies.
Ulla's ruling shows a betrothed woman is not a relative of her husband in matters of mourning, impurity and inheritance.
The ritual-impurity halakha does not prove testimony, since kinship there is based on a different criterion than affinity.
Baraita: a stepson alone is disqualified; Rabbi Yosei says brother-in-law, and another baraita says Rabbi Yehuda says stepson.
Asks which opinion the mishna follows, since neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosei fits its listing.
Rather, the baraita means the stepson alone is disqualified and the brother-in-law's relatives are too, matching Rabbi Yehuda.
Asks which opinion the baraita of Rabbi Ḥiyya follows, as it fits neither Rabbi Yosei nor Rabbi Yehuda.
The earlier reading is rejected: the baraita follows Rabbi Yosei, so the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Yehuda says Shmuel ruled that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Yosef upholds a deed of gift signed by brothers-in-law, reading Shmuel's ruling as following Rabbi Yosei in the mishna.
Abaye objects: Shmuel may have meant Rabbi Yosei in the baraita, who disqualifies the brother-in-law.
Rav Yosef replies that Shmuel's example of himself and Pineḥas shows only brothers-in-law are disqualified.
Abaye counters that Shmuel's example may have meant disqualification only because Pineḥas was his brother-in-law.
Rav Yosef tells the holder to acquire the gift through the witnesses who saw the delivery, following Rabbi Elazar.
Abaye objects: Rabbi Abba says Rabbi Elazar concedes a forged-in-itself document is invalid.
Rav Yosef dismisses the objection, saying the rabbis will not let him give the gift.
The mishna's Rabbi Yehuda rule on a witness married to a litigant's daughter; Rav and Rav Naḥman rule opposite views.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana cites a baraita of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: a judge from those days means one who was formerly related.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana says Rabbi Yoḥanan rules as Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, that a formerly related judge is fit.
Narrative aside about the sons of the father-in-law of Mar Ukva.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mar Ukva's relatives became unrelated to him, and he declares himself disqualified from judging their case.
The litigants ask which opinion Mar Ukva follows, since they would bring a ruling against Rabbi Yehuda.
Mar Ukva replies that they are not relatives, but he will not judge them because they would not obey the verdict.
The mishna lists the litigant's groomsman, according to Rabbi Yehuda, as disqualified because of love.
Asks how long the groomsman remains disqualified.
Rav, via Rabbi Yirmeya, says seven days of feasting; the Rabbis say from the first day after the wedding.
The mishna defines one who hates as someone who did not speak with the litigant for three days.
A baraita derives the rule from the verse about not being an enemy or seeking harm.
Asks where the disqualification of one who loves is derived from.
The verse can be read to include one who loves, as not being an enemy or loving him.
Asks whether one who loves is written in the verse, and proposes a logical extension instead.
Asks what the Rabbis, who disagree with Rabbi Yehuda, derive from the verse.
One part of the verse teaches that a judge who loves or hates a litigant is disqualified.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda derives that two scholars who hate each other cannot judge together.
Mishna: judges examine witnesses separately, intimidating them, and begin with the eldest witness.
Mishna: the witness must state that the defendant admitted the debt in the presence of witnesses.
Mishna: the second witness is examined in the same way, and if they agree the judges deliberate.
Mishna: with split judges, the majority rules, and an abstaining judge is treated as not on the court.
Mishna: after deciding, the greatest judge announces the verdict to the litigants.
A judge may not later reveal the division of opinions; verses on talebearing are cited as support.
Asks what the judges should say to intimidate the witnesses.
Rav Yehuda: the verse about clouds without rain shows a liar's deeds lack blessing.
Rava objects that false witnesses would not fear this, since a folk saying says famine missed the craftsman.
Rava instead cites the verse comparing a false witness to a hammer and sword, predicting premature death.
Rav Ashi objects that false witnesses would dismiss this, since everyone dies at his predestined time.
Natan bar Mar Zutra's suggestion: even those who hire false witnesses despise them, as Jezebel called them base fellows.
Mishna: the witness's report of an admission is disregarded unless he says the defendant admitted before witnesses.
Supports Rav Yehuda, who holds that a debtor must tell the witnesses to the loan that they are his witnesses.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: if the debtor later says he was teasing, he is exempt; this is also stated in a baraita.
A baraita states the same ruling about a debtor who says he was only teasing when asked to pay.
Even if witnesses were hidden behind a fence, the debtor who later says he was teasing is exempt.
Judges do not advance a claim on behalf of an inciter to idolatry.
Asks where the inciter was mentioned, since the baraita does not discuss him.
The baraita is incomplete: judges advance claims for a defendant in capital cases, but not for an inciter.
Asks what distinguishes an inciter, so that the court does not seek to exonerate him.
Rabbi Ḥama bar Ḥanina: the verse about not sparing or concealing an inciter removes the duty to exonerate.
The primordial snake that tempted Eve did not advance its own claims, so God did not advance them either.
Asks what the snake could have argued in its defense.
The snake could have said that the student's words should not outweigh the teacher's, since God commanded Adam and Eve.
Ḥizkiyya: Eve added to God's prohibition by saying not to touch the tree, showing that adding leads to subtraction.
Rav Mesharshiyya: the letter alef in amatayim shows that adding a letter reduces the measure.
Rav Ashi: the letter ayin in ashtei esrei reduces twelve to eleven, another example of addition reducing.
Abaye: the Sages taught that a debtor who denies a hidden-witness admission is exempt only if he says he was teasing.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Since witnesses heard the admission, the defendant is presumed a liar and cannot take an oath of exemption.
Rava's view, via Rav Pappa: a casual admission may be forgotten, so the denial is not an outright lie.
A case where the claimant hid witnesses under a bed; Rav Kahana rules the refusal means no liability.
A parallel case with witnesses hidden in a grave; Rabbi Shimon likewise rules the refusal means no liability.
Ravina infers from the earlier cases that silence, not refusal, would have made the admission binding.
A man nicknamed a kav of debts admitted owing many people, then claimed his admission was a joke before Rav Naḥman.
Rav Naḥman: people make false statements to avoid appearing wealthy, so an unspecific admission does not bind.
A miser nicknamed a mouse on dinars admitted debts on his deathbed, and the claimants sued his heirs.
Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei: the false-statement presumption applies in life, not to a deathbed admission.
Rabbi Ḥiyya's ruling: heirs cannot be sued for the rest, and the earlier verdict stands since the elder ruled.
Witnesses to an admission may write a document only if they performed an act of acquisition with the debtor.
Rav Ami and Rav Asi dispute whether three witnesses who are a court may write a record without acquisition.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: write the record only if the debtor gathered the witnesses; otherwise do not.
Rava: even if the debtor gathered them, write only if he explicitly asked them to serve as judges.
Mar bar Rav Ashi: write only if the full court procedure of a summons and a set place was carried out.
Movables with acquisition may be written; for land without acquisition, Ameimar forbids and Mar Zutra permits, and the halakha permits.
Rav Dimi asks Ravina whether movables available for collection are treated like land for writing a record.
Ravina says they are like land, while Rav Ashi says lack of physical collection makes them unlike land.
A document lacking the statement that the debtor asked for it: Abaye and Rava apply Reish Lakish's principle.
Reish Lakish: witnesses sign only when the transaction was properly done, so the missing detail does not invalidate it.
Rav Pappi, or Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, objects that the Sages would not know what court scribes know.
The Gemara tests this: the scribes of Abaye and Rava both knew the relevant halakhot, since writing is their profession.
Incident: a document of admission recorded that it reflected proceedings before witnesses, to be detailed next.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A court document lacks a note that one judge had left, so it may show only two judges sitting.
Ravina proposes applying Reish Lakish's principle that witnesses sign only when the action was done properly.
Rav Natan bar Ami objects: such cases raise concern for an erroneous court that thinks two judges form a court.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: a document saying the court convened needs no note, since a court is three judges.
Asks whether the document may reflect an impudent court of two judges, as Shmuel's view allows.
The document named the court of Rav Ashi, which presumably followed the rabbinic three-judge rule.
Asks whether Rav Ashi's court held Shmuel's view and so may have been an impudent court.
The document quotes Rav Ashi speaking to the court, so he would not have joined an impudent court.
A baraita: a father's hidden money is accepted as second tithe only if the witness could not have taken it for himself.
Principle: a witness's statement stands when it was in his power to take the money, and otherwise has no weight.
If the children saw the father's statement made as instruction to them, it stands; if it was a ruse, it does not.
A dream-revealed hidden amount of second tithe was accepted for spending, since dreams do not decide halakha.
Asks how the judges write the verdict when two exempt and one liable, given the dispute among judges.
Positions: Rabbi Yoḥanan omits the dispute; Reish Lakish names the judges; Rabbi Eliezer uses a general wording.
Asks what practical difference lies between these views.
The difference is whether the minority judge pays his share of restitution if the verdict was erroneous.
Asks why the minority judge would pay under the view that the verdict is written as exempt.
The difference is whether the majority judges pay the minority judge's share, depending on how the verdict is written.
Asks why the judges would pay his share, since without him there would be no verdict at all.
The dispute is only about wording, due to the prohibition of gossip, as Rabbi Yoḥanan derives from Leviticus.
Reish Lakish: naming the judges avoids the appearance of falsehood, since not all judges found him exempt.
Rabbi Elazar accepts both views, so the verdict is written generally, avoiding both falsehood and gossip.
Mishna: after deciding, the judges bring in the parties and the witnesses.
Asks whom the mishna brings in, since the litigants never left the room; so it must mean the witnesses.
The mishna does not follow Rabbi Natan; a baraita gives Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa's view on combining witnesses.
The baraita continues: Rabbi Natan allows witnesses to testify on different days, while the mishna requires them together.
Rabbi Neḥemya's custom of Jerusalem: judges hear the parties and witnesses, then deliberate outside, then call the parties back.
Asks whether a baraita says the witnesses are brought in after the decision, and answers it is not Rabbi Natan's view.
Restates that witnesses combine only if they saw together, per the first tanna versus Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa.
Asks what the disagreement is based on, and the Gemara offers an answer of logic or verse.
Logic: the first tanna needs joint sight, since each one-witness claim is insufficient, while Rabbi Yehoshua sees a whole claim.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa's view is based on the verse about a witness who has seen or known.
A baraita explains that one witness is singular in wording, so the verse teaches two witnesses unless stated otherwise.
Principle: wherever Torah says witness, it means two witnesses unless the verse specifies one.
The first tanna uses the singular form to show witnesses combine only if they saw together, per the verse on witness.
The baraita restated: Rabbi Natan allows testimony on separate days, combined by the judges.
Asks what the disagreement between these tannaim is based on.
It may be based on logic or on a verse, as the Gemara offers both options.
Logic: one witness comes to make the defendant swear, not to pay, so the judges combine the two testimonies.
Rabbi Natan objects: witnesses who testify one after the other are not testifying with one mouth.
If the disagreement is over a verse, it rests on the verse about bearing iniquity if one does not testify.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Both sides agree witnesses must see together; they dispute whether their court testimony must also be joint.
Narrative: Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim tried to advance Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina before Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asks who knows the halakha on Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa, and Rabbi Yosei is ordained.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asks Rabbi Yosei to tell him what he heard.
Rabbi Yosei reports that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa concedes to Rabbi Natan that joint testimony in court is unnecessary.
Rabbi Yoḥanan is disappointed: if the concession is so, the ordination was pointless; yet it stands.
Rabbi Zeira: once a great man is ordained, the ordination stands even if made in error.
Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin: the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa for both land and movables.
Ulla: the halakha follows him only for land, not for movables, where the items may differ.
Abaye objects to Ulla: the Rabbis concede to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa on land, implying they dispute on movables.
Rav Idi bar Avin's baraita lists cases such as firstborn blemishes and land, where the Rabbis concede to him.
The Gemara rejects Abaye: Ulla and Rav Idi simply differ on whether the Rabbis dispute land testimony.
Asks what the two pubic hairs case means, since two witnesses each seeing one hair would be invalid.
The case must be one witness seeing two hairs at the back and another two at the front, so their sightings need not match.
Rav Yosef: in Ulla's name, the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua for both land and movables; Meḥoza sages differ.
Rav's consistent principle: admission following admission, or admission following loan, testimonies combine.
Rav continues: loan following loan, and loan following admission, testimonies do not combine.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak challenges Rav Huna: why would a loan following loan not combine but an admission would?
Rav Huna: the admission refers to a loan the respondent told the second witness was also acknowledged to the first.
Rav Naḥman: the first witness still does not know it is the same loan, so the testimonies cannot combine.
Rav Huna: the respondent later told the first witness of the same acknowledgment, so both know it is the same loan.
Rav Huna says this is no real answer, since Rava rejected it as making admission following admission the same as admission following loan.
Rav Naḥman remarks wryly that the Meḥoza sages build and then undo their own good explanations.
Sages of Neharde'a: all four combinations combine, following Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa's view on one hundred dinars.
Rav Yehuda: contradictory witnesses are valid in monetary cases, though not in capital cases.
Rava upholds Rav Yehuda: a purse color is a minor detail, but a coin's color is a core contradiction.
Objection: Rav Ḥisda says a contradiction about a sword versus an ariran is invalid, but garment color is acceptable in capital cases.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Neither Rav Ḥisda nor Rav Yehuda is bound by the other's view on contradictions in secondary details.
The Sages of Neharde'a: even contradictory witnesses about a black coin and a white coin are combined.
Asks whether this follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa, who combines only non-contradicting testimony.
A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai agree a smaller sum is subsumed within a larger one.
Explains the dispute: in one set's contradiction, Beit Shammai disqualify while Beit Hillel combine; this is the Neharde'a source.
Incident: wine versus oil testimony came before Rabbi Ami, who awarded the lesser amount both witnesses agreed on.
Asks whether this ruling follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who applies subsumption only to amounts, not different items.
No direct contradiction here: the ruling only concerns monetary value, comparable to one hundred versus two hundred dinars.
Rabbi Ḥanina: a case of upper versus lower floor came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who combined the testimonies.
A baraita derives from the verses on talebearing that a judge must not reveal his colleagues' split decision.
Anecdote: a student who revealed a study-hall statement twenty-two years later was removed by Rav Ami as a revealer of secrets.
Mishna: a litigant may overturn a verdict with new proof found within thirty days, but not after.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: he may still overturn the verdict, since the litigant could not have found proof sooner.
Mishna: a proof or witnesses found after a claim of having none are worth nothing, as apparently false.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: one who did not know he had proof or witnesses may still overturn the verdict.
Mishna: proof produced only after a verdict looms, from a pouch or hidden witnesses, is worth nothing even for Rabban Shimon.
Rabba bar Rav Huna: the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and not the Rabbis.
Asks whether the second statement is obvious, since the first already implies the Rabbis' view is rejected.
Rabba bar Rav Huna teaches that if a court ruled like the Rabbis after the fact, the case is sent back to court.
Mishna's parallel case: Rabban Shimon accepts witnesses found after a claim of none; Rabba bar Rav Huna cites Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Asks whether the second statement is obvious, since the first already implies Rabban Shimon's view is rejected.
The statement teaches that only in this halakha is Rabban Shimon rejected, while elsewhere in the Mishna his view stands.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's exceptions to Rabban Shimon's rulings: guarantor liability, the Tzaidan incident, and the final evidence dispute.
A child brought before Rav Naḥman said he had no witnesses or proof, and was held liable in the claim.
Rav Naḥman: a child does not know his father's monetary matters, so his denial is ignorance, not artifice, and witnesses are accepted.
A woman holding a promissory note said it was repaid; Rav Naḥman accepted her claim and barred collection.
Rava asks whether the ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who says letters are acquired by transferring the document.
Rav Naḥman: the reason is different; she could have burned the note, so her claim is presumably true.
Another version: Rav Naḥman did not accept her testimony, and Rava objects that she could have burned the note.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava's objection continues: she could have burned the note, so why not accept her testimony?
Rav Naḥman: a note ratified in court cannot be nullified by testimony that she could have burned it, without evidence.
Rava objects from a baraita: a receipt from a trustee is valid even without signing witnesses, so his testimony is credible.
The Gemara concludes that Rava's refutation of Rav Naḥman's view is conclusive.
Rav Dimi cites Rabbi Yoḥanan: one may keep bringing proof until his claims are stopped up.
Asks how this is consistent: stopped claims follow the Rabbis, but the explicit call for witnesses follows Rabban Shimon.
Suggests the whole statement follows Rabban Shimon, but this clashes with Rabbi Yoḥanan's exceptions in the Mishna.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's version: witnesses from overseas or hidden documents may still be brought, without artifice.
Rav Dimi: one who tenaciously attacks in judgment must go to the Assembly's court when the other demands it.
Rabbi Elazar objects: this would force a claimant to travel far for a small debt, so one is judged in his own city.
Rav Safra cites Rabbi Yoḥanan: the litigant is judged locally, and local courts may write to a higher court for guidance.
A litigant may demand that the court write its reasons for a judgment, and the judges must do so.
A childless widow must go to her brother-in-law for ḥalitza, and the yavam does not come to her.
Asks how far the widow must travel, and Rabbi Ami says even from Tiberias to Tzippori.
Rav Kahana cites the verse about the elders of his city to show that ḥalitza is performed in his city.
Ameimar: if one litigant wants the Assembly's court, the other must go there.
Rav Ashi objects: Rabbi Elazar says the debtor is judged in his own city.
Ameimar: that applies when the borrower asks for the Assembly; if the lender asks, the request is accepted, as the borrower is a servant.
Sages' letter to Mar Ukva asking him to judge Ukvan's complaint against Yirmeya, or send him to Tiberias.
Asks how the letter can say both judge him yourselves and induce him to come to Tiberias.
The letter means: judge him locally, and if he refuses, send him to Tiberias.
Rav Ashi: the case concerns fines, which Babylonian courts do not adjudicate, so the wording only honors Mar Ukva.
Closing formula marking the end of the chapter.

ranges.en: Monetary and capital cases are alike in requiring inquiry and interrogation of witnesses.
Leviticus 24:22 is cited to show one uniform legal procedure for both kinds of case.
What distinguishes monetary cases from capital cases?
Monetary courts have three judges and may open for acquittal or conviction; capital courts have twenty-three and open only for acquittal.
Monetary rulings may be issued by a one-vote majority for either acquittal or conviction.
Capital rulings need a one-vote majority to acquit but a two-vote majority to convict.
Monetary cases may be reopened for either side, while capital cases may be reopened only for acquittal.
In monetary cases anyone present may argue either side; in capital cases only judges may argue for conviction.
Monetary arguers may switch sides freely, but in capital cases a pro-acquittal arguer may not later argue for conviction.
Monetary cases may conclude at night, but capital cases must be concluded during daytime.
Capital cases can end the same day only for acquittal; conviction waits a day, so they are not held on Shabbat or Festival eves.
Opinions begin with the greatest judge in monetary and purity cases, but from the side in capital cases.
All may judge monetary cases, but capital cases are restricted to priests, Levites and suitably lineaged Israelites.
Does monetary law really require inquiry and interrogation of witnesses?
A baraita about a promissory note dated Nisan of the Sabbatical Year is raised as a contradiction, with its rationale that the date may have been postdated.
If inquiry were required, the rationale about postdating would make no sense, since witnesses would simply be questioned on the signing date.
By the Gemara's own reasoning, a mishna elsewhere should pose a difficulty as well.
The mishna in Shevi'it states that antedated notes are invalid while postdated notes are valid.
If inquiry were required, postdated notes would be unacceptable, so why are they valid?
The baraita offers a stronger contradiction because even Nisan notes are postdated where debts rarely arise, yet they are upheld.
The contradiction nevertheless stands as difficult.
A mnemonic is given for the sages who offer answers.
Rabbi Hanina holds that by Torah law monetary and capital cases both require inquiry and interrogation.
Leviticus 24:22 is cited: one manner of law applies to both kinds of case.
What is the reason the sages said monetary cases need no inquiry?
It is a rabbinic ordinance so that lenders are not deterred, since rigorous examination could produce contradictory testimony.
If so, the Gemara continues to press the matter further.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If judges erred they need not pay, since that would lock the door before potential borrowers.
Rava limits the mishna's inquiry rule to fine cases, while the other sources concern admissions and loans.
Rav Pappa says both sources concern admissions and loans; the mishna addresses only possibly fraudulent trials.
Reish Lakish's approach is cited as the basis for the distinction.
Reish Lakish notes a contradiction between two verses on judging justly.
Leviticus 19:15 and Deuteronomy 16:20 are cited for the apparent contradiction.
How can the two verses be reconciled?
One verse applies to a possibly fraudulent trial and the other to a trial that is not fraudulent.
Rav Ashi holds the mishna follows the answers already given, with the verses concerning judgment and compromise.
A baraita explains the doubled justice verse as one term for judgment and one for compromise.
A baraita illustrates with two boats that cannot pass together on a river.
The baraita continues with two camels meeting on the narrow ascent of Beit Horon.
How does one decide which party goes first?
The laden boat or the boat nearer its destination goes first, and a fee compensates the one that waits.
A baraita cites the doubled justice verse as the basis for following the court.
One should follow the best court of the generation, illustrated by examples of famous sages and coded signals of mitzvah observance.
The doubled justice verse is cited again as the basis for following the Sages.
One should follow the Sages to whichever academy they are found in, listing examples of places and sages.
The mishna's rule that monetary cases open with an acquittal or a conviction claim is restated.
How does the court actually phrase the opening of the deliberations?
Rav Yehuda says the court tells the witnesses: who says it happened as you said, perhaps you erred?
Ulla objects that such a challenge silences the witnesses and so they will not testify.
Rav Yehuda cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Eliezer has witnesses moved to confuse them into retracting.
The comparison fails: there the witnesses are unsettled by themselves, whereas here the court acts directly.
Ulla proposes that the accused be asked whether he has witnesses to show the testifying witnesses are conspiring.
Rabba objects that opening with the accused's defense benefits one party at the other's expense, making it their liability.
A mishna states conspiring witnesses are not executed until the verdict is issued, supporting the objection.
Rabba restates that if the accused stays silent and conspiring witnesses surface later, the liability falls on the first witnesses.
Rabba instead says the accused should be asked whether he has witnesses to refute the testimony.
Rav Kahana says the witnesses are told that based on their statements the defendant is acquitted.
Abaye and Rava say the accused is told that if he did not kill, he should not fear the proceedings.
Rav Ashi says the court announces that anyone knowing a reason to acquit should come and teach it.
A baraita is cited as agreeing with Abaye and Rava.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi teaches the sota ritual formula.
The sota ritual verse in Numbers 5:19 is quoted, stating the innocent scenario first.
