ranges.en: A baraita derives that capital cases open by seeking acquittal, so the accused knows he has nothing to fear.
The mishna states that monetary cases may be reopened for new evidence.
A mishna in Bekhorot holds that an erring judge's decision stands and he pays from his own funds, contradicting the reopening rule.
Rav Yosef says the two mishnayot differ: reopening concerns an expert judge, while the Bekhorot ruling concerns a non-expert.
The Gemara objects that the Bekhorot mishna exempts an expert judge, so the expert case is not reopened either.
Rav Naḥman says reopening applies when a greater court exists to retry the case, and not otherwise.
Rav Sheshet says reopening applies to an error on a mishnaic matter, not to an error in deliberation.
Rav Asi's ruling is cited that a judge erring on a mishnaic matter has the decision revoked, while deliberation errors stand.
Ravina asks whether the category of mishnaic error includes later tanna'im and amora'im, and even the speakers themselves.
Rav Ashi replies that the category includes them all, since the speakers are merely reed-cutters in the pond.
What counts as an error in deliberation?
Rav Pappa says it is disagreement between two tanna'im or two amora'im, where the judge followed the minority view.
Rav Hamnuna raises an objection against Rav Sheshet from a case of a cow.
The mishna about Menachem's household cow is cited, in which Rabbi Tarfon ruled it a tereifah and Yavne's sages permitted it.
Rabbi Tarfon is told his donkey is gone, and Rabbi Akiva rules he is exempt as an expert accepted by the public.
Rav Hamnuna asks why Rabbi Akiva did not say Tarfon erred on a mishnaic matter and so must revoke the decision.
Rabbi Akiva gives two reasons: Tarfon erred on a mishnaic matter, and in any case an expert for the public is exempt.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzchak asks Rava what the objection was, since the cow was already fed to the dogs.
Rava explains that if the decision stands, Tarfon was reasonably worried, but if revoked, Akiva could say he did nothing.
Rav Ḥisda resolves the contradiction: the Bekhorot case is where the judge handed over the property, while here he did not.
How can the Bekhorot clause about exempting a liable party apply if the judge never handed over the property?
Once the judge declares the party exempt, it counts as if he had handed over the property.
How can reopening to find liable apply, if an exemption already counts as handing over the property?
The mishna teaches only one case: reopening to exempt, which is a liability for the other party, and parallel to capital cases.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna's rule is restated: the court retries to acquit, but not where acquittal would entail liability for another.
Liability for whom, when capital cases have no other litigant?
The liability is to the blood redeemer, who is harmed when the murderer is not put to death.
The explanation is challenged: why kill this man rather than reverse, and the two phrases must be separate matters.
Ravina says the case is a collateral item transferred to the wrong party, or a pure item made impure by touching a creeping animal.
The mishna on capital cases is cited for the retrial rules.
A baraita teaches that someone found liable who has a reason to acquit him is brought back to court.
From where is it derived that such a person is retried?
Exodus 23:7 is cited, reading the innocent as one not to be slain.
From where is it derived that an acquitted person who has a reason to convict is not retried?
From where is it derived that an acquitted person is not brought back?
Exodus 23:7 is cited again, reading the righteous as one whom you may not slay.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi says the opposite holds for an enticer to idolatry, who is retried only to convict.
Deuteronomy 13:9 is cited: do not spare or conceal the enticer.
Rav Kahana teaches this halakha.
Deuteronomy 13:10 is cited, with the repeated verb showing the enticer is killed in every case.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Sheshet how those liable to exile are derived as retried like intentional killers.
Rav Sheshet answers by verbal analogy: murderer for exile and wicked for lashes.
A baraita is cited with the same two verbal analogies, for exile and for lashes.
The mishna states that the court does not retry a convict for the purpose of finding liability.
Rabbi Yoḥanan limits this to errors on matters the Sadducees dispute, while errors on Torah-explicit matters are reversed.
What is the halakha if the judge erred regarding an adulterer and adulteress?
Rabbi Yoḥanan rebukes the questioner and repeats the principle: the verdict is revoked for an error about an adulterer.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling is repeated: an error regarding an adulterer is revoked.
What are the circumstances where the court does not revoke the acquittal?
Rabbi Yoḥanan says it is the case of acquitting an adulterer for atypical intercourse, which is not explicit in a verse.
The mishna states that in monetary cases all present may argue either side.
May even witnesses argue for acquittal in capital cases, and is the mishna per Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda?
Numbers 35:30 is cited: one witness shall not testify to convict a person.
The Rabbis forbid witnesses from arguing at all, while Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda allows arguing for acquittal only.
Rav Pappa explains that the mishna means one of the students before the court, so all agree.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What is the reason of Rabbi Yosei ben Yehuda?
Numbers 35:30 is read to bar testimony only for conviction, so a witness may argue for acquittal.
Reish Lakish says the Rabbis bar a witness's argument so he does not appear biased in his own testimony.
How do the Rabbis interpret the phrase that he die?
It is applied to a student of the court: an argument for acquittal or conviction from a student is not heard, per a baraita.
Rav holds the restriction applies only during the discussion, while at the verdict a judge may argue for conviction after acquittal.
A mishna is raised as an objection: the next day, each judge stands by his earlier view, and a conviction-side argument may follow an acquittal but not vice versa.
The following day is still during the deliberations, so the mishna is consistent with Rav's position.
The mishna's continuation is cited: the court deliberates until a convicting judge is persuaded, and a one-vote majority is not enough to convict.
A baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina says a student who argued for acquittal and then died is viewed as still standing and voting.
If he were alive, why not assume he might change his view to convict under Rav's position?
The assumption is that he would not have changed his view, though it was possible.
The Sages in Eretz Yisrael sent a different version of Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina, which places him in dispute with Rav.
A baraita says court scribes record the statements of both acquitting and convicting judges after the initial deliberations.
Recording convicting statements makes sense because a new conviction reason may appear the next day, requiring a postponement.
Why do the scribes record the acquitting statements, if new conviction reasons are ignored?
It prevents two judges from counting one acquittal reason derived from two verses as two votes; Rabbi Yoḥanan counts them as one.
From where is this rule derived?
Psalms 62:12 and Jeremiah 23:29 show one verse yields several explanations, while one explanation does not emerge from several verses.
What counts as one explanation from two verses?
Rav Zevid cites a mishna in Zevaḥim: Rabbi Yehoshua holds that an item fit to ascend the altar does not descend once it has ascended.
Leviticus 6:2 is cited, with the burnt-offering on the altar as the basis for Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling.
Rabban Gamliel holds that any item fit for the altar, if it ascended, does not descend, even if disqualified.
Leviticus 6:2 is cited again, with the words upon the altar as the basis for Rabban Gamliel's ruling.
What do both Sages include by these explanations?
Disqualified offerings, which do not descend once ascended; one Sage derives it from on the pyre and the other from upon the altar.
The example fails: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabban Gamliel disagree about disqualified blood and libations, so their explanations differ.
Rav Pappa cites a baraita of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who derives a rule from the wording of a verse.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita derives that anything touching the altar is sanctified, whether fit or unfit, by analogy to the lambs.
Rabbi Akiva derives from Exodus 29:42 that anything fit for the altar is included in the halakha of sanctification.
What do the two Sages exclude by their explanations?
Disqualified offerings are excluded: one Sage derives it from lambs and the other from burnt-offering.
Rav Adda bar Ahava holds the disagreement concerns a disqualified bird burnt-offering, which the Gemara uses to challenge the example.
Rav Ashi offers a different example of one explanation from two verses.
Leviticus 17 is cited: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva each include the sprinkler of blood outside the Tent of Meeting.
What do the two Sages include by these explanations?
They include one who sprinkles blood outside the Tent, derived from two different verses.
Rabbi Abbahu says they differ on one who slaughters and sprinkles, which would make the example a real dispute.
Abaye says Rabbi Akiva also holds only one liability, since Deuteronomy 12:14 combines all offering acts into one transgression.
The mishna's daytime and nighttime rules for monetary cases are introduced, with a mnemonic for the topics.
From where are the rules on the time of deliberation derived?
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Pappa derives it from Exodus 18:26, judging the people at all times.
If so, the initial trial should also be permitted at night, yet Deuteronomy 21:16 restricts inheritance judgments to daytime.
How can these verses be reconciled?
Rava says the daytime verse governs the initial trial and the night-inclusive verse governs the verdict.
The mishna is not in accordance with Rabbi Meir, as a baraita reports his view.
Rabbi Meir asks what disputes have to do with leprous sores, given the verse on priestly judgment in Deuteronomy 21:5.
The baraita derives that disputes and leprous sores share rules: daytime, sighted judges, and non-relative judges.
Leviticus 13:2 is cited to show that a single priest may examine leprous sores, against a three-judge analogy.
A blind judge in Rabbi Yoḥanan's neighborhood served, and the baraita's conclusion is reported as halakha.
How could Rabbi Yoḥanan allow a blind man to judge?
Rabbi Yoḥanan's own rule that the unattributed mishna prevails seems to bar a blind judge, since fit to judge is stricter than fit to testify.
Rabbi Yoḥanan found another unattributed mishna allowing a blind judge, so judging is not compared to examining leprous sores.
What makes this unattributed mishna stronger than the other?
It records many Sages' opinion, or it appears in the context of halakhot of judgment, the primary source on judging.
What does Rabbi Meir derive from the verse about judging at all times?
Rava says it includes a cloudy day, when a priest may not view leprous sores but the court may judge.
What does Rabbi Meir derive from the verse about the day of inheritance?
That verse teaches, as Rabba bar Ḥanina taught before Rav Naḥman, that inheritances are distributed only by day.
Deuteronomy 21:16 is cited for the rule that inheritance is distributed only during the day, not at night.
Rav Naḥman objects: then only a person dying by day would bequeath to children, which is absurd, so the rule must be about adjudication.
Numbers 27:11 is cited: the entire inheritance passage is a statute of judgment subject to court procedure.
Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name that three visitors to the sick may write and act as a court to transfer property.
Rav Ḥisda limits this to daytime; at night three can only witness, not act as a court.
A witness to the will cannot become its judge, and Rabba bar Ḥanina confirmed Rav Naḥman's view.
The mishna teaches that capital cases are judged in the daytime and concluded in the daytime.
From where are these matters derived?
Numbers 25:4 is cited: hang them before the Lord facing the sun, showing capital cases are judged by day.
From where is hoka'ah derived to mean hanging?
II Samuel 21:6 is cited: the Gibeonites hanged Saul's sons before the Lord, showing hoka'ah means hanging.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: II Samuel 21:10 and Numbers 25:4 are cited to show the bodies were hanged and the chiefs were summoned.
Why were the chiefs of the people punished if the verse records no transgression by them?
Rav says God told Moses to set up courts for the tribal chiefs, to judge and punish their own tribes' transgressors.
Why were multiple courts needed?
Rav Ḥisda's rule limits the one-day prohibition to two types of death, so one type could be judged in a day, weakening the explanation.
Rather, multiple courts were appointed so that God's anger would turn away from Israel, requiring haste.
The mishna states that monetary cases may conclude the same day, while capital cases conclude the next day to convict.
From where are these rules derived?
Rabbi Ḥanina cites Isaiah 1:21, linking justice with lodging overnight.
Rava cites Isaiah 1:17, reading ashru and ḥamotz as praising a judge who delays his verdict.
Rabbi Ḥanina reads the verse as relieving the robbery victim, not the robber, as wicked judges do.
What does Rava do with the verse about justice lodging overnight?
Rava follows Rabbi Elazar's teaching that delaying charity is like spilling the poor's blood, applying only to food.
The mishna states that capital cases are not judged on eves of Shabbat or Festivals.
What is the reason the verdict cannot be issued on the same day as the deliberations?
Trial on a Shabbat eve cannot be finished, since a verdict may not be on the same day and executions cannot occur on Shabbat or at night.
Reish Lakish argues by a fortiori that burying a met mitzvah overrides Shabbat, as the Temple service does, so the trial should too.
A baraita on the nazirite's prohibition on contact with the dead is cited, showing a met mitzvah overrides other duties like the Passover.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita rules that a priest may not become impure to attend a relative's funeral, even when it is a met mitzva.
Leviticus 21:2 is cited: the word for his sister shows he may become impure only for a met mitzva, not for a sister.
Reish Lakish suggests that burying a met mitzva overrides Shabbat, since Shabbat yields to the Temple service.
Rabbi Yoḥanan replies that murder overrides the Temple service but not Shabbat, so the inference fails.
The Gemara asks: murder itself should override Shabbat by a fortiori reasoning from the Temple service, citing Exodus 21:14.
Rava answers that the school of Rabbi Yishmael already settled the matter in the baraita on kindling fire on Shabbat.
What is the meaning of the verse singling out kindling fire?
Rabbi Yosei reads it as an ordinary prohibition, while Rabbi Natan reads it as dividing the labors for capital liability.
Rava asks what the word habitations adds, since the Shabbat obligation applies to the person everywhere.
A student of Rabbi Yishmael cites Deuteronomy 21:22 for the court's capital punishment on Shabbat, based on Exodus 31:14.
He reasons that the same verse permits a court to execute on Shabbat, to be considered as desecration of Shabbat.
How can the verses on putting to death on Shabbat be realized, whether they exclude or include court executions?
Numbers 35:29 is cited with habitations, read as the act of a court, so Exodus 35:3 excludes court executions on Shabbat.
Abaye argues a fortiori that if murder does not override Shabbat, it likewise does not override the Temple service.
The Gemara explains that Exodus 21:14 refers only to an individual's offering, which does not override Shabbat.
Rava argues a fortiori that murder should not override even an individual's offering.

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A fortiori argument: festivals yield to individual offerings, yet capital punishment does not override a festival, so it should not override such an offering.
Asks what can be said if vow and freewill offerings are sacrificed on festivals, since then the a fortiori inference has no explanation.
Rava replies that on every view the inference fails, because 'from My altar' cannot be restricted to individual offerings alone.
Objection: the verse 'from My altar' refers to the daily offering, which is communal, so it cannot be limited to individual offerings.
Mishna cited: in monetary cases and in ritual purity and impurity cases, judges begin voicing opinions with the greatest judge.
Rav reports that he sat in the quorum of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's court, where voting began with him.
Objection: we learned that judges begin from the greatest, yet Rav was among the junior judges.
Rabba responds that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's court was exceptional, as voting began from the side benches out of deference to him.
Rabba claims that from Moses until Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi no single person combined supreme Torah knowledge with worldly greatness.
Objection: wasn't there Joshua, who combined both?
Reply: Elazar was Joshua's equal in Torah knowledge during his time.
Objection: wasn't there Pinehas, who came after Elazar?
Reply: the elders were Pinehas's equals in Torah knowledge.
Objection: wasn't there Saul, who combined both?
Reply: Samuel was Saul's equal in Torah knowledge.
Objection: Samuel died during Saul's lifetime, so Saul was supreme in both.
Reply: the claim only means no one else was supreme in both for the whole period of leadership.
Objection: wasn't David the supreme figure in both domains?
Reply: Ira the Yairite was David's equal in Torah knowledge.
Objection: Ira died during David's lifetime.
Reply: the same clarification applies, that no other figure was supreme in both during the leadership period.
Objection: wasn't Solomon unparalleled in both domains?
Reply: Shimi ben Gera was Solomon's Torah master in his day.
Objection: Solomon killed Shimi ben Gera early in his reign.
Reply: the same clarification of the claim applies.
Objection: wasn't Hezekiah both the leading scholar and the king?
Reply: Shebnah was Hezekiah's equal in Torah knowledge.
Objection: Shebnah was killed in the war against Sennacherib.
Reply: the same clarification applies.
Objection: wasn't Ezra the greatest scholar and leader of his day?
Reply: Nehemiah son of Hakhaliah was Ezra's equal.
Rav Adda bar Ahava says the same: from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi until Rav Ashi no one combined supreme Torah with worldly greatness.
Objection: wasn't Huna bar Natan both learned and wealthy in Rav Ashi's time?
Reply: Huna bar Natan was subordinate to Rav Ashi, who surpassed him in both domains.
Mishna cited: in capital cases judges begin issuing opinions from the side benches, where the least significant judges sit.
Asks where these rules are derived from.
Rav Aha bar Pappa supplies the source for this practice.
Proof from Exodus 23:2: 'do not answer after a rav (riv)', read as not disputing the greatest judge.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports Rabbi Yohanan's teaching on the source of this practice.
Proof from I Samuel 25:13: David, the leader, girded his sword last among the men in a capital case.
Rav holds that a teacher may train a student and sit with him as a judge in capital cases.
Baraita objection: in ritual purity cases a father and son, or teacher and student, count as two votes.
Baraita contrast: in monetary, capital, and flogging cases, and in calendar matters, such a pair counts as only one vote.

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Resolves Rav's statement: it applies to students like Rav Kahana and Rav Asi, who needed Rav's rulings but not his reasoning.
Rabbi Abbahu: ten ways monetary cases differ from capital cases, and none applies to an ox to be stoned except the twenty-three judge requirement.
Asks where these differences are derived from.
Rav Aha bar Pappa gives the source.
Exodus 23:6 do not pervert the judgment of your poor: judges may lean toward acquitting a capital defendant, but may favor finding an ox liable.
Asks whether there are truly ten differences, since the mishna lists only nine.
The ten are really nine: the fitness requirement and the twenty-three judge rule are one halakha.
Points out that there is another difference not counted in the nine.
Baraita: an elderly person, a eunuch, or a childless person is not seated on the Sanhedrin; Rabbi Yehuda adds a cruel person.
The reverse applies to an enticer to idolatry, supported by Deuteronomy 13:9 'do not spare or conceal him'.
Mishna: all are fit to judge monetary cases.
Asks what the word 'all' is meant to add.
Rav Yehuda: it includes a mamzer among those qualified for monetary cases.
Objection: a baraita already teaches this, that those fit for capital cases are fit for monetary cases, but not vice versa.
Restates the question: what does the word 'all' add in the baraita?
Rav Yehuda: one source includes a convert and the other a mamzer.
Both sources are needed, since each status would otherwise be inferred differently from the other.
Mishna: not all are fit for capital cases.
Asks the reason for this restriction.
Rav Yosef's teaching: just as the court is clean in justice, it must be clean of every blemish.
Ameimar asks which verse is the source.
Song of Songs 4:7, 'you are all fair, my love, and there is no blemish in you', is cited as the source.
Objection: the verse may refer to an actual physical blemish, not lineage.
Rav Aha bar Pappa's reply: Numbers 11:16 'with you' means similar to you, so judges must be physically whole like Moses.
Objection: those with Moses had to be unblemished because of the Divine Presence, which does not apply to ordinary judges.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzhak: Exodus 18:22 'with you' requires regular judges to be unblemished too, and the Song verse teaches lineage.
Mishna: the Sanhedrin of twenty-three sits in a half-circle, with two scribes recording votes for conviction and acquittal.
Rabbi Yehuda: there were three scribes, one for acquittals, one for convictions, and a third recording both for cross-checking.

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: three rows of Torah scholars sit before the court in order of stature, and a vacancy is filled by advancing each row and seating a new member in the third.
Asks where these arrangements are derived from.
Rabbi Aha bar Hanina supplies the source.
Song of Songs 7:3, 'your navel is a round goblet, let no mingled wine be wanting', is cited as the basis.
Exegesis: the goblet is the Sanhedrin in the navel of the world, shielding it, and round like the moon, hence a semicircle.
Mixed wine: a member may leave only if twenty-three remain, the number of a lesser Sanhedrin.
'Your belly is a heap of wheat': all benefit from the Sanhedrin's rulings, as all benefit from a heap of wheat.
'Set about with lilies': even as a fence of lilies is not breached, the Jewish people do not breach Torah and rabbinic law.
Introduces an anecdote in which a heretic challenged Rav Kahana.
The heretic objects: a menstruating woman cannot be secluded with a man, as kindling near fire will surely ignite.
Rav Kahana replies that the Torah testifies that Israel is set about with lilies and does not breach such fences.
Reish Lakish: 'your temples are like a split pomegranate' shows even the empty among Israel are full of mitzvot.
Rabbi Zeira: Genesis 27:27 read as 'his traitors', showing even sinners among Israel have fragrant qualities.
Narrative: Rabbi Zeira befriended hooligans to lead them to repentance, and after his death they repented, proving his approach right.
Mishna cited briefly: three rows of Torah scholars.
Abaye infers that when one moves, all the rows move.
Objection: the one moved from the head of a row to its tail could protest that he was previously at the head.
Abaye's reply: better to be a tail to lions than a head to foxes, so the court's arrangement stands.
Mishna: how the court warns witnesses in capital cases, questioning whether their testimony rests on guesses, rumor, or hearsay.
The court's warning: unlike monetary cases, a false capital witness's victims' blood and offspring's blood are attributed to him forever.
Proof from Cain: Genesis 4:10 uses 'demei' in the plural, meaning his blood and his offspring's blood, or blood spattered everywhere.
Lesson: Adam was created alone, so that whoever destroys a single soul is charged as if he destroyed a whole world.
Another reason for a single Adam: to prevent people claiming superior ancestry and heretics positing many powers in Heaven.
Analogy: a king stamps coins with one seal, while God stamps all people with Adam's seal, so each must say the world was made for him.
The court begins a further warning to witnesses, cut off mid-sentence.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna continuation: the court asks why they would want this trouble, citing Leviticus 5:1 on the duty to testify and Proverbs 11:10 on wicked perishing.
Baraita: how the court describes testimony based on conjecture, e.g. a man seen chasing another into a ruin with a bloody sword over a dying victim.
Baraita story: Rabbi Shimon ben Shatah saw such a scene, could not testify, and a snake then killed the murderer.
Objection: was this murderer deserving of a snake death at all, rather than a court execution?
Rav Yosef: since the Temple's destruction the four types of court execution have not ceased in principle.
Objection: they have ceased, since courts no longer execute.
Reply: the four types of execution remain in the halakha, meaning their applicability persists.
Explains how the four death types persist: deaths like a fall from a roof, fire, sword, or drowning mirror the court's methods.
Explains the snakebite: the murderer had another liable sin, and the harsher burning penalty applies.
Mishna cited briefly: conjecture is not used in capital cases.
Infers that conjecture is not used in capital cases but is used in monetary cases.
Asks whose opinion the mishna follows.
A baraita of Rabbi Aha: a rampaging camel found beside a dead camel is presumed its killer, so monetary cases allow conjecture.
Asks whether, by the same reasoning, hearsay is allowed in monetary cases but not capital cases.
A mishna: witness hearsay is invalid in monetary cases, and testimony must be direct admission of debt.
Concludes that hearsay is invalid in monetary cases yet still warned against in capital cases, so conjecture is likewise warned against.
Mishna cited: the court tells the witnesses to be aware of these points.
Rav Yehuda son of Rabbi Hiyya: the plural 'demei' shows Cain struck Abel many times, not knowing where the soul leaves.
Rav Yehuda son of Rabbi Hiyya: since the earth received Abel's blood, it has never opened its mouth again.
Isaiah 24:16 'from the corner of the earth' is cited to support that the earth never opened its mouth again.
Objection from Hizkiyya: Numbers 16:32 says the earth opened its mouth to swallow Korah's company.
Reply: it opened for a harmful purpose, not a constructive one.
Rav Yehuda son of Rabbi Hiyya: exile atones for half of a sin, so Cain's punishment was only wandering.
Proof from Genesis 4:14 'fugitive and wanderer' and 4:16 'land of Nod', read as nad.
Rav Yehuda: exile atones for three matters.
Jeremiah 21:9: whoever goes out to the Chaldeans survives, showing exile saves from sword, famine and pestilence.
Rabbi Yohanan: exile atones for all transgressions.
Jeremiah 22:30 'write this man childless' applied to Jeconiah, who was exiled.
I Chronicles 3:17: Jeconiah's son was born in prison, and Shealtiel was planted in an unusual way, supporting a tradition about conception.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Alternative reading of Shealtiel: Zerubbabel was conceived in Babylon, and his true name was Nehemiah son of Hachaliah.
Story: Yehuda and Hizkiyya, sons of Rabbi Hiyya, claim over wine that the Messiah will not come until the Exilarch and Nasi houses are destroyed.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi objects that the young men are throwing thorns in his eyes by speaking this way before him.
Rabbi Hiyya defends them: wine and secrets share the numerical value seventy, so wine brings out what is hidden.
Attribution of the following interpretation to Rav Hisda, or alternatively to Mar Ukva.
Daniel 9:14: God hastened Zedekiah's exile for the good of Israel, since Jeconiah's earlier exile still had wise men who could teach the later exiles.
II Kings 24:16 'the craftsmen and the smiths': the hearsh are Torah scholars who silence others, and the masger closes the discussion.
Explains the verse: once scholars open their mouths others fall silent, and once they close a halakha it is not reopened; there were a thousand of them.
Ulla: the righteous act was hastening the exile by two years, based on the word venoshantem.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov infers from the word soon that the 852 years of the verse are the intended time until exile.
Mishna cited briefly: therefore Adam was created alone.
Baraita: Adam was created alone to refute heretics, and so neither the righteous nor the wicked can claim natural lineage.
Baraita: a single ancestor prevents family quarrels and robbery, and if one ancestor still fails, two would fail even more.
Mishna cited briefly: this shows the greatness of God.
Baraita: a king of flesh stamps identical coins with one seal, but God stamps every person with Adam's seal, so no two are alike.
Job 38:14, 'it is changed like clay under the seal', is cited to support that people are formed under one seal yet look different.
Explains why faces differ: so that no one can claim another's home or wife, since all identical faces would allow contradiction.
Job 38:15 'the wicked have their light withheld', supporting that differences thwart the wicked.
Rabbi Meir: people differ in voice, appearance, and thought, to prevent illicit spouse exchange and aid to robbers.
Baraita: Adam was created on Shabbat eve so no heretic can claim a partner, and so that a proud person is reminded he came last.
Another reason: Adam was created on Shabbat eve so he could enter a feast immediately, as the world was prepared for him.
A king's parable of building palaces and a feast, supported by Proverbs 9:1-3 on Wisdom building her house and sending out her maidens.
Explains the Proverbs verses: the house is Gods wisdom, the seven pillars are the days of Creation, the maidens are Adam and Eve.
Continuation of Proverbs 9:3, 'upon the top of the high places of the city'.
Rabba bar bar Hana objects: the verse says 'on the top' but Proverbs 9:14 says 'on a seat', so the two readings seem to conflict.
Explains the seat: Adam first stood on high ground, then sat on a bridegroom's seat once Eve was paired with him; the Holy One asks who led the man to sin.
Rabbi Meir: Adam's dust was gathered from the whole earth.
Psalm 139:15-16 and II Chronicles 16:9 are cited: God's eyes range across the whole earth, supporting that Adam was formed from all of it.
Rav Oshaya in Rav's name begins a further statement about Adam the first man, cut off mid-sentence.

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Adam's body was formed from dust of Babylonia, Eretz Yisrael, and other lands, and his buttocks from Akra de'Agma near Babylonia.
Rabbi Yohanan bar Hanina: Adam's creation unfolded hour by hour on the sixth day, ending with his expulsion from Eden.
Psalm 49:13 'man abides not in honor' is cited to show Adam did not stay even one night in honor.
Rami bar Hama reads Psalm 49:13 as meaning a wild beast only dominates a person who appears to it like a beast.
Mnemonic for the statements that follow, spelled by first letters of Aramaic cues.
Rav Yehuda: God proposed creating man, and the first group of angels was asked for their view of his conduct.
The angels object, quoting Psalm 8:5 that a creature such as man is not worth creating.
God burned the first group with a finger, and the same was done to a second group.
Introduces the third group of angels, who were asked about creating man.
The third group replies that the earlier objections accomplished nothing, since the whole world is God's to shape as He wishes.
When the generations of the flood and the dispersion arrived with corrupt deeds, the angels' argument returned.
The angels object that the first angels were right that man should not have been created.
God replies with Isaiah 46:4: even to old age I will bear and deliver man, despite his flaws.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: Adam spanned the world from one end to the other at first.
Deuteronomy 4:32, 'from the day God created man upon the earth to the one end of heaven', supports Adam's great height.
After Adam sinned, God laid His hand on him and diminished him.
Psalm 139:5 'behind and before You have created me and laid Your hand upon me' supports the diminishing.
Rabbi Eliezer: Adam's height reached from the earth up to the firmament.
Deuteronomy 4:32 is read as showing Adam stood on earth and rose to the end of heaven.
Once Adam sinned, God laid His hand on him and diminished him.
Psalm 139:5 is cited again as the basis for the diminishing.
Objection: the verses contradict each other, since one says the whole world and the other says earth to heaven.
Reply: both are one measure, the same distance from one end to the other.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: Adam spoke Aramaic.
Psalm 139:17 'how weighty are Your thoughts to me' is cited, spoken in Adam's voice.
Reish Lakish agrees that the psalm is spoken by Adam.
Genesis 5:1 'this is the book of the generations of Adam' shows God showed Adam every generation and its sages.
On seeing Rabbi Akiva's generation, Adam rejoiced in his Torah and grieved at his death.
Psalm 139:17 is restated as Adam's own words: how weighty are Your thoughts to me.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: Adam was a heretic.
Genesis 3:9 'Where are you' is cited as the supporting verse.
The phrase 'where are you' is read as asking where Adam's heart had turned from the truth.
Rabbi Yitzhak: Adam drew his foreskin forward to hide his circumcision.
Hosea 6:7 'they like men transgressed the covenant' is compared with Genesis 17:14 'he has broken My covenant'.
Rav Nahman: Adam denied the fundamental principle of belief in God.
Jeremiah 22:9 'they forsook the covenant of the Lord' is added to the earlier verses.
Mishna Avot 2:14 with Rabbi Yohanan: answer heretics only if they are gentiles, not Jewish heretics.
Rabbi Yohanan: where heretics cite a verse, the refutation lies alongside it in the same passage.
Genesis 1:26-27 and 11:5-7 and 35:3-7 show plural and singular forms for God, each with its own answer nearby.
Deuteronomy 4:7, II Samuel 7:23 and Daniel 7:9 show plural and singular in one verse, answering the heretics.
Asks why plural forms are used for God at all.
Rabbi Yohanan: God does not act without consulting the heavenly entourage, as Daniel 4:14 shows.
Asks what this explanation does for Daniel 7:9's thrones.
Baraita: one throne is for God and one for David, the view of Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Yosei objects that Akiva desacralizes the Divine Presence by equating God with a person.
Rabbi Yosei's view: both thrones are for God, one for judgment and one for righteousness.
Asks whether Akiva accepted Rabbi Yosei's explanation.
Another baraita: one throne for judgment and one for righteousness, the view of Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah objects that Akiva should stick to halakha, not aggada.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah's view: one seat is a throne and one a footstool.
Rav Nahman: only one who can answer heretics as well as Rav Idit should respond to them.
A heretic asks why Exodus 24:1 says come up to the Lord rather than to Me.
Rav Idit: the Lord refers to the angel Metatron, whose name is like his Master's, citing Exodus 23:21.
The heretic objects that the angel should then be worshipped, and asks why God would not pardon transgression.
Rav Idit: Israel did not accept even the angel as a guide, since Moses insisted that God Himself must go with them, citing Exodus 33:15.
A heretic asks Rabbi Yishmael why Genesis 19:24 says from the Lord rather than from Him.
A launderer answers: the Torah often speaks this way, as in Genesis 4:23 wives of Lemech.
Rabbi Yishmael asks the launderer where he got this interpretation.
The launderer heard it from Rabbi Meir's lecture, which Rabbi Yohanan said mixed halakha, aggada, and parables.

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Three verses, from Ezekiel, Leviticus and Proverbs, are cited as the basis of the parables
The heretic objects that Rabban Gamliel's God is a thief
Genesis 2:21 is cited: God cast a deep sleep on Adam and took a side from him
The emperor's daughter says she will answer the heretic and asks her father to leave him to her
She asks her father for a commander to avenge a theft
The emperor asks why she needs the commander
Bandits took a silver jug and left a golden one, so she explains the need
The emperor says he wishes such raids came every day
She argues that Adam's loss of a side and gift of a maidservant was also good for him
The emperor says God should have taken the side openly, not like a thief
She has raw meat roasted under embers and offers it to him as a demonstration
The emperor finds the meat repulsive
Adam too would have found the woman repulsive had she been taken openly
The emperor claims to know what God does and where He sits
Narration: the emperor moans and groans in distress
Rabban Gamliel asks what is the matter
The emperor says he has a son overseas he misses and asks to see him
The emperor replies that he does not know where his son is
Gamliel retorts that if the emperor cannot know earthly things, he cannot know heavenly ones
The emperor cites a verse praising God for counting the stars
Psalms 147:4 is cited on God counting the stars and naming them
The emperor asks what is special about God's counting, since he can count stars too
Gamliel demonstrates by spinning quinces in a sieve
Gamliel asks the emperor to count the moving fruit and the emperor asks for them to be held still
Gamliel says the firmament revolves in the same way, so counting is impossible
Some report that the exchange went differently
The emperor challenges Gamliel to count the stars for him
Gamliel asks the emperor how many teeth he has
The emperor puts his hand in his mouth and counts his teeth
Gamliel says the emperor does not know what is in his mouth yet claims to know the firmament
The emperor argues that the maker of mountains did not make wind, so different gods made them
Amos 4:13 is cited to support separate creators, one forming mountains and one creating wind
Gamliel replies that by the same logic Adam, created and formed, cannot have had separate makers
Gamliel argues that one creator made all parts of the face, so different gods are not possible
Psalms 94:9 is cited: the One who planted the ear hears, the One who formed the eye sees
The emperor concedes that different gods made different parts
Gamliel asks whether all these gods agree on the moment of death
A magus teaches that Hurmiz rules the upper body and Ahurmiz the lower body
Ameimar objects: if so, why does Ahurmiz allow Hurmiz to urinate in his territory
The emperor proposes that all become one people
R. Tanhum replies that the circumcised cannot become uncircumcised, so the others should become like them
The emperor grants that he speaks well
The emperor states that whoever defeats the king is thrown to beasts, and the beasts did not eat this one
A heretic says the beasts spared him because they were not hungry, and they then threw him in and ate him
The emperor says Gamliel holds that the Divine Presence rests among ten adults
The emperor asks sarcastically how many Divine Presences there are
Gamliel summons the servant and strikes him on the neck
Gamliel asks the servant why he let the sun into the emperor's house
The servant replies that the sun shines on all the world and no one objects
Gamliel argues a fortiori: if the sun, one of myriads of servants, shines on all, the Divine Presence rests on one all the more
A heretic says Rabbi Abbahu's God is a jester, given the contradictory instructions to Ezekiel
Ezekiel 4:4 is cited: lie on your left side
Ezekiel 4:6 is cited: lie on your right side
A student asks Abbahu the reason for the sabbatical year commandment
Abbahu says he will tell them something fitting for both of them
God commanded Israel to rest the land, they sinned and were exiled, so God afflicts Ezekiel as a king punishes his province
A heretic says Abbahu's God is a priest, since offerings are given to Him
Exodus 25:2 is cited: take for Me an offering
The heretic asks in what immersion God purified Moses's body after burial
If God immersed in water, the heretic says, that is impossible
Isaiah 40:12 is cited: who has measured the waters in His palm
Abbahu replies that God immersed in fire
Isaiah 66:15 is cited: the Lord will come in fire
The heretic asks whether immersion in fire is effective
Abbahu replies that fire is the main form of immersion
Numbers 31:23 is cited: what cannot endure fire must pass through water, showing fire purifies more
A heretic says to R. Avina that Israel is a unique nation
II Samuel 7:23 is cited: who is like Your people Israel, one nation on earth
The heretic asks what Israel's greatness is, since they too are mixed with the nations
Isaiah 40:17 is cited: all nations are as nothing before Him
R. Avina replies that Balaam, one of their own prophets, testified in Israel's favor, as written

39b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Numbers 23:9 is cited: Israel is not reckoned among the nations
R. Elazar raises a contradiction between two verses about God's goodness
Psalms 145:9 and Lamentations 3:25 are cited as the two contradicting verses
A parable resolves it: watering the whole orchard shows God's general goodness, hoeing only good trees shows selective protection
The Mishnah teaches that all humanity descends from one person, so each person must say the world was created for him
I Kings 22:36 is cited: the cry went through the camp when Ahab died
R. Aha bar Hanina introduces his reading of the song as a reference to an earlier event
Proverbs 11:10 is cited: when the wicked perish there is song
R. Aha explains that the verse alludes to the song at the downfall of Ahab ben Omri
The Gemara asks whether the Holy One is gladdened by the downfall of the wicked
II Chronicles 20:21 is cited: give thanks to the Lord, for His mercy endures forever
R. Yonatan asks why the praise omits the phrase for He is good
The phrase is omitted because God does not rejoice in the downfall of the wicked
R. Yonatan, relayed by R. Shmuel bar Nahman, asks what a verse about the Red Sea means
Exodus 14:20 is cited: the one came not near the other all night
The ministering angels wanted to sing a song before God at the Red Sea
God rebukes them: My handiwork is drowning in the sea, and you sing before Me
R. Yosei bar Hanina teaches that God does not rejoice at their downfall, though He causes others joy
Deuteronomy 28:63 is cited, noting the verse uses the causative yasis rather than yasus
The Gemara concludes that the inference is correct
I Kings 22:38 is cited: the harlots washed themselves by the pool of Samaria
R. Eliezer reads hazzonot as visions, saying the death fulfilled two visions, of Micaiah and of Elijah
I Kings 22:28 and 21:19 are cited to show how Micaiah's and Elijah's visions were fulfilled
Rava explains that the harlots were literal: Jezebel put two harlots in Ahab's chariot to warm him
I Kings 22:34 is cited: a man drew a bow offhandedly and struck the king
R. Elazar reads letummo as lefi tummo, meaning without aiming at Ahab
Rava reads letammem as making whole two visions, of Micaiah and of Elijah
A mnemonic is recorded for the cases that follow
I Kings 18:3 is cited: Ahab called Obadiah, who feared the Lord greatly
The Gemara asks what the verse is saying, and R. Yitzchak responds
Ahab says to Obadiah that it is written about Jacob
Genesis 30:27 and 39:5 are cited: God blessed Laban and Potiphar's house for the sake of Jacob and Joseph
Ahab objects that his house was not blessed, so perhaps Obadiah does not fear God
A divine voice answers that Obadiah feared the Lord greatly, while Ahab's house is not fit for blessing
Ahab's house is not fit for blessing like the houses of such masters
R. Abba says Obadiah's praise is greater than Abraham's, since the word greatly is written of Obadiah but not of Abraham
R. Yitzchak asks why Obadiah merited prophecy
Because he concealed one hundred prophets in a cave
I Kings 18:4 is cited: Obadiah hid one hundred prophets, fifty men in a cave
The Gemara asks why he hid them in groups of fifty
R. Elazar says he learned it from Jacob's division of his camp
Genesis 32:9 is cited: if Esau smites one camp, the camp that is left shall escape
R. Abbahu says no cave can hold more than fifty people
Obadiah 1:1 is cited: the vision of Obadiah concerning Edom
The Gemara asks why Obadiah specifically prophesied concerning Edom
R. Yitzchak says God sent Obadiah, who dwelled among wicked Ahab and Jezebel yet did not learn from them, to prophesy about Esau
Efrayim Miksha'a, a student of R. Meir, says in R. Meir's name that Obadiah was an Edomite convert
A proverb: the ax handle comes from the forest it will chop
II Samuel 8:2 is cited: David smote Moab and measured them with a line
R. Yochanan, citing R. Shimon bar Yochai, applies the same proverb: David descended from Ruth the Moabite
Rav Dimi from Eretz Yisrael says a thigh rots from within, so the same nation punishes
II Kings 3:27 is cited: the king of Moab offered his eldest son as a burnt offering on the wall
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether the king sacrificed for the sake of Heaven or for idolatry
The Gemara asks how the view that it was for Heaven accounts for the great indignation
II Kings 3:27 is cited: there was great indignation against Israel
The Gemara asks how the view that it was for idolatry explains the indignation
The indignation is explained by the teaching of R. Yehoshua ben Levi
R. Yehoshua ben Levi raises a contradiction between two verses in Ezekiel
Ezekiel 5:7 is cited: you did not act according to the statutes of the nations around you
Ezekiel 11:12 is cited: you did act according to the statutes of the nations around you
You did not act like the proper among the nations, but you did act like the flawed among them
II Kings 3:27 is cited for the words that they departed and returned to their land
R. Hanina bar Pappa says at that time Israel's wicked descended to the lowest level
I Kings 1:4 is cited: the damsel was very fair, yafa ad me'od
R. Hanina bar Pappa says Abishag did not reach half the beauty of Sarah
The word ad me'od is read as not including the praise of very fair, and Sarah is called very fair in Genesis 12:14
Chapter-closing formula: the end of the chapter on monetary laws

ranges.en: Witnesses are examined with seven lines of inquiry about the week, year, month, day, hour and place
R. Yosei adds inquiries about the day, hour and place of the event
Do you recognize him, and did you warn the idolater before he worshipped
Whom did he serve and with what did he serve
Whoever multiplies examinations is praiseworthy
A case in which Ben Zakkai examined witnesses with fig stalks
What is the difference between inquiries and examinations
In inquiries, if a witness says he does not know, his testimony is void
In examinations, testimony stands even if some say they do not know, but is void if witnesses contradict each other
One witness says the second of the month and another the third, and the testimony stands
The testimony stands because one witness knows the intercalation of the month and the other does not
One says the third and another says the fifth of the month, so the testimony is void
One says two hours and another three hours, and the testimony stands
One says three hours and another five hours, and the testimony is void
R. Yehuda disagrees and holds that the testimony stands
One says five hours and another seven hours, and the testimony is void
Explains the contradiction: at five the sun is in the east, and at seven it is in the west
The second witness is brought in and examined, and if the words align the case opens with merit
A witness or disciple may say he has something to teach in favor of or against the accused
The court silences the speaker who offers guilt-teaching after the defense has begun
A disciple says he has merit to teach, so the accused is raised and seated among the judges
The accused may not leave all day, and if his words have substance they are heard
Even if the accused says he has merit to teach in his own favor, he is heard
Provided there is substance, if merit is found he is acquitted, and otherwise the case is postponed
The case is postponed to the next day, and the judges meet in pairs
The judges eat less that day and do not drink wine
They deliberate all night and return to court in the morning
The one who acquits says he acquits and does so in his place
The one who convicts says he convicts and does so in his place
One who taught guilt may later teach merit, but one who taught merit may not later teach guilt
If judges erred, the scribes remind them; if merit is found they acquit, otherwise they stand for the count
Twelve for acquittal against eleven for conviction, and the other combinations of the count
If one judge says I do not know, the counting rule still applies
Even twenty-two judges acquitting or convicting are subject to the same rule
If one says I do not know, the judges add more
The judges are added two at a time up to seventy-one, with the numbers for acquittal and conviction specified
The judges are paired one against one until one of the convicting judges shifts, and the view of the acquitting judges prevails
From where are these matters derived
Rav Yehuda says the matter is derived from a verse
Deuteronomy 13:15, 17:4 and 19:18 are cited: inquire, search and ask thoroughly

40b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why not say each case is written separately, and let the Merciful One write all seven interrogations in one place
Since the three cases are written together and use analogous terms, the halakhot are learned from one another
But the three cases are not similar to each other, so how can their halakhot be learned from one another
A mnemonic is given for the terms: escapes, sword, forewarning
Explains the differences: an idolatrous city loses its property, idolatry is stoning and not the sword, and conspiring witnesses are not forewarned
The link is a verbal analogy using the word diligently, and the word is free in its context so it cannot be refuted
The word is free on only one side, since it is superfluous in two of the three verses but not in the third
The word is superfluous in the idolatrous-city verse too, since the Torah could have written the verb in doubled form
By a fortiori inference, the seven interrogations apply to the strangled, and to the burned from the stoned
This works only if stoning is more severe than burning, so it fails on the view of R. Shimon
Rav Yehuda says there are additional phrases in the verses used to teach the halakha
Deuteronomy 13:15 and 17:4 are cited, each containing the phrase the matter is true and certain
Eleven phrases remain after seven are used for interrogations and three for the verbal analogy, leaving one for an extra halakha
For R. Shimon the extra phrase includes burning, and for the Rabbis it teaches what an a fortiori inference would have shown
R. Abbahu ridicules this by suggesting the extra phrase adds an eighth interrogation
Are there really eight interrogations, and what could be added
Yes, one could add at what time within the hour the event occurred
A baraita teaches that they examined the witness with eight interrogations
This works out according to Abaye's reading of Rabbi Meir, who holds that a person errs a little, so asking about the hour is reasonable
Abaye's reading of Rabbi Yehuda, and Rava's view that people err much more, leave no reason to ask about the hour
Suggests instead asking in how many years within the jubilee the event occurred
This is the same as asking in which seven-year period, so it adds nothing
Abbahu reasons that once the seven-year period is known, there is no need to ask the jubilee cycle, since the court would not assume a fifty-year-old event
R. Yosei holds that witnesses are asked only about day, hour and place
R. Yosei challenges the Rabbis: if a witness says the accused killed last night, why ask the year, month and day
The Rabbis reply: if a witness says the killing just happened, why ask the day, hour and place
The Rabbis respond that all interrogations are required anyway, following R. Shimon ben Elazar on confusing witnesses
R. Yosei holds that testimony of a killing last night is common, so it counts, while just-now testimony is rare, so it does not
Do you recognize him
A baraita is introduced
The baraita lists further questions: did a gentile or a Jew kill, did you forewarn him, did he accept the warning, and did he kill within a short phrase
In an idolatry case the witness is asked which idol was served, and in what manner
Ulla asks from where in the Torah forewarning is derived
Leviticus 20:17 is cited about one who takes his sister and sees her nakedness
Does this mean the matter depends on seeing, when the transgression is intercourse
Rather, seeing means he must understand the reason and be forewarned, which is needed because excision is in Heaven's hands

41a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The forewarning principle is applied to the matter of lashes as well
The school of Hizkiyya taught a source for the requirement of forewarning
Exodus 21:14 is cited: a man who comes intentionally to slay with guile, so forewarning shows intent
The school of R. Yishmael taught a source for forewarning transgressors
Numbers 15:33 is cited: the wood-gatherer was found gathering, so he had been forewarned and still gathered
The school of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi taught a source for forewarning
Deuteronomy 22:24 is cited: the matter of speech, requiring a verbal forewarning
All these sources are needed, since without the sister verse one might exempt capital cases from forewarning
Without the intentional verse one might exempt stoning, which is severe, so the verse is needed
Two verses are needed to cover the stoned cases
Why do I need two verses for those liable to be stoned
According to R. Shimon, burning is more severe, so one verse teaches burning by a fortiori reasoning
Why not write it once for stoning and derive the rest from it
According to the Rabbis, the verse writes explicitly what could be derived a fortiori, since the Torah takes the trouble
One of the questions asked of witnesses: did he release himself to death
From where do we derive that he must release himself to death
Rava says, or some say Hizkiyya, that the verse requires the condemned to release himself first
Deuteronomy 17:6 is cited: the dead shall be put to death only once he has released himself
Rav Hanan rules that conspiring witnesses against a betrothed woman are not executed, since they can say they came to forbid her to her husband
Witnesses must have forewarned her, so how can they claim they only meant to forbid her to her husband
Rav Hanan's ruling concerns a learned woman, a ḥavera, following R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda
A baraita: R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda holds a ḥavera needs no forewarning, since forewarning only distinguishes unintentional from intentional acts
If the witnesses are not executed for conspiracy, how can she be executed
Testimony that cannot be made conspiratory is not counted as testimony
The witnesses are not executed since they may say they meant to forbid her, so she is not executed either
If forewarning is not needed for a ḥavera, how can such a case arise according to R. Yosei
It arises when she committed adultery, returned, and committed adultery again
The witnesses could claim they meant to forbid her to her second paramour
Alternatively, it arises when she committed adultery with her relatives
What is different about a betrothed young woman that Rav Hanan chose to state the case of her
Yes, the case works even for one not living under her husband, and the witnesses may still claim they meant to forbid her to her husband
Rav Hisda rules that a contradiction about the weapon is not congruent testimony, but about the color of garments it is
A baraita seems to say that a contradiction about the weapon, or color of garments, is not congruent
Rav Hisda explains the baraita: the killing was by strangling with a cloth, which is both sword and ariran
A baraita on sandal colors is not congruent testimony, which contradicts Rav Hisda
Rav Hisda can explain that there the murderer kicked the victim with his sandal
A mishna: ben Zakkai examined the witnesses about the stems of figs, showing even minor contradictions matter
Rami bar Hama says the mishna refers to a case where the murderer picked a fig on Shabbat, so he is executed for that act
A baraita says the witnesses said the killing was beneath a fig tree, which indicates a murder case
Rami bar Hama says the murderer stabbed the victim with a fig branch, and contradictions about branches are testimony
Ben Zakkai asked whether the fig tree's stems were thin or thick and figs black or white, showing fruit details matter
Rav Yosef says ben Zakkai is different, as he treated examination like inquiry
Who is this ben Zakkai, and could R. Yohanan ben Zakkai have sat on a Sanhedrin
A baraita says R. Yohanan ben Zakkai lived 120 years: forty in business, forty studying, forty teaching
A baraita says the Sanhedrin was exiled forty years before the Temple's destruction to a store
R. Yitzchak bar Avudimi explains that the Sanhedrin stopped judging monetary-penalty cases only, not capital cases
Since R. Yohanan ben Zakkai instituted the lulav ordinance after the destruction, he must have been prominent then
Rather, this was a different ben Zakkai, not the well-known sage
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would not call Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai merely ben Zakkai, so the referent must be someone else
A baraita says R. Yohanan ben Zakkai examined the witnesses about fig stems, which would identify him as the sage
Rather, at that time he was a student sitting before his teacher, and his reasoning is sensible

41b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains why he is called ben Zakkai while a student and Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai once he was teaching
The mishna's incident of ben Zakkai examining witnesses about fig stems is cited
What is the difference between interrogations and examinations
What does even two witnesses saying we know mean, and is it obvious
The Gemara restates the mishna's rule that testimony stands when one witness does not know, for either procedure
Rav Sheshet explains that the mishna's first clause applies to interrogations, following Rabbi Akiva's comparison of three to two
Rava objects that the mishna says testimony stands, not that it is void
Rava reads the mishna as saying that even in interrogations testimony stands, following a view other than Rabbi Akiva's
Rav Kahana and Rav Safra studied the tractate in Rabba's school, and Rami bar Hama met them
Rami bar Hama asks what they said about tractate Sanhedrin in Rabba's school
They ask what they say about the plain tractate Sanhedrin
Rami asks what difficulty they have
Rami raises a difficulty from the mishna on the difference between interrogations and examinations
The mishna states that in interrogations testimony is void if one says he does not know, while in examinations it stands even if two say they do not know
Since both procedures are Torah law, what is the difference between interrogations and examinations
In interrogations a single 'I do not know' voids testimony, since it is testimony that cannot be rendered conspiratory
In examinations testimony stands, since the witnesses are testimony that can be rendered conspiratory
Rami says that if they speak so incisively about this tractate, they have said much
Kahana and Safra reply that Rami's goodwill drew out much from them, but his challenge would draw out nothing
The mishna states that if one witness says the second and another says the third, testimony stands
Until how many days into the month is the event counted
R. Yohanan teaches that the testing extends until the majority of the month has passed
Rava says that the mishna also teaches this rule
The mishna states that if one witness says the third and another says the fifth, testimony is void
Why not say one witness knows of two intercalations and the other of one, so there is no contradiction
The Gemara rejects the proof: a witness may not know the day even after the majority, since the shofar blasts are the basis for the ruling
R. Aha bar Hanina, citing R. Asi and R. Yohanan, teaches until when one may bless the new month, until its flaw is filled
R. Yaakov bar Idi, citing Rav Yehuda, says seven days, while the Neharde'ans say sixteen days

42a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that both opinions follow R. Yohanan, who permits the blessing until the moon's flaw is filled
Rav Aha of Difti proposes that the blessing over the moon's light be the blessing for Him who is good and does good
Ravina objects: the blessing for good is for good news, and the moon does not diminish only to be blessed as true judgment
R. Yohanan teaches that one who blesses the new month at its proper time greets the face of the Divine Presence
Exodus 12:2 and 15:2 are linked: this month, and this is my God, so the new month reveals God
A baraita of R. Yishmael's school: without the new month Israel would only greet their Father in Heaven once a month
Abaye rules that they should recite the blessing standing, and Mareimar and Mar Zutra would lean on each other's shoulders
Rav Aha tells Rav Ashi that in the West they recite the blessing that renews the months
Rav Ashi replies that their women also recite that blessing
The full blessing is Rav Yehuda's version, in which God created the heavens and set their law and time
Proverbs 24:6 is cited: by wise counsel you shall make your war
R. Yohanan teaches that the war of Torah is found in one who has bundles of mishna in his hand
Rav Yosef applies Proverbs 14:4 to himself, and the plenty comes by the strength of the ox
The mishna states that if one witness says two hours and another three hours, testimony stands
Rav Shimi bar Ashi says this applies only to differences in hours, not to other kinds of time
The mishna states that if one witness says before sunrise and another says after sunrise, testimony is void
Isn't this obvious, and what of one who says before sunrise and another during sunrise
The mishna teaches that a light seen during dawn is not clearly daylight, and a glimmer is what was seen
The mishna states that the court brings in the second witness and examines him, all on that same day only
A baraita says that if the words have substance he never descends, and otherwise he does not descend all day
Abaye translates the baraita: if there is no substance to his words
The mishna states that if they find merit for him, they acquit him
What is the reason the judges did not drink wine
R. Aha bar Hanina says the reason is stated in a verse
Proverbs 31:4 is cited: it is not for rulers to drink wine, lest they forget the law
The mishna states that if they find merit for him, they acquit him
What is the meaning of if they did not see
R. Aha says they release him
R. Yohanan likewise says they release him
Rav Pappa asks Abaye why not release him from the outset if they release him anyway
Abaye replies that R. Yohanan's reason is so that they do not leave the court confused
Some say that Rav Pappa asks why add judges at all when the first court should release him
Abaye replies that R. Yosei holds like this, as is taught
A baraita: R. Yosei says just as one may not add to a court of seventy-one, one may not add to a court of twenty-three
The Sages taught that in monetary cases one says the judgment has grown aged, but not in capital cases
What is the meaning of the judgment has grown aged, and why would one say the reverse in capital cases
Rav Huna reports in Rav's name that the reverse should be said
Rav Ashi says it should never be reversed
The judgment has grown wise, meaning it is a wise judgment
A baraita says the greatest judge says the judgment has grown aged, which would not fit the reading that the judgment is shaky
Yes, the greatest judge must announce it, since being shamed by oneself is not like being shamed by others
Some object to the second reading: if the judgment is wise, the greatest judge would be praising himself
Proverbs 27:2 is cited: let another praise you and not your own mouth
A matter of the court differs, since its administration rests on the greatest judge
A mishna: when they finished deliberating, the greatest judge tells each litigant whether he is acquitted or liable
Chapter-closing formula: the end of the chapter that begins with the witnesses being examined

ranges.en: Mishna: a condemned man is taken out to be stoned, and the place of stoning is outside the court, as stated
Leviticus 24:14 is cited: take out the blasphemer outside the camp
A man stands at the court entrance with cloths, and another on a horse signals when a judge offers a reason to acquit
Even if the accused says he has merit to teach in his own favor, he is returned four or five times, provided there is substance
Was the place of stoning just outside the court and nothing more, given a baraita that says otherwise
The baraita states the place of stoning was outside three camps, which seems to contradict the Gemara's reading
Yes, it was outside three camps, and the practical difference is that the court's own location must not look like murderers
Alternatively, it is so that the condemned has a chance of rescue
From where is this derived, as the Sages taught
Leviticus 24:14 is cited: take out the blasphemer to outside the camp
Do we say outside three camps, or only outside one camp
Rather, the verse says outside the camp, meaning only outside one camp
The bulls burned outside the camp are cited as the model: as there, outside three camps, so here
From where do we know this, as the Sages taught
Leviticus 4:12 is cited: he shall carry the whole bull outside the camp
Do we say outside three camps, or only outside one camp
The baraita reasons that the phrase outside the camp is needed for the bull of the congregation, since it is already stated
Leviticus 4:21 is cited: he shall burn it as he burned the first bull, giving it a second camp
The baraita reasons the phrase outside the camp for ashes is needed, since it is already stated
Leviticus 4:12 is cited: the ashes are burned on the place where the ashes are poured out
The baraita concludes a third camp is given, and the case should be learned from slaughter outside the courtyard, which is outside one camp
It is reasonable to learn from the bulls that are burned, since it is a similar case
On the contrary, the halakha should be learned from slaughter outside the Temple courtyard, which is also outside one camp
Learning from burned bulls is better, since the sinner is excised and the rendering-fit case is preferred
Rav Pappa says
Moses sat in the Levite camp when God told him the blasphemer must be taken out
Leviticus 24:14 is cited again: they took the blasphemer outside the camp, outside the camp of the Levites
The phrase outside the camp of Israel seems needed to teach implementation, but the implementation is written explicitly

43a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Leviticus 24:23 is cited: the children of Israel did as God commanded Moses
If so, what is the point of the verse
Leviticus 24:23 is cited again: they stoned him with a stone
What do they need the phrase for
That phrase is needed, as taught in a baraita
Stoning with a stone, not with the clothing, is derived from the verse: a single stone that kills suffices
The singular and plural forms are both needed, since one stone would otherwise permit bringing another, and stones would otherwise permit two
The objection: the baraita reasons from a verbal analogy, so Rav Pappa's derivation is unnecessary
Rav Ashi says the place of stoning can be derived directly from the blasphemer verse
Leviticus 24:14 is cited: Moses sat in the Levite camp and was told to take the blasphemer outside the camp
The objection: the implementation is written explicitly, as the verse says the children of Israel did as commanded
That verse is needed for two purposes: one to support the derivation and one to exclude another
The Sages ask Rav Ashi what he derives from the bull verses if his reading holds
A mishna: one man stands at the court entrance with cloths ready to signal
Rav Huna says it is obvious to him that stoning, hanging, the sword and strangling are all public matters
Why do we not tell the one who has a reason to acquit him to go and fetch it, and let him kill himself
Rav Huna asks whether the cloth and the racing horse come from the condemned man's property or from the community's
Rav Hiyya bar Rav Ashi reports Rav Hisda's teaching that a condemned person is given frankincense in wine to confuse his mind
Proverbs 31:6 is cited: give strong drink to one who is perishing, and wine to the bitter of soul
A baraita: the noble women of Jerusalem would volunteer to bring such drink
The drink comes from the community's property, since it says give
Rav Aha bar Huna asks Rav Sheshet: if one student says he can teach merit and then falls silent, what is the halakha
Rav Sheshet answers that even if he falls silent the court disregards him, since there he did not speak
The Gemara introduces a proof from R. Yosei bar Hanina
R. Yosei bar Hanina teaches that a student who argued to acquit and died is regarded as standing in his place
The Gemara rejects the proof: the student who argued to acquit is obviously counted, but one who only proposes it is not
The mishna teaches that even the condemned man himself may return four or five times if there is substance to his words
A baraita seems to contradict the mishna: the first and second returns are made whether or not there is substance
Rav Pappa explains that the substance requirement applies from the second return onward
How do we know whether there is substance to his words
Abaye says that after two returns, the court sends two rabbis with him to evaluate the claim
Why not send the rabbis from the outset, since the condemned man can say everything he has
A mishna: if the judges find merit they acquit, otherwise he is led out, and a crier proclaims his offense and calls any with merit to speak
Abaye adds that the crier must state the day, hour and place of the offense, in case others could refute the witnesses
The crier goes out before the condemned man only once he is led out, not from the outset
A baraita about the trial of the Nazarene: the crier proclaimed forty days, and he was hanged on the eve of Passover without finding merit
Ulla challenges: how could one search for merit for an inciter to idolatry, when the Torah forbids sparing him
Deuteronomy 13:9 is cited: do not spare him or conceal him
The Nazarene's case was special, since he was close to the kingdom
A baraita: the Nazarene had five disciples, and they brought the first, Mattai, to trial
Mattai asks: shall I be executed, when it is written that I shall come and see God's face
Psalms 42:3 is cited: when shall I come and see the face of God
The judges reply: yes, Mattai shall be executed
Psalms 41:6 is cited: when shall he die and his name perish
The second disciple, Nakai, is brought to trial
Nakai asks: shall I be executed, when it is written not to slay the innocent and righteous
Exodus 23:7 is cited: the innocent and righteous you shall not slay
The judges reply: yes, Nakai shall be executed, since the innocent is slain in secret places
Psalms 10:8 is cited: in secret places he kills the innocent
The third disciple, Netzer, is brought to trial
Netzer asks: shall I be executed, when it is written that a branch shall grow from his roots
Isaiah 11:1 is cited: a branch shall grow out of his roots
The judges reply: yes, Netzer shall be executed, since he is cast out like an abominable branch
Isaiah 14:19 is cited: you are cast out like an abominable branch
The fourth disciple, Buni, is brought to trial
Buni asks: shall I be executed, when it is written that Israel is My firstborn son
Exodus 4:22 is cited: Israel is My firstborn son
The judges reply: yes, Buni shall be executed, since it is written I will kill your firstborn son
Exodus 4:23 is cited: behold, I will kill your firstborn son
The fifth disciple, Toda, is brought to trial
Toda asks: shall I be executed, when it is written a psalm of thanksgiving
Psalms 100:1 is cited: a psalm of thanksgiving
The judges reply: yes, Toda shall be executed, since it is written whoever offers a thanksgiving sacrifice
Psalms 50:23 is cited: whoever offers a thanksgiving sacrifice honors Me

43b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one who subdues his evil inclination and confesses is credited as honoring God in both worlds
Psalms 50:23 is cited: whoever offers a thanksgiving sacrifice honors Me
R. Yehoshua ben Levi adds that while the Temple stands, the one who brings a sacrifice receives the reward for bringing it
One whose mind is humble is credited as if he had offered all the sacrifices
Psalms 51:19 is cited: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, and a broken and crushed heart God will not despise
Mishna: when the condemned is about ten cubits from the stoning place, they tell him to confess, since whoever confesses has a share in the world to come
The Gemara notes that Joshua told Achan to confess, showing the practice
Joshua 7:19 and 7:20 are cited: give glory to the Lord God of Israel and make confession to Him
Achan answers Joshua that he indeed sinned, and describes what he did
From where do we learn that confession atones
Joshua 7:25 is cited: Joshua said, why did you trouble us
Joshua's words continue: the Lord will trouble you this day, and you are troubled, and not in the world to come
Mishna: if the condemned cannot confess, they tell him to say that his death atones for all his sins
R. Yehuda says that if the condemned knows he is guilty he should not say this, and the sages reply that otherwise everyone would say it to clear himself
A baraita: the word na is only a term of request
Joshua 7:11 is cited: Israel has sinned
Joshua asks God: master of the universe, who sinned
God replies: am I an informer to you
God tells Joshua to cast lots, and the lot falls on Achan
Joshua tells Achan that he is in the lot, and that he and Eleazar the priest are the leaders of the generation, so the lot falls on one of them
Joshua asks Achan not to bring disrepute upon the lots, since the land of Israel will be divided by lot
Numbers 26:55 is cited: the land shall be divided by lot
Ravina explains that Joshua won Achan over with words: they asked only for a confession, so he is discharged
Achan confesses to the Lord, God of Israel, that he sinned in this and that way
R. Hanina teaches that Achan misused consecrated property from three dedications, two in Moses's time and one in Joshua's
R. Yohanan, citing R. Elazar son of R. Shimon, teaches that the sins were four or five in Moses's time and one in Joshua's
If so, why was Israel not punished for Achan's sin until now
Because God did not punish for hidden sins until Israel crossed the Jordan, according to a tannaitic dispute
Deuteronomy 29:28 is cited: the hidden things belong to the Lord our God, and the revealed to us forever
Why is the word for us dotted in the verse
The dot teaches that God did not punish for hidden sins until Israel crossed the Jordan, the words of R. Yehuda
R. Nehemiah objects: does God punish a nation for hidden sins at all, since the verse says forever, and as God does not punish hidden sins, He does not punish revealed ones until the crossing

44a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why was Achan punished, given the Gemara's point about hidden matters
His offense was not hidden, since his wife and children knew of it and did not protest
Joshua 7:11 is cited: Israel has sinned
R. Abba bar Zavda infers that even when Israel sinned, the verse still calls it Israel
R. Abba's proverb about a stake in the middle of a cultivated field and its name
Joshua 7:11 continues: they transgressed the covenant, took the dedicated property, stole, dissembled and hid it
R. Ile'a, citing R. Yehuda bar Masparta, teaches that Achan transgressed all five books of the Torah
The word five in the verse is cited for that teaching
R. Ile'a adds that Achan stretched his foreskin to conceal that he was circumcised
The covenant phrase in Joshua is compared with Genesis 17:14, which says the uncircumcised man has broken the covenant
Is it not obvious that he concealed his circumcision, and so why teach it
Joshua 7:15 is cited: he has committed a wanton deed in Israel
R. Abba bar Zavda teaches that Achan had intercourse with a betrothed young woman
Deuteronomy 22:21 is compared with Joshua's wanton deed, since the same term appears
Is it not obvious, since he violated the whole Torah, and why teach this
Ravina holds that Achan's law is like that of the betrothed young woman, who is stoned
The Exilarch says to Rav Huna that it is written
Joshua 7:24 is cited: Joshua took Achan, his sons, daughters, livestock and tent
If Achan sinned, what did his children sin
Rav Huna replies that by that reasoning, if Achan sinned, all Israel sinned
Joshua 7:24 continues: and all Israel with him
Rather, Joshua brought them down to the valley so as to make them descend
Joshua 7:25 is cited: they burned them with fire and stoned them with stones
Ravina explains: those fit for burning are burned, and those fit for stoning are stoned
Joshua 7:21 is cited: a fine mantle of Shinar and two hundred shekels of silver
Rav and Shmuel explain the term mantle of Shinar differently, as a cloak of wool and as a coat
Joshua 7:23 is cited: they laid them out before the Lord
Rav Nahman says Joshua came and cast the spoils down before God
Joshua says to God that for these, most of the Sanhedrin will be killed
Joshua 7:5 is cited: the men of Ai struck them, about thirty-six men
The verse's figure of about thirty-six men is cited
A baraita: exactly thirty-six, the words of R. Yehuda
R. Nehemiah objects: were there really thirty-six, since the verse says about thirty-six
Rather, Zeh Yair ben Menashe, who was equal to the majority of the Sanhedrin
