Rav Nahman says that Rav says the verse on entreaties and impudence refers to Moses and Joshua
Proverbs 18:23 is cited: the poor man speaks entreaties, and the rich answers with impudence
The poor man refers to Moses, who entreated, and the rich refers to Joshua, who answered with impudence
What is the reason Joshua answered God with impudence, since Phinehas did not do so
Psalms 106:30 is cited: Phinehas stood and prayed, and the plague was stayed
R. Elazar explains that the verse says prayed, not interceded, teaching that Phinehas acted in judgment with God
Phinehas says before God: for these twenty-four thousand of Israel should fall
Numbers 25:9 is cited: those that died in the plague were twenty-four thousand
But should one not derive it from another verse
Joshua's complaint is quoted: why did You bring this people across the Jordan
Exodus 5:22 is cited: why have You done evil to this people, as Moses also said
Joshua 7:7 is cited: we would have been content to dwell beyond the Jordan
Joshua 7:10 is cited
Joshua 7:10 continues: the Lord said to Joshua, get up
R. Sheila teaches that God told Joshua that his own sin is harder than theirs
Deuteronomy 27:4 is cited: you shall set up stones on Mount Ebal after you cross the Jordan
The stones were set sixty mil away from the place the Jordan crossed
Joshua 11:15 is cited, with Rav's reading: as the Lord commanded Moses his servant
Rav explains the verse: Joshua did not depart from anything the Lord commanded Moses
If so, why does the verse say get up
God said to Joshua: you caused them to sin, and that is what God means by get up
Joshua 8:2 and 5:13 are cited about Ai and Jericho and the angel who came to Joshua
Joshua 5:13 is cited: when Joshua was by Jericho he lifted his eyes and saw a man
Joshua 5:14 is cited: no, but as captain of the host of the Lord I have come now, and Joshua fell on his face
The Gemara objects: how could Joshua do this, since R. Yohanan forbids greeting a person at night lest he be a demon
It is different there, since the stranger said I am captain of the host of the Lord
Perhaps he was lying, but we learn that one does not take the name of Heaven in vain

44b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The angel rebukes Joshua: yesterday you neglected the daily offerings at twilight, and now you neglected Torah study, so which of them did you come for
The angel replies that he has now come, and Joshua acts immediately
Joshua 8:9 and 8:13 are cited: Joshua lodged that night in the midst of the valley
R. Yohanan teaches that this means Joshua lodged in the depths of halakha
Shmuel bar Unya teaches in Rav's name that Torah study outweighs the daily offerings
Joshua 5:14 is cited: I have now come
Abaye asks Rav Dimi how he explains a verse in the West
Proverbs 25:8-9 is cited: do not hastily go to strife, lest your neighbor shame you
Rav Dimi explains the time when God told Ezekiel to speak to Israel
Ezekiel 16:3 is cited: your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite
The spirit Paskonit speaks before God
The spirit argues: if Abraham and Sarah came before You, You would say to them that their strife is with their neighbor
Who has such authority to rebuke God in this way
Yes: R. Yosei bar Hanina teaches that the angel Gabriel has three names, one of which stops the sins of Israel from being spoken
Job 36:19 is cited: will your cry avail, so as not to be in distress
R. Elazar teaches that one should always pray before trouble comes, since Abraham prayed before trouble at Bethel and Ai
Resh Lakish teaches that one who strains himself in prayer from below has no troubles from above
R. Yohanan teaches that one should always ask for mercy, so that all strive with their strength and no troubles come from above
From where do we know that Achan's confession atoned for him
Joshua 7:20 is cited: Joshua said, why have you troubled us, and you shall be troubled for the world to come
I Chronicles 2:6 is cited: the sons of Zerah, Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Darda, all five
What is the meaning of all five, and why are they all in the world to come
The verse names Zimri and elsewhere Achan, so the two are compared
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether Achan's name is Achan or Zimri, and the reason for the name
Mishna: if the condemned cannot confess, they tell him to say it, and R. Yehuda says he should clear himself
They clear themselves so as not to bring disrepute on the courts and the witnesses
A baraita introduces a case of a man led out to be executed
The condemned man says: if I have this sin, let my death not atone; if I have no such sin, let my death atone for all my sins
The court and all Israel are cleared, while the witnesses will never be forgiven
When the sages heard, they said it could not be reversed, since the decree was made, so he is executed and the rope hangs on the witnesses' neck
Is this not obvious, since a man cannot be released merely by his own claim
It is needed for the case where the witnesses retract their testimony
Even if the witnesses retract, what difference does it make, since once testimony is given it cannot be retracted
It is needed because the witnesses give reasons for their retraction, as in the case where a man sought to be covered

Mishna: at four cubits from the stoning place, the condemned's clothes are removed, a man is covered in front, and a woman in front and back; R. Yehuda and the Sages disagree on the nudity of the woman

45a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: a man is covered by one cloth in front, a woman by two pieces front and back, and R. Yehuda and the Sages disagree on stoning a woman naked
What is the reasoning of the Rabbis
Leviticus 24:14 is cited: all the congregation shall stone him, with the word him
What does the word him, and not her, teach
Objection: Deuteronomy 17:5 explicitly mentions the man or the woman, so the word him cannot exclude women
Rather, him means him without his clothing, and her means her with her clothing
R. Yehuda holds that him without clothing applies whether man or woman
Is it that the Rabbis fear sexual thoughts in the onlookers
Objection: we learned the reverse, that R. Yehuda is concerned about the sota's exposure
Mishna on the sota: the priest tears her garments, and R. Yehuda says he exposes her heart and unbraids her hair only if they are not beautiful
Rabba explains that in the sota case the priests might be tempted if she is found innocent, whereas here she is executed
Rabba says we learned that the evil inclination rules only over one whose eyes see
Rava resolves the apparent contradiction between R. Yehuda's two rulings, and between the Rabbis' rulings, by distinguishing the cases
Rava offers a further resolution: the Rabbis' two rulings also do not conflict
Ezekiel 23:48 is cited: all women shall be chastened, so that they do not act as you
Here there is no greater chastening than this
What if one says both should be done to her
Rav Nahman says in the name of Rabba bar Avuh that the verse about loving one's neighbor applies
Leviticus 19:18 is cited: you shall love your neighbor as yourself, and a choice death is the condemned's right
The Gemara suggests that Rav Nahman's view is a dispute among the tannaim
Rejected: not everyone holds Rav Nahman's view, and here the dispute is between the other positions
The dispute is whether a person's dignity or his body is the greater concern for a choice death
Mishna: the platform on which the condemned is pushed is twice a person's height, and the second witness casts a stone on the chest if he survives the fall
A tanna teaches that adding the platform's height and the condemned's height gives three times his height
Do we require all this height
A baraita seems to contradict: a pit kills at ten handbreadths, so all such heights should be ten handbreadths
Rav Nahman says that Rabba bar Avuh says the verse about loving one's neighbor applies to a choice death for the condemned
Leviticus 19:18 is cited again: you shall love your neighbor as yourself, a choice death
If so, the platform should be higher, so that he is not mutilated
One of the witnesses pushes him, and the Sages taught a baraita on the pushing and stoning
Exodus 19:13 is cited: he shall be pushed, using the word yarah, to derive the pushing punishment
The derivations of stoning from the word stone, and of stoning and pushing from the same word, are cited
Exodus 19:13 is cited: whether he is stoned or shot, he shall be stoned or shot
From where do we know that if he dies from the pushing he is released
The verse says or shot, which teaches that if he dies from the pushing he is released
From where do we know this applies to all generations

45b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The doubled verb in Leviticus 24:16 shows the halakha applies everywhere and always
Mishna: if the condemned does not die from the first stone, the second witness takes the stone and casts it
A baraita of R. Shimon ben Elazar says two people carry the stone and place it on his chest, which seems to contradict the mishna
Both lift the stone together, but the second witness alone casts it so it falls with force
Mishna: if he does not die from the first stone, all of Israel completes the stoning
A baraita says no one ever repeated the stoning, which conflicts with the mishna
The Gemara clarifies that it means one repeats only if needed
A baraita: the stone, the tree, the sword and the cloth are all buried with the executed person
That is needed for the case where the implements were replaced by others
Another baraita says they are not buried with him
Rav Pappa explains that with him means together with his possession
Shmuel rules that if the witnesses' hands were severed after sentencing, the condemned is exempt
What is the reason for Shmuel's ruling
Deuteronomy 17:7 is cited: the hand of the witnesses shall be first upon him
If so, the same should apply when witnesses were lame from the outset
There the verse speaks of the hand of the witnesses which was already there, so the case is different
Objection from a mishna: where two witnesses testify that a death sentence was passed, the witnesses are themselves executed
Shmuel explains that the witnesses in the case are themselves the witnesses
Do we need to fulfill the verse exactly as written
Numbers 35:21 is cited: he that smote him is a murderer, he shall surely be put to death
If this applies only to the death written in the verse, from where do we know other means
The verse says he shall be put to death from any place, which teaches all methods of execution
That case is different, since the verse says he shall surely die
Why not learn a general principle from this case
This case proves no general principle, since two verses about the murderer and the avenger come together
What is the halakha of the avenger of blood, as taught in a baraita
Numbers 35:21 is cited: the avenger of blood shall slay the murderer
It is a mitzva to be the avenger, and if there is no avenger the court appoints one
Numbers 35:19 is cited: when he meets him, he may slay him, from any place
Mar Kashisha asks Rav Ashi whether we do not need to fulfill the verse as written
A mishna: a stubborn and rebellious son cannot be one who is maimed, lame, mute, blind or deaf
Deuteronomy 21:19-20 is cited, with the terms for the hands, mute, lame, blind and deaf
What is the reason for this exclusion
It is because the verse must be followed as written, and the distinction is that the whole verse is superfluous there
A baraita about an idolatrous city and its street: R. Yishmael and R. Akiva disagree on whether it needs a street
The dispute is whether the street must be prepared from the outset or may be prepared now, and all agree the verse requires it
The dispute is a tannaitic one, as in a mishna on the purification of a leper, where R. Eliezer and R. Shimon differ on the side of the body
Mishna: R. Eliezer says all the stoned are hung after death, while the Sages say only the blasphemer and the idolater
Mishna: R. Eliezer says the man's corpse faces the people and the woman's faces the tree out of modesty; the Sages disagree
The Sages say the man is hung but the woman is not
Objection to R. Eliezer from Shimon ben Shetach, who hung eighty women in Ashkelon on one day
Deuteronomy 21:22-23 is cited: if a man has committed a sin, and he is put to death and hanged, for the cursed of God is the hanged one
A baraita: as the blasphemer is hung, so all who are stoned are hung, and the Sages say the same of one who denies a principle of faith
In what do the Rabbis and R. Eliezer disagree in method
The Rabbis expound by generalization and detail, while R. Eliezer expounds by inclusions and exclusions
The Rabbis explain: the generalization he is put to death and you shall hang him is limited by the detail of the cursed of God, so only the blasphemer and idolater are hung

46a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Since the general rule and the specific detail are in separate verses, the verses include idolatry as similar to the blasphemer
R. Eliezer expounds by amplifications and restrictions, so the idolatry case is included and the other stoned offenders are hung as well
Mishna: according to R. Eliezer a man's corpse is hung facing the people and a woman's facing the tree
From where do the Rabbis derive that the executed man is hung without his clothing
Deuteronomy 21:22 is cited: you shall hang him, him and not her
R. Eliezer reads him as meaning him without his clothing
Yes, they agree the word him indicates that the corpse is hung without clothing
Deuteronomy 21:22 is cited: if a man has committed a sin, the verse refers to a man and not a woman
What does R. Eliezer derive from the words if a man has committed a sin
Resh Lakish says it excludes the stubborn and rebellious son
A baraita says a stubborn and rebellious son is stoned and hung, in R. Eliezer's view
Rather, R. Nahman bar Yitzchak says the verse includes the stubborn and rebellious son
What is the reason for that
The verse says a man, not a child, and the specific exclusions show the inclusion of the stubborn son
R. Eliezer objects that Shimon ben Shetach hanged women in Ashkelon
Rav Hisda rules the Sages taught only about two kinds of death, and one court may judge a case with one death
Objection: the case of Shimon ben Shetach involved a single death, which contradicts the ruling
Rather, the ruling is stated as applying only to a single death that resembles two deaths, such as two offenses
Rav Hisda adds that one court may judge one death and one offense
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects from a baraita: a court may not judge two capital cases in one day, even an adulterer and adulteress
Rav Hisda explains that the baraita speaks of a priest's daughter with her lover, or of conspiring witnesses
A baraita: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov says courts may administer lashes and capital punishment, not from the Torah but as a fence for the Torah
An incident on Shabbat during the days of the Greeks: a man ridden a horse was stoned not because he deserved it, but because the time required it
Mishna: how they hang the one who was stoned, with a post and a crossbeam; R. Yosei says the beam leans on the wall
The body is untied immediately, and leaving it overnight transgresses a prohibition
Deuteronomy 21:23 is cited: his body shall not remain all night on the tree
Deuteronomy 21:23 is cited: he who is hanged is a curse of God, and you shall bury him
Explains why the hanged man is cursed: he blessed the Name, and the Name is profaned
R. Meir teaches that when a man suffers, the Divine Presence says: I am light-headed from My head, from My arm
If God grieves over the blood of the wicked, all the more so over the blood of the righteous
One who leaves his dead overnight without burying him transgresses a prohibition, and must provide a coffin and shrouds
The executed are not buried in their ancestral plots, but in two court cemeteries, one for the executed by strangling and beheading, one for stoning and burning
The bones are gathered and buried in place after the flesh decays, and relatives come to greet the judges and witnesses
This means that we bear no grudge, since the judgment you gave was true

46b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The relatives of the executed do not observe the full mourning rites, since mourning is only in the heart
A baraita: had the verse said hang him, one would hang first and kill afterward, as the government does
Deuteronomy 21:22 is cited: and he shall be put to death and you shall hang him
He is executed first, then hung; the procedure is delayed until near sunset and one ties while another unties to fulfill the hanging
Deuteronomy 21:22 is cited: a tree, and the baraita asks whether it is detached or attached
The baraita infers that the body may be hung on a detached or attached tree
Deuteronomy 21:23 is cited: for he that is hanged is cursed of God, so the body must be buried
Tannaitic dispute on the verse: R. Yosei holds the tree must be detached and buried, while the Sages disagree
That is, why is this one hung: because he blessed the Name
R. Meir's parable of two twin brothers, one made king and one a robber, to explain why the hanged man is a curse
What does kilelat imply
Abaye and Rava debate whether kilelat means lightness or heaviness, and the Divine Presence says distress
If kilelat is needed for the blasphemer's hanging, how can it also allude to God's distress
Mishna: not only the executed but everyone must be buried on the day of death
R. Yohanan teaches in the name of R. Shimon bar Yohai the source for the duty to bury
From where is the prohibition of leaving the dead unburied derived
Deuteronomy 21:23 is cited: you shall bury him
The prohibition is derived from the verse: you shall bury him
Some say R. Yohanan teaches a hint to burial in the Torah
Deuteronomy 21:23 is cited again: you shall bury him, a hint to burial in the Torah
King Shapur asks Rav Hama where in the Torah burial is required
Rav Hama is silent and gives no reply
Rav Aha bar Yaakov responds that the verse only requires a coffin, and burial is a custom God kept for Moses
I Kings 14:13 and Jeremiah 16:4 are cited to show that burial is a custom
Is burial needed for dignity or for atonement, and what is the practical difference
The practical difference is whether a person who asked not to be buried is honored
Ecclesiastes 7:20 is cited: there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin, so the righteous need atonement
I Kings 14:13 is cited: all Israel shall lament and bury him
If burial atones, the wicked would also need burial to atone, so the case is not a proof
Jeremiah 16:4 is cited: they shall not be lamented or buried, so it is not for atonement
Is the eulogy for the honor of the living or the honor of the dead
The practical difference is whether a person may forbid a eulogy for himself, and whether it excludes heirs
Genesis 23:2 is cited: Abraham came to eulogize Sarah and weep for her
If the eulogy honors the living, Abraham's delay would honor him, while Sarah herself would want it, so the proof is weak
I Kings 14:13 is cited again: all Israel shall lament and bury him
If the eulogy is for the honor of the living, then the honor of the wicked's sons is not for the righteous
Jeremiah 16:4 is cited again: they shall not be lamented or buried
It is not pleasing for the righteous to be honored by the wicked
Jeremiah 34:5 is cited: you shall die in peace, and with the burnings of your fathers the former kings shall be burned for you
If the eulogy honors the living, the point is that Israel should honor the king as they honored his fathers

47a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Scriptural verse and Hezekiah's treatment of his father are cited as a proof.
Asks why Hezekiah's act would matter if eulogy honors the living.
Hezekiah acted for his father's atonement, and the people accepted forgoing their honor for that purpose.
A baraita is cited in which the Tanna asks not to be eulogized in small towns.
Objects that if eulogy honors the living, the baraita's request makes no practical difference.
Replies that the Tanna wanted Israel to be more greatly honored by gatherings in large cities.
A mishna is cited permitting overnight delay of burial for the sake of honor.
Asks whether the honor in the mishna refers to the deceased.
Answers that the honor meant is that of the living relatives, not the deceased.
Asks whether delay for the living's honor is allowed despite the overnight prohibition.
Explains the prohibition applies only where the corpse suffers disgrace, so delay for honor is allowed.
A baraita is cited saying acts for honoring the living do not transgress, since they honor the dead.
Explains the baraita refers to honoring the living, since the dead suffer no disgrace.
Rabbi Natan's baraita: lacking eulogy or burial is a good sign, showing the dead atone through it.
Concludes that eulogy is an honor for the dead, whose lack brings atonement.
Asks why such a rule about burial location is necessary.
Explains that a wicked person is not buried beside a righteous one.
Asks for the scriptural source of the rule that a wicked man is not buried next to a righteous one.
Cites II Kings: a man revived by touching Elisha's bones, shown as support for the rule.
Rav Pappa objects that the revival may have fulfilled Elisha's request for a double portion of spirit.
Rav Aha replies with a baraita that the revived man did not go home, so the revival had another purpose.
Asks where Elisha is shown to have revived a second person, if not for that request.
Rabbi Yoḥanan answers that curing Naaman's leprosy counts as a kind of death revived, as with Miriam.
Explains that as a righteous man is not buried with the wicked, a more wicked man is not buried with a less wicked one.
Objects that four graveyards should then be established, one for each mode of execution.
Answers that tradition holds there are only two graveyards for those executed by the court.
Ulla cites Rabbi Yoḥanan: one who ate forbidden fat, offered for it, then apostatized and returned, remains rejected.
Another version: the same offering stays rejected when the offerer became insane and later recovered.
Explains both cases must be taught: apostasy is self-caused rejection, while insanity is involuntary.
Explains the insanity case must be taught separately, since one cannot cure oneself, unlike an apostate.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita on consecrated items in an idolatrous city, where animal offerings must die.
Asks why those animal offerings must die if the idolaters' death atoned for them.
Abaye objects that one who dies unrepentant in sin does not achieve atonement.
Rav Shemaya's baraita: a priest is defiled only for kin who act as the people do.
Rava objects that one killed in wickedness is not comparable to one who died in wickedness.
Explains that a natural death brings no atonement, while execution atones even without repentance.
Psalm 79 is cited: executed transgressors are called servants, implying their death atones.
Asks what the terms 'Your servants' and 'Your pious ones' mean in the verse.
Explains that 'pious ones' are truly pious, while 'servants' refers to those later executed.
Abaye objects to Rava's comparison of the two cases.

47b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Distinguishes those killed by a foreign government from those executed by a Jewish court regarding atonement.
A mishna is cited: an executed transgressor is not buried in his ancestral plot.
Objects that if execution alone atones, the executed should be buried in ancestral plots.
Replies that both death and burial are required for atonement.
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects from a mishna that mourning rites were not observed, and asks why if burial atones.
Asserts that flesh must also decay before atonement is complete.
A mishna is cited about gathering bones after the flesh decays, supporting that decay is needed.
Rav Ashi holds that mourning and atonement begin at different moments in the burial process.
Asks why flesh decay is needed at all if the atonement is already complete.
Explains that decay was required because Rav's body could not be buried, so dust was taken from it.
Shmuel rules that the people acted properly, since land of eternity is not forbidden.
Cites II Kings: dust was cast on graves, and an analogy to idolatry is drawn to show graves are not forbidden.
Deuteronomy's verse on idols on high hills supports the analogy that a grave attached to land is not forbidden.
Objects from a baraita: one who carved a grave for his father and buried him elsewhere may never be buried there.
Explains that the case concerns a built tomb, not a carved one.
A baraita is cited: a new grave may be used for benefit, but a grave into which one fell is forbidden.
Explains that the same distinction applies here: the case concerns a built tomb.
A baraita on three kinds of graves is cited to show which may be moved and which may not.
Explains that the built tomb is the concern and that a found grave may be moved.
Objects that a grave of a met mitzvah might be different, since its place is not forbidden.
Introduces a dispute about whether one may weave a shroud for a dead person.
Abaye holds it is forbidden while Rava holds it is permitted.
Gives each side's reasoning: Abaye says a prior arrangement makes it a matter, Rava says it does not.
Asks what Abaye's reason is for his ruling.
Abaye derives his ruling from verses on the heifer whose neck is broken, applying it to prior arrangement.
Rava derives his ruling from verses on idolatry, arguing prior arrangement does not make it forbidden.
Asks what Rava's reason is for not deriving the ruling from the heifer.
Begins Rava's answer to why the heifer verse is not his basis for the ruling.

48a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the derivation: the heifer is excluded because it is itself sanctified.
Asks Abaye's reason for not deriving the ruling from idolatry.
Rava answers that a matter is derived from a similar matter, excluding idolatry, with a mnemonic list.
Objects from a baraita on a corpse-carrying cover, asking why the wording of giving and wrapping is needed.
Explains that the wording refers to the ruling of Rav Hisda.
Rav Hisda rules on a cloth set aside for tefillin, distinguishing whether it was wrapped with them.
Gives Abaye's view that prior arrangement is a matter, so the cloth is forbidden even if not wrapped.
A baraita on a soul built for a living person is permitted, but forbidden if added to for a dead person.
Asks what case is meant here, and why the addition matters.
Explains the case where a dead person was cast in, so adding or not adding is both relevant.
Rav Hisda rules, as reported by Rafram, that if one knows the owner the cloth may be removed and used.
A baraita: one who cut a grave for his father and buried him in another may never be buried there.
Explains the ruling there is for the honor of the father, and the same reasoning is sound here.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's clause in the mishna is cited, applying the same rule to hewn stones.
If the reason is honor of the father, fine, but if it is prior arrangement like spun yarn, who holds that view?
A baraita: a new grave may be used for benefit, but forbidden if a person fell into it.
Explains the baraita's wording on casting, and that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view on stillborns is taught separately.
A baraita: a grave may pass from one dead person to another, and the estate passes to heirs.
Asks what case the baraita addresses, and whether the mishna should be read the same way.
The mishna is cited with the same rule that a grave may pass to the dead and the estate to heirs.
A baraita explains how the collection is made: for the dead and for one who collected for the dead.
Asks, by your own reasoning, why not say the latter clause of the mishna instead.
Rabbi Meir holds one may not touch the money until Elijah comes; Rabbi Natan permits a bed-side arrangement.
Abaye and Rava each reconcile the views according to their own principles.
Everyone agrees that a prior arrangement is a matter of concern.
Explains the first tanna holds a grasped item differs when it is seen or not seen, while Rabbi Meir is in doubt.
Therefore one may not touch the items until Elijah comes.
Rabbi Natan is certain the item is grasped, so the bed-side arrangement is permitted.
Rava reconciles on his own principle: all agree that prior arrangement is not a matter.
Explains the first tanna holds the heirs may forgo the honor, while Rabbi Meir is uncertain whether it is waived.
Explains that Rabbi Natan is certain it is not waived, so a bed-side arrangement is allowed.
A baraita: a father and mother who throw vessels on the dead, and others have the duty to save them.

48b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the reason is their bitterness, and that this is what the earlier teaching meant.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling on a bed that touched the dead, with Ula's gloss on the burial shroud.
A baraita: a pouch made for tefillin may not hold money, but one used for tefillin may hold money.
Reinterprets the baraita as a case where the pouch was made and used for tefillin, so money is forbidden.
A baraita: a case of a scribe making a case for a book or tefillin, permitted for ordinary use only if not used for sacred items.
Explains the rule is conditional.
A baraita: gold-covered or hide-covered items are fit or unfit depending on whether the hide came from a clean animal.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that even a clean animal's hide is unfit until it has been worked for its purpose.
Ravina asks Rava whether there is any place where a corpse was cast and cloth was woven for the dead.
Rava answers yes, as in the case of the dead of Harpania, as Mar taught.
Rules that the halakha follows Abaye, though the Rabbis say it follows Rava, and the halakha follows Rava.
A baraita: property of those killed by a king goes to the king, but of those killed by court goes to heirs; Rabbi Yehuda disagrees.
Objects to Rabbi Yehuda from the verse about Naboth's vineyard, noting Naboth had many sons who could inherit.
Rabbi Yehuda replies with a verse that God required the blood of Naboth and of his sons.
The Rabbis respond that the sons were the ones able to inherit from him.
Kings I 21:13 is cited: the verse says Naboth cursed God and the king, supporting property going to the king.
Asks, on the view that property goes to heirs, why the verse says 'and king' at all.
Presses the same point: why say 'God and king' if the heirs view applies.
Explains the words are included only to vent anger.
Kings I 2:28 is cited: Joab fled to the Tent and held the altar horns, supporting the king's claim.
A second verse is cited, Joab saying he will die here, supporting the same reading.
Asks, on the view that property goes to heirs, what difference the matter makes.
Explains it matters for a temporary life, as stated in the verse about Solomon's sentence.
Cites the verse where Benaiah reports Joab's words to the king.
Benaiah relays the king's instruction to Joab, which would make his killing the only remedy.
Kings I 2:31 is cited: the king tells Benaiah to do as he said and bury him.
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, says all the curses David placed on Joab were fulfilled in David's seed.
Samuel II 3:29 is cited with the list of curses, including one with a discharge, a leper, and one who lacks bread.
Kings I 12:18 is cited: King Rehoboam hurried to flee to Jerusalem in a chariot, showing the curse on Rehoboam.
Leviticus 15:9 is cited: every saddle a discharge-sufferer rides becomes unclean, linking to Rehoboam's flight.
Chronicles II 26:16-19 is cited: Uzziah became a leper after entering the Temple to burn incense.
Kings I 15:23 is cited: Asa was diseased in his feet in old age, linking the curse to the king.
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, says Asa was seized by gout.
Mar Zutra asks Rav Naḥman what the affliction is like.
Rav Naḥman answers that it is like a needle in living flesh.
Asks how Rav Naḥman knew what the affliction was like.
Offers three possible explanations: he was attentive, he was taught, or he learned it through the text.
Psalm 25:14 is cited about God's secret being with those who fear him, and a sword fall.
Chronicles II 35:23 is cited: archers shot King Josiah, linking the case to a king's death.
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, says Mikhaya's whole body was reduced to a sieve and he lacked bread.
Kings II 25:30 is cited: Jehoiachin was given a regular daily ration, supporting that a dead man lacking bread can be fed.
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, concludes with a common saying of people.

49a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrates that Yoav was brought before the court and was asked to answer for his conduct.
Asks why Yoav killed Abner.
Yoav replies that Abner was an avenger of blood, since Asahel had been a pursuer.
The court objects that Yoav could have saved Asahel by striking one of his limbs.
Yoav replies that one cannot be saved by a limb now, since the spear struck at the fifth rib.
Samuel II 2:23 is cited: Abner struck Asahel with the butt of his spear at the fifth rib.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the blow was at the fifth rib, where liver and gall hang, so it cannot be saved by a limb.
The narrative moves on to Yoav's killing of Amasa.
Asks why Yoav killed Amasa.
Amasa is answered as a rebel against the kingdom.
Samuel II 20:4 is cited: the king ordered Amasa to summon the men of Judah within three days.
Amasa reports that he was taught a teaching, which he explains by studying it.
Joshua 1:18 is cited: whoever rebels against your word and does not obey shall be put to death.
Explains that one might think it applies even to Torah words, but Scripture limits it to rebels against the kingdom.
Kings I 2:28 is cited: news reached Joab, who had turned after Adonijah and Absalom but did not turn.
Asks what is meant by 'he did not turn'.
Rav Yehuda says Joab sought to turn but did not turn.
Asks why he did not turn.
Rabbi Elazar says the moisture of David still remained.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina says David's astrologers still remained.
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, says David had four hundred children, all handsome and long-haired, who walked at the head of armies.
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana disagrees: were it not for David, Joab would not have waged war.
Continues Rabbi Abba's view: Joab waged war so that David would not be occupied with Torah.
Samuel II 8:15 and 3:26 are cited about David doing justice while Joab was over the army.
Samuel II 3:26 continues: Joab left David and sent messengers after Abner, who brought him back from the cistern.
Asks what 'from the cistern' means.
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana says the cistern and the pit caused Abner to be killed.
Samuel II 3:27 is cited: Joab took Abner aside to speak with him in the gate.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the Sanhedrin judged the case by their verdict.
The court objects to Yoav: why did you kill Asahel, who was a pursuer, when you could have saved him by a limb?
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, says the matter concerns Yoav's own affairs.
Samuel II 3:27 is cited: Joab struck Abner there at the fifth rib.
Rabbi Yoḥanan repeats that the blow was at the fifth rib, where the organs hang.
Kings I 2:32 is cited: the Lord returns Joab's blood on his head, for he struck two men more righteous than he.
Explains that those two men taught the halakha of akhin vrakin, while Joab did not teach it.
Samuel II 20:10 is cited: Amasa was not guarded against the sword in Joab's hand.
Rav says Joab was not suspected, since he was not accused of the murder.
Kings I 2:34 is cited: Joab was buried in his house in the wilderness.
Asks whether his house was a wilderness.
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, says like a wilderness: as a wilderness is open to all and free of theft and sexual sins, so Joab's house was open and free of them.
Chronicles I 11:8 is cited: Joab revived the rest of the city.
Rav Yehuda says even the defeated cities and the stench are sweet to them.
Closing formula of the chapter: the chapter is complete and the judgment concluded.

49b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna lists the four court death penalties and Rabbi Shimon's order, identifying stoning as the mitzva of the stoned.
Rav Huna, in the name of the sages, says that where the sages say 'the way' there is no earlier or later order, except for seven items.
A mishna on seven substances that remove a stain is cited, including the ordering rule for the latter clause.
Rav Pappa, citing Rav, says the four death penalties are also taught in a fixed order, with Rabbi Shimon's dispute limited.
Rav Pappa adds that the Yom Kippur rites likewise follow a fixed order, so an out-of-order act has no effect.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua says the same applies to the order of the daily offering, which is a mere mitzva.
A mishna on the mitzva of chalitza is cited: the court gave the man proper counsel before the rite.
Deuteronomy 25:7-10 is cited with the full procedure of chalitza, the spitting before the elders and the name made known.
Rav Yehuda states that the chalitza is recited with the one who recites it, and the woman removes the shoe and spits.
Asks what the teaching adds, since the mishna already states it.
Explains the mishna teaches that it is a mitzva to be done in this way, and there is no objection in principle.
A baraita is cited: whether the removal of the shoe came before or after the spitting, what was done stands.
Explains that the teaching excludes the priestly garments, where the high priest adds more garments than an ordinary priest.
A baraita is cited: linen breeches must be on the flesh, so nothing is placed before the breeches.
Asks why the tunic is listed before the breeches in the mishna.
Explains the verse itself put the tunic first.
Asks the reason the verse puts it first.
Explains it is first because the tunic covers the whole body, so it is more important.
Opens the comparison of the severity of stoning and burning.
Asserts stoning is more severe, since it is applied to a blasphemer and one who worships idols.
Asks what the severity is, since stoning applies to one who raises his hand against the root of the matter.
Counter-argues that burning is more severe, since it applies to a priest's daughter who profanes her father.

50a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Rabbis hold a married woman goes out to burning, and the verse's wording for a betrothed woman shows stoning.
Asserts stoning is more severe than the sword, since it applies to a blasphemer and one who worships idols.
Asks what the severity is, repeating the earlier point.
Counter-argues that the sword is more severe, since it applies to the men of an apostate city, and asks which strength is greater.
A baraita is cited: those who lead a city astray are stoned.
Stoning is more severe than strangling, since stoning applies to a blasphemer and an idolater.
Asks what the severity is, as previously stated.
Counter-argues that strangling is more severe, since it applies to one who strikes his father and mother, whose honor is compared to God's.
The verse's wording for a betrothed Israelite woman is used to derive that stoning is more severe than strangling.
Stoning is more severe than burning, and burning is more severe than the sword.
Burning is more severe than the sword, since it applies to a priest's daughter who committed adultery.
Asks what the severity is: she profanes her father.
Counter-argues that the sword is more severe, since it applies to the men of an apostate city, and asks what the severity is.
Derives from the repeated wording about the father that stoning and burning are each more severe than the sword.
Strangling is more severe than burning, since it applies to a priest's daughter who committed adultery.
Counter-argues that strangling is more severe, since it applies to one who strikes his father and mother.
Derives from the wording for a married priest's daughter and a married Israelite woman that strangling applies to burning.
Burning is more severe than the sword, and the sword is more severe than strangling, since it applies to an apostate city.
Asks what the severity is, since their property is lost.
Counter-argues that strangling is more severe, since it applies to one who strikes his parents, a comparison to God's honor.
Replies that even so, one who stretches his hand against the root is more severe.
Rabbi Shimon says the same in his own way.
Burning is more severe than stoning, since it applies to a priest's daughter who committed adultery.
Counter-argues that stoning is more severe, since it applies to a blasphemer and an idolater, and asks what the severity is.
Rabbi Shimon holds that of betrothed and married women, the one who goes out goes to burning.
Derives from the verse for a betrothed priest's daughter that a betrothed Israelite goes to burning, not stoning.
Burning is more severe than strangling, since it applies to a priest's daughter who committed adultery.
Asks what the severity is, as stated before.
Counter-argues that strangling is more severe, since it applies to one who strikes his father and mother.
Asks what the severity is, since it is the father and mother of the one who strikes.
Explains the severity is that the strike against father and mother is compared to honor of the Omnipresent.
Derives from the verse for a married priest's daughter that a married Israelite woman goes to burning, not strangling.
Burning is more severe than the sword, since it applies to a priest's daughter who committed adultery.
Asks what the severity is, as stated before.
Counter-argues that the sword is more severe, since it applies to the men of an apostate city, and asks what the severity is.
Asks which strength is greater, the strength of the one who leads astray or of the one who is led astray.

50b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A kal vachomer argues that if strangling is more severe than the sword, burning is more severe, and so on.
Stoning is more severe than strangling, since it applies to a blasphemer and one who worships idols.
Asks what the severity is, as stated before.
Counter-argues that strangling is more severe, since it applies to one who strikes his father and mother.
The verse's wording for a betrothed Israelite woman is used to derive that stoning is more severe than strangling.
Stoning is more severe than the sword, since it applies to a blasphemer and an idolater.
Counter-argues that the sword is more severe, since it applies to the men of an apostate city, and asks what the severity is.
Asks which strength is greater, that of the one who leads astray or the one who is led astray.
Concludes that the strength of the one who leads astray is greater.
A kal vachomer: if strangling is more severe than the sword, stoning is more severe than strangling, so the sword is lighter.
Strangling is more severe than the sword, since it applies to one who strikes his father and mother.
Asks what the severity is, as stated before.
Counter-argues that the sword is more severe, since it applies to the men of an apostate city, and asks what the severity is.
Asks again which strength is greater, the one who leads astray or the one who is led astray.
Concludes that the strength of the one who leads astray is greater.
A baraita is cited: those who lead a city astray are stoned.
Rabbi Shimon says the apostate city is punished by strangling, as Rabbi Yoḥanan often said.
Rabbi Shimon says a betrothed priest's daughter who committed adultery is burned, while others say stoning.
Asks what this teaches the Rabbis.
Explains that for the Rabbis a married woman goes to burning, not a betrothed one, while Rabbi Shimon holds one of each goes to burning.
Asks what the reason is.
Explains that for the Rabbis stoning is more severe, while for Rabbi Shimon burning is, so one condemned to two deaths is judged by the more severe.
Asks what Rabbi Shimon's view is, as taught in a baraita.
Rabbi Shimon's baraita: two general rules are stated about a priest's daughter, and the derivation of which women are included.
Continues the derivation: a married priest's daughter is included in the rule for conspirators against a married Israelite woman.
A baraita on Leviticus 21:9: the verse on a priest's daughter who profanes herself is taught in a particular sense.
Derives that the verse speaks of adultery with a woman of a husband's betrothal, as in the parallel verse about the father.
Asks whether the verse means only to exclude all people when it says she profanes.
Derives that adultery with a betrothed woman is the same in both the father's and the priest's daughter verse.
Concludes the rule applies to a betrothed or married woman and a grown woman, even one who is old.
Asks where the verse teaching a priest's daughter in every case is derived.
Leviticus 21:9 is cited: a priest's daughter in every case is included.

51a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks from where we know which women beyond the priest's daughter are included in the rule.
Leviticus 21:9 is cited: a priest's daughter, even if not a priestess, is burned.
States that one who has relations with her is burned, but her seducers are not burned.
Rabbi Eliezer says her father is burned and her father-in-law is stoned.
Quotes a baraita on the scope of the verse about profaning the Sabbath, concluding she is stoned.
Rava explains this is Rabbi Shimon's view, which holds burning is more severe, so priestly cases get burning.
States what the ruling teaches us.
Asks what the difference is from his own view.
Proposes that the Sabbath is permitted for service, so a priest's daughter is not permitted the Sabbath.
Concludes the case is still to be judged by burning, as taught.
Objects that one might think even a single woman is included, and asks whether the verse says her father only.
Explains that the verse only excludes all people, and what is meant is adultery in her father's house.
Asks why the teaching is specific to a priest's daughter and not an Israelite daughter as well.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Avudimi reports a teaching on the matter.
A verbal analogy from the wording 'coming' and 'coming' is used to derive that the verse teaches the priest's daughter.
Explains Scripture specified the priest's daughter and not the Israelite daughter, to teach this.
Asks from where we know the rule applies to the others, such as the priest's wife.
Scripture says the priest's daughter, even though she is not a priestess, so the rule applies to her.
Explains that because she married them, she is not a priest's daughter and nothing else applies to her.
Proposes that the verse means only the case where she begins now, not one who began from the start.
Leviticus 22:12 is cited: a priest's daughter who marries a stranger.
States that once she has been defiled by a relative of a Levite or an Israelite, she is disqualified.
Leviticus 22:13 is cited: she returns to her father's house as in her youth.
Explains that if she was with him she did not eat, so she is not burned, and this is taught.
A baraita, against Rabbi Meir: a priest's daughter married to an Israelite pays the principal and is burned.
Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute the fines and the death penalty for a priest's daughter married to a disqualified man.
Rabbi Eliezer again says her father is burned and her father-in-law is stoned.
Asks what 'her father and her father-in-law' means, and whether it is from her father or her father-in-law.
Asks why the rule is specific to the priest's daughter, since an Israelite's daughter is also burned and her daughter-in-law stoned.
Explains it means with her father's permission and her father-in-law's permission, and asks whose view this is.
If it follows the Sages, a married woman goes to burning, not a betrothed one.
If it follows Rabbi Shimon, one betrothed and one married woman both go to burning.
If it follows Rabbi Yishmael, a betrothed woman goes to burning and her father-in-law is strangled.
Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Ḥanina that the mishna's proposal is really like the Sages.
Anything below her father's death penalty: a married Israelite woman is strangled, while here the priest's daughter is burned.
Anything above her father's death penalty: a betrothed Israelite woman is stoned, while here her father-in-law is stoned.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects that the mishna teaches nothing above or below, and proposes a different reading.

51b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: States that the view is always like Rabbi Yishmael: the father's death penalty is burning with permission, the father-in-law's stoning, and all others strangling.
Asks what the difference is between both being done by the same means and both being permitted.
Rava explains it is Rabbi Shimon's view, with Rabbi Elazar holding a married woman is like a betrothed one, one rank of penalty each.
Rabbi Ḥanina objects that Rabbi Shimon's view must hold that both cases are burning, not a mix.
Ravina explains the view is that of the Sages, and the reversed order is only a manner of speech.
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabbah son of Avuh citing Rav, rules the halakha follows the teaching Ravin reported from Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Ḥanina.
Rav Yosef says the halakha is reserved for the Messiah, as the matter remains undetermined.
Abaye objects: then the slaughter of sacrifices should not be taught as halakha, but as expounded for reward.
Explains that here too one expounds and receives reward, since they say the halakha is for the Messiah.
Asks why they must say the halakha is for the Messiah.
Explains the sugya is about a matter of halakha, which the Gemara states.
Asks what Rabbi Yishmael's view is, as taught in a baraita.
Leviticus 21:9 is cited: a priest's daughter who commits adultery with a betrothed girl, the verse speaks of a betrothed woman.
Asks whether one says the verse covers only a betrothed woman, or even a married one, and answers by another verse.
Leviticus 20:10 is cited: whoever commits adultery is put to death, so the Israelite daughter is stoned and the priest's daughter burned.
Derives by analogy: as the verse excludes an Israelite daughter for stoning only if betrothed, so too the priest's daughter for burning only if betrothed.
Deuteronomy 19:19 is cited: the conspirator is included with the one who lies with her, in the punishment.
Asks what 'as he planned' means, if the conspirator is already included.
Explains the conspirator is included with the death penalty of the one who lies with her, since the verse says 'to do to his brother, not his sister'.
States the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva, with Rabbi Akiva holding one betrothed and one married woman both go out to burning.
Rabbi Akiva derives from the 'father' verses that adultery with a betrothed woman is included, as the verse says 'even a single woman'.
Rabbi Yishmael objects: as there the girl is betrothed, so here the girl is betrothed.
Rabbi Akiva replies that he expounds 'daughter and daughter', which is his derivation.
Rabbi Yishmael objects that if the verse includes the married woman, it excludes the single one, and asks why this one is excluded from burning.
Rabbi Akiva replies that the verbal analogy excludes the single woman, while 'daughter and daughter' includes the married one.
Rabbi Yishmael holds the verse says 'daughter and daughter', so he withdraws from the verbal analogy.
Explains Rabbi Yishmael's use of 'daughter and daughter', citing a baraita on the distinction among priests' sons and their daughters.
A baraita is cited: the verse distinguishes sons from their daughters, so one might think to divide their daughters, and the verse says 'daughter and daughter'.
Rabbi Akiva derives from Leviticus 21:6 that the priests' daughters are included, citing the verse about offering sacrifices.
Rabbi Yishmael explains that without the verse one would have thought only the sons are included, not their daughters, so it teaches the daughters.

52a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what the verse about her father is needed for, since it is already stated.
A baraita of Rabbi Meir: the verse says she profanes, so that if sacred things are treated as profane, she is treated as a disgrace.
Explains the baraita's reasoning: those treating her with disgrace say cursed is the one who bore her and cursed is the one who raised her.
Rav Ashi asks which view this follows, and says it follows this tanna even for an evil son.
States that the mishna's category of stoning is what is meant here.
Asks why the tanna says this is the mitzva of those stoned.
Explains it was taught because the court's stoning place was two stories high, and since the burning rule was mentioned, the stoning rule was repeated.
The mishna on the mitzva of burning: they sank the offender in dung and wrapped a cord around his neck, then lit a wick thrown into his mouth.
Rabbi Yehuda says if he died in their hands they could not carry out burning, but must open his mouth with pincers and throw the wick in.
Rabbi Elazar son of Tzadok reports a case of a priest's daughter who was burned by a bundle of sticks, since the court was not expert then.
Asks what the wick is.
Rav Matna says the wick is made of the flesh of a limb.
Asks from where we know that burning applies here.
Derives that burning is burning from the congregation of Korah: as there the soul burns and the body remains, so here.
Rabbi Elazar derives burning from the sons of Aaron, as there the soul burns and the body remains.
Asks from where the one who derives from Korah's congregation has this.
Numbers 17:3 is cited: the censers of the sinners, their souls burned while their bodies remain, and that burning is actual burning.
Explains 'for their lives' means they were liable to burning over matters of their lives, as Resh Lakish said.
Psalm 35:16 is cited: the teeth of the Prince of Gehenna gnash over the flattering of Korah's congregation.
Asks from where the one who derives from the sons of Aaron has this.
Leviticus 10:2 is cited: they died before the Lord like a death, and that burning is actual burning.
Explains that 'they died' began inside, so it is like a death, as taught.
A baraita of Abba Yosei son of Dostai: two fiery threads came out of the Holy of Holies, split into four, and burned them.
Objects that it is written 'and it consumed them, and not their garments', so the burning was not actual burning.
Derives from the burnt cows that burning is actual burning, as there, so here.
Argues that one should learn from a sinning man instead, or rather from the burnt cows, which serve for generations.
Asks why the one who derives from Korah's congregation does not derive from the sons of Aaron.
Explains that the sons of Aaron's case was actual burning, so one learns from it.
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabbah son of Avuh, says the verse 'love your neighbor as yourself' means the death must be clear and good.
Asks why there is need for the verbal analogy, if the matter is already established.
Explains that without the verbal analogy one would think burning of soul and body remaining is not burning at all.
Explains the 'love your neighbor' verse teaches that one may bind bundles of sticks to burn a calf, as taught.
Recounts that Moses and Aaron walked ahead, and Nadab and Abihu followed, with all Israel after them.
Nadab says to Abihu: when will these two elders die, so that you and I may lead the generation.
The Holy One, blessed be He, replies: who will bury whom?
Rav Pappa says this is what people say: the camels are many, the old men who lead astray must be guided.
Rabbi Eliezer says the same.

52b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An analogy: a scholar is like a golden pitcher, then silver, then clay that once broken cannot be repaired.
Relates the case of a priest's daughter who committed adultery, whom Rav Ḥama son of Tuvia burned with bundles of sticks.
Rav Yosef says he erred in two matters: in Rav Mattana's ruling and in a baraita.
Deuteronomy 17:9 is cited: in the days when there is a priest there is judgment, and when there is no priest there is no judgment.
Rabbi Elazar son of Tzadok relates a case of a priest's daughter who committed adultery.
Rav Yosef says it was a Sadducee court, which said this to them and they answered him.
Objects with a baraita: Rabbi Elazar recounts that as a child he was carried on his father's shoulders when a priest's daughter was burned, and he was told he was a child.
Replies that testimony from a child is not admissible proof.
Explains there were two incidents, and the first court said something that the later court did not accept because it was not expert.
Mishna on capital punishment by decapitation: the sword is used as the state does, but Rabbi Yehuda says it is disgraceful and the block and axe are used.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda tells the Sages he knows death by decapitation is disgraceful, but the Torah says not to follow the practices of the nations.
The Rabbis object: since the sword is in the Torah, we should not derive from the nations, but how can we burn kings if the Torah forbids the practices of the Amorites?
Explains that since burning is written in the Torah in Jeremiah, we do not derive it from the nations, and the same applies to the sword.
Notes that we learned in another chapter the list of those executed: the murderer and the people of the apostate city.
Asks how we know the murderer is put to death by the sword, since the apostate city is explicitly so.
A baraita on Exodus 21:20 and Leviticus 26:25: a sword brings vengeance and the covenant, so the murderer is punished by the sword.
Objects that the verse could mean a dagger, which is concealed, and the verse says 'by the sword'.
Objects that the verse may mean a sword struck with a club, or a dagger.
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabbah son of Avuh, says Leviticus 19:18 shows that a clear death is good, so the death should be quick.
Asks how we know that a free man who kills a slave is punished by the sword, while a slave is strangled.
Argues by a fortiori that this would follow if strangling is lighter, but not if it is harsher.
Asks what can be said on the view that strangling is harsher.
Deuteronomy 21:9 is cited: the verse about the blood of the innocent is compared to the heifer whose neck is broken, so the killer is punished by the sword.
Derives that as there the sword is used from the neck, so here the sword is used from the neck.
Counter-argues that the mattock is used from the back of the neck, so here the mattock is used from the back of the neck.
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabbah son of Avuh, again cites Leviticus 19:18 that a clear death is good.
Mishna on strangling: they sank the offender in dung to his knees, placed a stiff cloth around his neck, and pulled it from both sides until he died.
The Sages teach from Leviticus 20:10 and 20:2 that the verses limit adultery to a man and a married woman, with death by strangling.
Asks whether the verse means strangling or any of the death penalties stated in the Torah.
Rabbi Yoshiyah says whenever a death penalty is stated without specification, one may only ease it, not make it harsher.
Rabbi Yonatan says the rule is not that it is lighter, but that any death penalty stated without specification is strangling.
Rabbi says death by heaven and death by man are both stated, and death by heaven leaves no mark, so death by man leaves no mark either.
Objects that burning should be inferred since the verse says a priest's daughter by burning, implying burning is not for every case.

53a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how Rabbi Yonatan's reasoning fits, and from where Rabbi Yoshiyah derives the penalty.
Rava says strangling exists because the four death penalties are learned by tradition, so the sword is not the only one.
Explains that the point is not that strangling is light, but the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages.
Rabbi Zeira objects to Abaye: the other stoned offenders are not written with stoning, so from where do they learn 'die they shall die' or 'their blood on them'.
A baraita on Numbers 35:21: 'the smiter is a murderer', so he is put to death by any means, and not only the one written.
Rav Aḥa of Difti asks Ravina what is still difficult if they learn from 'die they shall die'.
Objects: if the case is a married woman, then why learn from a wizard's verse, if the verse on stoning is read differently?
Compares Leviticus 20:27 to the verse on betrothed women stoned, implying a married woman is not stoned.
Objects that the one who strikes his father and mother should be learned from the verse on a wizard, and the other stoned offenders from the verse on a married woman.
The mishna lists the stoned offenders: one who has relations with his mother, father's wife, daughter-in-law, a male, an animal, and others.
The mishna says one who has relations with his mother is liable for her, and Rabbi Yehuda says only for the mother.
The mishna says one who has relations with his father's wife is liable for her and the wife of a man, and likewise for a daughter-in-law and a wife of a man.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says if his mother was not fit for his father, he is liable only for the mother.
Asks what is meant by 'not fit for him'.
Explains that if it means those liable to karet or the court's death, the Sages hold she is not fit for him, and the Sages hold no betrothal applies.
Rabbi Yehuda holds like Rabbi Akiva, that betrothal does not take effect with those liable for prohibitions.
Rav Oshaya objects: a prohibited mitzva and a prohibited holiness release the widow from levirate marriage, but do not take her in levirate marriage.

53b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Prohibitions of a mitzva are rabbinic, meaning the rule is a matter of the Sages' words.
Asks why they are called prohibitions of a mitzva.
Explains that a mitzva is to listen to the Sages, and that the prohibition of holiness applies to a widow to a High Priest, and a divorcee or halutza to an ordinary priest.
Repeats the question of why they are called prohibitions of holiness.
Leviticus 21:6 is cited: they shall be holy to their God, which grounds the prohibition of holiness.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda switches the terms, and here levirate is required.
Objects: if Rabbi Yehuda holds like Rabbi Akiva, those liable for prohibitions are like those liable for karet, and so the Tanna kamma would not hold this.
When Rabbi Yitzḥak came, he taught it as we learned in the mishna.
The mishna: Rabbi Yehuda says one is liable only for the mother.
Asks what the reason is.
Abaye explains that the verse says 'your mother is she', so one is liable for the mother but not for the father's wife.
Objects: from now on, the verse about the father's wife also says 'the nakedness of your father', so one is liable for the father's wife but not for the mother.
Explains the verse is referenced here and excludes the other case, so for the mother who is the father's wife, one is not liable at all.
Objects that for the Sages too the verse says 'your mother is she', so it must be needed for the case of Rav Shishah son of Rav Idi, which also applies to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Aḥa son of Rav Eika says the verse refers to a single nakedness, so one is liable for one prohibition, not two.
Objects: the verse on a son's wife also says 'the nakedness of her', so why does the mishna say one is liable for both, if Rabbi Yehuda does not dispute.
Explains that since it is one body, even though there are two prohibitions, the verse says 'her nakedness' here too.
Rava explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds 'the nakedness of your father' is the father's wife, and derives it by a verbal analogy, including the mother who is the father's wife.
Leviticus 18:7 is cited again: 'the nakedness of your mother', that she is your mother so one is liable for her, and not for the father's wife.

54a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita taught in accordance with Rava's view.
Leviticus 20:11 is cited: a man who lies with his father's wife, the word 'man' excludes a minor.
Notes the wording implies both his father's wife who is his mother and one who is not, and asks where the other case comes from.
Leviticus 20:11 is cited: the nakedness of the father is uncovered, drawn near to derive by a verbal analogy.
Asks whether 'they shall surely die' means stoning, or any of the death penalties in the Torah.
Derives by verbal analogy from the wording on blood and the wizard, so the punishment is stoning.
Asks where the warning for this prohibition comes from.
Leviticus 18:7 is cited: the nakedness of your father, that is the father's wife, as the warning.
Asks whether it means the father's wife, or the nakedness of the father itself.
The phrase 'the nakedness of your father' is compared to 'the nakedness of his father' and shown to concern marriage.
Asks again where we learn about the mother who is not the father's wife, and the father's wife who is not the mother.
Scripture teaches that the warning covers the mother who is not the father's wife, as it does the mother who is.
Compares the warning and punishment for the mother and the father's wife by analogy.
Concludes that the verse makes the mother who is not the father's wife like the mother who is, in punishment as well.
Says the verse 'your mother is she' makes one liable for the mother, but not for the father's wife.
The Sages hold the phrase 'the nakedness of your father' is literal, and this verse is one.
Leviticus 18:22 is cited: 'from a male' is derived to make one liable twice, as Rav Yehuda said.
Rav Yehuda says a gentile who lies with his father is liable twice, and one who lies with his father's brother is liable twice.
Rava says Rav Yehuda's ruling is reasonable for an Israelite who sinned unwittingly, and the word 'gentile' is a fine expression.
Objects: if a gentile is meant literally, what is his penalty? He is killed for two, and it was taught so too.
A baraita: one who lies with his father is liable twice, and one who lies with his father's brother is liable twice.
Some say this is not like Rabbi Yehuda, and some say even according to Rabbi Yehuda.
A kal vachomer: if one who lies with his father's brother, who is more distant, is liable twice, then with his father, all the more so.
Explains the dispute is between Abaye and Rava: one holds punishments are not from the law, and the other holds they are.
Asks from where the Sages derive the warning for the father's wife.
Explains it is derived from the verse 'the nakedness of your father's wife you shall not uncover'.
Rabbi Yehuda says the verse is needed for the warning to the father's wife after death.
The Sages derive it from the end of the verse, which says 'the nakedness of your father'.
Rabbi Yehuda needs the verse for the warning about the father's wife, making one liable for the wife of a father or a man.
Objects that the mishna teaches one who lies with his father's wife is liable for her and for another's wife, and Rabbi Yehuda does not dispute.
Abaye says Rabbi Yehuda disputes in the baraita, and the Sages hold the penalty for the father's wife after death.
Asks from where the Sages derive the penalty for the father's wife after death, since Rabbi Yehuda uses a verbal analogy.
The Sages reply that the verse excludes the father's wife for a verbal analogy, but they derive the penalty for the father's wife after death from it.
Asks from where the Sages derive the penalty for the mother who is not the father's wife.
Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi says the verse 'your mother is she' makes the mother who is not the father's wife like the mother who is.
Abaye explains the verse begins with the daughter-in-law and ends with the son's wife, to show they are the same.
The mishna on bestiality: one who lies with a male, an animal, or a woman who brings an animal is stoned, and the animal is stoned too.
Asks from where we know the law for a male.
A baraita on Leviticus 20:13: the verse teaches a male, minor or adult, and that the penalty is stoning by verbal analogy with the wizard.

54b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: We have heard the penalty; asks where the warning for the prohibition comes from.
Leviticus 18:22 is cited: 'you shall not lie with a male as with a woman', teaching the warning for the one who lies.
Asks where the warning for the one who is lain with comes from.
Deuteronomy 23:18 and Kings I 14:24 are cited: there shall be no sodomite of Israel, and sodomy was in the land.
Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva dispute whether the verse is needed, and the verse 'do not lie with a male' is read with the female case.
Asks from where we know the prohibition on lying with an animal, as the Rabbis taught.
Leviticus 20:15 is cited: whoever lies with an animal, the word 'man' excludes a minor, whether large or small.
Asks whether the animal case is stoned, or punished by any of the death penalties in the Torah.
Derives by verbal analogy from 'you shall kill' and 'killing kill him' that the penalty is stoning.
Asks how we know that the penalty applies both to the one who lies and the one who is lain with.
Exodus 22:18 is cited: whoever lies with an animal shall die, so the verse covers both cases, and a warning is taught from Leviticus 18:23.
Deuteronomy 23:18 and Kings I 14:24 are cited again to show the warning for the one who lies with a male.
Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva dispute whether the verse 'you shall not give your lying' is needed, with Rabbi Akiva saying it is not.
Rabbi Abbahu says that for one who lies with a male and brings a male upon him, Rabbi Yishmael makes him liable twice, Rabbi Akiva once.
Rabbi Abbahu says that for one who lies with an animal and brings an animal upon him, Rabbi Yishmael makes him liable twice, Rabbi Akiva once.
Abaye says that even by Rabbi Yishmael's view, one is liable only once, since the verse about holiness is written about men.
Asks, if Rabbi Yishmael's warning for the one who is lain with is taught, from where he derives it.
Exodus 22:18 is cited: the Torah uses the word 'lies' for the one who is lain with, so he is punished and warned like the one who lies.
Rabbi Abbahu says that by Rabbi Akiva one is liable twice, and by Rabbi Yishmael only once.
Both views are the same: the verse about holiness is said of both.
Abaye says even by Rabbi Yishmael one is liable twice, since the verse says 'whoever lies with an animal'.
Explains by the wording that the Torah uses 'lies' for the one who is lain with, making him punished and warned.
Whether Rabbi Abbahu or Abaye, by Rabbi Yishmael one who lies with a male and brings one upon him is liable three times, and by Rabbi Akiva twice.
A baraita: the Sages taught that a male is not treated like a minor, but an animal is treated the same whether small or large.
Asks what is meant by 'not treated like a minor, as an adult'.
Rav says the act of a minor is not valid unless he is at least nine years old, like a nine-year-old.
Shmuel says the act of a minor is not valid unless he is at least three years old, like a three-year-old.
Explains the dispute: Rav holds whatever is present in the one who lies is present in the one who is lain with, and whatever is absent is absent in both.
Shmuel holds that the verse about women is written, so a minor is not included.
A baraita agrees with Rav: a male nine years and a day old.

55a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: States that one who lies with an animal is liable whether in the usual manner or not, and a woman who brings an animal upon herself is liable likewise.
Rav Naḥman son of Rav Ḥisda explains that a woman has two modes of intercourse, while an animal has only one mode.
Rav Pappa objects: a woman's usual manner is for intercourse, so why hold her liable, while an animal's manner is not usual, so why hold one liable for every orifice?
A baraita: a male nine years and a day old, whether he lies with an animal in the usual or unusual manner, is liable.
Repeats the baraita on the animal and the woman who brings an animal upon herself, liable either way.
Ravina asks Rava: what about one who penetrates a male, and what about penetrating an animal?
Rava explains that the verse on the father's sister is not needed for the analogy, and the animal is subject to court death penalties, so why need it.
Explains the verse of the animal is needed to make it a case of the death penalty by the court, and the verse is used for interpretation.
Asks Rav Aḥadvoi son of Ami what the law is for one who penetrates himself, a case Rav Ashi asks Rav Sheshet about.
Rav Kabestan and Rav Ashi explain the difficulty: a case is found only in a dead person's penetration, which is exempt by one view and liable by the other.
On the view that one is liable, one is liable for both the one who lies and the one who is lain with.
Asks Rav Sheshet whether a gentile who lies with an animal requires disgrace and penalty, or whether the mere offense suffices.
Rav Sheshet answers: we learned that trees neither eat nor drink, yet the Torah says destroy and burn, since the animal leads people astray, and a fortiori.
Objects: then a gentile who worships his animal should be forbidden, and the animal should be killed, but that is not so.
Abaye explains the disgrace is greater in one case and smaller in the other, so the rules differ.
Explains that trees have no great disgrace, and the Torah's statement about burning concerns living beings, as the verse shows mercy for them.
Rava says the Torah states that an animal that benefits from the transgression is killed, while trees do not benefit, so the rule about living beings is distinct.
Cites a baraita: the animal must not pass in the street, so people do not say this is the one by whom the man was stoned; objects that this seems to be the same point.

55b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Infers from the latter clause that the first clause means calamity without shame, a gentile with an animal.
Rejects the inference: the first clause may teach that shame alone suffices, with calamity meaning transgression.
Rav Hamnuna asks whether an animal unwittingly mated with must die when there is shame but no execution calamity.
Rav Yosef cites a Nidda mishna on a three-year-old girl and the animal and forbidden-relations rulings as support.
Objects that a minor's case has shame without calamity yet the mishna still orders execution, so shame suffices.
Replies that calamity is present since she sinned deliberately, and the Merciful One pitied only her, not the animal.
Rava brings a proof from the next mishna on a nine-year-old boy and his yevama.
The mishna continues: an animal and forbidden relations are stoned or executed based on the man's intercourse.
Objects that the animal case has shame without calamity, yet the mishna has the animal stoned, so shame suffices.
Replies the same way: intentional sin supplies calamity, and the Merciful One pitied the man, not the animal.
Offers a resolution from another mishna: the animal is killed so it is not paraded, implying a shame-only case.
Rejects this: the latter clause may be calamity plus shame, the first calamity alone; the dilemma stays unresolved.
Mishna: one who blasphemes is liable only if he pronounces God's name; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha disagrees.

56a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: witnesses name the blasphemy by an appellation, the eldest repeats it privately, and judges tear their garments.
Baraita: a blasphemer is liable only if he curses the divine name using the name itself.
Shmuel derives this rule from the repeated phrase 'blasphemes the name' in Leviticus 24:16.
Asks from where we know that the word nokev means cursing rather than something else.
Balaam's 'how shall I curse' and the prohibition 'you shall not curse God' show nokev means cursing.
Objects that nokev may mean making a hole, citing the verse of drilling a hole in a lid.
The prohibition on destroying God's name, in Deuteronomy, is cited to support the hole-making reading.
Replies that liability needs name-with-name, which a hole-making act cannot involve, so nokev means cursing.
Objects that one can pierce one divine name with another, or with a knife point, so name-with-name is possible.
Suggests nokev means uttering the ineffable name, citing Numbers 1:17 and the fear-of-God verse in Deuteronomy.
Replies that name-with-name excludes that reading, and a positive commandment does not count as a prohibition.
Offers an alternative proof from Leviticus 24:11 that the verb vayyikkov means cursing.
Objects that perhaps one is liable only if he both made the nokev and cursed God.
Replies that the verse says bring out the one who cursed, not the nokev and the cursor, so it is one act.
Baraita: 'ish ish' includes gentiles, who are liable for blessing God's name and executed only by the sword.
Objects that this is derived from the earlier verse, and asks why not derive it from there instead.
Derives it from Genesis 2:16, where the Lord means the blessing of God's name.
Rav Yitzhak Nappaha holds the verse is needed only to include gentiles cursing by appellations, following Rabbi Meir.
Baraita asks why 'ish ish' is needed when the verse already says whoever blasphemes the name shall die.
Suggests one might think only the ineffable name is punishable, so appellations would not be included.
Derives from 'ish' that appellations are included too, which is Rabbi Meir's view.
The Rabbis hold death for the ineffable name and warning only for appellations.
Contradicts Rav Yitzhak Nappaha: Rav Meyasha holds a gentile is liable for appellations even by the Rabbis' view.
Cites Leviticus 24:16, 'convert as well as homeborn', to show the name-with-name condition applies only to Jews.
Asks what Rabbi Meir does with the phrase 'as the convert, as the native', since it is not needed for the sword case.
Gentiles are executed by the sword, not stoning, and the phrase is included to teach this.
Asks the same about Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, who follows the Rabbis, regarding the 'as the convert' phrase.
For gentiles the name-with-name condition is not required, which the phrase teaches.
Asks why the verse needs 'ish ish' if not to derive gentile liability for appellations.
No law is derived from it; the Torah simply spoke in ordinary human idiom.
Baraita: the descendants of Noah were commanded seven mitzvot, including courts, blessing God, idolatry, and not eating a limb from a live animal.

56b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Hananya ben Gamla, Rabbi Hideka and Rabbi Shimon add blood from a live animal, castration and sorcery to Noahide duties.
Rabbi Yosei: every sorcery listed in the sorcery passage is forbidden to a descendant of Noah.
Cites the Deuteronomy verses on sorcery and the abominations of the nations as support for Rabbi Yosei.
