Rabbi Elazar: diverse kinds are forbidden to Noahides only in breeding animals and grafting trees, not in wearing or sowing.
Asks from where the Noahide commandments are derived.
Rabbi Yohanan derives them from Genesis 2:16-17, God commanding the man about the garden trees.
Homiletically, 'commanded' alludes to courts of judgment, supported by Genesis 18:19.
'The Lord' alludes to blessing God's name, supported by Leviticus 24:16 on one who blasphemes the name.
'God' alludes to idolatry and 'the man' to bloodshed, supported by Exodus 20:2 and Genesis 9:6.
'Saying' alludes to forbidden relations, supported by Jeremiah 3:1.
'Of every tree' alludes to robbery and 'you may freely eat' to the prohibition on eating a limb from a live animal.
Rav Yitzhak taught the two expositions in reverse order when he came to Babylonia: commanded means idolatry, God means courts.
Asks how we know 'commanded' alludes to idolatry, given that 'God' clearly alludes to judges.
Rav Hisda and Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi each derive idolatry from a verse using the root tzav.
Asks what practical difference lies between the two sources.
The difference: a gentile who made an idol but did not worship it is liable under one view only once he worships it.
Rava objects: is there anyone who holds a gentile who made an idol but did not bow is liable, given a baraita?
Rav Pappa replies that the baraita excludes embracing and kissing an idol, so no proof follows.
Asks what kind of embracing and kissing of an idol is meant.
If done in the idol's standard manner it is capital; the exclusion covers doing it in a non-standard manner.
Asks whether the descendants of Noah were commanded to establish courts.
Objects with a baraita stating that courts were given at Marah, so Noahides were not commanded to establish them.
Judgment, Shabbat and honoring parents were given at Marah, with Rav Yehuda reading 'as the Lord commanded you'.
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, holds Noahides had courts, and Marah added only the details of procedure.
Asks how the baraita can say God added judgment if it was already a Noahide commandment.
Rava: Marah added only the halakhot of fines.
Asks why the baraita then does not say that more halakhot of judgment were added.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov: Marah added the requirement to establish courts in every province and city.
Asks whether the descendants of Noah were not commanded in this matter at all.
Objects with a baraita stating Noahides were commanded to establish courts in every province and city like Israel.
Rava: this is the Menashe school tanna, who swapped out the dalet-kaf mitzvot for samekh-kaf.
The school of Menashe taught seven Noahide mitzvot: idolatry, sexual sins, bloodshed, robbery, live-animal limb, castration, diverse kinds.
Rabbi Yehuda: Adam was commanded only about idolatry.
Supports Rabbi Yehuda from Genesis 2:16, 'the Lord God commanded the man'.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira adds blessing God's name, and some say also courts of judgment.
Asks whose opinion Rav Yehuda's exposition of Rav follows, that cursing, idolatry and courts are included.
Rav's exposition: I am God, so do not curse me, do not exchange me, let my fear be upon you.
It follows the view of those who say the verse includes these prohibitions and courts.
Objects: if the school of Menashe expounds 'commanded' homiletically, why not include cursing and courts; if not, where do the seven come from?
The Menashe school does not expound 'commanded'; each mitzva is written separately in the Torah, such as idolatry and sexual sins.

57a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites Genesis 6:11, 'the earth was corrupt before God', as the source for the Noahide prohibitions.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael: wherever corruption is stated it means only licentiousness and idolatry.
Supports this with Genesis 6:12 on corrupting one's way, and Deuteronomy 4:16 on corrupting oneself with idols.
The other tanna'im explain that the verse only exposes the behavior of Noah's generation.
Bloodshed is derived from Genesis 9:6, 'whoever sheds the blood of man'.
For the other tanna'im the verse only sets the death penalty for Noahides, not the prohibition itself.
Robbery is derived from Genesis 9:3, read by Rabbi Levi as ownerless herbs of the field.
The other tanna'im read that verse as permitting the eating of meat.
Eating a limb from a living animal is derived from Genesis 9:4, 'only flesh with its life'.
The other tanna'im read that verse as permitting limbs of living creeping things.
Castration is derived from Genesis 9:7, 'be fruitful and multiply'.
For the other tanna'im that verse is only a blessing, not a commandment.
Diverse kinds is derived from Genesis 6:20, 'after their kind'.
The other tanna'im hold that the separation in the ark was only for companionship.
Rav Yosef: a Noahide is executed for three mitzvot, given by the mnemonic gimmel-shin-reish: sexual sins, bloodshed, and blessing God's name.
Rav Sheshet objects: why derive the others from the bloodshed verse, and if by inclusion, why not idolatry too?
Rav Sheshet's own version: a Noahide is executed for four mitzvot, the three listed plus idolatry.
Asks whether a Noahide is executed for idolatry, citing a baraita that only a prohibition with no death penalty is implied.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: their prohibition is their death penalty, since the Torah prescribes execution for them.
Rav Huna, Rav Yehuda and Rav's students: a Noahide is executed for violating any of the seven mitzvot.
Asks whether a Noahide is executed for robbery, citing a baraita that treats robbery as prohibited for gentiles but not for Jews.
The tanna taught 'prohibited' in the first clause because the second clause uses 'permitted', so liability is not implied.
Objects that elsewhere a capital matter is taught with the word liable, so the baraita should have used that word here.
Using 'prohibited' and 'permitted' fits here, since a Jew may not rescue a gentile from a pit but also may not kill him.
Asks what actions similar to robbery the baraita refers to.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov: a laborer in a vineyard who eats the fruit is like a robber.
Asks when the laborer eats: if at harvest it is permitted, and if not, it is full robbery and not novel.
Rav Pappa: the baraita teaches robbing less than a peruta's worth.
Asks why it is prohibited for a gentile to rob a Jew, since a Jew would forgive such a small debt.
The owner forgives later, but the robber causes distress at the time of the robbery, so it is a transgression.
Objects: if so, what is new in a gentile robbing a gentile of a small sum, since they do not forgive?
Rav Aha son of Rav Ika: the case is withholding a hired laborer's wages, which is less obvious than other robbery.
Asks what action is similar to intercourse with a captive beautiful woman that the baraita means.
Rav Dimi cites Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Hanina: a Noahide who gives his maidservant to his slave and sleeps with her is executed for it.
The Gemara notes the baraita does not teach that a Noahide is liable for actions similar to bloodshed.
Abaye: if a baraita teaches it, it accords with the opinion of Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul.
Baraita: a pursuer who could be stopped by maiming one limb but is killed instead is the view of Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul.

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A descendant of Noah is executed for killing even in a case where the victim is attacking, as with a Jew.
Book of Aggadot: a Noahide is executed on one judge, one witness and without forewarning; Rabbi Yishmael adds fetuses.
Asks from where these halakhot are derived.
Rav Yehuda derives the one-judge rule from Genesis 9:5, where the Hebrew 'I will require' is singular.
'At the hand of every animal' shows execution without forewarning, since an animal cannot forewarn.
'At the hand of man' with the singular 'I' shows one witness suffices, and 'every man' excludes women as witnesses.
'At the hand of his brother' shows the testimony of a relative is valid.
Rabbi Yishmael: a Noahide is executed even for killing a fetus.
Asks what the reason is for Rabbi Yishmael's view.
Genesis 9:6 'ba'adam' homiletically means 'in a person', which is a fetus in its mother's womb.
The school of Menashe, the first tanna, holds all Noahide death penalties are strangulation.
Reads the verse 'in a person his blood shall be shed' homiletically, as shedding blood inside the body.
Explains that bloodshed inside a person's body is strangulation.
Rav Hamnuna objects: a Noahide woman must establish courts, since Abraham commanded his household per Genesis 18:19.
Abraham commanded his sons to do justice, and his household to give charity, since tzedek can mean charity.
Rav Avya asks why a female Noahide who killed should not be executed, since the text says 'man' not 'woman'.
Rav Pappa: Rav Yehuda derives from 'one who sheds the blood of a person' that murder applies to either sex.
Rav Avya asks why a female Noahide who committed adultery should not be executed, since Genesis 2:24 says 'a man'.
Rav Yehuda: 'they shall be one flesh' at the verse's end combines men and women, so the law applies to both.
Baraita: 'no one' in Leviticus 18:6 includes gentiles in the prohibition of forbidden relations.
Asks whether this is derived from there, the Genesis 2:16 verse instead.
Genesis 2:16 'the Lord God commanded the man' alludes to forbidden sexual relations, per the earlier discussion.
The Genesis verse refers to gentile women, while the baraita concerns Jewish women: a gentile with a married Jewish woman is liable.
Asks what halakha is taught by judging such a gentile by Jewish law.
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh: it teaches a Sanhedrin trial, two witnesses and forewarning.
Asks why the law for a gentile with a Jewish woman would then be less strict than for a gentile woman.
Rabbi Yohanan: the baraita is about a gentile with a betrothed Jewish woman, since gentiles recognize only marriage.
Asks whether gentiles with a married Jewish woman are judged by their law, given a baraita prescribing strangulation.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzhak: a woman who entered the canopy but was not yet intimate is married by Jewish law only.
Rabbi Hanina: gentiles can have a married woman who has been intimate, but not one only under the canopy.
Baraita in line with Rabbi Yohanan: a capital forbidden relation applies to Noahides, and a non-capital one does not, per Rabbi Meir.
The Rabbis: many forbidden relations for which Israel does not execute still apply to Noahides.
A gentile with forbidden Jewish women is judged by Jewish law, and so only the betrothed woman case is an exception.
Asks whether the case of a woman who entered the canopy but was not intimate should also be counted.
The tanna is of the school of Menashe, who holds all Noahide death penalties are strangulation, as is the Jewish penalty for adultery.
Asks whether Rabbi Meir holds that any capital forbidden relation applies to Noahides, citing a baraita on converts.

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Sets up the case: conceived as a gentile but born after conversion, so only maternal kinship applies.
Asks how the principle works out in practice.
Gives concrete cases of a convert's marriages to half siblings and relatives, and which must be divorced.
Rabbi Meir says divorce; the Sages say the marriage may be maintained.
Rabbi Meir's rule: relatives forbidden through maternal kinship must be divorced, paternal kinship may stay.
States that the convert may marry his brother's wife and other relatives forbidden to a born Jew.
Explains that the phrase including the father's wife is added to cover her case.
A gentile who married a mother and daughter: one may be kept, but the mother-in-law question is disputed.
Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction: the two baraitas cite Rabbi Meir according to different tannaim.
Baraita citing the verse about a man leaving his father and mother.
Rabbi Eliezer's position: father and mother refer to the parents' sisters.
Rabbi Akiva's position: father refers to the father's wife and mother literally to the mother.
Derives prohibitions from the verse's phrases: cleaving, his wife, and one flesh.
Explains that one flesh excludes animals, which cannot become one flesh with a person.
Restates Rabbi Eliezer's position that father means the father's sister.
Asks why father should not be read literally.
The prohibition is derived from the phrase about cleaving, not to a male.
Asks why father should not refer to the father's wife.
The phrase to his wife excludes another man's wife.
Asks why not read it as the father's wife after the father's death.
By analogy to mother, who is forbidden through relation rather than marriage, so is father.
Rabbi Eliezer reads mother as the mother's sister.
Asks why mother should not be read literally.
The phrase to his wife excludes another's wife, and mother is the father's wife.
Asks why not read it as mother after the father's death.
By analogy to father, neither term is interpreted literally.
Rabbi Akiva's reading: father refers to the father's wife.
Asks why father should not be read literally.
The prohibition is derived from the cleaving phrase, not from the literal father.
Objects: if so, the father's wife would also be derived from to his wife.
Explains that to his wife refers to the father's widow, after the death.
Rabbi Akiva says mother refers literally to his mother.
Objects that this prohibition is derived from the phrase to his wife instead.
For Rabbi Akiva, mother refers to a woman his father raped, who was never his wife.
Asks what the dispute between the two tannaim rests on.
States Rabbi Eliezer's view on the point of dispute.

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates that father and mother terms are interpreted alike, and only in the case of sisters.
Rabbi Akiva prefers reading father as the father's wife, excluding the father's sister.
Brings a proof from Amram marrying his aunt Jochebed in support of the view.
Objects that she may have been his maternal aunt, so the proof fails.
Replies that she was his paternal aunt, upholding the proof.
Cites Abraham's words about Sarah, inferring that a mother's daughter is forbidden.
Objects that Sarah was actually his brother's daughter, so the proof fails.
Explains Abraham's words as a relationship through the father only, not literal sisterhood.
Cites a baraita on Adam and Cain marrying sisters, inferring that it was once permitted.
States Rav Huna's view that a gentile may marry his daughter.
Cites the Adam and Cain reasoning as support for Rav Huna's view.
Reports the other version: Rav Huna prohibits a gentile from marrying his daughter.
Cites Adam's abstention from marrying his daughter as evidence for the prohibition.
Rav Hisda: a Canaanite slave may marry his mother and his daughter.
Explains that the slave left gentile status but did not enter Jewish status.
Reports Rabbi Hanina's ruling on a gentile who assigns a maidservant to his slave and sleeps with her.
Asks from when the maidservant counts as the slave's mate.
Rav Nachman: from the time she is called by her owner's name.
Asks from when she is released from the slave's relationship.
Rav Huna: from the time she uncovers her head in the marketplace.
Rabbi Hanina: a gentile who has atypical intercourse with his wife is liable.
Cites Genesis 2:24's cleaving as indicating only natural intercourse.
Rava objects: is there an act a Jew is exempt from but a gentile is liable for?
Rava narrows the ruling to one's own wife, preserving the view and exempting adultery with another's wife.
Explains the distinction through the verse's wording, to his wife and not another's wife.
Rabbi Hanina: a gentile who strikes a Jew is liable to the death penalty.
Cites Moses killing the Egyptian who struck a Hebrew as support.
Rabbi Hanina: slapping a Jew's cheek is like slapping the Divine Presence's cheek.
Cites Proverbs 20:25, read homiletically as striking the Holy One's cheek.
Gives a mnemonic for the Reish Lakish statements that follow.
Reish Lakish: one who raises a hand against another is wicked even without striking.
Cites Exodus 2:13 to show that raising the hand alone makes one wicked.
Ze'eiri, citing Rabbi Hanina: one who raises a hand against another is called a sinner.
Cites Samuel's account of the youths' sin as support for the sinner label.
Rav Huna: the hand of one who habitually strikes others should be cut off.
Cites Job 38:15 about the broken arm as support.
Reports that Rav Huna actually cut off the hand of such a person.
Rabbi Elazar: such a violent person has no remedy but burial.
Cites Job 22:8 read homiletically to mean the violent deserve burial.
Rabbi Elazar's second view: land is given only to those who can protect it.
Cites Job 22:8 as support for the view that land belongs to the strong.
Asks what Proverbs 12:11 means.
Explains the verse: one who makes himself a slave to the land will have bread.
Reish Lakish: a gentile who observes Shabbat is liable to the death penalty.
Cites Genesis 8:22, read homiletically to mean Noahides may not rest.
Recalls the teaching that the Noahide warning is also their death penalty.
Ravina: even a Noahide who rests on a Monday is liable.
Objects: the tanna should have counted this among the seven Noahide mitzvot.
Explains the tanna counts only prohibitions requiring refraining, not mitzvot requiring action.

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that establishing courts requires action, yet it is counted among the seven mitzvot.
Rabbi Yochanan: a gentile who studies Torah is liable to the death penalty.
Cites Deuteronomy 33:4 that the Torah is an inheritance for Israel and not for gentiles.
Objects: then the tanna should count this among the seven Noahide mitzvot.
Explains it as robbing Israel's inheritance, or as a betrothed woman's punishment by stoning.
Objects from a baraita: Rabbi Meir says a gentile who studies Torah is like a High Priest.
Answers that the baraita refers to a gentile studying the seven Noahide mitzvot.
Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel: blood of a living animal is also forbidden to Noahides.
Cites Genesis 9:4 as the baraita's source for forbidding a limb from a living animal.
Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel restates that blood from a living animal is also forbidden.
Asks what the reasoning of Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel is.
Explains that he reads the verse to forbid blood of a living animal.
Asks how the Rabbis read the blood mention, since they see no such prohibition.
Answers that the mention permits limbs of living creeping animals.
Cites Deuteronomy 12:23 to show blood of a living animal is also forbidden to Jews.
Asks how the Rabbis read this verse, given their view on living-animal blood.
Answers that it teaches the prohibition on blood spilled in bloodletting.
Asks why the Torah writes this for Noahides and repeats it at Sinai for Jews.
Answers per Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina: a mitzva given to both groups applies to both.
Concludes that a Noahide mitzva not repeated at Sinai applies to Israel alone, as with the sciatic nerve.
Presents the baraita: a Noahide mitzva repeated at Sinai applies to both groups.
Objects: if repeated at Sinai, it seems meant for Israel alone, since Israel are also Noahides.
Answers that idolatry was repeated at Sinai and gentiles were punished for it, so both groups are bound.
Restates the baraita: a Noahide mitzva not repeated at Sinai applies to Israel and not to Noahides.
Objects: if not repeated at Sinai, it should be meant for Noahides and not for Israel.
Answers that nothing is permitted to a Jew but forbidden to a gentile.
Asks whether there is not: a Jew may take a beautiful captive woman but a gentile may not.
Explains the exception: gentiles may not wage conquest, so the rule applies only to Jewish wars.
Asks whether stealing less than a peruta is forbidden to a gentile yet permitted to a Jew.
Explains gentiles do not forgive small debts, so taking such amounts counts as robbery.
Concludes: any mitzva stated to Noahides and repeated at Sinai applies to both groups.

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that circumcision was stated to Noahides, yet was repeated and given to Israel alone.
Answers that the Sinai verse only permits circumcision on Shabbat, so it was not truly repeated.
Objects that procreation was stated to Noahides, yet repeated at Sinai for Israel alone.
Answers that the Sinai repetition teaches that a prohibition needs a new vote to be lifted.
Asks: if so, each Noahide mitzva repeated could carry a further teaching, exempting Noahides from all.
Explains Rabbi Yosei's view: repeating a full prohibition shows it applies to both groups.
Presents the baraita's conclusion that only the sciatic nerve prohibition applies to Israel alone.
Objects that procreation and circumcision were repeated for other purposes, so they too should be Israel-only.
Gives an alternative: circumcision was commanded to Abraham himself, not to all Noahides.
Objects: Ishmael's descendants, as Abraham's offspring, should also be obligated to circumcision.
Answers that the verse says through Isaac offspring is called yours, excluding Ishmael's line.
Objects: Esau, Isaac's son, should be obligated to circumcision too.
Answers that the verse says of Isaac, so only some of Isaac's offspring are included, excluding Esau.
Rav Oshaya objects: then Keturah's descendants should not be obligated to circumcision.
Answers from a verse, citing Rabbi Yosei, that the verse includes Keturah's descendants.
States Rav's view that Adam was not permitted to eat meat.
Cites Genesis 1:29, where Adam's food is only herbs and fruit.
States that when Noah's children came, God permitted meat to them.
Cites Genesis 9:3-4 to derive the limb-from-a-living-animal and creeping-animal prohibitions.
Asks what the derivation is that excludes creeping animals.
Rav Huna: the word its blood indicates animals whose blood is separate from their flesh.
Objects from Genesis 1:28 that the verse about fish refers to eating, not labor.
Answers that fish can labor, citing Rahava's hypothetical about a fish yoked to a wagon.
Cites Genesis 1:28 about the birds of the air, asking whether it refers to eating.
Answers that the verse refers to labor.
Asks whether birds can perform labor.
Answers yes, citing Rabba bar Rav Huna's dilemma about geese and chickens threshing.
Objects from Genesis 1:28 that creeping things cannot labor, so the verse must mean eating them.
Answers that the phrase includes the snake, which could labor before its curse.
Cites a baraita about a snake that served its owner, as evidence that snakes could labor.
Objects from a baraita: Adam dined in Eden on meat roasted for him by the angels.
Answers that this meat descended from heaven by miracle, not from animals.
Asks whether meat descending from heaven actually exists.
Answers yes, citing an incident involving Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta.
Tells how Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta was menaced by roaring lions on the road.
Cites Psalms 104:21 to show that lions seek their food from God.
Recounts that two thighs descended, the lions ate one, and he brought the other to the study hall.
Asks whether this heavenly thigh is a pure or an impure item.
The Sages answer: it must be kosher, since an impure item does not descend from heaven.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Abbahu what the halakha would be if a donkey's likeness had descended.
Rabbi Abbahu answers that an impure item cannot descend from heaven, so it must be kosher.
States Rabbi Shimon's view that the Noahides were also commanded to avoid sorcery.
Asks the reasoning behind Rabbi Shimon's view, citing the verse he relies on.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Derives from the adjacent animal verse that gentiles are also included in the prohibition against letting a witch live.
Rabbi Elazar says the Noahides were also commanded against diverse kinds.
Asks from where Shmuel derives the prohibition of diverse kinds.
Shmuel: the verse My statutes you shall keep refers to statutes already given to Noahides.
Cites Leviticus 19:19 forbidding breeding animals of diverse kinds and sowing diverse seeds.
Derives the details: breeding and grafting are forbidden to Noahides, inside and outside the Land.
Asks: if so, the verse keep My statutes in Leviticus 18:5 should also obligate Noahides.
Answers that the two verses differ: the one in Leviticus 18 refers to statutes given now.
States the mishna: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says judges use an appellation for God's name.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov: the blasphemer is liable only for cursing a four-letter divine name.
Asks whether this is not obvious, since the mishna's example has four letters.
Answers: lest one think the example is incidental, it teaches liability only for the Tetragrammaton.
Some say Rav Acha bar Yaakov teaches that the Tetragrammaton itself is a liable name.
Asks whether this is not obvious, given the mishna's example.
Answers: lest one think liability requires the forty-two-letter name, it teaches liability for the Tetragrammaton.
Mishna: the eldest witness repeats the curse, and the judges stand and tear their garments.
Asks from where the judges derive that they must stand.
Cites Judges 3:20: Eglon stood for Ehud, so a Jew must stand all the more for the ineffable name.
Asks from where the judges derive the tearing of garments.
Cites II Kings 18:37: officials came to Hezekiah with torn garments after hearing Rabshakeh's blasphemy.
Mishna: the judges never fully stitch the tear back together.
Asks from where the rule against stitching the tear derives.
Rabbi Abbahu derives it by verbal analogy from Elisha's torn garment after Elijah's ascent.
Baraita: whoever hears the curse, directly or from a hearer, must tear; witnesses need not, having already torn.
Asks: if they tore when first hearing, why not tear again while hearing the testimony?
Answers from II Kings 19:1: Hezekiah tore his clothes, but the reporters did not tear again.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: one who hears God's name cursed by a gentile need not tear.
Objects: Rabshakeh was a gentile, yet the officials tore their clothes at his blasphemy.
Answers: Rabshakeh was an apostate Jew, so the case differs.
Shmuel: one tears only for the ineffable name, not for an appellation.
Rav Hiyya disagrees: nowadays hearing God's name cursed need not be torn for, or garments would be full of tears.
Asks from whom such curses are heard, since an Israelite would hardly be so irreverent.
Answers that it is obviously from a gentile.
Objects: gentiles do not know the ineffable name, so the curse must be by an appellation.
Concludes that nowadays no tearing is required, whereas earlier it was required.
Mishna: the second witness says I too heard as he did.
Reish Lakish: this testimony is valid by Torah law in both monetary and capital cases.
Explains that the Sages instituted the higher standard of separate testimony, which here cannot be met, so they relaxed it.
Argues that if the testimony were invalid, a man would be executed without proper testimony, so it must be valid.
Mishna: the third witness says I too heard as he did.
Explains the mishna follows Rabbi Akiva, who compares three witnesses to two.

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: one who worships idols is stoned, including by sacrifice, libation, bowing, or declaring the idol a god.
Mishna: hugging, cleaning or dressing an idol, or vowing in its name, transgresses a prohibition but is not capital.
Mishna: defecating before Ba'al-Peor or stoning Mercury is capital, since that is the idol's form of worship.
Asks what the phrase one who worships adds, since worship covers all the listed acts.
Rabbi Yirmeya: the mishna means worship in its typical manner, and also these Temple rites even if atypical.
Objects: sprinkling blood should be counted among the mishna's listed sacrificial rites.
Abaye: sprinkling blood is the same as libation, as Psalms 16:4 suggests.
Asks from where the Sages derived these matters.
Baraita: the verse to the gods refers to slaughtering a sacrifice to idols, not only outside the Temple.
Baraita asks how burning incense and pouring libations are derived, since only slaughter is stated.
Answers: the verse except to the Lord alone designates all sacrificial rites for the ineffable name.
Asks why slaughter is singled out, and from where bowing is included.
Answers from Deuteronomy 17:3-5: one who bows to idols is liable, as the verses are juxtaposed.
Asks from where the prohibition against bowing to an idol is derived.
Answers from Exodus 34:14: you shall bow to no other god.
Objects: one might include hugging, kissing and shoe-putting among the capital cases.
Answers: slaughter is singled out as an analogy, so every Temple rite performed for idolatry is capital.
Restates the Master's baraita: one might think slaughtering outside the Temple is capital.
Asks: isn't slaughtering outside the Temple punished by karet, not death?
Answers: one might think death if warned and karet if not, but the baraita teaches no death even if warned.
Rava bar Rav Hanan proposes that bowing is singled out to teach that any honorable worship is capital.
Objects: if so, why is slaughter mentioned in the verse at all?
Answers that slaughter is mentioned to teach that intention may shift from one Temple rite to another.
Rabbi Yochanan states his view on slaughtering to sprinkle blood or burn fat for idolatry.

61a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: States that the slaughtered animal is forbidden for benefit, while Reish Lakish says it is permitted.
Rava bar Rav Hanan explains the verse is superfluous for Rabbi Yochanan but needed for Reish Lakish's intention principle.
Rav Pappa objects: Rabbi Yochanan too needs the verse to make the slaughterer liable to death.
Rav Aha son of Rav Ika objects: Reish Lakish too can impose liability without the verse, as with bowing to a mountain.
Asks Ravina what Deuteronomy 12:30 is meant to exclude, given Rava's reading of it.
Answers that the verse excludes defecating before Mercury, which might otherwise seem liable as a degrading act.
Objects: Rava's reading conflicts with Rabbi Eliezer, who derives liability for sacrificing to Mercury from Leviticus 17:7.
Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: the verse applies to worship not in the idol's typical manner, such as sacrificing to Mercury.
Answers that Rabbi Eliezer's verse concerns sacrificing to Mercury out of insolence, not as worship.
Relates that Rav Hamnuna lost his oxen, and Rabba met him and raised a contradiction between two mishnayot.
Rabba's contradiction: one mishna exempts mere speech of idol worship, while another makes speaking of it liable.
Rav Hamnuna answers that the mishna refers to one who accepts the idol as a god only through actual worship.
Rav Yosef rejects that answer: the mishnayot reflect a dispute between tanna'im over inciting others.
Explains the dispute concerns mere speech: Rabbi Meir deems speech significant, Rabbi Yehuda deems it nothing.
Rav Yosef retracts: even Rabbi Yehuda deems one liable for speech alone in incitement.
Cites Rabbi Yehuda's baraita that one is liable upon saying I will worship, showing speech alone suffices.
Asks what principle Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree about.
Answers they disagree about an inciter whose listeners reply yes, as to a self-incitement case.
States Rabbi Meir's view that the listeners' yes is sincere, so the incitement takes effect.
States Rabbi Yehuda's view that listeners are unlikely to heed the inciter and say yes only to themselves.

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks in what way the idol-inciter differs from us, that one should worship him.
Answers that the Yes they say to him is mocking, not sincere.
Resolves the mishnah conflict: an incited individual does not change his mind, while a multitude does, so only the individual is liable for speech.
Rav Yosef: Deuteronomy 13:9 do not approve nor listen shows that approving the inciter's words makes one liable.
Abaye objects from a baraita: individual and multitude are both included, each singled out from the other.
Cites the baraita's distinctions: the individual is treated more stringently in body and more leniently in property, and the reverse for multitudes.
Abaye concludes: they differ only in those matters, so no distinction applies to verbal commitment to idol worship.
Abaye resolves: the mishnah on actual worship concerns a self-incited person, while the other concerns those incited by others.
Abaye's proof from Deuteronomy 13:9: approval alone suffices when one listens to an inciter.
Rava resolves: liability for mere approval applies only when the inciter described the idol's benefits and harms.
Rava derives this from Deuteronomy 13:7-8: near idols reveal the nature of distant ones, so only described idols make approval liable.
Rav Ashi: the latter mishnah concerns an apostate Jew, whose commitment is final and so is liable on speech alone.
Ravina: there is no contradiction; the tanna teaches the elementary halakha first, then the novel one about speech.
Amoraim dispute whether one who worships out of love or fear, without faith in the idol, is liable: Abaye says liable, Rava says exempt.
Abaye: he is liable since he worshipped; Rava: liability requires sincerely accepting the idol as a god.
Gives a mnemonic, a slave bows to the anointed, for the proofs Abaye cites next.
Abaye cites the mishnah's repeated one who worships as including worship out of love or fear.
Rava replies that one who worships is explained by Rabbi Yirmeya's reading of typical manner of worship.
Abaye cites Exodus 20:5 and the Haman example, noting Haman was worshipped out of fear, so fear-based worship is liable.
Rava: the Haman comparison covers only one who believes in the person's divinity, not one who worships out of fear.
Abaye cites a baraita on the High Priest's unwitting idol worship, where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Sages differ on an offering.
Agreement: a High Priest brings a female goat for idol worship like an individual, and no provisional guilt-offering.
Asks what the case of an unwitting act of idol worship is, given the Sages' requirement.
Abaye answers: the case is bowing to a statue of a person; if accepted as a god, it is intentional and capital.

62a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Infers from the baraita that the High Priest's unwitting worship out of love or fear counts as idol worship.
Rava replies: the baraita concerns a High Priest who says to himself that idol worship is permitted.
Objects: that is a lapse the Rabbis also make liable, so what differs between the two opinions?
Resolves: the difference is between thinking idol worship entirely permitted and upholding part of its prohibition.
Rabbi Zakkai's baraita: one lapse covering several idolatrous acts requires only one sin-offering.
Rabbi Yochanan tells him to teach it outside, since the halakha is an offering for each act.
Rabbi Abba: Rabbi Zakkai's view reflects the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Natan about Shabbat fire-kindling.
Rabbi Natan: kindling fire is singled out to divide Shabbat labors into separate prohibitions, each with its own offering.
Rabbi Abba concludes: each reading of the fire verse parallels how bowing is read in idolatry.
Rav Yosef objects: Rabbi Yosei may derive the division of Shabbat labors from Leviticus 4:2, not from the fire verse.
Cites Rabbi Yosei's baraita: Leviticus 4:2 sometimes gives one offering for many transgressions and sometimes one per transgression.
Rabbi Yonatan explains: one and them in that verse show one violation may count as many, and several as one.
Rabbi Yonatan's example: writing a whole name versus only some of its letters, requiring an offering for two letters.
Rabbi Yonatan applies it: knowing it is Shabbat but not the prohibition yields an offering per labor, and the reverse yields one.
Rav Yosef continues: with idol worship perhaps all agree bowing is singled out to divide prohibitions, and so it is capital.
Asks why the division of idolatrous acts is not derived from the same from one of them verse.
Explains the categories: one is the complete act, them the primary rites, of them the subcategories, such as breaking a stick.
Applies the principle: knowing idolatry is forbidden but not a specific rite yields many offerings, and the reverse yields one.
Asks what the case of an unwitting act of idol worship is.
Answers: a synagogue mistake is no transgression, so the case must be bowing to a person's statue, capital if accepted as a god.
Clarifies that the case concerns love or fear, which Abaye would hold liable.
Asks what can be said for Rava, who holds one exempt in that case.
Rather, Rava's case is one who thinks idolatry permitted in general, which also bears on Rava's Shabbat dilemma.
Notes that Rava's dilemma was left unresolved, and that the difficulty is no difficulty: resolve it from here.
Asks whether Leviticus 4 can apply to idol worship at all, since it addresses priests, kings and individuals.
Cites the baraita on the High Priest's unwitting idolatry, bringing a female goat, showing a different source.
Concludes that the suggested derivation is groundless, so Rav Yosef's objection stands.
Introduces Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's arrival from Eretz Yisrael to Babylonia, where he said the following.

62b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita Rabbi Zakkai taught: Shabbat is stricter in one respect and other mitzvot in another, about offerings for multiple or unwitting acts.
Quotes the Master's baraita: Shabbat is stricter, since two acts in one lapse require an offering for each.
Asks what the circumstances of this Shabbat ruling are.
Hypothesizes reaping and grinding on Shabbat, paralleled by forbidden fat and blood, so there is no difference between Shabbat and other mitzvot.
Asks what circumstances would make other mitzvot liable for only one offering.
Answers: forbidden fat consumed twice in one lapse, paralleled by reaping twice, again yields no difference.
Explains Rabbi Yochanan's rebuke to Rabbi Zakkai: the baraita is not worthy of the study hall.
Asks what difficulty caused Rabbi Yochanan to disregard the baraita.
Proposes the baraita's Shabbat rule concerns labor, and the idolatry rule follows Rabbi Ami: one offering for several rites in one lapse.
Rejects that reading: the last clause, unwitting acts without intent, cannot refer to idolatry.
Explains why unwitting idolatry without intent is impossible: a synagogue mistake is exempt, and a person's statue is capital if accepted as a god.
Proposes the case of idolatry from love or fear, which Abaye holds liable and Rava holds exempt.
Proposes the case of one who thinks idolatry permitted in general, whereas unwitting Shabbat permission is fully exempt.
Objects: Rava's question to Rav Nachman shows no one holds the Shabbat case fully exempt, so this reading fails.
Challenges the conclusion: the first clause may contrast Shabbat with idolatry and the last with other mitzvot.
Explains the unwitting case for other mitzvot: forbidden fat swallowed thinking it spittle is liable, while unwitting Shabbat labor is exempt.
Cites Shmuel as transmitted by Rav Nachman: unwitting forbidden fat is liable, while unwitting Shabbat labor is exempt.
Rabbi Yochanan's principle: he does not explain two clauses of one baraita by different reasons.
Quotes Rabbi Yochanan's barrel remark, then turns to the matter itself: several idolatrous acts in one lapse.

ranges.en: Rabbi Ami: sacrificing, burning incense and pouring a libation within one lapse yields only one sin-offering.
Abaye gives Rabbi Ami's reason: the verse Nor worship them treats all worship as one rite.
Asks whether Abaye really holds this, since he says the three bowing prohibitions divide idolatry into categories.
Explains that Abaye spoke according to Rabbi Ami's view, though he himself does not hold it.
Restates Abaye's view: the three bowing prohibitions cover a standard manner, a non-standard manner, and category division.
Asks why a verse is needed for bowing as standard worship, when Deuteronomy 12:30 already covers it.
Rather, Abaye's standard-manner mention covers worship similar to bowing, with separate mentions for non-standard worship and category division.
Mishnah: one who accepts an idol as a god, or says to it you are my god, is liable.
Rav, citing Rabba bar Avuh: saying to an idol you are my god makes one liable even without worship.
Asks which punishment is meant and whether Rav holds it even by the Rabbis, who require a significant action.
Answers that Rav states this according to Rabbi Akiva, who requires no significant action.
Asks: if so, is it not obvious, since Rabbi Akiva obligates a blasphemer without any action?
Rav teaches it lest one think Rabbi Akiva's offering applies only to a blasphemer, since karet is explicit there.
The Torah compares accepting an idol as a god to active worship, citing Exodus 32:8.
Rabbi Yochanan: were it not for the vav in he'elukha, Israel would have been destroyed, and others say the same.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai objects: linking God's name with another is idolatry, and the plural shows they wanted many gods.
Mishnah: hugging, kissing or cleaning an idol transgresses a prohibition without capital liability.
Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Elazar: one is flogged for all these except vowing and swearing in an idol's name.
Asks what distinguishes vowing and swearing in an idol's name from the other cases.
Answers: those are no-action prohibitions, and one is not flogged for a general prohibition covering several acts.
Baraita: Leviticus 19:26 yields prohibitions on eating from an animal before death and on eating offering meat before sprinkling.
Rabbi Dosa: from the same blood verse, mourners may not be fed a meal after an executed person's burial.
Rabbi Akiva: judges who sentenced someone to death may not taste food that day, derived from the same verse.
Rabbi Yochanan: the prohibition on a stubborn and rebellious son's eating is derived from the same verse.
Rabbi Avin: no flogging for prohibitions derived from a general prohibition covering several actions.
Ravin reports a version of Rabbi Elazar: no flogging except for vowing and swearing in an idol's name.
Asks what distinguishes those vow cases from the flogged ones.
Answers that this halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, who flogs for no-action prohibitions.
Baraita on the Paschal offering: Exodus 12:10 adds a positive mitzva to burn leftovers after a prohibition was violated.

63b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: States Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on whether one is flogged for the violation discussed.
Rabbi Yaakov: no flogging because it is a no-action prohibition, so Rabbi Yehuda must hold flogging applies to such prohibitions.
Mishnah: one who vows in an idol's name or affirms by an oath in its name transgresses a prohibition.
Asks from where we derive that vowing in an idol's name is a prohibition.
Derives from Exodus 23:13 that one may not vow in an idol's name, cause others to, or incite others to idolatry.
Asks why the incitement prohibition is derived here, when Deuteronomy 13:12 states it explicitly.
Supports Shmuel's father: a partnership with a gentile is forbidden lest he swear by his idol, which the verse covers.
Narrates that Ulla lodged in Kalnevo, and Rava asks where the Master lodged.
Rava objects: Kalnevo is an idol's name, and Exodus 23:13 forbids mentioning other gods.
Ulla answers: Rabbi Yochanan permits mentioning any idol written in the Torah.
Rava asks where this idol is written in the Torah.
Ulla: Isaiah 46:1 mentions Bel and Nevo, so Nevo is written.
Asks whether an idol not written in the Torah may not be mentioned.
Rav Mesharshiyya objects from a mishnah in Zavim that mentions the idol Gadyon.
Ravina: Gad is also written in Isaiah 65:11, so the premise holds.
Rav Naḥman: all mockery is forbidden except mockery of idolatry, which is permitted, citing Isaiah 46:1-2.
Hosea 10:4-5: read kevodo as keveido, the idol's burden, showing derogatory statements are permitted only about idols.
Rav Yitzchak asks what Hosea 13:2 means, including the word kitvunam.
Explains kitvunam as their image: each person carried an idol image in his pocket and kissed it.
Asks what Hosea 13:2 means by those who sacrifice men kiss calves.
Rabbi Yitzchak of Rabbi Ami's school: idol priests starved calves and used the wealthy's statues to lure and despoil them.
Rava objects: the wording should have been calves kiss those who sacrifice men, so this reading fails.
Rava reads it: one who sacrifices his son to an idol is kissed by the calf as the reward for a great gift.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, identifies the idols of II Kings 17:30-31 as images of a hen, a rooster, a bald goat, a dog and a donkey.
Identifies the Sepharvites' gods Adrammelech and Anammelech as a mule and a horse, by their functions.
Hezekiah's father tried to burn him as an offering to an idol, but his mother saved him with salamander blood.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: Israel knew idolatry was empty and worshipped only to permit forbidden sexual relations in public.
Rav Mesharshiyya objects from Jeremiah 17:2: Israel longed for their idols, showing real attachment.
Answers: the attachment came after they began to believe in idols; initially they were drawn only by lust.
Proof from Leviticus 26:30 that Israel worshipped idols for their own sake, not for lust.
Narrates Elijah the Righteous searching for the starving, and finding a child lying swollen in the garbage.
Elijah asks the child's family and offers to teach him a way to live: to say the Shema every day.
The child agrees, and Elijah teaches him the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4.

64a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The child did not want even to hear God's name, which his parents never taught him.
The child clings to his idol until his stomach bursts and the idol falls on him, fulfilling Leviticus 26:30.
Cites Nehemiah 9:4, the people crying out to God, as a further proof about attachment to idolatry.
Asks what they said in that cry.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: the cry was that the evil inclination for idolatry destroyed the Temple and exiled Israel, and it came after they became attached to idolatry.
The people fasted three days, and a note fell from heaven reading truth, showing God accepted the prayer.
Rabbi Hanina: from this one learns that the seal of the Holy One is truth.
A lion cub of fire emerges from the Holy of Holies, which Zechariah identifies as the evil inclination for idolatry; when caught, it shrieks.
Asks what to do, since perhaps Heaven will pity it if they try to kill it.
The prophet advises throwing it into a lead container, since lead muffles sound, citing Zechariah 5:8.
The Sages suggest praying for mercy regarding the evil inclination of sexual sin, which is then delivered to them.
They imprisoned it for three days, and no fresh egg could be found, as reproduction stopped.
Asks what to do, since praying for only half the inclination will achieve nothing.
They gouged out its eyes, so that a person is no longer aroused to incest with close relatives.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: a gentile woman who recovered vowed to worship every idol, but at Peor, learning the rite, preferred her illness.
Rav Yehuda contrasts attachment to Ba'al-Peor, Numbers 25:5, with cleaving to God, Deuteronomy 4:4, using tight and loose images.
A baraita reverses the conclusion: attachment to Ba'al-Peor is like a loosely worn bracelet, while cleaving to God is tight.
Sabbeta ben Alas, a Jew, defecated before Ba'al-Peor to demean it, but the priests praised his worship.
Halakha: defecating before Ba'al-Peor, or stoning Mercury, is liable idol worship even when intended as demeaning.
Rav Menashe threw a stone at a Mercury idol to demean it, and the locals told him that is its form of worship.
The Sages answer: throwing a stone at Mercury is liable even when demeaning, and both taking and placing a stone are liable.
Mishnah: one who gives offspring to Molekh is liable only if he both hands the child to its priests and passes him through fire.
Asks why the mishna teaches idolatry and then Molekh separately.
Answers that the mishna follows the view that Molekh is not idolatry, and cites the baraita's dispute between Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon and the others.
Abaye: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus share one opinion; a baraita says the Molekh term covers any so named.
Rava objects: they differ, since a temporary Molekh is liable only according to Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus.

ranges.en: Rabbi Yannai: one is liable only if he hands the child to Molekh's priests, based on the verb to give in Leviticus 18:21.
A baraita shows through the verbs give and pass that handing over and passing are both required, and only for Molekh.
A baraita cites Deuteronomy 18:10 to confirm that passing through fire and handing over to Molekh's priests are both required.
Rav Acha son of Rava: one who passes all his offspring is exempt, since the verse says of your offspring, not all of them.
Rav Ashi raises dilemmas: a blind child, a sleeping child, and a grandchild passed through fire.
Resolves one dilemma via a baraita: Leviticus 20:4's offspring includes grandchildren, so a grandchild is liable.
Asks why the tanna cites two different verses for the same halakha.
Answers: the second verse teaches that offspring of flawed lineage, such as a mamzer, are also included.
Rav Yehuda: one is liable only if he passes the child in the typical manner of passing.
Asks what counts as the typical manner of passing.
Abaye: the child walks along a brick lattice between two fires.
Rava: the typical manner is leaping, like children over Purim bonfires.
A baraita supports Rava: walking the child through is exempt, so passing is done by leaping.
Baraita: one is liable only for his descendants; father, mother, siblings or himself are exempt, though Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon deems self liable.
Baraita: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon holds liability only for passing to Molekh, not to other idols.
Ulla explains that Rabbi Elazar reads among you as among yourself, so passing oneself is liable.
Asks whether the Rabbis do not read among you as oneself, given the mishnah on lost items and one's own needs.
Answers: there the halakha comes from the limiting word only, so one begins with himself.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina asks why karet is mentioned three times for idolatry.
Answers: one mention for typical idolatry, one for atypical idolatry, and one for the Molekh ritual.
Asks: if Molekh is idolatry, why is a separate karet needed for Molekh?
Asks: if the blasphemy verse refers to idolatry, why does blasphemy need its own karet?
Answers from Numbers 15:31: hikkaret means excised in this world, tikkaret in the World to Come, per Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Yishmael objects: the earlier verse already states karet, and the Torah speaks in ordinary human language.

65a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: necromancers and sorcerers are stoned, and one who inquires through them transgresses a prohibition.
Asks why the mishnah here lists both necromancer and sorcerer, while Karetot lists only the necromancer.
Rabbi Yochanan: both are stated in one prohibition, so the sorcerer is not counted separately for karet.
Reish Lakish: the sorcerer is omitted in Karetot because his transgression involves only speech, not an action.
Rabbi Yochanan asks why the mishnah in Karetot names the necromancer specifically.
Answers that the necromancer is named because the verse opens the prohibition with him.
Asks why Reish Lakish did not explain the matter as Rabbi Yochanan does.
Rav Pappa: the two are divided in the death penalty, so Reish Lakish disagrees with Rabbi Yochanan's reading.
Rabbi Yochanan replies: a division in the penalty is not counted as a division for sin-offerings.
Asks why Rabbi Yochanan did not explain the matter as Reish Lakish does.
Rabbi Yochanan: the Karetot mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva, who requires no action.
Reish Lakish: even Rabbi Akiva requires at least a minor action, which sorcery lacks.
Asks what action a blasphemer performs.
Answers that twisting his lips while speaking is an action.
Asks what action a necromancer performs.
Answers that striking his arms together to produce a voice is an action.
Asks whether this counts as action for the Rabbis, who require a significant action, citing the baraita on idolatry.
Reish Lakish: the baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, who counts bowing even with a minimal action.
Rabbi Yochanan: even per the Rabbis, bending one's height is a significant action.
Asks: if bending is not significant for the Rabbis, how can arm-striking be significant?
Reish Lakish concedes arm-striking is an action only per Rabbi Akiva, not per the Rabbis.
Objects: then the Karetot mishnah should have excluded blasphemer and necromancer for lack of action.
Ulla: the necromancer in Karetot burns incense to a demon to raise the dead, which is a significant action.
Rava objects: burning incense to a demon is idolatry, already listed in Karetot.
Rava: the mishnah means burning incense to demons to gather them, as a form of sorcery.
Abaye objects: gathering demons makes one a charmer, which has its own prohibition without karet.
A baraita: charmers include gatherers of large animals, small animals, even snakes and scorpions.
Abaye concludes: one who gathers scorpions and hornets to harm others is forbidden, even to prevent harm to himself.
Asks Rabbi Yochanan why bending counts as action for the Rabbis, but twisting the lips does not.
Rava: a blasphemer's case differs, since the transgression is in the heart too, so speech without intent is not blasphemy.

ranges.en: Rabbi Zeira objects: false witnesses' speech is an action, not purely in the heart, so why are they exempt?
Rava: conspiring witnesses differ, since their speech only makes them heard by the court, which involves no action.
Asks whether, per Rabbi Yochanan, projecting one's voice is an action, citing the dispute over muzzling an ox by voice.
Explains: Rabbi Yochanan holds that twisting the mouth to speak is an action, while Reish Lakish denies it, which is the source of the dispute.
Rava's alternative: conspiring witnesses are liable mainly for what they saw, which involves no action.
Baraita defines the necromancer as one who makes the dead speak from his joints or armpit, and the sorcerer as one using a bone in his mouth.
Objects from Isaiah 29:4: does the dead speak from the grave on its own? The Gemara answers no, it is done by sorcery.
Cites I Samuel 28:13, the woman's words to Saul, as proof that the dead speak on their own; the Gemara refutes this.
Baraita: one who raises the dead by zekhur appears upside down and does not rise on Shabbat, unlike one who inquires via a skull.
Asks how the dead rise, since the skull lies before him, and suggests the dead answers instead.
Narrates Turnus Rufus asking Rabbi Akiva why Shabbat is different from other days.
Turnus Rufus: perhaps some other day of the week is Shabbat.
Rabbi Akiva: the Sabbatyon River, necromancy and the father's grave prove today is Shabbat; Turnus Rufus then rebukes him.
Asks why necromancy and directing inquiries to the dead are mentioned separately in Deuteronomy 18:11.
Baraita: directing inquiries to the dead means starving oneself and sleeping in a cemetery to receive an impure spirit.
Rabbi Akiva weeps: if the starving draw an impure spirit, the righteous should draw a pure one, but sins prevent it, citing Isaiah 59:2.
Rava: if the righteous wished, they could create a world, since only sins separate people from God.
Rava created a golem, which did not answer Rabbi Zeira, who told it to return to dust.
Rav Hanina and Rav Oshaya studied Sefer Yetzira each Shabbat eve and created a calf to eat.
Baraita defines the soothsayer by the views of Rabbi Shimon, the Rabbis, and Rabbi Akiva.
Baraita defines the enchanter as one who relies on omens such as falling bread, a raven's call, or a fox on one's left.

66a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita explains that the verse forbidding divination covers those who read omens from a weasel, birds or fish, and the collector example.
The mishna states that one who desecrates Shabbat is liable to karet for willful violation and a sin-offering for unwitting violation.
The Gemara infers from the mishna's wording that some Shabbat desecration carries neither karet nor a sin-offering.
The Gemara asks what the labor is that is prohibited but carries no karet or sin-offering.
The answer: it is boundary-crossing, following Rabbi Akiva, or kindling fire, following Rabbi Yosei.
The mishna rules that one who curses parents is liable only if he uses the divine name; Rabbi Meir disagrees.
The Gemara asks who the Rabbis of the mishna are.
The answer: they are Rabbi Menachem son of Rabbi Yosei, whose view is cited in a baraita.
Rabbi Menachem son of Rabbi Yosei's baraita derives from the repeated words of Leviticus 24:16 the limit of liability to cursing by name.
A baraita uses the repeated word ish in Leviticus 20:9 to include a daughter, a tumtum and an androgynos.
Rabbi Yoshiya derives liability for cursing only one parent from the proximity of the word curses in the verse.
Rabbi Yonatan rejects that derivation, reading the verse as making liability for either parent alone unless specified otherwise.
The phrase shall be put to death is taken to mean that the punishment is stoning.
The baraita asks whether the penalty is stoning or one of the other death penalties stated in the Torah.
The baraita compares the phrase his blood upon him in Leviticus 20:9 with the stoning of sorcerers in Leviticus 20:27 to fix stoning.
The baraita asks where the prohibition against cursing a parent is derived from.
Exodus 22:27 is read to prohibit cursing judges, the elohim, and the verse about a king of your people is cited as well.
If the parent is neither judge nor king, the Gemara asks how the prohibition is derived.
The answer is an inference by paradigm: the defining traits of king and judge are dissimilar and each lacks the other's features.
The common element is being of your people, so the father is included in the prohibition against cursing.
Objection: the common element is their prominence, so the prohibition may apply only to prominent figures.
The baraita brings a third case, Leviticus 19:14 about cursing the deaf, to show the prohibition covers even the wretched.
Objection: the deaf case is prohibited only because of the deafness, like misleading the blind, so it proves nothing general.
Defense: the king and judge cases show prominence is not the determining factor, so the deaf case can still prove the point.
The baraita restates the combined inference from the three cases, concluding the parent is included.
Objection: the common element is that these are unusual people, so perhaps ordinary people may be cursed.
If only unusual people are protected, the verse would be superfluous in naming judges, so it should apply to cursing a father.
The Gemara asks how this works if elohim is non-sacred, but if it is sacred, what can be said?
Baraitot cite Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on whether elohim is non-sacred or sacred, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov on cursing God.
The answer: each side derives the other meaning by a gezera shava from its own reading of elohim.
The Gemara asks whether the derivation of the non-sacred meaning from the sacred meaning is valid by inference.
The answer: the verse should then have written takel, meaning demean, instead of tekallel, to prohibit cursing God alone.

ranges.en: The Gemara asks what halakha is derived from the superfluous lamed in the word tekallel.
The answer: the word includes two prohibitions, against cursing God and against cursing a judge.
The mishna rules that one who has intercourse with a betrothed young woman is stoned, and a second man is strangled.
A baraita derives the conditions of young, virgin, betrothed and in her father's house from the verse in Deuteronomy 22.
Rav says the mishna follows Rabbi Meir, who includes a minor girl; the Rabbis include even a minor in the term.
Rav Aha asks Ravina how we know the mishna follows Rabbi Meir rather than the Rabbis.
Ravina replies that the phrase until she is a young woman shows the age condition is essential, so the mishna excludes minors.
Rabbi Ya'akov bar Adda asks Rav whether Rabbi Meir exempts a minor completely or only from stoning.
Rav answers that it stands to reason Rabbi Meir excludes such a case only from stoning, not from strangulation.
Rabbi Ya'akov objects from Deuteronomy 22:22 that both must be equally liable, so a minor's partner is exempt.
Shmuel asks why Rav stayed silent and did not answer the objection.
Shmuel says Rav could cite Deuteronomy 22:25, where the man is stoned even though the woman is exempt.
The Gemara explains the matter is a tannaitic dispute, with Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan reading the verse differently, as a baraita shows.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yonatan derives from the phrase they shall both die.
Rava says it excludes an act of sharpening, which is not sexual intercourse, so the couple is exempt.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yoshiya derives from the phrase the man who lay with her alone shall die.
A baraita shows that if ten men had intercourse with her, only the first is stoned and the others are strangled.
A baraita cites Leviticus 21:9 and Deuteronomy 22:25, reading the word teḥel as teḥila, meaning first.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is saying.
Rav Huna explains he follows Rabbi Yishmael: a betrothed priest's daughter is burned for her first act of adultery, otherwise strangled.
The Gemara asks what the end of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's statement is doing and how the verse is relevant.
The answer: the halakha here, for the priest's daughter, is like there, referring to the first act of intercourse.
Rav Beivai bar Abaye objects that his master Rav Yosef does not explain Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's statement that way.
Rav Yosef's alternative: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi follows Rabbi Meir, so a priest's daughter who married a mamzer is strangled.
This explains the statement: if she first disqualified herself by adultery she is burned, otherwise she is strangled.
The Gemara asks what the end of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's statement, and likewise, is meant to convey.
