ranges.en: The Gemara calls the verse a mere mnemonic sign, not a true source for the halakha.
The mishna defines the inciter as an ordinary person who tells one man or two men that an idol eats, drinks and helps its worshippers.
If the inciter speaks to one man, that man is told to bring friends so there are witnesses; if he is naked, witnesses are hidden.
The mishna describes hiding witnesses behind a fence, the inciter retracting or persisting, and the court stoning him if he persists.
The mishna lists the phrasings of incitement that count, such as I shall go and worship, I shall sacrifice, burn incense or bow.
The Gemara infers from the wording ordinary person and individual that a prophet or a multitude gets strangulation instead.
The Gemara asks whose opinion the mishna states.
The mishna follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a prophet or a subverter of a city is strangled, as a baraita shows.
The Gemara challenges: the last clause may be Rabbis' view while the first clause is Rabbi Shimon's, as Rav Yehuda reports Rav.
Ravina defends the mishna as wholly the Rabbis' view, read in the not only this but also that style.
Rav Pappa explains that calling the inciter an ordinary person refers to the hiding of witnesses, treating him as a simpleton.
A baraita shows that hiding witnesses to ensnare a condemned person is done only for the inciter.
A baraita describes the procedure: a candle in the inner room, witnesses outside, the inciter stoned, and the court hanged ben Setada on Passover eve.
The Gemara asks why he was called ben Setada if he was the son of Pandeira.
Rav Hisda suggests the husband was Setada and the paramour Pandeira, so the mamzer is named after the husband.
The Gemara objects that his mother's husband was Pappos ben Yehuda, not Setada.
Perhaps his mother was named Setada and he was named after her, instead.
The Gemara objects that his mother was Miriam, who braided women's hair, so she could not be named Setada.
Setada was a nickname, as the people of Pumbedita say: she strayed from her husband.
The mishna says the subverter liable to stoning is one who says to a multitude: let us go and worship idols.
The mishna says the warlock is liable for a real act of sorcery, but not one who merely deceives the eyes.
Rabbi Akiva in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua illustrates: of two men gathering cucumbers by sorcery, one really did so and is liable, the other is exempt.
Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name that the mishna's subverters refers to subverting an idolatrous city, resolving the difficulty.
The warlock is explained as one who performs a real act, the mishna's point about the deceiver.
A baraita infers from the word witch, which includes men, that most women practice sorcery, so the verse names the female form.
The Gemara asks by what means the witch is put to death.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives death by the sword from the verse about the Canaanites, by a verbal analogy.
Rabbi Akiva derives stoning from the Sinai verse, where the phrase shall not live refers to stoning.
Rabbi Yosei objects that Akiva's analogy is weaker, since the phrase shall not live is less similar than his own.
Rabbi Akiva replies that the phrase shall not live is especially significant for Jews, for whom the verse lists many death penalties.

67b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Decapitation is the only capital punishment applying to gentiles, so it cannot be transferred by verbal analogy to a Jewish sorcerer.
Ben Azzai derives from the juxtaposition of witch and bestiality verses that a warlock is stoned like one who lies with an animal.
Rabbi Yehuda objects that mere juxtaposition should not lead to the most severe punishment of stoning.
Rabbi Yehuda's own source: necromancers and sorcerers are singled out from the warlock category to be compared to it for stoning.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehuda should also hold that two verses coming together teach only those cases.
Rabbi Zekharya explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds two verses that come together do teach about other cases.
Rabbi Yohanan explains the name keshafim as an acronym meaning that sorcery contradicts the heavenly entourage.
Deuteronomy 4:35, there is none else besides Him, is cited as a verse against the efficacy of sorcery.
Rabbi Hanina holds that sorcery has no effect on a righteous person, illustrated by a woman who failed to harm him.
The Gemara asks: is that so, given that Rabbi Yohanan says sorcery contradicts the heavenly entourage and warns against it?
Rabbi Hanina is different, since his merit is great and sorcery has no effect on him.
Rabbi Aivu bar Nagri, citing Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, distinguishes demonic acts from sorcery by the Hebrew words for hidden arts and flaming sword.
Abaye says that a sorcerer particular about a utensil works with a demon, while one indifferent to it performs sorcery.
Abaye says the halakhot of sorcery parallel those of Shabbat: some are capital, some prohibited only rabbinically, some permitted.
Abaye elaborates the three categories, and gives Rav Hanina and Rav Oshaya as examples of what is permitted ab initio.
Rav Ashi reports seeing Karna's father produce silk rolls from his nostrils, a deception of the eyes.
Rabbi Eliezer derives from Exodus 8:15, the finger of God, that a demon cannot create anything smaller than a barley grain.
Rav Pappa says demons cannot create even a camel-sized entity, but can only gather large animals to move them.
Rav recounts seeing an Arab slice a camel and revive it, to which he later reports Rabbi Hiyya's response.
Rabbi Hiyya replies that the absence of blood and excretion shows it was a deception of the eyes, not sorcery.
Ze'eiri in Alexandria finds a donkey that was really a bridge plank, showing sorcery was common and items were tested with water.
Yannai is served a drink that turns to scorpions, then bewitches the innkeeper into a donkey, which he rides through the marketplace.
Exodus 8:2 writes the frog in the singular, which Rabbi Elazar reads as one frog that spawned and filled Egypt.
The matter is a dispute between tanna'im: Rabbi Akiva also holds that one frog spawned and filled the entire land of Egypt.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah rebukes Rabbi Akiva for expounding aggada, urging him to stick to halakhot of impurity.
Rabbi Elazar's reading: it was one frog that whistled, and the other frogs came after it.
The mishna's cucumber example is recalled: Rabbi Akiva in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua holds that sorcery is either real or only deception.

68a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Akiva learned these halakhot from Rabbi Yehoshua, since a baraita reports a different visit.
A baraita recounts that when Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, Rabbi Akiva and colleagues visited, and his son Hyrcanus was rebuked as he removed phylacteries.
Hyrcanus thinks his father is insane; Rabbi Eliezer replies that they neglect Shabbat prohibitions punishable by stoning while fussing over rabbinic ones.
The Sages, seeing his mind was stable, sat before him at four cubits, since an ostracized person may not be sat within four cubits.
Rabbi Eliezer asks the Sages why they have come.
They reply that they came to study Torah, not to visit him.
Rabbi Eliezer asks why they did not come until now.
They reply that they had no spare time.
Rabbi Eliezer predicts the Sages will be tortured by the Romans, and that Akiva's death will be worse since he neglected to study.
Rabbi Eliezer laments that he learned much and taught much, but his students took only as much as a paintbrush takes from a tube.
Rabbi Eliezer says he can teach hundreds of halakhot on leprosy and thousands on planting cucumbers by sorcery, but only Akiva ever asked.
Rabbi Eliezer recounts how, walking with Akiva, he taught him to plant cucumbers by one statement and uproot them by another.
The Sages ask the halakha on impurity of a leather-covered ball, a shoe last, an amulet and a pearl pouch.
Rabbi Eliezer rules they are susceptible to impurity and purified by immersion as they are.
The Sages ask whether a shoe on a last is a complete vessel subject to impurity.
Rabbi Eliezer rules it is pure, and with these words his soul departs in purity.
Rabbi Yehoshua rises and declares the vow permitted, lifting the ostracism on Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Akiva, returning from Caesarea, meets the funeral procession and eulogizes Eliezer with the verse from II Kings 2:12.
The Gemara objects that Akiva evidently learned cucumber sorcery from Eliezer, not from Yehoshua.
He learned it from Eliezer without understanding it, and later Yehoshua explained it to him.
The Gemara asks how Eliezer could perform sorcery, since the mishna makes performing it liable.
Performing it to learn and understand is permitted; the verse in Deuteronomy 18 forbids learning in order to do, not in order to understand and teach.
The chapter-closing formula: this concludes the chapter of the four capital punishments.

68b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna defines when a stubborn and rebellious son becomes liable: from two pubic hairs until a lower beard, and a minor is exempt.
The Gemara asks from where we derive that a minor is exempt from the death penalty of a stubborn son.
The reason, as the mishna states, is that the minor has not yet entered the category of mitzvah obligation.
The Gemara asks where else the verse punishes a minor, so that a special verse would be needed to exempt him.
The Gemara explains the death penalty is for what he will become, so a minor could be included, but the word son rather than man excludes him.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, derives from If a man has a son that the law applies to a son close to manhood, not a boy.
The mishna's lower beard is reaffirmed: the boy's liability ends once the lower beard surrounds the genitals.
Rabbi Hiyya's baraita says until the hair surrounds the corona, and Rav Dimi explains this means the penis, not the sac.
Rav Hisda holds a minor's son cannot be a stubborn son, citing the verse's wording if a man has a son.
The Gemara asks, on Rav Yehuda's view, why the verse should not say ki yihye ben le-ish, and what le-ish means here.
The verse's unusual wording is read as teaching two halakhot, so it supports Rav Hisda's ruling as well.
The Gemara asks whether the entire verse may instead be for Rav Hisda's ruling, and why it does not say ben ish.
The wording If a man has a son teaches two conclusions: a minor cannot be a rebel, and his son cannot be one either.
Rabba holds a minor cannot father a child, deriving it from Numbers 5:8 about a man with no redeemer, which is taught in the Jewish people context.
The verse concerns the robbery of a convert, who has no relatives, so Numbers 5:8 does not refute Rav Hisda.

69a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse But if the man has no relative means one must search for a convert's relatives only when he is a man, not a minor.
A minor convert needs no search for relatives, because it is known he has none, since a minor cannot father a child.
Abaye raises an objection to Rabba from a baraita.
The baraita derives from the extra vav in Leviticus 19:20 that a nine-year-old boy, fit for intercourse, is included in the halakha.
Rabba replies that a nine-year-old has sperm but cannot father a child, like grain cut before a third of its growth.
A Sage of the school of Hizkiyya derives from the word yazid in Exodus 21:14 that a minor cannot heat himself to produce viable sperm.
Rav Mordekhai asks Rav Ashi how we know that mezid means heating up.
Rav Ashi answers that the word is used in Genesis 25:29 for cooking pottage, so it means heating.
The Gemara asks why the school of Rabbi Yishmael's baraita would say that a father is not a rebellious son, given this.
The Gemara asks whether a rebellious son's entire liability period of three months leaves room for conception and birth.
The Gemara suggests the child was conceived before the first hairs, so a minor can father a child.
The Gemara rejects this: conception came after the hairs, and Rav Dimi explains the verse excludes only one whose wife conceived in this period.
Rabbi Kruspedai says in the name of Rabbi Shabbtai that a rebellious son is liable only during three months.
The Gemara asks: but we learned the mishna makes liability depend on hair and beard, not a three-month period.
If the beard surrounds him he is no longer liable even before three months; and after three months he is exempt even without the beard.
Rabbi Ya'akov from Nehar Pekod infers from Kruspedai's view on seven-month births that the three-month period is needed for discernment.
Ravina replies that the rule follows the majority, since most women give birth at nine months.
Rav Huna objects: in capital cases do we follow the majority, when the court must seek exculpatory arguments?
Rav Huna cites Numbers 35:24-25, the congregation shall judge and deliver, to require searching for exculpatory grounds.
The Sages bring Rav Huna's analysis back to Ravina and present it before him.
Ravina challenges: do we not follow the majority in cases of capital law?
Mishnaic cases on witnesses to the addition of a day, and on betrothal of a three-year-old girl, show the majority is followed even in capital law.
The mishna states the rules of a three-year-old girl's betrothal, levirate, impurity, priesthood and the execution of relatives, with the minor exempt.

69b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yirmeya argues that a three-year-old married girl is presumed capable of bearing, so the majority rule applies even to capital cases.
The Gemara refutes this: the mishna's phrase about a married girl refers to an unwitting sin-offering, not the death penalty.
The Gemara asks why the mishna's death penalty clause, for any forbidden relation, does not apply when the husband is a different man.
The case must be one where the husband explicitly accepted her as a wife, so an outsider is liable to death.
A baraita records the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on whether a minor's intercourse disqualifies a woman from the priesthood.
Rav Hisda and Ze'eiri report that all agree a boy nine years and one day counts, and dispute only the eight-year-old.
The Gemara asks from where we derive that men in earlier generations fathered children at this age.
Scriptural chronology of Bathsheba, Eliam, Ahithophel and Solomon is cited to show Solomon's birth was early in the family line.
Verses on Absalom's sheepshearers and exile are used to tally the years after Solomon's birth.
Verses on Absalom's two years in Jerusalem and the forty years, and Ahithophel's suicide, fix Solomon's age at the rebellion.
Psalms 55:24 and a baraita on the life spans of Doeg and Ahithophel are used to compute that each parent fathered at eight.
The Gemara objects that the parents may each have fathered at nine, and Bathsheba conceived earlier because women mature sooner.
Genesis 11 on Terah's sons is cited to show Abraham was two years older than Haran, so Haran fathered at about eight.
Rabbi Yitzhak identifies Iscah with Sarah, explaining the name by her hidden visions and her beauty.
Abraham was ten years older than Sarah and two older than Haran, so Haran fathered Sarah at about eight.
The Gemara objects that Abraham may have been the youngest brother, listed first only for his wisdom.
The Gemara answers that the verse sometimes lists brothers by wisdom rather than by birth order.
Genesis 5:32 and 7:6 show Shem was two years older than Japheth yet at 600 years Noah's sons are reckoned at Japheth's age.
Genesis 11:10 shows Shem was only 100 at a time when he would have to be older, so the order must be by wisdom.
Shem was in fact the youngest brother, and the list order reflects wisdom, as in the Terah case.
Rav Kahana reports his discussion before Rav Zevid, who showed from Genesis 10:21 that Japheth was the eldest.
The Gemara asks from where we derive that men in earlier generations fathered children at eight, beyond the tabernacle example.
Exodus 38:22 and Chronicles 2:19-20 show Bezalel was a grandson of Caleb's wife and Hur, establishing the generational chain.
The Gemara asks how old Bezalel was when he built the Tabernacle.
He must have been at least thirteen, since the verse calls the craftsmen men, and one under thirteen is not a man.
A baraita: in the first year Moses made the Tabernacle, in the second he erected it and sent the spies.
Caleb's age at the spy mission and his statements to Joshua are used to show each of three generations fathered at eight.
The mishna's rule covers a son and not a daughter, the son alone being liable.
A baraita: Rabbi Shimon holds it reasonable that a daughter who sins like a rebellious son should also be punished like him.

70a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The reason a daughter is excluded is that she is commonly drawn into sin, but the Torah's edict limits the penalty to a son.
The mishna sets when the rebellious son becomes liable: eating a tarteimar of meat and drinking wine, and the verse in Proverbs on gluttons and drunkards.
Rabbi Zeira says he does not know what a tarteimar is.
It is derived from Rabbi Yosei's doubling for wine that the measure for meat is doubled too, making a tarteimar half a maneh.
Rav Huna rules the son is liable only if he buys meat and wine cheaply, as the verse zolel and sovei implies.
Rav Huna also rules he is liable only if he eats raw meat and drinks raw wine.
The Gemara objects: Rabbah and Rav Yosef both say that eating raw meat and drinking raw wine does not make him a rebel.
Ravina distinguishes: wine is liable raw but mixed, meat is liable raw but not cooked, like a fox's meat that thieves eat.
Rabbah and Rav Yosef both say that eating salted meat and drinking wine from its press does not make him a rebel.
The mishna on Tisha B'Av forbids two cooked dishes, and a baraita permits mourners to eat salted meat and drink wine from the press.
Rabbi Hanina bar Kahana answers the limit: meat remains like peace-offerings and wine remains fermenting.
A baraita states fermenting wine does not raise concern of revealing, and that fermentation lasts three days.
The difference is that here the wine's pull is the concern, while in the case of peace-offerings it is rejoicing.
Rabbi Hanan says wine was created only to comfort mourners and to repay the wicked, citing Proverbs 31:6.
Rabbi Yitzhak explains Proverbs 23:31 as saying the wicked have red faces in this world and white faces in the next.
Rava reads Proverbs 23:31 as meaning the end of wine is blood.
Rav Kahana raises a contradiction: the verse is written tirosh but read tirosh, the same word with different effects.
Rava raises a similar contradiction over Psalms 104:15, with the verse written and read differently.
Rava's saying that wine makes the wise cunning resolves the contradiction in favor of wine's effect.
Rav Amram, citing Rabbi Hanina, reads Proverbs 23:29-30 as describing the various woes of those who linger over wine.
Rav Dimi explains the method of exposition: a verse read from start to end and back, with thirteen and vav letters tied to wine.
Genesis 9:20-24 tells of Noah planting a vineyard, drinking, and Ham seeing his nakedness.
Noah awoke from his wine and knew what his youngest son had done to him.
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether Ham castrated Noah or sodomized him, and the dispute on cursing Canaan follows from it.
Verbal analogy on the word saw in Genesis 9:22 and 34:2 is used to support the view that Ham sodomized Noah.
The Gemara asks why, on the view that Ham castrated, the curse fell on the fourth son, and why sodomy would be stated explicitly.
Both views are true, and the verse about Noah planting a vineyard is read together with the other.
Rav Hisda, citing Rav Ukva and Rabbi Zakkai, says God told Noah he should have taught from the first man not to fall into wine.
A baraita holds that the tree the first man ate from was a vine, as Rabbi Meir says.

70b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Wine alone is said to bring wailing and trouble upon a person
Rabbi Yehuda identifies the Tree of Knowledge as wheat
A baby cannot call its father or mother until it tastes grain
Rabbi Nehemya identifies the Tree of Knowledge as a fig tree
Genesis verse about the fig leaves supports Nehemya
Proverbs verse about the words of King Lemuel introduces the mother's correction
Rabbi Yohanan teaches in the name of Rabbi Shimon that the mother tied him to a pillar
The mother asks what her son is doing, questioning her own vows
Explanation that everyone knows the father feared Heaven, so people will blame the mother
The mother asks about the pregnancies of all the women of the household
Women stop seeing the king once pregnant, so she pushed in to get a zealous son
The mother asks about the vows of all the women of the household
The women vowed for a son fit for the kingdom; she vowed a son fit for prophecy
She wished for a son diligent in Torah, fit for prophecy and not for kings
Proverbs verse that kings should not drink wine is quoted
The mother asks what Lemuel has to do with kings who drink wine and become drunk
Verse about strong drink for rulers is quoted
Continuation of the verse: one whose secrets are revealed may drink wine and get drunk
An alternative version: whoever rulers rise early to attend may drink and become drunk
Rabbi Yitzhak asks from where we learn that Solomon repented and admitted to his mother
Proverbs verse in which Agur says he is too ignorant to understand man
Genesis verse about Noah with the same wording is cited as a parallel
One who eats in a group performing a mitzva is not liable
Rabbi Abahu says one is not liable unless he eats in a group entirely of idlers
The Mishnah teaches that one who eats in a mitzva group does not become a rebellious son
The ruling applies because it is a mitzva meal, even though not all are idlers
The point is that even if all are idlers, one engaged in a mitzva does not get dragged
Case of one who eats during the intercalation of the month
Does this mean that meat and wine were raised as the intended food
A baraita says one only goes up to the Temple on bread of grain and legumes
This teaches that even though one goes up on bread and legumes, if he ate meat and wine he is not dragged
A baraita: one does not go up at intercalation unless there are at least ten people
One goes up only on bread of grain and legumes, and only by the light of the intercalation
One goes up only by day, not at night
A baraita says one goes up only at night, not by day
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba told his sons to go up and come down quickly so people would hear and weep
Case of one who eats second tithe in Jerusalem
Since eating is his usual way, he is not dragged
Case of one who eats carrion, non-kosher meat and creeping things
Rava says one who eats the flesh of a bird does not become a rebellious son
The Mishnah teaches that one who eats carrion and creeping things does not become a rebellious son
The Mishnah speaks of ritually pure foods that are consumed, so the rule applies to them
The Mishnah is quoted to complete the discussion
Mishnah: one may eat what is a mitzva or a sin, such as consoling mourners or fasting for the public
What is the reason for this ruling
A verse about not listening to the voice of the people, nor to the voice of God, is cited
Mishnah: one who eats any food but not meat, or drinks any drink but not wine
This explains that the case of eating any food but not meat comes to include a dabilah of Kaila
Drinking any drink but not wine comes to include honey and milk
A baraita: one who eats a dabilah of Kaila and drinks honey and milk is cited
And he enters the Temple, which is the conclusion of the case

71a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: He is not a stubborn and rebellious son unless he eats meat and drinks wine
Baraita: one who eats any food but not meat, or drinks any drink but not wine, is not a rebellious son
Verse describing the glutton and the drunkard is cited
Although there is no proof for this, it is a memorial to the matter
Proverbs verse: do not be among drunkards of wine or gluttons of meat
Another Proverbs verse: the drunkard and glutton will become poor and wear rags
Rabbi Zeira says whoever sleeps in the study hall has his Torah turned to tatters
The verse about clothing a sleeper in tatters is cited for that teaching
Mishnah: a son who steals from his father to eat at his father's table is not rebellious unless he steals from father and eats elsewhere
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says he must steal from both his father and his mother
Gemara explains the Mishnah's cases of stealing and eating in different combinations of houses
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda repeats that stealing from father and mother is required
Where do we learn that a wife's acquisitions belong to her husband
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina derives it from a feast prepared for father and mother
Objection: Rabbi Hanan bar Mulda said in Rav Huna's name that he is not liable
Rav Huna's view: he must buy meat cheaply and drink wine cheaply
Reply: the case is like a feast prepared for parents, or a stranger gave it on condition her husband has no right
Mishnah: if father wants and mother does not, or the reverse, he is not rebellious unless both want
Rabbi Yehuda says if his mother is not worthy of his father, he is not rebellious
What does not worthy mean here
Suppose it means she is liable for karet or capital punishment by court
Rejected: father is still father and mother is still mother, so that cannot be the meaning
Rather, the Mishnah means she must be equal to the father
A baraita says the same: Rabbi Yehuda says if his mother is not equal to his father
He is not rebellious if equal in voice, appearance and height
What is the reason for this ruling
The verse: he does not listen to our voice is cited
From voice we learn that appearance and height must also be equal
Like whom does this follow
Baraita: a rebellious son never existed and never will exist
Why was it written then, and does one receive reward for studying it
It follows Rabbi Yehuda, or alternatively Rabbi Shimon
Rabbi Shimon's baraita begins to be cited
Rabbi Shimon asks whether the parents would stone a son who ate meat and drank wine
Rather, such a son never existed and never will, and it was written to be expounded
Rabbi Yonatan's anecdote: I saw him and sat on his grave
Like whom does this follow
Baraita: an apostate city never existed and never will, and was written to be expounded
It follows Rabbi Eliezer
Rabbi Eliezer says any city with even one mezuzah is not an apostate city
What is the reason
The verse about gathering the spoil into the square and burning the city is cited
If a mezuzah were present, the destruction would be impossible
Verse: you shall not do so to the Lord your God is cited
Rabbi Yonatan's anecdote: I saw it and sat on its ruins
Like whom does this follow
Baraita: a house with leprosy never existed and never will, and was written to be expounded
It follows Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon
As we learned in a Mishnah
Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon says a house is impure only if the spot is the size of two lentils on two stones in a corner
What is the reason of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon
The verse uses both wall in the singular and walls in the plural
Which wall is like walls? It means the corner angle
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer ben Tzadok said a place in the area of Gaza was called a sealed ruin
Rabbi Shimon's anecdote: in the Galilee he saw a place marked by stones that were declared impure
Mishnah: one who was maimed, lame, mute, blind or deaf is not a rebellious son
Deuteronomy verse about the parents seizing him and bringing him out is cited
Mishnah: the verse excludes those who cannot speak or hear, and they are warned before three
They are warned before three judges and flogged
If he repeats the offense, he is judged by twenty-three judges and not stoned unless the first three are present
The verse: our son, this one, is cited to show he was flogged before you
We learn from this that a verse is needed, as written; this case is different

71b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The whole verse would be superfluous if it only teaches warning before three
Why do we need the warning before two and the flogging before three
Abaye explains: warned before two, flogged before three, for the rebellious son
Where is this written
Rabbi Abahu says we learn it from the verses
Deuteronomy verses about chastising, flogging and the wicked man are cited
One who repeats the offense is judged by twenty-three judges
Why would the verse need our son this one, if not to exclude the blind and deaf
From our son this one we learn two things
Mishnah: one who fled before his judgment was final and then the lower elder encircled him is exempt, but after it is final he is liable
Rabbi Hanina says a Noahide who blessed the Name and then converted is exempt
Since his law has changed, shall we say this supports the Mishnah
Restating the Mishnah case of fleeing before the judgment became final
What is the reason
No, it is different here, since if he does it now he is no longer one fit to be killed
A baraita says one who fled after judgment and was encircled is liable
You speak of a final judgment, but then the man is already one to be killed
Another baraita: a Noahide who struck and committed adultery and converted is exempt, but liable if an Israelite did it
Why not say that since his judgment has changed it is the same
We require both the judgment and the death; here the judgment changed but the death did not
For a murderer the method is the sword before and after, but for an adulteress it differs
The baraita teaches that such a case among Israel parallels another man's wife
Rather, how can a lighter penalty be made into a heavier one
This works for the Rabbis who hold the sword is the more severe penalty
But according to Rabbi Shimon, who holds strangling is more severe, what can be said
Rabbi Shimon holds like the tanna of the house of Menashe
The tanna of the house of Menashe says every death penalty stated for the sons of Noah is only strangling
Granted the adulteress is strangled before and after, but the murderer is strangled before and then by the sword
Shall we say it supports him: a baraita that she was seduced and then grew up is judged by strangling or stoning
What is the reason
It is because if the law changed, the law changes, and certainly here it changed completely
Rabbi Yohanan tells the tanna to teach that the case is judged by stoning
Mishnah: the rebellious son is judged by his end; if he dies innocent, he should not die, and if he dies guilty he is liable
Mishnah continues with the opposite fates of the wicked and the righteous, such as death, wine, sleep, scattering, gathering and quiet

72a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita attributed to Rabbi Yosei the Galilean
Rhetorical question: is it because he ate meat and drank Italian wine that he should be stoned
The Torah said he goes out to court to be stoned
Rather, the Torah reaches the end of the rebellious son's intention
The rebellious son eventually consumes his father's property, seeks learning, fails, and turns to robbery
The Torah's verdict: he should die innocent, and not die guilty
The list repeated: the death of the wicked is pleasure to them and to the world, while the righteous get the opposite
Mishnah: one who tunnels in and breaks a jar is liable if the owner has money and exempt if not
What is the reason
Rava explains: a person does not stand by his property, since the intruder would otherwise say he would not leave him alone
The verse: if one comes to kill you, rise early and kill him
Rav says one who tunnels in and takes utensils and leaves is exempt
What is the reason
When he took the money it is considered as if he has acquired it
Rava says Rav's view is reasonable when he broke and has no money, but not when he took
Rav says even if he took, he is liable since the owner has money and it was lost
Evidently his property stands, so here too his property stands, and it is not the same
When we explained the verse as applying to his property for damages, but for acquisition it is the owner's property
Mishnah: if he broke the jar and has money he is liable, but if not he is exempt
The reason for the exemption without money is that breaking was not done for gain
The same law applies even if he took, as in the Mishnah
Why does the Mishnah teach that he broke the jar
It teaches that when he has money he is liable even though he broke it, which is obvious as a damager
He is a damager, and the Mishnah teaches that even unintentional damage is liable
What does this teach us
A person is always a damager, as we learned, even by accident, which contradicts the ruling
Rav Bibi bar Abaye raises an objection
Objection: one who steals a purse on Shabbat is liable, since the theft came before the Shabbat prohibition
Reply: the prohibitions of theft and of stoning arise together
Rava's conduct: he returned stolen rams rather than accept them, since it came from Rav's mouth
A baraita cites the verse: if the sun shined on him, there is no blood guilt, and if certain it is like the sun
A different baraita contradicts it: if the sun shined on him there is blood guilt
This is a difficulty; the general case is not a difficulty

72b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Here it is the father over the son, and here the son over the father, as two cases
Rav says anyone who comes to tunnel in may be killed
Rav Hanina bar Shila disagrees with Rav
What is the reason for his disagreement
Suppose it is because he is righteous, but he came to tunnel, which is not righteous
Rather, I know he has compassion for me, as a father has for a son
Baraita: blood guilt applies on weekdays and Shabbat, and if no money, there is no guilt on either day
Granted the no-money case needs both days stated, since one might think it is like court executions
We might think it is like court executions not done on Shabbat, so it teaches we do kill
Rather, if he has money, both weekday and Shabbat: on a weekday we do not kill, so is Shabbat in doubt
Rav Sheshet says it is needed to teach that one may put a stone on him to protect him
Baraita cites the verse: the one who strikes any man and kills, in any death you can kill him
Granted, the verse about any man is needed, since one might think it applies only to the owner
The owner is one who does not stand by his property, but for another it is not so, which we teach
It teaches that the pursuer is included, even another, and he dies in any death
Why do I need this, since it is derived from the murderer
Baraita cites the verse: the smiter is a murderer, and he shall surely be put to death
I have only the death specified in the verse
From where do we learn that if you cannot kill him by the stated death, you may kill him by any death
The verse says he shall surely die, which teaches the murderer and redeemer of blood have two verses that come together
Since two verses come together and both apply, we cannot derive one from the other
Baraita: a tunneling is only the roof, courtyard and enclosure, from where
From where do we learn this, from the verse
The verse: the thief shall be found, which suggests the rule is general
If so, why does the verse say tunneling
Because most thieves are found tunneling
Another baraita: the tunnel is only its roof, courtyard and enclosure, and it contradicts the earlier derivation
If so, why does the verse say tunneling again
His tunnel is his warning, which means the pursuer needs no warning if he tunneled
Rav Huna says a small pursuer may be saved with his own life, holding that a pursuer needs no warning, whether adult or minor
Rav Hisda objects to Rav Huna: if his head came out, one does not touch him, since one life does not override another, so why is he a pursuer
That case is different, since they pursue him from Heaven, so shall we say it supports him
Baraita: one who pursues another to kill him is told: see, he is an Israelite and a son of the covenant
The Torah verse: whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed
The Torah says to save the blood of this one by the blood of that one
This is the view of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says a warning is not needed, since warning was given only to distinguish unintentional from intentional
Come and hear: a baraita on one who pursues another to kill him
The baraita: he says to him he is Israelite and covenant son, and if he says I know he is so, he is exempt on that condition, but liable if I do it
It is needed for one standing on the far bank of a river who cannot rescue him, and one wanting to bring him to court needs a warning

Proposes that the parent-striker dies only if he actually kills the parent.
Rejects that proposal as absurd: beheading for killing others but strangling for parents.
If strangulation is lenient or severe, what can explain the limitation to killing?
Derives from two verses that unspecified striking does not itself cause death.
Argues both verses are needed to include adults and non-viable or eight-month newborns.
Why not liable without drawing blood, given the Mishnah says a wound is required?
Verse juxtaposing striking a man with striking an animal shows a wound is needed.
Rav Yirmeya objects: an animal weighed down by stones is liable without bleeding.
If the juxtaposition is not needed for that, why is it written at all?
A baraita on healing: striking for medical purposes is exempt, as with animals.
Is a son permitted to draw blood from his father for treatment?
Rav Mattana derives it from the command to love your neighbor as yourself.
Rav Dimi bar Ḥinnana derives it from the man and animal juxtaposition.
Rav and Mar son of Ravina would not let their sons treat them, out of caution.
If so, anyone else treating him would also risk an unwitting capital violation.
The Mishnah permits removing a thorn on Shabbat; why not fear wounding and stoning?
There the act is destructive, and he is liable only for constructive labor.
This works if destructive labor is exempt, but what if it is liable?
The one who holds destructive labor liable is Rabbi Shimon.

85a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon's principle: labor not needed for itself makes the actor exempt.
Can a court-designated agent be a son who flogs or curses his own father?
Heaven's honor overrides a parent's honor, so a son may serve as agent.
A baraita implies a general prohibition on striking, even when not commanded.
The baraita's clauses differ only in whether the agent is the son or another person.
No difference between son and other agents; the clauses differ only by the mitzva case.
Deuteronomy's forty-lash limit shows a general prohibition on striking beyond it.
A baraita: a son who strikes a condemned father is liable, another person is exempt.
What is the difference between a son and another person in that baraita?
Rav Ḥisda: the baraita concerns a condemned man refusing to leave, so force is needed.
Rav Sheshet: the case is one where he goes willingly and another strikes him.
If so, anyone striking a condemned man should be liable, which the baraita denies.
Rav Sheshet holds a humiliator liable to heirs, so why is the condemned man different?
If another is exempt only from payment, does the son owe payment? The baraita must mean punishment.
The verse forbidding cursing a ruler of your people limits the prohibition to conduct befitting a Jew.
That explains cursing, but where is the same halakha for striking derived?
If the prohibition is limited, the son of a penitent should be exempt too; Rav Pineḥas explains repentance.
If so, another person who strikes the condemned should also be liable.
Rav Mari: the phrase of your people means only one remaining among the people, not one facing execution.
If so, the son should be exempt because his father's execution is imminent.

85b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The son's liability to curse after death applies here too, even before the death.
What halakhic conclusion was reached about a son serving as agent?
Rabba bar Rav Huna and the school of Rabbi Yishmael: a son is not an agent against a father, except an inciter.
Cites Deuteronomy 13:9 about not sparing or concealing an inciter as the exception.
Mishnah: striking a parent is not capital unless a wound results, while cursing is stricter.
Baraita cites Leviticus 20:9 to include cursing a parent after death.
A fortiori argument from striking to cursing, showing no liability for cursing after death.
The extra phrase in the verse is taken to include cursing a parent after death.
If the extra phrase serves Rabbi Yonatan, what does it do for Rabbi Yoshiya?
Rabbi Yoshiya's baraita: the redundant ish ish includes a daughter, tumtum and hermaphrodite curses.
Rabbi Yonatan: a vav joining two subjects means both together or each alone, unless stated together.
From where does Rabbi Yoshiya derive liability for cursing a parent after death?
Derives it from Exodus 21:17 on one who curses a father or mother.
What does Rabbi Yonatan derive from that verse?
He uses it to include a daughter, tumtum and hermaphrodite among those liable for cursing.
Why not derive that from the redundant ish ish, as Rabbi Yoshiya does?
Why does the mishna not teach the second stringency about striking versus cursing?
The mishna's tanna holds that striking is likened to cursing through the verses' juxtaposition.
Suggests the Samaritan disputes parallel the earlier disputes among the tanna'im.
First baraita: one must refrain from striking a Samaritan but not from cursing him.
Second baraita: one must refrain from neither cursing nor striking a Samaritan.
Everyone agrees Samaritans are true converts, so they are like sinning Jews.
Do the baraitot disagree on whether striking is likened to cursing?
No: they disagree on whether Samaritans are true converts or converts under threat.
The baraita on an ox treats Samaritans as Jews, so the dispute must concern the verse juxtaposition.
Mishna on abduction: liability requires bringing the victim into one's domain and exploiting him, with Rabbi Yehuda's stricter view.
Why does the first tanna not require exploitation, since the verse states it explicitly?
Rabbi Aha son of Rava: the dispute concerns exploitation worth less than one peruta.
Dilemmas of Rabbi Yirmeya: abducting a sleeping man, or a pregnant woman for her fetus.
Why not rule the abductor exempt, since there is no exploitation at all?
The dilemmas concern lying on a sleeper or shielding from wind with a pregnant woman; left unresolved.
Baraita derives from Deuteronomy 24:7 and Exodus 21:16 that men and women abductors and victims are liable.
Another baraita: abducting any person, including converts and minors, creates liability if sold or kept.
Abducting slaves is exempt; selling to the victim's father or relatives makes the abductor liable.

86a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Sheshet objects: Rabbi Shimon limits abduction to removing the victim from his brothers, so the baraita must say exempt.
Is the baraita perhaps the view of the Rabbis, against Rabbi Shimon?
Unattributed baraitot in the Sifrei follow Rabbi Shimon, and all these tanna'im followed Rabbi Akiva.
What is the reason for the Rabbis who exempt one who abducts his son?
Abaye: the verse if a man is found excludes one already in the abductor's custody.
Rav Pappa objects: by that logic adulterers found in a known house would also be exempt.
Abaye: the Rabbis derive it from or if found in his possession, excluding the already found.
Rava rules that teachers of children are exempt for abducting their students, who count as held in their possession.
Mishna and baraita: Rabbi Yehuda holds a slave has no indemnity for humiliation, as he is not a full brother.
What is the reason for the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda?
Deuteronomy 25:11 on the brother who has family ties receiving payment, excluding slaves.
The Rabbis say a slave is a brother regarding the fulfillment of mitzvot.
How does Rabbi Yehuda read brother to make half-slaves liable for abduction?
Rabbi Yehuda: from his brethren excludes slaves, and from the children of Israel excludes the half-slave, a restriction after restriction.
The Rabbis read the two expressions to exclude slaves and half-slaves separately.
From where is the prohibition against abducting a person derived?
Rabbi Yoshiya cites You shall not steal and Rabbi Yohanan cites Leviticus 25:42 on selling a slave.
The two Sages do not disagree; each verse is needed, one for abduction and one for selling.
Baraita: the steal prohibition speaks of abduction, learned by context from the capital prohibitions beside it.
Second baraita: the same verse speaks of property theft, learned by context from the adjacent property prohibitions.
If the abduction and sale witnesses are proven conspiring, the dispute over their execution is stated.
Hizkiyya says they are not executed; Rabbi Yohanan says they are.
Hizkiyya follows Rabbi Akiva that testimony must cover a whole matter; Rabbi Yohanan follows the Rabbis who accept half-matter testimony.
Hizkiyya concedes that the final witnesses against a rebellious son are executed, which challenges his general view.

86b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The abduction witnesses came only to flog, but the later witnesses are responsible for the whole execution.
Rav Pappa objects: by that logic the sale witnesses should be executed too, and Hizkiyya cannot flog abductors.
Recalls that Hizkiyya and Rabbi Yohanan disagree on flogging abduction witnesses, and Hizkiyya holds they are not executed.
Rabbi Yohanan's view would make it a warning for capital punishment, so flogging the witnesses cannot follow.
Rav Pappa: they dispute only abduction witnesses, since abduction is the start of the sale.
Rabbi Yohanan concedes that the early witnesses against a rebellious son are not executed.
Abaye summarizes: all agree on the rebellious son cases, and the dispute lies only in the middle case.
For the early witnesses, all agree they are not executed, since they came only to flog for past conduct.
For the final witnesses, all agree they are executed, because they are responsible for the entire execution.
The dispute over a rebellious son arises when two pairs of witnesses testify to stealing and eating separately.
Rav Asi: witnesses to a sale are not executed, since the accused could claim it was his slave.
Rav Yosef: Rav Asi follows Rabbi Akiva, that testimony must cover an entire matter.
Abaye objects: if the Rabbis were the source, Rav Asi's slave reasoning would still defeat execution.
Rav Asi may follow the Rabbis, when only sale witnesses testify and the abduction witnesses are absent.
If that is so, what is the point of the ruling, since it is obvious?
It covers later abduction witnesses and gestures between the pairs, which Rav Asi says are insignificant.
Mishna: a rebellious elder who defies the court is strangled; the three courts in Jerusalem are described.
The elder appeals first to the court at the Temple Mount entrance, with the same procedure for each court.
If unresolved, the case moves to the court at the Temple courtyard, then the two courts jointly appear before the High Court.
The High Court's ruling binds; an elder who only teaches his old view is exempt, but one who instructs others is liable.
A student not yet ordained who instructs others against the Sanhedrin is exempt, as his ruling carries no authority.
Tannaitic baraita on Deuteronomy 17:8, reading yippaleh to show the court decides hard matters.

87a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Verse Deuteronomy 17:8 refers to a distinguished adviser, with a Sinai halakha and a logical inference.
Each pair of matters in the verse stands for distinct halakhot about blood, cases, and leprosy.
The verse's remaining phrases name sacred gifts, sota and the heifer, and gleanings, and teach that the Temple is highest.
From where does the tanna derive that Eretz Yisrael is higher than all other lands?
Jeremiah 23:7-8 shows that coming to Eretz Yisrael is also called ascent.
Baraita: the rebellious elder is liable only for karet or sin-offering matters, per Rabbi Meir, with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon differing.
What is the reason for Rabbi Meir's opinion?
Verbal analogy from matter in Deuteronomy 17:8 to matter in Leviticus 4:13 limits liability to karet cases.
Rabbi Yehuda reads according to the Torah they will instruct you, requiring both Written and oral teaching.
Rabbi Shimon reads from that place, making any deviation from the Sanhedrin liable.
Rav Huna asks Rava to explain the baraita according to Rabbi Meir, showing karet for each category.
Rav Pappa explains the adviser as one who intercalates years, citing a mishna on intercalation in Adar.
A contrary ruling on intercalation could permit leaven on Passover, making karet or sin-offering apply.
The matter of the eleven days is a halakha from Sinai involving a greater zava's karet and purification.
Rabbi Yohanan: the tenth day counts as the ninth, so a clean day is needed on the eleventh.
Reish Lakish: the tenth day counts as the eleventh, so no clean day is needed, changing the karet liability.
Judgment is a logical inference, one of the hermeneutical principles.

87b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Example of the prohibition against intercourse with a daughter born of a rape victim.
Verbal analogies between henna and zimma in Leviticus show that intercourse with a daughter is forbidden and capital.
Blood case: Akavya ben Mahalalel and the Rabbis dispute whether green blood is menstrual.
Childbirth blood: Rav and Levi dispute whether the blood comes from one source or two.
Zava blood: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute when a woman who gave birth becomes a zava.
Monetary-law cases: Shmuel and Rabbi Abbahu dispute whether a two-judge court's rulings are valid.
Capital cases: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Rabbis dispute whether a life for a life means money.
Lashes cases: Rabbi Yishmael and the Rabbis dispute the number of judges required for lashes.
The three kinds of leprous marks are listed: on persons, houses, and garments.
Human leprosy: Rabbi Yehoshua and the Rabbis dispute an uncertain order of baheret and white hair, with Rava's explanation.
House leprosy: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon requires a mark on two walls, as the mishna states.
What is the reason for the opinion of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon?
The verse's wall and walls is read to require a corner between two walls for a leprous house.
Garment leprosy: Rabbi Yonatan ben Avtolemos and the Rabbis dispute, as a baraita begins to show.

88a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Would garment leprosy that spreads over the whole garment be pure, as in human leprosy?
Karahat and gabbahat in both leprosy contexts are read by analogy, so a fully spread mark is pure for garments too.
Valuations: Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis dispute whether a child valued under a month old gives a monetary value.
Dedications: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says undesignated dedications go to Temple maintenance, per Leviticus 27:28.
The Rabbis say undesignated dedications go to the priest, per Leviticus 27:21, which affects betrothal and liability.
Consecrations: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov requires ten judges to redeem, while the Rabbis require three.
Sota and heifer: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute warning a wife on one or two witnesses.
Rabbi Yehoshua holds that both the warning and the bitter waters require two witnesses.
Heifer: the tanna's dispute over where the corpse is measured, from navel, nose, or neck.
Leper purification: Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis dispute whether blood and oil can go on a missing body part.
Gleanings and forgotten sheaves: the mishna sets stalk and sheaf counts that define them.
Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute the portions and betrothal effect for those gleanings.
Pe'a: Rabbi Yishmael and the Rabbis dispute the designation sequence, from standing grain to flour.
Rabbi Yishmael allows designating pe'a from dough, so a poor person's betrothal with it takes effect.
Mishna: three courts in Jerusalem are described for the rebellious elder's procedure.
Rav Kahana: a ruling based on a received tradition is not executed, since there is a basis for it.
An elder who asserts his own understanding is not executed, as Akavya ben Mahalalel shows.
Rabbi Elazar holds even a traditional-basis elder is executed to prevent discord, while Akavya was theoretical.
Does the mishna's phrase include an elder who rules on tradition against the court's understanding?
No: the mishna means he says the understanding is his own while the court relies on tradition.
A baraita from Rabbi Yoshiya on a husband's retracted warning, as proof for the mishna's interpretation.

88b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A stubborn and rebellious son's parents may forgive him and decline to bring him to court.
A court may forgive a rebellious elder who deviated, which supports Rabbi Elazar against Rav Kahana.
Baraita (Rabbi Yosei): originally the Sanhedrin's tiers of courts stood across Israel, with no discord.
Procedure: those seeking a ruling ask their local court, then move up through the courts toward the Temple.
The deviating elder appeals to the Chamber of Hewn Stone, which sat between the morning and afternoon offerings.
On Shabbat and festivals the courts sat at the rampart and decided by vote when no ruling was clear.
Disciples of Shammai and Hillel did not serve their masters fully, so Torah became two Torahs.
The Sanhedrin sends the appointment criteria and promotes a qualified judge upward through the courts.
Sages send a statement on the qualities for the World-to-Come, and they judge Rav Ulla bar Abba fits.
Mishna: the elder who teaches at home is exempt unless he instructs others; the Sages add that acting on his ruling suffices.
If he is liable only for instructing, the death penalty is new for a ruling on fat and blood, but not for capital-level rulings.
Even when he acts on his ruling, the change is that forewarning is no longer required before execution.
If his ruling was about idolatrous incitement, which needs no forewarning, what is the change?
Before the divergent ruling, his stated reason was accepted; afterward it is not, since he already held incitement permitted.
Mishna: greater stringency applies to rabbinic interpretations than to Torah matters, with the phylacteries example.
Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Oshaya: liability requires a matter rooted in Torah, extended by rabbinic addition, following Rabbi Yehuda.
Does the lulav mitzva, with its rabbinic addition of species, not also meet that test?
Lulav: if the species stand separately, an added species is inconsequential, so the elder is not liable.
Does the mitzva of ritual fringes, with rabbinic additions of fringes and threads, meet the test?
Fringes: if the upper knot is not Torah law, extra threads are independent and do not compromise the mitzva.

89a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Four-compartment phylacteries with an added separate compartment remain valid, the same as fringes.
Challenge: a fifth phylactery compartment should spoil the mitzva, as the outer compartment unexposed to air shows.
Rabbi Zeira's ruling on a covered outer compartment makes any fifth compartment unfit.
Mishna: a rebellious elder is not executed locally or at Yavne, but taken to Jerusalem and executed on a festival, per Rabbi Akiva.
Baraita repeats the Jerusalem and festival procedure, with Rabbi Akiva's view on the nation hearing and fearing.
Rabbi Yehuda objects to Rabbi Akiva: the verse says hear, so the execution should be immediate.
Four offenders require public proclamation, and the verse on those remaining who hear and fear limits who must heed it.
Mishna: the false prophet is executed by man if he prophesies unheard words, and by Heaven if he suppresses or breaks his prophecy.
One prophesying in the name of idol worship is strangled, even if his halakhic ruling is correct.
Adultery with a married woman who entered the husband's domain is a strangulation offense.
Conspiring witnesses against a priest's daughter are strangled, as her paramour is, unlike the burning penalty.
Baraita sorts prophecy offenses: three executed by man and three by Heaven.
From where are these categories derived?
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, derives them from Deuteronomy 18:20, and every unspecified death means strangulation.
Deuteronomy 18:19 with the reading of its words yields the three Heaven-executed offenses.
The mishna's example of one who prophesies unheard words.
Example: Zedekiah son of Chenaanah prophesied victory for Ahab with iron horns.
What could Zedekiah do, since the spirit of Naboth misled him, and why was he held responsible?
I Kings 22 shows God permitting the spirit to entice Ahab, cited to explain the prophetic deception.
Rav Yehuda: Go forth means the spirit left God's proximity by volunteering deceit, so it is not prophetic.
Rabbi Yitzhak: one style of prophecy suits many prophets, but two prophets do not share one style.
Obadiah and Jeremiah verses show that pride and self-deception lead prophets astray.
Those who cite these examples together seem to say nothing decisive.
Perhaps they did not know Rabbi Yitzhak's principle about one style of prophecy.
Jehoshaphat's question, Is there not yet a prophet of the Lord, is cited as evidence.
Jehoshaphat was told the tradition of his father's house: one style rises to many prophets.
Hananiah son of Azzur prophesied against Jeremiah's word, the example of an unsent prophecy.
Hananiah reasons a fortiori: if Elam came only to help Babylon, God will break Elam, and Babylon's power too.
Jeremiah 28:2 records Hananiah's prophecy that God would break the yoke of Babylon.
Rav Pappa objects to Abaye: the same should not be said of the other prophet, so the principle is undermined.
Abaye: a fortiori, since the verse is given to be expounded, this one is not said, as with the false prophet.
Examples: the prophets of Baal who spoke in the name of idolatry, Jonah ben Amittai who suppressed prophecy, and one who forgoes a prophet.

89b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Colleague of the prophet Micah: a prophet struck by a lion for disobeying the word of God, per I Kings 20.
Iddo the prophet violated his own word and was killed by a lion, shown by I Kings 13.
A baraita says one who suppresses prophecy is flogged, but Rav Hisda doubts he can be forewarned.
Abaye: his fellow prophets forewarn him.
From where do the prophets know that a colleague received a prophecy?
Amos 3:7 says God reveals His counsel to His prophets, showing they know of each other's prophecies.
Perhaps the heavenly court reconsidered, and the prophets were not told.
If it were revoked, all prophets would have been informed.
Jonah's case shows a revoked prophecy was not announced to Jonah's people.
Jonah was told from the outset, and the prophecy could be read as good or bad, so it was fulfilled as stated.
How does a prophet's colleague know he is a prophet, when no sign was given, as with Micah?
Without a sign, Isaac and the people at Mount Carmel would not have obeyed Abraham or Elijah.
After what matters does the verse place God's testing of Abraham?
Rabbi Yohanan: after Satan's remark that Abraham's feast had no offering, God tested Abraham's willingness.
Rabbi Shimon bar Abba: na is an entreaty, as in the parable of a king and his warrior in a final war.
God's words your only whom you love are gradually clarified, since Abraham had two sons.
Satan quotes Job 4 to make Abraham regret the binding, and Abraham answers from Psalms 26.
Satan reports from behind the heavenly curtain that the sheep alone is to be offered, and Abraham does not believe him.
Rabbi Levi: after Ishmael mocks Isaac for circumcision, Isaac offers himself, so God tests Abraham.
Baraita: a prophet who incites idolatry is stoned, while Rabbi Shimon says strangulation.
The Rabbis derive stoning by verbal analogy from the incitement of a layman who incites idolatry.
Rabbi Shimon reads death in the verse as strangulation, following the general rule.
Those who incite a city to idolatry are stoned, derived by verbal analogy from laymen and prophets.
Rabbi Shimon derives the city incitement from the prophet's incitement, which is strangulation.
Why not derive the punishment from a non-prophet who incites multitudes or an individual?
Rav Hisda: once a prophet has incited, no ordinary person is greater than him, so he is stoned.

90a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Dispute over a prophet uprooting idolatry: Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis on strangulation or stoning; other mitzvot differ.
Rav Hamnuna objects from a baraita that the verse's walk and on which refer to positive and negative mitzvot.
Rav Hisda: the positive mitzva is destroying idolatrous altars and images, as in Deuteronomy 12:3.
Rav Hamnuna's alternative: the dispute concerns uprooting idolatry or a whole mitzva, with partial espousal exempt.
Baraita: a false prophet who abolishes a Torah matter is strangled, and idolatry is always liable.
Abaye follows Rav Hisda and Rava follows Rav Hamnuna in reconciling the baraita.
Abaye's reading: abolishing a Torah matter is strangled, and idolatry is stoned per the Rabbis and strangled per Rabbi Shimon.
Rava's reading follows Rav Hamnuna: abolishing any Torah matter is capital, with stoning or strangulation disputed.
Rabbi Abbahu for Rabbi Yohanan: a prophet urging temporary violation of Torah is heeded, except for idolatry.
Baraita of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: the Torah gave the false prophet authority against idolatry, even with a stopped sun.
Rabbi Akiva: the sun is not stopped for sinners, but a prophet turned false, like Hananiah son of Azzur, is warned.
Mishna: conspiring witnesses against a priest's daughter and her paramour are strangled.
From where are these matters derived?
Rav Aha son of Ika cites Rabbi Yosei's baraita on Deuteronomy 19:19 to derive strangulation for conspiring witnesses.
Closing formula of the chapter, These are the strangled.
Mishna: all Israel has a share in the World-to-Come, except deniers of resurrection, Torah from Heaven, and epikoros.
Rabbi Akiva adds external books and healing charms; Abba Shaul adds pronouncing the ineffable Name.
Three kings and four commoners lack a share in the World-to-Come; Rabbi Yehuda says Manasseh has one.
Why is one so severely punished for denying resurrection?
Baraita: measure for measure, so the denier loses his share in resurrection.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani: II Kings 7 shows measure-for-measure, as the officer who doubted Elisha's word saw but did not eat.

90b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Perhaps Elisha's curse, not measure-for-measure, killed the officer, since a sage's curse comes true.
If so, the verse would simply say he was trampled; in the gate teaches death over the gate matter.
Rabbi Yohanan derives resurrection from Numbers 18:28, since Aaron must live to receive teruma.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael reads to Aaron as requiring teruma for his meticulous descendants.
Rabbi Yonatan: teruma is not given to an am ha'aretz, per II Chronicles 31:4.
Rav Yehuda: giving teruma to an am ha'aretz is like placing it before a lion, unsure whether it is eaten pure.
Rabbi Yohanan: giving teruma to an am ha'aretz causes the priest's death, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds guilt.
Rabbi Simai derives resurrection from Exodus 6:4, which speaks of giving the land to them, the Patriarchs.
Mnemonic for the sages cited in the coming discussion.
Heretics ask Rabban Gamliel for proof of resurrection; he cites Torah, Prophets and Writings, but they reject it.
Proof from the Torah: Deuteronomy 31:16, lie with your fathers and arise.
Heretics: the verse can be divided so the people arise and stray.
Proof from Isaiah 26:19: your dead shall live.
Heretics: the verse refers only to the dead Ezekiel revived.
Proof from Song of Songs 7:10: the lips of those that sleep move, showing the dead will speak.
Heretics: their lips only move as they repeat halakhot cited in their names, so the verse is unrelated.
Rabban Gamliel cites Deuteronomy 11:21: to give them, meaning the Patriarchs, who will inherit the land.
Deuteronomy 4:4: you shall live every one of you, meaning in the World-to-Come, as today.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya tells the Romans that Deuteronomy 31:16 shows resurrection and divine foreknowledge.
The Romans object that the verse can be split to read that the people will arise and go astray.
Rabbi Yehoshua answers half, and Rabbi Yohanan cites Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, that God knows and revives the dead.
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yosei refuted Samaritans, who denied resurrection from the Torah.
Numbers 15:31: the soul is excised in this world, and his iniquity is upon him for the World-to-Come.
Rav Pappa asks why Rabbi Eliezer did not cite hikkaret tikkaret, excised from both worlds, to the Samaritans.
Abaye: Torah speaks in human language, and the tanna'im dispute this verse's meaning, with Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Ishmael cites Numbers 15:30 to show the excision is only in this world, so the sinner repents.
Excision in this world applies only if the sinner has not repented, as the Torah speaks of the case where he does not.
Cleopatra asks Rabbi Meir how the dead rise, and he answers with grain that is buried bare and grows clothed.
A fortiori: wheat buried bare sprouts in many garments, so righteous buried in their clothes will surely rise.
Caesar tells Rabban Gamliel that the dead are dust, and the dust is still living.

91a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The emperor's daughter's parable of two craftsmen: water vessels are finer, so God can revive from dust.
Rabbi Yishmael's school argues a fortiori from glass vessels, which can be remade, to human resurrection.
A heretic asks Rabbi Ami: the dead are dust, so how can dust come to life?
Rabbi Ami's parable of a palace built where no water or earth was, then rebuilt where both exist.
The king's anger and the examples of the akhbar creature and a snail show creation from earth over time.
Geviha ben Pesisa and a heretic dispute the resurrection; Geviha calls the heretic a wicked hunchback-taunter, and they trade insults.
Megillat Ta'anit: the twenty-fourth of Nisan celebrates expelling usurpers, and Afrikiya claims Canaan's land before Alexander.
Geviha volunteers to argue for the Sages before Alexander, with a fallback either way.
Geviha's argument: Genesis 9:25 makes Canaan a slave, and a slave's property belongs to his master.
Alexander gives three days; Afrikiya cannot answer and flees, so the Sabbatical year benefits Israel.
Egypt claims Israel borrowed gold and silver, citing Exodus 12:36.
Geviha again volunteers and is allowed to argue before Alexander.
Geviha cites Exodus 12:40: 430 years of enslavement, so the Egyptians owe wages for 600,000 men.
Egypt asks for three days, finds no answer, and flees during the Sabbatical year.
Ishmael and Keturah's descendants claim the land, citing Genesis 25:12 and 25:19.
Geviha again volunteers to argue against the descendants of Ishmael.
Geviha cites Genesis 25:5-6: Abraham gave gifts to his sons while alive, so Isaac alone inherits the land.
What were the gifts Abraham gave to the sons of the concubines?
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba: the gifts were the name of impurity, passing ritual defilement to them.
Antoninus asks Rabbi how body and soul can each exempt themselves from judgment.
The body and soul each blame the other for sin, in a dialogue of the body as corpse and the soul as bird.
Rabbi begins a parable of a king with a fine orchard, introducing the analogy of guilt and care.

91b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Parable of the orchard: a lame guard rides a blind guard to steal figs.
The owner cannot tell which guard stole, so he judges them as one, like soul and body together.
Psalm 50:4 applies to the soul, heavenly, and the body, earthly, judged together.
Antoninus asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi why the sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
Rabbi Yehuda: if it were reversed, you would ask the reverse; the question is the same.
Antoninus asks why the sun sets in the west rather than deviating elsewhere.
The sun sets to greet its Creator, and to serve workers and travelers, as Nehemiah 9:6 suggests.
Antoninus asks whether the soul enters at conception or at formation of the embryo.
Rabbi Yehuda: from formation.
Antoninus objects that an embryo cannot survive days without a soul, so the soul enters at conception.
Rabbi Yehuda, taught by Antoninus, cites Job 10:12 on pekudah, preservation from conception.
Antoninus asks from when the evil inclination dominates a person.
Rabbi Yehuda: from formation.
Antoninus objects that the evil inclination would kick the mother's innards, so it starts at birth.
Rabbi Yehuda, taught by Antoninus, cites Genesis 4:7, sin crouches at the entrance, showing birth.
Reish Lakish: verses conflict on whether the resurrected keep their defects.
The dead rise with their defects and are then healed.
Ulla: verses conflict on whether death will end, Isaiah 25:8 against Isaiah 65:20.
Isaiah 25 speaks of Israel and Isaiah 65 of idolaters, who live long.
What do gentiles seek in that era, that they merit long life?
The verse of Isaiah 61:5 refers to strangers who serve Israel as plowmen and vinedressers.
Rav Hisda: verses conflict on whether the sun and moon shine at the end of days.
Isaiah 30 refers to the Messianic age, Isaiah 24 to the World-to-Come.
How is the conflict resolved according to Shmuel, who sees only the subjugation of exile as the difference?
Isaiah 30 refers to the light of the righteous camp, and Isaiah 24 to the light of the Divine Presence.
Rava: Deuteronomy 32:39 says I kill and I bring to life, then I wounded and I will heal, a contradiction.
God's statement: what I kill I also revive, and then what I wound I heal.
Baraita: death and life occur in one person, as wounding and healing do, answering the denial of resurrection.
Rabbi Meir derives resurrection from Exodus 15:1 and Joshua 8:30, where the future tense shows Moses and Joshua will act again.
The same reasoning would have Solomon build the altar for Chemosh in the future, so the proof fails.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: Psalm 84:5 says they will praise You, not they praised, showing resurrection.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: whoever sings in this world will sing in the World-to-Come, per Psalm 84:5.
Rabbi Yohanan: Isaiah 52:8 says they will sing, showing that resurrection is from the Torah.
Rabbi Yohanan: all the prophets will sing in one voice in the future, per Isaiah 52:8.
Rav Yehuda: one who withholds halakha from a student is like one who robs him of his inheritance, per Deuteronomy 33:4.
Rav Hanna bar Bizna and Rabbi Shimon Hasida: whoever withholds halakha from a student is cursed even in the womb, per Proverbs 11:26.

92a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proverbs 11:26 read word by word: leom means fetuses, kabbo means curse, and bar means Torah.
Ulla bar Yishmael: one who withholds halakha is perforated like a sieve; Abaye compares it to a launderer's sprinkler.
If one teaches halakha to a student, what is his reward?
Rava, citing Rav Sheshet: the teacher is blessed like Joseph, the mashbir who provided grain.
Rav Sheshet: one who teaches Torah in this world will teach it in the World-to-Come, per Proverbs 11:25.
Rava, Ravina and Rav Ashi each derive resurrection from Deuteronomy 33:6, Daniel 12:2 and Daniel 12:13.
Rabbi Elazar: a communal leader who guides calmly is rewarded by leading in the World-to-Come.
Rabbi Elazar: knowledge is great, since it sits between two names of God, per I Samuel 2:3.
Rabbi Elazar: the Temple is great, as it too sits between two divine names, per Exodus 15:17.
Rav Adda Karhina'a: if being between names gives greatness, vengeance should be great too.
Rabbi Elazar answers with Ulla: vengeance is great in its context, with both divine attributes of good and punishment.
Rabbi Elazar: one with knowledge is as if the Temple was built in his days, since both sit between two letters.
Rabbi Elazar: one with knowledge becomes wealthy, per Proverbs 24:4.
Rabbi Elazar: one without knowledge may not be shown mercy, since God shows none to such a people, per Isaiah 27:11.
Rabbi Elazar: one who gives bread to the ignorant falls ill, per Obadiah 1:7 and Hosea 5:13.
Rabbi Elazar: a person without knowledge is ultimately exiled, per Isaiah 5:13.
Rabbi Elazar: a house where Torah is not heard at night is consumed by Gehenna, per Job 20:26 and Joel 3:5.
Rabbi Elazar: one who does not support Torah scholars from his property never sees a sign of blessing.
Rabbi Elazar: one who does not leave bread on the table after a meal never sees blessing.
Rabbi Elazar also says leaving bread on the table is idol worship, per Isaiah 65:11, which seems contradictory.
Leaving bread is idolatry only with a whole loaf present, and blamed only when no whole loaf is there.
Rabbi Elazar: one who alters the truth in speech is as if he worships idols, per Genesis 27:12 and Jeremiah 10:15.
Rabbi Elazar: one who looks at nakedness loses his potency, per Habakkuk 3:9.
Rabbi Elazar: remain obscure and you will endure, supported by Rabbi Zeira's mishna on a dark house.
Rabbi Tavi and Rabbi Yoshiya: the grave and the womb are juxtaposed in Proverbs 30:16, showing resurrection.
A fortiori: if a womb takes in and gives forth, a grave, which takes in, can give forth too.
Isaiah 4:3: the righteous who are holy will not return to dust but remain, as God is eternal.

92b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: if the dead revive in the future, what will the righteous do to survive that era?
God will give the righteous wings like eagles so they can fly over the water.
Psalm 46 is cited to show the righteous will not fear when the earth changes.
Objection: perhaps the righteous will still suffer some distress from flying.
Isaiah 40 is cited to show that those who wait for God gain strength and do not tire.
Objection drawing on Ezekiel's revived dead, who would then have died again.
Reply: the school of Eliyahu follows the view that Ezekiel's revival was a parable.
Baraita: Ezekiel's revived dead stood, sang a song, and died again, and the song is given.
Rabbi Yehoshua says the song was a verse about God killing and giving life.
A verse from Samuel 1 is cited as the text of the song about killing and raising.
Rabbi Yehuda says Ezekiel's revival was true but also a parable.
Rabbi Nehemya challenges the contradiction: if true, why a parable, and if a parable, why true.
Reply upholding Rabbi Yehuda: the revival was in truth a parable.
Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says the revived dead went to Israel and had children.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says he descends from them and holds tefillin they left behind.
Who were the dead that Ezekiel revived?
Rav says they were Ephraim's descendants who miscalculated the end of the enslavement and died.
Chronicles verses are cited to support Rav's identification of the sons of Ephraim.
Shmuel says they were people who denied the resurrection of the dead.
Ezekiel 37 is cited: the people say their bones are dried out and their hope is lost.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says they lacked even a trace of a mitzva.
Ezekiel 37 is cited: the dry bones are told to hear the word of God.
Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha says they filled the Sanctuary with repugnant creeping things.
Ezekiel 8 and 37 are linked by the shared word around to identify the same people.
Rabbi Yohanan says they were the dead of the Dura Valley and specifies its boundaries.
Story: Nebuchadnezzar's youths were so beautiful that women desired them, so they were killed and trampled.
Baraita: when Nebuchadnezzar threw three men into the furnace, God told Ezekiel to revive the Dura dead.
The revived bones came and struck the wicked king in the face.
Nebuchadnezzar asks what these revived ones are.
His servants reply that the friend of the three men revives the dead in the Dura Valley.
Nebuchadnezzar praises God, quoting Daniel's verse about God's everlasting kingdom.
Rabbi Yitzhak says molten gold should fill that king's mouth, since he would outdo David's psalms.
Baraita lists six miracles of that day, including the furnace rising and Ezekiel reviving the dead.
The Gemara notes the miracles are known by tradition, while the four ranks are derived from a verse.
Daniel 3:2 is cited to show Nebuchadnezzar gathered the ranks of officials.
Daniel 3 verses are cited: certain Jews refused to bow, and officials saw the men emerge unharmed.
The school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches that one should not demean his rank even in danger.
Daniel 3:21 is cited: the men were cast into the furnace still wearing their own garments.
Rabbi Yohanan begins a statement that continues on the next daf.

93a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Righteous people are said to be greater than the ministering angels.
Daniel 3:25 is cited about four men walking unharmed in the furnace, with an angel-like figure.
Rabbi Tanhum bar Hanilai describes nations striking Israel and mocking their God after the three men emerged.
The three men reply with a verse from Daniel 9 acknowledging God's righteousness and their own shame.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani attributes to Rabbi Yonatan a similar teaching.
What is the meaning of the verse from Song of Songs about climbing the palm tree?
The palm is Israel; God could grasp only the one bough of the three men, who alone gave their lives.
Rabbi Yohanan offers a further explanation of a verse.
Zechariah 1:8 is cited about a man on a red horse standing among myrtles.
What is the meaning of the phrase I saw the night?
God sought to turn the world into night because there were no righteous; the man is God.
Exodus 15:3 is cited: the Lord is a man of war, His name, on a red horse.
God sought to turn the whole world into blood.
Once God looked at the three men, His mind was calmed.
Zechariah 1:8 is cited about the one standing among the myrtles in the depths.
Myrtles here refer to the righteous.
Esther 2:7 is cited, where Hadassah is identified as Esther.
Depths here refer to Babylonia.
Isaiah 44:27 is cited about the deep being told to dry up.
The angry horses turned gray and red turned white; Rav Pappa draws a lesson that white horses in dreams are good.
Where did the three men go after their deliverance?
Rav says they died from the evil eye.
Shmuel says they drowned in the spittle of the nations.
Rabbi Yohanan says they ascended to Eretz Yisrael, married, and had children.
