A parallel tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua give the first two views, and the Sages the third.
Zechariah 3:8 is cited: Joshua and his fellows are men of wonder.
Who are the men for whom a wonder was performed?
Those are Hananiah, Mishael, Azariah, and Daniel.
Where did Daniel go?
Rav says Daniel went to dig the great river in Tiberias.
Shmuel says Daniel went to bring choice alfalfa seed.
Rabbi Yohanan says Daniel went to bring high-quality pigs from Alexandria in Egypt.
Objection from a baraita: no sow from Alexandria gives birth, since its womb is severed.
Reply: they were small pigs brought without the knowledge of the people of Alexandria.
Baraita: God, Daniel, and Nebuchadnezzar agreed Daniel should leave Babylonia so the miracle is not credited to him.
Daniel says he will leave so that the verse about idols will not apply to him.
Deuteronomy 7:25 is cited about burning the graven images of their gods.
Nebuchadnezzar says Daniel should leave so people will not say he burned his own god.
From where is it derived that Nebuchadnezzar bowed to Daniel?
Daniel 2:46 is cited: Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face and worshipped Daniel.
Jeremiah 29:21 is cited about Ahab and Zedekiah prophesying lies in God's name.
Jeremiah 29:22 is cited about the curse of Ahab and Zedekiah, who were toasted in the fire.
Rabbi Yohanan, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, explains they were made like toasted grain.
Jeremiah 29:23 is cited about committing adultery with the wives of their neighbors.
What did they do?
They went to Nebuchadnezzar's daughter, each urged her to lie with them, and she told her father.
Nebuchadnezzar says the God of these people abhors lewdness, so the prophecy is likely false.
Nebuchadnezzar instructs her to send them to him when they come.
Who told you to do this? Nebuchadnezzar asks them.
They reply that the Holy One, Blessed be He, told them.
Nebuchadnezzar objects that he asked Hananiah and the others, who prohibited it.
They reply that they are prophets too, and the prophecy was given to them.
They answer that God did not say it to the three men but to them.
Nebuchadnezzar proposes to test them as he tested the three men.
Ahab and Zedekiah say they are two, not three, so their merit is insufficient.
Nebuchadnezzar tells them to choose a third person to be tested with them.
They choose Joshua the High Priest, thinking his great merit will protect them.
They cast the three into the furnace, and Joshua's garments were singed.
Zechariah 3:1 is cited: Joshua the High Priest standing before the angel of the Lord.
Zechariah 3:2 is cited: the Lord rebukes Satan, who stands at Joshua's side.
Satan objects: the fire helped the righteous one only a little and did not help the other three at all.
God replies that they were three and He was one, explaining the uneven effect of the fire.
Objection: Abraham was alone without wicked companions, but here the wicked were present and the fire was permitted.
A proverb is cited: two dry logs and one wet log, where the dry logs burn the wet one.
Why was Joshua punished?
Rav Pappa says his sons married women unfit for the priesthood and he did not object.
Zechariah 3:3 is cited: Joshua was dressed in filthy garments.
The filthy garments teach that his sons married unsuitable women and he did not rebuke them.
Rabbi Tanhum bar Kapara taught in Zippori.
Ruth 3:17 is cited: Boaz gave Ruth these six measures of barley.
Does six barley mean literally six grains?
Objection: was it Boaz's way to give six grains as a gift?

93b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: it is not a woman's way to take six se'ah, so the amount needs an explanation.
Reply: the six measures are a hint that six sons would descend from her, blessed with six blessings.
Lists the six who were blessed: David, the Messiah, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.
1 Samuel 16:18 is cited describing David as skilled in music, a warrior, and wise in speech.
Rav Yehuda says the whole verse was said of Doeg in a derogatory sense.
Explains the same words as praise for Torah scholars: skill in debate, wisdom, and God being with them.
A comparison is drawn to Jonathan and his sons, who were of a similar character.
Contrasts the verses about Saul and David, showing the matter was not reversed for David.
How do we know that Doeg was the one described?
1 Samuel 21:8 is cited, where Doeg appears as a servant of Saul.
Doeg the Edomite, chief of Saul's shepherds, is identified with the figure in the verse.
Isaiah 11:2 is cited about the spirit of the Lord resting on the Messiah.
Isaiah 11:3 is cited: the Messiah's delight is in the fear of the Lord.
Rabbi Alexandri says the verse teaches the Messiah is loaded with mitzvot and suffering, like millstones.
Rava says the Messiah judges by smell, as derived from the verse.
Isaiah 11:3-4 is cited: he will not judge by sight but will judge the poor with righteousness.
Bar Kokhba reigned as king for two and a half years.
Bar Kokhba tells the Sages that he is the Messiah.
Sages object: the Messiah is said to judge by smell, so let us test whether he does.
When they saw he did not judge by smell, they killed him.
Daniel 1:4 is cited describing the youths as without blemish, wise, and fit to serve in the palace.
What does 'without any blemish' mean?
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina says they had no blemish even of the smallest kind.
What does 'strength to stand in the king's palace' mean?
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina says they restrained themselves from laughter, talk, and sleep out of fear of royal power.
Daniel 1:6 is cited: among the Judeans were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.
Rabbi Eliezer says all of them were from the tribe of Judah.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani says Daniel was from Judah, while the other three were from other tribes.
Isaiah 39:7 is cited: some of your sons will be eunuchs in the palace of Babylon.
What does 'eunuchs' mean here?
Rav says it means literal eunuchs.
Rabbi Hanina says idolatry was castrated in their days, meaning its power was removed.
On the view that idolatry was castrated in their days, the verse about no harm is explained.
Daniel 3:25 is cited: no harm from the fire was found in them.
Objection: on the view of literal eunuchs, why is the verse about no harm from the fire needed?
Daniel 3:27 is cited: the fire had no effect on their bodies or on their smell.
On the view that idolatry was castrated in their days, Isaiah 56 is clear.
Isaiah 56:4 is cited: to the eunuchs who keep My Sabbaths.
On the literal eunuch view, the verse disparages the righteous, and both kinds were present among them.
On the literal eunuch view, the following verse fits.
Isaiah 56:5 is cited: a memorial and a name better than sons and daughters.
The other view is that idolatry was castrated in their days.
What does 'better than sons and daughters' mean?
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak says it means the children they had before they died.
What does 'an everlasting name' refer to?
Rabbi Tanhum taught in Tzippori that this is the book named after Daniel.
Since all those matters were spoken by Nehemiah, why is the book not named for him?
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says Nehemiah claimed credit for himself, so the book is not named for him.
Nehemiah 5:19 is cited: remember me, my God, for good.
Psalm 106:4 is cited: remember me, Lord, with the favor You show Your people.
David, too, asked for mercy, as the verse indicates.
Rav Yosef says Nehemiah recounted the faults of the earlier governors.
Nehemiah 5:15 is cited about earlier governors who burdened the people with bread and wine.
Also Daniel, who was greater than Nehemiah, recounted matters in his book.
From where do we know that Daniel was greater than Nehemiah?
Daniel 10:7 is cited: Daniel alone saw the vision, while the men with him did not see it.
Who were the men who were with Daniel?
Rabbi Yirmeya, or Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, identifies them as Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

94a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Compares two groups of prophets, arguing that one is superior to the other in a specific respect.
One of them saw the matter, while the others did not see it.
Objection: since they did not see, why does the reasoning still hold?
What is the reason?
Their star sees even when they see nothing, so the stars can reveal what is hidden.
Ravina concludes from this that the reasoning is sound.
The one who is frightened, though he does not see, has his star see.
What is the remedy for one who is frightened: to move from his place?
Answer: move four cubits, or call the city by a different name.
If he stands in a filthy place, should he say this?
Gives a proverb about the butcher's goat, which is fatter than the others in the house.
Isaiah 9:6 is cited about the increase of dominion and endless peace.
Rabbi Tanhum bar Kapara taught in Tzippori on this verse.
Why is every mem in the middle of a word open, while this one is closed?
God wanted to make Hezekiah the Messiah and Sennacherib Gog and Magog, but the attribute of justice objected.
Objection: David composed many praises yet was not made Messiah, while Hezekiah got miracles without song.
The earth opened and said it would sing a song before God instead of that righteous man.
Isaiah 24:16 is cited: from the corners of the earth we heard songs of praise to the righteous.
The minister of the world asks God to make His beauty for the righteous, and a heavenly voice speaks of secrets.
The prophet laments and asks how long this will last.
A heavenly voice says the treacherous have dealt treacherously.
Isaiah 24:16 is cited: the treacherous have dealt treacherously, and the treacherous have dealt very treacherously.
Rava, or perhaps Rabbi Yitzhak, interprets the verse about spoil being brought.
Isaiah 21:11 is cited: a prophecy about a watchman called from Seir.
Rabbi Yohanan says the angel in charge of the winds is named Dumah.
The winds gather to Dumah and ask the watchman what of the night.
The watchman replies: morning comes, and also night; if you wish to ask, return and come.
A tanna in the name of Rabbi Pappeus says it is a disgrace to Hezekiah and his group that they did not sing until the earth did.
Isaiah 24:16 is cited again.
Exodus 18:10 is cited, where Jethro says blessed is the Lord who saved you.
A tanna in the name of Rabbi Pappeus says it is a disgrace to Moses and the six hundred thousand that they did not bless until Jethro did.
Jethro says blessed is the Lord, and he rejoices.
Rav says Jethro passed a sharp sword over his flesh.
Shmuel says Jethro's flesh was made sharp, cut all over.
Rav cites a proverb: do not despise a convert before ten generations have passed.
Isaiah 10:16 is cited: the Lord will send wasting among his fat ones.
What does 'wasting among his fat ones' mean?
God says Hezekiah will come, who has eight names, and Sennacherib will be punished, who has eight names.
Isaiah 9:5 is cited, naming the child Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, and Prince of Peace.
Objection: but there is Hezekiah, who strengthened Yah.
Another interpretation: Hezekiah strengthened Israel toward their Father in heaven.
The Gemara lists the Assyrian kings named in Kings and Chronicles, including Sennacherib.
Objection: Sennacherib spoke a dispute, and another explanation is that he spoke against heaven.
Rabbi Yohanan asks why that wicked man merited being called Osnappar, the great and honored.
He did not speak against the land of Israel, as Kings II 18:32 promises a land like your own.
Rav and Shmuel disagree on whether that king was wise or foolish.
On the view that the king was wise, saying the land is better would be taken as a lie.
On the view that the king was foolish, the account lacks any point of greatness.
What is his greatness, then?
Where did they exile them?
Mar Zutra says they were exiled to Africa.
Rabbi Hanina says they were exiled to the mountains of Salug.
Israel spoke of the faults of the land of Israel, and so they were exiled.
A saying about a people reaching Shush.
A saying: two say about one, two.
Isaiah 10:16 is cited: the glory of the Lord burns like a fire.
Rabbi Yohanan says 'instead of his glory' does not mean literal glory.
Gives an example from Rabbi Yohanan's reading of a word as meaning honors.
Rabbi Eliezer says 'instead of his glory' means literal glory.
Analogy: as the soul and body of Aaron's sons remained after burning, so here.
A tanna in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha: Pharaoh blasphemed and God punished him directly, and likewise Sennacherib.

94b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: God punishes a person through a messenger.
Pharaoh was punished through a messenger.
Exodus 5:2 is cited: Pharaoh asks who the Lord is, that he should heed His voice.
God punished Pharaoh Himself, directly.
Exodus 14:27 and Habakkuk 3:15 are cited about the Lord shaking Egypt into the sea.
Kings II 19:23 is cited: Sennacherib reproached the name of the Lord.
Sennacherib was punished through a messenger.
Kings II 19:35 is cited: the angel of the Lord struck the Assyrian camp.
Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa raises a contradiction between Isaiah 37:24 and Kings II 19:23 about Sennacherib's end.
Resolution: the wicked one said he would first destroy the lower house and then the upper one.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi offers an explanation.
What does Kings II 18:25 mean, and what did Sennacherib hear from the prophet?
Isaiah 8:6 is cited: this people rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah.
Rav Yosef says without the Targum of this verse he would not know what it means.
Rabbi Yohanan states a principle.
What is the meaning of the verse about the curse of the Lord in the house of the wicked?
Proverbs 3:33 is cited: the curse of the Lord is in the house of the wicked.
The wicked is Pekah ben Remaliah, who ate forty se'ah of pigeons; the righteous is Hezekiah, who ate a litra of greens.
Isaiah 8:7-8 is cited about the king of Assyria flooding through Judah up to the neck.
Why was the prophet punished over the ten tribes, when he set his mind on all of Jerusalem?
Isaiah 8:23 is cited: the prophet told him that there is no gloom for the one who was oppressed.
Rabbi Elazar bar Berekhiah says one who is weary in Torah is not handed over to his oppressor.
What is the meaning of the verse about the former time?
Isaiah 8:23 is cited about the former and later times of the land of Zebulun and Naphtali.
The earlier ones were lightened of the yoke of Torah; the later ones were burdened with it.
These are deserving of a miracle, like those who crossed the sea and the Jordan.
If he returns, good; if not, I will make Galilee among the nations.
II Chronicles 32:1 is cited about Sennacherib coming to Judah and besieging the fortified cities.
What do 'after these words and this truth' and 'after what' mean?
Ravina explains that God swore an oath to hand Sennacherib over to Hezekiah, and then acted at once.
God swore that He would bring Sennacherib.
Isaiah 14:24-25 is cited: the Lord swore that Assyria would be broken in His land.
Rabbi Yohanan says God will make Sennacherib and his allies a manger for Hezekiah and his allies.
Isaiah 10:27 is cited: on that day his burden will leave his shoulder and his yoke from his neck.
The yoke is destroyed because of oil.
Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha says Sennacherib's yoke was destroyed because of Hezekiah's oil, lit in synagogues and study halls.
What did Hezekiah do?
Hezekiah placed a sword at the study hall door, declaring that whoever did not study Torah would be stabbed; none untaught were found.
Isaiah 7:21 is cited: on that day a man will keep a cow and two sheep.
Isaiah 7:23 and 33:4 are cited about vines turned to thorns and spoil gathered like locusts.
A prophet tells Israel to gather their spoil, and they ask whether it is for plunder or division.
He replies: as the locust gathers each for itself, so each of you should gather his spoil for himself.
Objection: but the wealth of the ten tribes is mixed in with it.
Isaiah 33:4 is cited: like the gathering of tax collectors that surges with wealth.
Tax collectors lift a person from impurity to purity; likewise Israel's property, once fallen among idolaters, is purified.
Ammon and Moab were purified through the conquest of Sihon, as in the parallel case.
Rav Huna says that wicked one traveled ten stages on that very day.
Isaiah 10:28-32 is cited about the enemy advancing on Ai, Migron, Michmash, and Gibeah.
The Gemara explains that the prophet speaking was addressing the Assembly of Israel.
The Assembly of Israel is the daughter of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who performed mitzvot like the waves of the sea.
The Gemara says: do not fear, but be afraid of the wicked Nebuchadnezzar, who is compared to a lion.
Jeremiah 4:7 is cited: a lion has gone up from his thicket.
Begins a question that continues on the next daf.

95a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Isaiah 10:30 is cited about the town of Anathoth.
Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, from the priests of Anathoth, is destined to prophesy there.
Jeremiah 1:1 is cited: the words of Jeremiah from the priests in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin.
What is the comparison between the word for lion used there and the word used here?
Rabbi Yohanan says the lion has six names, and he lists them.
Verses are cited giving the names of the lion: ari, kefir, lavi, lish, shahal, and shahatz.
Objection: if so, the two phrases about passing over refer to two separate matters.
What does the next verse mean?
Isaiah 10:32 is cited: yet today he will stand at Nob.
Rav Huna says the city of Nob was left standing that day, and the Chaldeans told Sennacherib to take it today.
Sennacherib boasts that Jerusalem is the smallest and weakest of the cities he conquered by his own hand.
He shakes his head toward the Temple Mount and orders each man to bring a stone; one was killed at once.
Kings II 19:35 is cited: the angel of the Lord struck the camp of Assyria, and in the morning all were dead bodies.
Rav Pappa cites a saying that a daughter of judgment nullifies the judgment itself.
Samuel II 21:16 is cited about the men of Nob who bore a sword and wished to strike David.
What does 'the men of Nob' mean?
Rav Yehuda says it refers to a man involved in the Nob affair, and God rebuked David that the sin lay on him.
David replies: better that I be handed over to the enemy than that my descendants be lost.
One day David went hunting; a demon took the form of a bird, and David was carried to the land of the Philistines.
Psalm 18:37 is cited: You enlarge my steps beneath me, so my ankles did not slip.
Abishai son of Zeruiah was washing his head in a basin on Friday evening and saw blood stains.
A dove came fluttering before him, and Abishai said the Assembly of Israel is like a dove.
Psalm 68:14 is cited: the wings of a dove covered with silver.
The Gemara concludes that David was in distress, came home, and did not find her.
A mishnah is cited: in a time of danger, a king may not ride his horse, sit on his throne, or use his scepter.
What happened when he came to ask in the study house?
They told him that in a time of danger it is fine to ride his mule and go.
He mounted his mule and went; a story follows about Arpha, the mother of the giant, who struck him with a spindle.
Ishbi of Nob says that now there are two, and they will kill him, and he throws his spear at David.
Abishai places David between heaven and earth and rescues him, as one set free from prison escapes.
What does David seek here?
He replies that the Holy One, Blessed be He, told him this.
God tells David to pray, and his prayers will be accepted so he need not grieve.
If so, join his help to theirs, as the verse indicates.
Samuel II 21:17 is cited: Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, says they helped him through prayer.
Abishai's sister was pursuing them, and two men killed the giant.
They told the giant to go and find his mother in the grave.
When his mother's name was recalled to him, Ishbi's strength failed and he was killed.
Samuel II 21:17 is cited: David's men swore he should no longer go out to battle, lest he quench Israel's lamp.
A baraita teaches that three had the earth shrink for them.
The baraita lists Eliezer, Abraham's servant, Jacob our father, and Abishai son of Zeruiah.
The Gemara says: as we said, Eliezer was Abraham's servant.
Genesis 24:42 is cited: I came today to the spring.
The Gemara explains that on that day Jacob our father went out.

95b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Genesis 28:10 is cited: Jacob left Beersheba and went to Haran.
Genesis 28:11 is cited: he encountered the place and lodged there.
When the sun set, Jacob reached Haran.
Jacob thinks he passed a place where his fathers prayed, and considers going back to pray there.
As he resolved to return, the earth shrank for him immediately.
Explains that the encounter in the verse means prayer, not a chance meeting.
Jeremiah 7:16 is cited: do not pray for this people or lift up cry or prayer for them.
Jacob lodged there because the sun set after he prayed, and he wanted to return.
God says this righteous man should leave without lodging, and immediately the sun rose.
Genesis 32:32 is cited: the sun rose upon him.
Did the sun rise only for him, when it shone on the entire world?
Rabbi Yitzhak says the sun rose for his sake, though it shone everywhere.
How do we know that David's seed was destroyed?
Kings II 11:1 is cited about Athaliah destroying all the seed of the kingdom.
Objection: Joash survived there, and Abiathar also survived.
Samuel I 22:20 is cited: one son, Abiathar son of Ahimelech, escaped.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, says if Abiathar had not survived, none of David's seed would remain.
Rav describes Sennacherib's army: forty-five thousand royal men in golden chariots, a thousand armored heroes, and sixty thousand sword-bearers running ahead.
The same happened with Abraham, and the same will happen with Gog and Magog.
A baraita gives the length of the camp as four hundred parasangs and its total as two hundred sixty myriad thousands, less one.
Abaye asks whether the total is less one myriad, less one thousand, or less one hundred, and it stays unresolved.
A tanna teaches that the first of the enemy crossed the river up to the armpit.
Isaiah 8:8 is cited: it will flood through Judah and pass over.
The middle group crossed at standing height.
Isaiah 8:8 is cited again: it reaches up to the neck.
The last group raised dust with their feet, found no water in the river, and brought water from elsewhere to drink.
Isaiah 37:25 is cited: I dug and drank water.
Objection: the verse says the angel struck the Assyrian camp, and all of them were dead corpses.
Rabbi Abahu says these were the heads of the divisions.
Rav Ashi says this is also derived from the verse about leanness among his fat ones.
Ravina says this too is derived from a verse in Chronicles.
Chronicles II 32:21 is cited: the Lord sent an angel who destroyed every mighty man and leader in the camp.
By whose hand was he struck?
Rabbi Eliezer says it was by the hand of God, as the verse about the great hand at the sea shows.
Rabbi Yehoshua says it was by the finger of God, as the magicians told Pharaoh.
Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says God told Gabriel the matter was abandoned, and Gabriel replies it has stood since creation.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai says that time was the season for ripening fruit, and God told Gabriel to go out and ripen it.
Isaiah 28:19 is cited: from the time it passes it will take you.
Rav Pappa says to go along with your enemy's road, and some say the wind blows through their noses and they die.
Isaiah 40:24 is cited: the wind blows on them and they wither.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says God clapped His hands for them, and they died.
Ezekiel 21:22 is cited: I will also clap My hands together and My wrath will rest.
Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha says God revealed their ears, and they heard song from the living creatures and died.
Isaiah 33:3 is cited: at the nations' lifting up, they scattered.
How many were left of them?
Rav says ten were left.
Isaiah 10:19 is cited: the rest of the trees will be few, and a child could write them.
Shmuel says nine were left.
Isaiah 17:6 is cited: gleanings will remain in it, like the shaking of an olive tree.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says fourteen were left.
Isaiah 17:6 is cited again: two, three, four, and five.
Rabbi Yohanan says five were left: Sennacherib, two of his sons, Nebuchadnezzar, and Nebuzaradan.
The Gemara turns to Nebuchadnezzar.
Daniel 3:25 is cited: the fourth appears like a son of the gods.
Sennacherib and his two sons would not have known it without seeing it.
Kings II 19:37 is cited: Sennacherib was worshipping in the house of his god when his sons struck him with the sword.
Rabbi Abahu says that without the written verse one could not say this.
Isaiah 7:20 is cited: the Lord will shave with a razor hired from beyond the river, the king of Assyria.
The Holy One, Blessed be He, appeared like an old man.
God asks the old man what he said to the kings of East and West whose children he brought and killed.
He replies that the man sat in that same fear too.
The old man asks what they should do.
God says: go.

96a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Begins a story in which one man asks another to fetch scissors and cut his hair.
He tells him to go into a house and bring the scissors.
Angels came and appeared to them as men while they were grinding at a mill.
The man asks them to grind scissors; they agree to grind one grain of the mill until it grows dark.
He orders him to bring fire; the fire catches his beard, and he cuts his head and beard.
They say this is what is written.
Isaiah 7:20 is cited: the Lord will also shave the beard.
Rav Pappa cites a saying: dragging a stranger is fine, though fire catches his beard and he gets no laughter from it.
A story of the great God who saved Noah, with two sons who come and kill the man who came to them.
Kings II 19:37 and Genesis 14:15 are cited, the latter about Abraham dividing against the enemies at night.
Rabbi Yohanan says the angel who met Abraham at night was named Lilah, as Job 3:3 indicates.
Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha says a night event occurred with him, as the verse about stars shows.
Judges 5:20 is cited: from heaven the stars fought against Sisera.
Resh Lakish says Nappaha's teaching is good.
A verse is cited: he pursued them as far as Dan.
Rabbi Yohanan says when that righteous one reached Dan, his strength failed.
He saw that his grandsons would worship idols in Dan, as the verse says.
Kings I 12:29 is cited: one calf he placed in Beth-El and the other he placed in Dan.
Even that wicked one was not strengthened until he reached Dan, as the verse says.
Jeremiah 8:16 is cited: from Dan the snorting of his horses is heard.
Rabbi Zeira says one should beware of an elder who forgot his learning due to illness, as Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira taught.
Warns to beware of an elder who forgot his learning, of the veins, and of ignorant people, since from them Torah goes out.
The Gemara says we are informing them of this matter.
Jeremiah 12:1 is cited: why does the way of the wicked prosper? You planted them and they took root.
What did they answer him?
Jeremiah 12:5 is cited: if you race with footmen and they tire you, how will you race with horses?
A parable: one claims he can outrun horses for three parasangs over water, and a runner outruns him on land.
Applies the argument: if a runner beats him, how much more should God reward Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who ran like horses.
Jeremiah 23:9 is cited: my heart is broken within me, and all my bones tremble.
What are these four paces?
Isaiah 39:1 is cited: at that time Merodach-Baladan sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah.
Because Hezekiah was ill and then recovered, the king sent letters and a gift.
Chronicles II 32:31 is cited: to inquire about the wonder that was in the land.
Rabbi Yohanan says the day on which Ahaz died was two hours long, which relates to the miracle.
When Hezekiah recovered, God returned ten degrees to him, as the sundial of Ahaz shows.
Isaiah 38:8 is cited: I will bring back the shadow of the steps ten degrees.
What is this sign?
Hezekiah was weak and recovered.
Berodach says there is no one like him and wants to send peace to King Hezekiah.
Peace to the city of Jerusalem and to the great God; the letter was from Berodach, and at that time Nebuchadnezzar was not there.
Dialogue: he asks how the letter was written, and they say it was written this way; he tells them to call God great.
They say the reader of the letter should be a messenger who runs after it four paces.
Gabriel came and set him in place after four paces.
Rabbi Yohanan says had Gabriel not come and established him, Israel's enemies would have had no remedy.
Who was Berodach son of Berodach?
They say Berodach was king; his face changed, and his son sat on the kingdom, and both names were written.
Malachi 1:6 is cited: a son honors a father, and a servant his master.
Jeremiah 52:12-13 is cited: Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, came to Jerusalem and burned the house of the Lord and the king's house.

96b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether Nebuchadnezzar went up to Jerusalem.
Kings II 25:6 is cited: they brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
Rabbi Abahu says Riblah is Antioch.
Rav Hisda and Rabbi Yitzhak bar Avdimi offer two views: an image of Nebuchadnezzar engraved on his chariot, or great dread of him.
Rava describes an iron power that Nebuchadnezzar sent to Nebuzaradan, who swallowed all the rest.
Nebuchadnezzar's agents swallowed everything, including the one grass of Jerusalem.
Psalm 74:6 is cited: they break its carved work down with axes and hammers.
Nebuzaradan wants to return, fearing they will do to him as they did to Sennacherib; a voice says the time has come to destroy the Temple.
The Temple is opened when one iron rod strikes it.
Psalm 74:5 is cited: a man who lifts axes in a thicket of trees.
He kills with axes until he reaches the Temple and sets fire to it.
The Temple was lifted high from the heavens.
Lamentations 1:15 is cited: the Lord trod the virgin daughter of Judah in a winepress.
A daughter of a voice tells Nebuzaradan: you killed the people and burned the Temple.
The Gemara notes a wordplay on grinding flour.
Isaiah 47:2 is cited: take millstones and grind flour, uncover your locks.
The Gemara explains the verse says flour, not wheat.
Nebuchadnezzar saw the blood of Zechariah boiling.
Nebuchadnezzar asks what this is.
They tell him it is the blood of sacrifices that was spilled.
He tells them to bring the blood and see whether it stops; otherwise he will comb their flesh with iron combs.
They say this was a priest and prophet who warned Israel of Jerusalem's destruction, and they killed him.
He says: I will appease it.
He kills the sages, students, and young priests upon it, ninety-four myriads in all, and the blood does not stop.
He approaches Zechariah's blood and says: I destroyed the best of them; does it please you that I kill them all? Then it rests, and he reflects on repentance.
He thinks: if they did not destroy more than one soul, what then will befall this man?
He fled, sent a note to his house, and converted.
A baraita: Naaman was a resident proselyte.
Nebuzaradan was a righteous proselyte.
Descendants of Sisera taught Torah in Jerusalem, and descendants of Sennacherib taught Torah publicly.
Shemaiah and Avtalyon, descendants of Haman, taught Torah to the people of Bnei Berak.
God wished to bring the descendants of that wicked man under the wings of the Shekhinah.
The ministering angels object: this is the one who destroyed Your house and burned Your Temple, and You bring him under the wings of the Shekhinah?
Jeremiah 51:9 is cited: we would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed.
Ulla says this refers to Nebuchadnezzar.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani says these are the rivers of Babylon, and the translation of the verse.
Ulla says Ammon and Moab were the bad cries of Jerusalem.
When they heard the prophets foretelling Jerusalem's destruction, they sent to Nebuchadnezzar: come, I fear you will do to me what you did to the earlier ones.
Proverbs 7:19 is cited: the man is not at home; he went on a long journey.
But the Holy One, Blessed be He, is the one who is not at home.
Exodus 15:3 is cited: the Lord is a man of war.
They sent to him: he is near, and he came.
They sent him word: he went on a long journey.
They sent: there are righteous people who pray for mercy and bring him back.
Proverbs 7:20 is cited about the bag of money, and Hosea 3:2 about buying for fifteen pieces of silver.
He sent: the wicked may return in repentance, pray for mercy, and be brought back.
They sent to him: he set them a time.
Proverbs 7:20 is cited: he will come on the appointed day.
A home has no appointed time except a time, as the Gemara explains.
Psalm 81:4 is cited: blow the horn on the new moon, on the appointed day of our feast.
They sent him a message: it is a hot day, and we do not know whether rain will come.
They sent: come, the sheep of the mountain.
Isaiah 16:1 is cited: send the lamb of the ruler of the land from Sela in the wilderness to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.
He sent: if I come, I have no place to sit.
They sent: their graves are better than yours.
Jeremiah 8:1-2 is cited: at that time the bones of the kings of Judah and of its officials shall be brought out and spread before the sun and the moon.
Rav Nahman said to Rabbi Yitzhak.
Did you hear when bar Nafli will come?
Who is bar Nafli?
He answers: the Messiah is the son of Nafli, yes.
Amos 9:11 is cited: on that day I will raise up the fallen booth of David.

97a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Amos 9:11 is cited: the fallen booth of David.
Rabbi Yohanan says this is the teaching he gave.
Rabbi Yohanan says that in the generation of the son of David scholars will dwindle, and others will suffer grief and harsh decrees.
A tanna teaches that in the first year after the son of David comes, the following verse applies.
Amos 4:7 is cited: rain on one city and none on another, followed by famine, death, and Torah forgotten.
The fourth year brings satiety without satisfaction, and the fifth brings great abundance and joy.
The sixth year brings voices, the seventh wars, and after the seventh the son of David comes.
The son of David comes at the end of a seventh year.
Rav Yosef objects: how many seventh years have been like this, and he did not come?
Abaye asks whether the voices and wars actually happened, and whether they happened in order.
Psalm 89:52 is cited: with which Your enemies have reproached the footsteps of Your anointed.
Rabbi Yehuda says in the generation of the son of David the house of assembly will become a place of harlotry.
Rabbi Yehuda describes the corruption of that generation: Galilee destroyed, scholars' wisdom rotting, God-fearers despised, and truth absent.
Isaiah 59:15 is cited: truth is absent, and one who departs from evil is plundered.
What does 'truth is absent' mean?
The school of Rav says truth became scattered in flocks.
What does 'one who departs from evil is plundered' mean?
The school of Rabbi Shila says everyone who departs from evil is plundered by people.
Rava recounts that he once thought there was no truth in the world, until a scholar named Rav Tavyomi told him otherwise.
Rava recounts a place named Kushta where no one could be refuted and no one died outside his appointed time.
Rava tells of his wife sitting and combing her hair, and of his two sons who died.
The people of the place came to Rava and asked what this was; he said it happened like this.
Rabbi Nehorai says in the generation of the son of David youths will shame elders, and a son will not be ashamed before his father.
Rabbi Nehemiah says in that generation boldness will increase, prices will rise, and the kingdom will turn to heresy with no rebuke.
Rabbi Yitzhak says the son of David will not come until the whole kingdom turns to heresy.
Leviticus 13:13 is cited: it has turned all white, so he is clean.
Deuteronomy 32:36 is cited: the Lord will judge His people; their hand is weak, and none is left.
The son of David will not come until that verse is fulfilled.
The Gemara gives several readings: until traditions multiply, until students diminish, until the purse is empty, or until they despair of redemption.
Rabbi Zeira, finding scholars discussing this, asks them not to push it away.
Three things come unexpectedly: the Messiah, a found object, and a scorpion.
Rav Kattina says the world lasts six thousand years, and one of them is desolate.
Isaiah 2:11 is cited: the Lord alone will be exalted on that day.
Abaye says two of the thousand years are desolate.
Hosea 6:2 is cited: after two days He will revive us, and on the third day He will raise us up.
A baraita teaches like Rav Kattina: as the seventh year is released, so the world is released every thousand years out of seven thousand.
Isaiah 2:11 is cited again: the Lord alone will be exalted on that day.
Psalm 92:1 is cited: a psalm for the Sabbath day, a day that is entirely Sabbath.
Psalm 90:4 is cited: a thousand years in Your eyes are like yesterday when it passes.
A tanna of the school of Elijah teaches: the world lasts six thousand years, two thousand desolate, two thousand Torah, and two thousand the days of the Messiah.

97b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Due to our sins, which multiplied, many things went out from them.
Elijah said the following to Rav Yehuda.
The world is not less than eighty-five jubilees, and the son of David comes in the last jubilee.
Elijah is asked whether the son of David comes at the beginning or the end of that jubilee.
Elijah answers that he does not know.
Asks whether the world ends at that point or does not end.
Elijah again answers that he does not know.
Rav Ashi says Elijah told him: up to here do not look, and from here on you may look.
Rav Hanan bar Tahlifa wrote to Rav Yosef that he found a man with a scroll.
The man said he was hired by Roman soldiers and found the scroll among the treasures of Rome, written in Ashuri script and Hebrew.
The scroll says that after 4,291 years from creation the world will be orphaned, with wars of dragons, Gog and Magog, and the rest of the Messiah's days.
God renews His world only after seven thousand years.
Rav Aha son of Rava says it will be after five thousand years.
A baraita: Rabbi Natan says this verse pierces and descends to the abyss.
Habakkuk 2:3 is cited: the vision is for an appointed time; though it tarries, wait for it.
Not as our masters interpreted Daniel's time, times, and half a time.
Not as Rabbi Shmelai interpreted Psalm 80:6 about bread of tears.
Not as Rabbi Akiva interpreted Haggai 2:6 about yet once, it is a little while.
The first kingdom lasted seventy years, the second fifty-two, and the kingdom of Ben Kozeva two and a half years.
What does 'it will hasten to the end and not lie' mean?
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani, citing Rabbi Yonatan, says those who calculated the end are to be damned; if he does not come when expected, wait for him.
Isaiah 30:18 is cited: therefore the Lord waits to be gracious to you, and therefore He rises to have mercy on you.
If we wait and He waits, who is delaying? Justice delays; why then do we wait for reward?
Waiting is to receive the reward.
Isaiah 30:18 is cited: happy are all who wait for Him.
Abaye says there are never fewer than thirty-six righteous people in each generation who receive the presence of the Shekhina.
Objection: Rava said the generation before God is eighteen thousand parasangs.
Ezekiel 48:35 is cited: around, eighteen thousand.
Answer: some look through a bright mirror, and some through a dim mirror.
Are there really that many?
Objection: Hezekiah cites Rabbi Yirmeya quoting Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai about the few righteous, with himself and his sons among them.
Answer: some enter with a son and some without a son.
Rav says all the calculated ends have passed, and the matter depends only on repentance and good deeds.
Shmuel says it is enough for a mourner to stand in his mourning.
As in a tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says if Israel repents they are redeemed, and if not they are not; Rabbi Yehoshua says God appoints a harsh king like Haman, and Israel repents and returns.
A baraita: Rabbi Eliezer says if Israel repents they are redeemed.
Jeremiah 3:22 is cited: return, backsliding children, and I will heal your backsliding.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects, citing Isaiah 52:3: you were sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money, not by repentance.
Rabbi Eliezer counters with Malachi 3:7: return to Me, and I will return to you.
Rabbi Yehoshua replies with Jeremiah 3:14: I will take you, one from a city and two from a family.
Rabbi Eliezer cites Isaiah 30:15: in returning and rest you will be saved.
Rabbi Yehoshua replies with Isaiah 49:7: thus says the Lord, Redeemer of Israel, to one despised.

98a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Isaiah 49:7 is cited: kings will see and arise, princes will bow down.
Rabbi Eliezer said the following to him.
Jeremiah 4:1 is cited: if Israel returns, says the Lord, return to Me.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects: but it is already said in Daniel 12:7 about the man clothed in linen.
Daniel 12:7 is cited: all these things will be finished when the power of the holy people is scattered.
Rabbi Eliezer falls silent, and Rabbi Abba speaks.
There is no revealed end beyond this.
Ezekiel 36:8 is cited: you, mountains of Israel, shall give your branches and bear your fruit.
Rabbi Eliezer says: also from this, as stated in Zechariah.
Zechariah 8:10 is cited: before those days there was no wage for man or beast, and no peace from the adversary.
What does 'no peace from the adversary for one who goes out and comes in' mean?
Rav says even Torah scholars, of whom peace is written, have no peace from the adversary.
Shmuel says the end comes only when all the gates are equally balanced.
Rabbi Hanina says the son of David will not come until a fish is requested for the sick and not found.
Ezekiel 32:14 is cited: then I will make their waters settle and their rivers flow like oil.
Ezekiel 29:21 is cited: on that day I will cause a horn to sprout for the house of Israel.
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina says the son of David will not come until the dominion of the stalk is cut off from Israel.
Isaiah 18:5 is cited about cutting the sprigs with pruning knives, and the following verse about a present.
Zeiri says in the name of Rabbi Hanina: the son of David will not come until the proud are gone from Israel.
Zephaniah 3:11-12 is cited: I will remove those who rejoice in your pride, and leave a poor and humble people.
Rabbi Shmelai says in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon: the son of David will not come until all judges and officers are gone from Israel.
Isaiah 1:25 is cited: I will turn My hand upon you and smelt away your dross.
Ulla says Jerusalem will be redeemed only with righteousness.
Isaiah 1:27 is cited: Zion will be redeemed with justice, and her captives with righteousness.
Rav Pappa lists those who must be gone: the arrogant, the liars, the judges, and the decree-makers.
Isaiah 1:25 is cited: I will smelt away your dross and remove all your lead.
Rav Pappa continues the list of those who must be gone.
Zephaniah 3:15 is cited: the Lord has removed your judgments and turned away your enemy.
Rabbi Yohanan says: if you see a generation that dwindles, wait for it.
II Samuel 22:28 is cited: you will save the afflicted people.
Rabbi Yohanan says: if you see a generation on which many troubles come like a river, wait for it.
Isaiah 59:19 is cited: when the enemy comes like a flood, a redeemer will come to Zion.
Rabbi Yohanan says the son of David comes only in a generation that is entirely righteous or entirely guilty.
In a generation entirely righteous, the son of David comes.
Isaiah 60:21 is cited: your people are all righteous and will inherit the land forever.
In a generation entirely guilty, the son of David comes too.
Isaiah 59:16 and 48:11 are cited: God saw there was no intercessor and will act for His own sake.
Rabbi Alexandri and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi raise a contradiction about the verse on timing.
Isaiah 60:22 is cited: in its time, and also I will hasten it, so the verse appears to contradict itself.
Rabbi Alexandri and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi raise a contradiction with Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 9:9.
Daniel 7:13 is cited: one like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven.
Zechariah 9:9 is cited: lowly and riding on a donkey.
Shavor Malka tells Shmuel: you said the Messiah comes on a donkey; I will send him my white horse.
Asks whether Shmuel has a son with white features.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi found Elijah standing at the entrance of Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai's cave and asked him about the world to come.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: I saw two and heard the voice of three.
Asks when the Messiah will come; Elijah tells him to go ask the Messiah himself where he sits.
Elijah describes him: he sits among poor people who are sick, and he unbinds one and binds one.
He thinks he will go and not be delayed, and goes to him.
Rabbi Yehoshua says: peace upon you, my master; the Messiah replies: peace upon you, son of Levi.
He asks when the Messiah will come.
The Messiah answers that he comes today.
Elijah asks what the Messiah told him.
Elijah says he will promise him and his father a place in the world to come.
The Messiah says Elijah lied, since he said he would come today and did not come; Elijah replies.
Psalm 95:7 is cited: today, if you hearken to His voice.
His students ask Rabbi Yose ben Kisma when the son of David comes; he fears they will ask him for a sign, and they promise they will not.
He says: when this gate falls, is rebuilt, and falls again, and no one can rebuild it, then the son of David comes.
The students insist on a sign, and he reminds them they said they would not ask; they reply nevertheless.
He says: then let the waters of the cave of Pamyas turn to blood; they turned to blood at his death, and he tells them to dig for him.

98b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Compares Babylon, where every palm has a Persian horse tied to it, with Israel, where no Median horse eats straw.
Rav says the son of David comes only after the kingdom spreads over Israel for nine months.
Micah 5:2 is cited: He will give them up until she who labors gives birth.
Ulla says the Messiah will come but I will not see him, and Rabbah says the same.
Rav Yosef says let him come, so that I may merit sitting in the shade of the Messiah's donkey.
Abaye asks Rava and Rabbah what the reason for this view is.
Proposes that the reason is the birth pangs of the Messiah.
Objection: it is taught that Rabbi Elazar was asked how to avoid the Messiah's birth pangs, and he said study Torah and do acts of kindness.
Answer: perhaps sin causes the delay.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi raises a contradiction about Jacob's fear.
Genesis 28:15 and 32:8 are cited: God promised to guard Jacob, yet Jacob was afraid.
Jacob feared that sin would cause the delay, as a baraita teaches.
Exodus 15:16 is cited: until Your people pass over, the first coming, and until this people you acquired, the second coming.
Had Israel been worthy, a miracle would have happened in the second coming as in the first, but sin caused the delay.
Rabbi Yohanan says the same: he will come, but I will not see him.
Resh Lakish asks why.
Proposes that the reason is the verse about a man fleeing a lion.
Amos 5:19 is cited: as a man flees from a lion, and a bear meets him, and a serpent bites him.
Come and I will show you the parallel of this in this world.
When a man goes out to the field and a wild boar meets him, it is like a lion meeting him.
A lion entering the city meets an official, which is like a bear entering a house.
A bear enters a man's house and finds his children lying hungry, like one bitten by a serpent.
Rather, the reason is that it is written in Jeremiah.
Jeremiah 30:6 is cited: ask now and see whether a male gives birth; why does every man hold his loins like a woman in labor?
What is the meaning of 'I see every man'?
Rava bar Yitzhak, citing Rav, says it refers to one whose whole strength is his own.
What does 'all faces turn pale' mean?
Rabbi Yohanan says: when God said these are My handiwork and those are My handiwork, how can I destroy these because of those?
Rav Pappa cites a saying: when an ox runs and falls, the donkey goes and drops hay in front of it.
Rav Gidel, citing Rav, says Israel will eat the years of the Messiah.
Rav Yosef says this is obvious; otherwise, who would eat them? Chelek and Bilek will eat them.
This contrasts with Rabbi Hillel, who said there is no Messiah for Israel, since they were already eaten in Hezekiah's days.
Rav says the world was created only for David.
Shmuel says the world was created for Moses, and Rabbi Yohanan says for the Messiah.
What is the Messiah's name?
The school of Rabbi Shila says his name is Shiloh.
Genesis 49:10 is cited: until Shiloh comes.
The school of Rabbi Yannai says his name is Yinnon.
Psalm 72:17 is cited: his name will endure before the sun, and Yinnon is his name.
The school of Rabbi Hanina says his name is Hanina.
Jeremiah 16:13 is cited: I will not give you grace.
Some say his name is Menahem son of Hezekiah.
Lamentations 1:16 is cited: because Menahem who should comfort me is far from me.
The Sages say his name is the Leper of the school of Rabbi.
Isaiah 53:4 is cited: surely he has borne our sickness, yet we considered him stricken and afflicted.
Rav Nahman says: if the Messiah is from the living, I am like him.
Jeremiah 30:21 is cited: his mighty one will be from him, and his ruler will come from within him.
Rav says: if he is from the living, he is like our holy teacher; if from the dead, like Daniel, a man of desires.
Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name that God will appoint another David for them.
Jeremiah 30:9 is cited: they will serve the Lord their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them.
Rav Pappa says to Abaye: but it is written that David My servant will be their prince forever.
Ezekiel 37:25 is cited: David My servant will be their prince forever.
Explains: like a Caesar and a half-Caesar, a kind of royal title.
Rabbi Shmelai taught the following.
What is written?
Amos 5:18 is cited: woe to those who desire the day of the Lord; it is darkness and not light.
A parable: a rooster and a bat both waited for light.
The rooster tells the bat: I wait for light, because its light is mine; why do you want light?

ranges.en: A heretic said the following to Rabbi Abahu.
Asks when the Messiah will come.
Abahu replies dismissively that he is cursing him and should cover those people with darkness instead.
He says a verse is written about it.
Isaiah 60:2 is cited: darkness covers the earth, but the Lord will shine upon you.
Rabbi Eliezer says the days of the Messiah last forty years.
Psalm 95:10 is cited: forty years I was wearied with that generation.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says seventy years, as the verse indicates.
Isaiah 23:15 is cited: Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, like the days of one king.
Asks which king is singled out; the answer is that this is the Messiah.
Rabbi says three generations, as the verse indicates.
Psalm 72:5 is cited: they shall fear You with the sun and before the moon, generation after generation.
Rabbi Hillel says Israel has no Messiah, since they already ate him in Hezekiah's days.
Rav Yosef objects: Hezekiah lived in the First Temple, but Zechariah prophesied in the Second Temple.
Zechariah 9:9 is cited: rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; your king comes to you, lowly, riding on a donkey.
Another teaching: Rabbi Eliezer says the days of the Messiah last forty years.
Deuteronomy 8:3 and Psalm 90:15 are cited: He afflicted you and fed you; gladden us according to the days you afflicted us.
Rabbi Dosa says four hundred years.
Genesis 15:13 is cited: they will enslave and afflict them four hundred years.
Rabbi says three hundred and sixty-five years, matching the number of the sun's days.
Isaiah 63:4 is cited: the day of vengeance is in My heart, and the year of My redeemed has come.
What does 'the day of vengeance is in My heart' mean?
Rabbi Yohanan says: I revealed it to My heart, but I did not reveal it to My limbs.
Resh Lakish says: I revealed it to My heart, and I did not reveal it to the ministering angels.
Abimi, son of Rabbi Abahu, teaches that the days of the Messiah for Israel are seven thousand years.
Says seven thousand years, as the verse says.
Isaiah 62:5 is cited: as a bridegroom rejoices over a bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, says the days of the Messiah are like the days from creation until now.
Deuteronomy 11:21 is cited: as the days of heaven upon the earth.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak says the days of the Messiah are like the days of Noah until now.
Isaiah 54:9 is cited: this is to Me like the waters of Noah, as I swore.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, citing Rabbi Yohanan, says all the prophets prophesied only for the days of the Messiah.
But for the world to come, the Gemara turns to the next verse.
Isaiah 64:3 is cited: eye has not seen, God beside You, who acts for the one who waits for Him.
Objection: this disagrees with Shmuel, who said the only difference between this world and the Messiah's days is the subjugation of kingdoms.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, citing Rabbi Yohanan, says the prophets prophesied only for those who repent.
The completely righteous are not addressed by the prophets.
Isaiah 64:3 is cited again: eye has not seen God beside You.
Objection: this disagrees with Rabbi Abahu, who said the righteous do not stand in the place where those who repent stand.
Isaiah 57:19 is cited: peace, peace to the far and to the near; the far first and then the near.
What do 'far first' and 'near now' mean?
Rabbi Yohanan says the far is far from sin and the near is near to sin, and one who withdraws from it is the far.

Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, citing Rabbi Yohanan, says the prophets prophesied only about marrying one's daughter to a scholar and benefiting scholars from one's property, but scholars themselves are different.
Isaiah 64:3 is cited: eye has not seen God beside You.
What is the meaning of 'eye has not seen'?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says this is wine preserved in its grapes since the six days of creation.
Resh Lakish says this is Eden, which no eye has ever seen.
Objection: where did Adam dwell? If you say the garden is Eden, the verse about a river going out of Eden must be explained.
Genesis 2:10 is cited: a river went out of Eden to water the garden.
Whoever says the Torah is not from heaven is the one who despises the word of the Lord.
Numbers 15:31 is cited: because he despised the word of the Lord, that soul shall be utterly cut off.
A baraita reads this as referring to one who says there is no Torah from heaven, or to an apikoros.
Another reading: one who reveals faces in Torah and breaks His commandments, who breaks the covenant of flesh, is cut off in this world and in the world to come.
Rabbi Eliezer the Modai lists those who profane sacred things, despise festivals, break Abraham's covenant, and shame others publicly.
Even one who has Torah and good deeds has no share in the world to come.
A different baraita: the one who says there is no Torah from heaven is the one who despises the word of the Lord.
Even one who says all the Torah is from heaven except one verse that Moses said on his own is the one who despises the word of the Lord.
Even one who says all the Torah is from heaven except a detail of reasoning, or a verbal analogy, is the one who despises the word of the Lord.
Rabbi Meir says: one who learns Torah and does not teach it is the one who despises the word of the Lord.
Rabbi Natan says: anyone who does not pay attention to the Mishnah is the one who despises the word of the Lord.
Rabbi Nehorai says: anyone who can study Torah and does not is the one who despises it.
Rabbi Yishmael says: this is one who worships idols.
What is the meaning of this?
The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: it refers to one who despises the speech spoken to Moses at Sinai.
Exodus 20:2 is cited: I am the Lord your God; you shall have no other gods before Me.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha says: one who learns Torah and does not review it is like one who sows and does not reap.
Rabbi Yehoshua says: one who learns Torah and forgets it is like a woman who gives birth and buries her child.
Rabbi Akiva says the following.

99b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One should be engaged in Torah every day.
Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi says the following.
What verse is this?
Proverbs 16:26 is cited: the appetite of the laborer labors for him, for his mouth urges him on.
He toils in one place, and his Torah toils for him in another place.
Rabbi Elazar says every person is created for toil.
Job 5:7 is cited: man is born to toil.
I do not know whether he is created for toil of the mouth or toil of labor.
When one says that his mouth urges him on, this is the reference.
He says he is created for toil of the mouth, but I still do not know whether for toil of Torah or toil of speech.
Joshua 1:8 is cited: this book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth.
He says: one is created for the toil of Torah.
Rava says all of them are the vessels of Torah, and the good ones are fit to be the vessels of Torah.
Proverbs 6:32 is cited: whoever commits adultery lacks understanding.
Resh Lakish says this refers to one who learns Torah intermittently.
Proverbs 22:18 is cited: it is pleasant if you keep them within you, that they be ready on your lips.
Numbers 15:30 is cited: the soul that acts with a high hand.
This is Manasseh son of Hezekiah.
He sat and taught homilies that cast doubt.
Manasseh objects: did Moses have nothing to write but Genesis 36:22 about the sister of Lotan?
Genesis 36:22 and 30:14 are cited about Timna and Reuben in the wheat harvest.
Reuben went in the wheat harvest, found mandrakes in the field, and a bat kol came out and spoke to him.
Psalm 50:20-21 is cited: you sit and speak against your brother, you slander your mother's son.
This is explicit in the tradition.
Isaiah 5:18 is cited: woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity and sin as with the cart rope.
What is 'the cart rope'?
Rabbi Asi says the evil inclination is at first like a thread of a spider, and in the end like a cart rope.
What is Timna, the sister of Lotan?
Timna was a daughter of kings.
Genesis 36:29 is cited: the chief of Lotan, the chief of Timna.
Timna, a princess, wanted to convert and came to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but they did not accept her; she became a concubine of Eliphaz, and Amalek descended from her, who afflicted Israel.
What is the reason they did not push her away?
Genesis 30:14 is cited again: Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest.
Rava, citing Rav Yitzhak, says from here it is derived that the righteous do not stretch out their hands to robbery.
What are the mandrakes?
Rav says they are yavrukhei; Levi says sigli; Rabbi Yonatan says the Hebrew term for them.
Rabbi Alexandri says whoever engages in Torah for its own sake makes peace in the heavenly and earthly hosts.
Isaiah 27:5 is cited: let him hold to My strength, and make peace with Me.
Rav says it is as if he built palaces above and below.
Isaiah 51:16 is cited: I have put My words in your mouth and covered you in the shadow of My hand, to plant heavens and found the earth.
Resh Lakish, and Rabbi Yohanan, say such a person shields the whole world, as the verse says: I covered you in the shadow of My hand.
Levi says such a person also hastens the redemption.
Isaiah 51:16 is cited: to say to Zion, you are My people.
Resh Lakish says whoever teaches his fellow's son Torah is considered by Scripture as if he had made him.
Genesis 12:5 is cited: the souls they made in Haran.
Rabbi Eliezer says he is considered as if he made them for the words of Torah.
Deuteronomy 29:8 is cited: keep the words of this covenant and do them.
Rava says he is considered as if he made himself.
Deuteronomy 29:8 is read again: and you shall do them, not read them as 'them' but as 'you'.
Rabbi Abahu says anyone who makes another do a mitzva is considered by Scripture as if he did it.
Exodus 17:5 is cited: take in your hand the staff with which you struck the river.
Did Moses strike? Aaron struck it; this teaches that one who makes another do a mitzva is credited as if he did it.
Rav and Rabbi Hanina say the one who despises a Torah scholar is the one meant; Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi say likewise.
Another version: one who despises his fellow in front of a scholar.
Fine according to the view that one who despises his fellow in front of a scholar is an apikoros.
One who despises a scholar himself reveals faces in Torah improperly.
According to the view that one who despises a scholar himself is an apikoros, he reveals faces in Torah, for example.
What is an example?
Manasseh son of Hezekiah.
Some teach it at the end: he reveals faces in Torah.
Rav and Rabbi Hanina say this is one who despises a scholar.
Rabbi Yohanan and Resh Lakish say this is one who despises his fellow in front of a scholar.
According to the view that one who despises a scholar himself reveals faces in Torah, one who despises his fellow in front of a scholar is an apikoros.
But according to the view that one who despises his fellow in front of a scholar reveals faces in Torah, it is an apikoros.
Rav Yosef gives examples: these who say, what did the rabbis benefit us, and they called them names and taught them.
Abaye objects: this one who reveals faces in Torah is also the one of whom it is written: if not My covenant of day and night.
Jeremiah 33:25 is cited: if not My covenant of day and night, the laws of heaven and earth I did not establish.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak says from here too we learn.
Genesis 18:26 is cited: I will spare the whole place for their sake.
Rather, the example is one who sat before his teacher and a teaching fell to him in another place, and he said it as we say there.
Rava says the example is like those of the house of Benjamin the physician, who say: what did the rabbis benefit us at all?

ranges.en: Says that the raven was not permitted and the dove was not forbidden, concerning the status of these birds.
Rava, when the trefah of the house of Benjamin was brought before him, saw a reason to permit it.
Rava tells them to see that he permitted the raven for them.
When Rava saw a reason to forbid it, he did so.
Rava says to see that he forbade the dove for them.
Rav Pappa says it is like the case of these rabbis who said the following.
Rav Pappa forgot and said like these rabbis, and he fasted.
Levi bar Shmuel and Rav Huna bar Hiyya were preparing book-wrappers for the books of the house of Rav Yehuda.
When they reached the Scroll of Esther, they said it does not need a wrapper, since such a thing appears like disrespect.
Rav Nahman, citing Rabbi Yohanan, says Gehazi was punished because he called his master by name.
II Kings 8:5 is cited: Gehazi said to the king, this is the woman and this is her son whom Elisha restored.
Rabbi Yirmeya sat before Rabbi Zeira and said God will bring out a river from the Holy of Holies, with fruit trees on its banks.
Ezekiel 47:12 is cited: on the river's banks will grow every tree for food; its leaves for healing.
An elder said yasher to him.
Rabbi Yohanan likewise said yasher; Rabbi Yirmeya told Rabbi Zeira that such a thing appears like disrespect.
He says: this one supports you; but if you heard this, you heard that.
Rabbi Yohanan expounds that God will bring precious stones, thirty by thirty cubits, and set them in the gates of Jerusalem.
Isaiah 54:12 is cited: I will make your windows of agate and your gates of carbuncle.
A student mocked him.
The student says: we do not find such pearls on land, but we find them at sea.
His ship sailed at sea, he saw angels sawing precious stones, and they said these are for the gates of Jerusalem.
When he returned, he found Rabbi Yohanan teaching, and told him: I saw this, so you should expound it.
Rabbi Yohanan says: empty one, if you did not see it you did not believe; you mock the words of the sages.
He looked at him and made him a heap of bones.
Leviticus 26:13 is cited: I led you upright.
Rabbi Meir says the height was two hundred cubits, like two statures of the first man.
Rabbi Yehuda says one hundred cubits, corresponding to the Temple and its walls.
Psalm 144:12 is cited: our sons like plants grown in their youth, our daughters like the corners of a palace.
Rabbi Yohanan asks the Kuyi of the house of Ziqa: what is 'its leaves for healing'?
Rabbi Yitzhak bar Avdimi and Rav Hisda: one says to open the mouth of the upper world, the other the mouth of the lower world.
Hizkiya says to open the mouth of the dumb; bar Kapara says to open the mouth of barren women.
Rabbi Yohanan says healing in the literal sense.
What does 'healing' mean?
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani says it refers to the beauty of the faces of those who speak.
Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Simon, taught: whoever darkens his face over the words of Torah in this world, God brightens his radiance in the world to come.
God brightens the radiance of such a person for the world to come.
Song of Songs 5:15 is cited: his appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars.
Rabbi Tanhum bar Hanilai says whoever starves himself over the words of Torah in this world, God satisfies him in the world to come.
Psalm 36:9 is cited: they shall be satisfied with the fatness of Your house, and You give them drink from the river of Your delights.
Rav Dimi says God is destined to give every righteous person his full load.
Psalm 68:20 is cited: blessed is the Lord, day by day He bears our burden.
Abaye objects: is it possible to say so, when Isaiah 40:12 asks who measured the waters with his hollow hand?
What is the reason?
It is taught in the West, in the name of Rava bar Mari, that God will give every righteous person three hundred and ten worlds, as Proverbs 8:21 indicates.
Rabbi Meir says: by the measure a person measures, he is measured.
Isaiah 27:8 is cited: in measure, when You send her away, You contend with her.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects: is it possible to say a person gives full load to the poor in this world, and God gives full load in the world to come?
Isaiah 40:12 is cited: who has measured the waters in the hollow of His hand and the heavens with a span?
If so, which is the greater measure: the measure of good, or the measure of punishment?

100b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The attribute of reward is greater than the attribute of punishment.
Psalms describes manna rained down from the open doors of heaven as reward.
Genesis describes only windows opened in the flood, a smaller opening, for punishment.
Isaiah cites the carcasses of rebels as the punishment described in the verse.
Continuing Isaiah: their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched.
The Gemara asks how one can endure Gehenna's fire when a finger in this world burns at once.
God gives strength to the wicked to endure punishment and to the righteous to receive reward.
Rabbi Akiva teaches that one who reads outside books has no share in the World-to-Come.
A baraita applies this to heretical books, and Rav Yosef bans reading the book of Ben Sira.
Abaye asks what the reason is for prohibiting Ben Sira.
If the reason is a foolish remark about roasting fish skin, that is not a sufficient reason.
The literal sense also appears in the Torah, so a literal reading cannot be the objection.
On the homiletic reading, Ben Sira teaches proper conduct against anal intercourse with a wife.
Ben Sira's advice about daughters may be a problem, since it seems to disparage them.
The Sages said the same about women, and a world needs both sons and daughters.
Ben Sira's warning against anxiety may be a problem as it is in the book.
Solomon already said that anxiety in the heart dejects a man in Proverbs.
Rabbis Ami and Asi read the verb homiletically, and both readings agree with Ben Sira.
Ben Sira's advice to limit visitors to one's house may be a problem.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi taught the same point, citing a verse about friends who ruin a person.
Ben Sira's list of physical traits and sayings is nonsense, so reading it is unsuitable.
Rav Yosef teaches the book's good sayings publicly, including on good and bad wives.
Asks what the remedy is for a bad wife.
The remedy is to divorce her and be healed of her leprosy.
A beautiful wife makes her husband's days doubled, as Ben Sira says.
The teaching warns to avert one's eyes from a graceful woman, as many were ruined by beauty.
The wounds of a peddler refer to those who accustom others to forbidden sexual matters.
Jeremiah compares deceitful houses to a cage full of birds, supporting the image.
Ben Sira advises limited company, few confidants, and guarding one's speech.
Proverbs says not to boast about tomorrow, supporting the caution against worrying.
You do not know what tomorrow holds, so worrying over a world not yours is futile.
Cites Proverbs 15:15 on the days of the poor, supporting the preceding caution.
Ben Sira says even nights are bad for the poor, describing roofs and vineyards by elevation.
A mnemonic lists the Amoraim whose statements follow, by their names.
Rabbi Zeira says in Rav's name a teaching about the poor and the good-hearted.
Asks what the verse about all the days of the poor being terrible means.
Days of the poor are Talmud scholars, and the feast is for Mishnah scholars.
Rava says the opposite, as Rav Mesharshiyya reported in his name.
Asks what the verse in Ecclesiastes 10:9 means.
Stone quarrying refers to Mishnah scholars, and wood chopping refers to Talmud scholars.
Rabbi Hanina says the poor man's bad days refer to a bad wife, and feasts to a good wife.
Rabbi Yannai says the poor man's bad days refer to the delicate, and feasts to the broad-minded.
Rabbi Yohanan says the poor man's bad days refer to the compassionate, and feasts to the cruel.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi opens his statement on the poor man's days, which continues onto the next daf.

101a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continuing Rabbi Yannai: one with a broad mind accepts others' actions and is a good-hearted feast.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reads the poor man's bad days as a verse about his lack of rest.
Asks: but there are Shabbatot and festivals when the poor man rests and eats festive meals.
Shmuel's principle: a change of routine in eating and rest brings on an intestinal illness.
Baraita: one who treats a Song of Songs verse as secular song or reads verses at banquets harms the world.
God asks the Torah what people should occupy themselves with while eating and drinking.
The Torah replies: Bible, Mishna, and Talmud scholars each have a proper study for their stage.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Hananya, says timely reading brings good.
Proverbs 15:23 cited: a word in its season, how good it is.
The Mishna lists one who whispers invocations over a wound among those without a share in the World-to-Come.
Rabbi Yohanan limits the ruling to spitting while whispering, since God's name is not mentioned over spittle.
Rav and Rabbi Hanina extend the prohibition to verses used as incantations, even unrelated ones.
Baraita permits oil, rubbing, and cool vessels on Shabbat for pain and inflammation, and whispering for bites.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel limits this to movable vessels and bans consulting demons on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yosei forbids consulting demons even on weekdays.
Rav Huna rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Yosei's prohibition is only due to danger, not the Torah ban on witchcraft.
Example: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef swallowed into a cedar after consulting a demon, and a miracle split it.
Baraita allows rubbing oil on the intestines on Shabbat, provided it is not done as one does on weekdays.
Asks how one then performs the rubbing on Shabbat.
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina: first smear oil, then rub.
Rabbi Yohanan: smear and rub at the same time.
Baraita: oil and eggs used for consulting demons are permitted but futile, since they deceive.
The reason is that such practices are deceptive.
Incantations go over oil in a vessel, so one may smear oil brought in another's hand but not from a vessel.
Story: Rav Yitzhak bar Shmuel bar Marta got boils from oil in a vessel and was healed by a woman's incantation.
Rabbi Abba raises an apparent contradiction and cites Exodus 15:26.
The verse quoted: no disease will be placed on you, for I am God your healer.
Asks why healing is needed if God does not place disease on the people.
Rabbi Yohanan says the verse resolves itself from its own content.
Exodus 15:26 continues: if you hearken, no disease; and even if not, I am your healer.
Rabba bar bar Hana: when Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, his disciples came to visit him.
Rabbi Eliezer says there is intense heat in the world, meaning divine anger, causing his suffering.
The disciples weep while Rabbi Akiva laughs.
The disciples ask why Akiva laughs, and he asks back why they weep.
The disciples reply that a Torah scroll is in distress and they cannot help but weep.
Akiva explains he laughs because his teacher's possessions show no sign of spoiling, so he may lack reward.
Akiva reasons that suffering now means full reward later, so he rejoices.
Eliezer asks Akiva whether he has failed to teach any part of the whole Torah.
Akiva replies that Eliezer taught them, citing Ecclesiastes 7:20 on the righteous who sin not.
Baraita: four elders visit the ill Rabbi Eliezer: Tarfon, Yehoshua, Elazar ben Azarya, and Akiva.
Rabbi Tarfon encourages him: he is better for Israel than a drop of rain, benefiting both worlds.
Rabbi Yehoshua says he is better for Israel than the sun's orb, benefiting both worlds.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says he is better for Israel than a father and mother, benefiting both worlds.
Rabbi Akiva says he is beloved by sufferings and wants his disciples to hear his words.
Akiva's disciple asks where this teaching comes from.
Akiva answers that he expounds a verse.
The verse in Kings about Manasseh, who did evil in God's eyes, begins to be cited.

101b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites Proverbs 25:1 about the proverbs of Solomon that the men of Hezekiah copied.
Rhetorically asks whether Hezekiah taught Torah to the entire world.
Hezekiah taught Torah to the world, but did not teach it to his son Manasseh, who was brought only to suffering.
Chronicles: God spoke to Manasseh and the people, who did not listen, so Manasseh was seized and bound.
Chronicles continues: Manasseh humbled himself, prayed, and God restored him to his kingdom.
Manasseh knew God is God, and so the lesson is that sufferings are beloved.
Baraita: three came with accusations, namely Cain, Esau, and Manasseh, starting with Cain.
Genesis 4:13 cited: Cain says his sin is greater than can be borne.
Cain argues that his sin is not greater than the six hundred thousand who will sin, which you forgive.
Genesis 27:38 cited: Esau says there is one blessing, for you, my father.
Manasseh at first called many gods, but at the end called on the God of his fathers.
Abba Shaul says one who pronounces God's name by its letters is also included.
The baraita adds that this applies in provinces and in the Aramaic language.
Baraita: three kings and four commoners, listing names that are among the wicked.
Tannaitic explanations of Jeroboam's name and the people who peered, identifying Nevat, Micah, and Sheva.
Baraita: three peered but did not see, namely Nevat, Ahitophel, and Pharaoh's magicians, with Nevat producing Jeroboam.
Ahitophel saw leprosy on his mother's side and thought he was king, but Bat Sheva was his daughter.
Solomon was among Pharaoh's magicians, as Rabbi Hama bar Hanina said.
Asks what the verse in Numbers 20:13 means about the waters of Meribah.
The magicians saw Israel's savior in the waters and erred, so the one who sinned at Meribah was punished.
Exodus 1:22 cited: every son born shall be cast into the river, and they did not know it.
They did not know that one is punished over matters of the waters of Meribah.
Asks how we know Jeroboam does not enter the World-to-Come.
First Kings 13:34 cited: this matter caused the house of Jeroboam to sin and be cut off from the world.
Rabbi Yohanan explains Jeroboam gained kingship for rebuking Solomon, and was punished for rebuking him publicly.
First Kings 11:27 cited: Solomon built the Millo and closed the breach of the city of David.
David tells Solomon that his father breached the wall for Israel's festivals, and Solomon closed them for Pharaoh's daughter.
Asks what the verse about lifting a hand against the king means.
Rav Nachman says Jeroboam's pride, shown by removing tefillin before Rehoboam, led to his removal from the world.
First Kings 12:26 cited: Jeroboam thought the kingdom would return to the house of David if the people went up to Jerusalem.
Jeroboam reasons that only Judah's kings may sit in the Temple court, but Rehoboam sits while he stands, so he fears for his life.
First Kings 12:28 cited: the king consulted and made two golden calves, placing one in Bethel and one in Dan.
Asks what the word and he consulted means.
Rabbi Yehuda says it means the wicked man was seated next to the righteous one.
Jeroboam asks the righteous man to agree to everything he says, even to worship idols, and all agree.
The righteous man says Heaven forbid, and the wicked man speaks to him.
Explains that the wicked man is not really like Jeroboam, but seeks to test whether the other accepts his words.
